articles.title: Google lanzó sus primeros lentes con Android XR a USD 1.099, 200 dólares menos que la Meta VR Glasses
articles.text:
Google y la empresa Xreal lanzaron las Aura, los primeros lentes con el sistema Android XR, con un precio de USD 1.099 hasta fin de año. El modelo básico costaba USD 1.279 en las reservas de octubre. Las ventas abrieron el 28 de octubre en Estados Unidos, Canadá y Corea del Sur.
Las Aura se presentaron en la Cumbre de Desarrolladores de Android, según Android Authority. Pesan menos de 95 gramos porque el procesador y la batería van en una unidad aparte, del tamaño de un teléfono, conectada por cable. Esa unidad también funciona como panel táctil, según Google.
El modelo de 12 GB de memoria y 256 GB de almacenamiento cuesta USD 1.279 a precio regular y USD 1.099 con la oferta. El de 16 GB y 512 GB cuesta USD 1.499, o USD 1.299 con descuento. Ambos descuentos rigen hasta diciembre, según Notebookcheck y 9to5Google.
Las entregas comenzarán a mediados de noviembre. En Japón, los pedidos abrirán el 2 de noviembre. Google precisó que la compra está limitada a mayores de 18 años. Xreal prevé llegar a más países en 2027.
Un precio que se ubica por debajo de Meta
Meta presentó el 23 de septiembre sus Meta VR Glasses, de unos 100 gramos y con una unidad de procesamiento similar. Costarán USD 1.299,99 y saldrán a la venta en la primavera boreal de 2027, según la compañía. La Aura de entrada queda USD 200 por debajo.
The Verge señaló que la rebaja respecto de los USD 1.279 iniciales posiblemente responda a esa competencia. El medio sostiene que Google y Xreal habrían quedado frente a frente con Meta al mismo precio. Es una interpretación del medio citado, no una explicación de las empresas.
Las dos propuestas se diferencian en el tipo de pantalla. Las Aura usan lentes transparentes, con campo de visión de 70 grados en diagonal, y permiten ver el entorno. Las Meta VR Glasses, según The Verge, tienen lentes oscurecidos por fuera. También advirtió que ese campo de visión no es amplio.
Gemini ve lo que ve el usuario
Google afirma que su asistente Gemini entiende lo que el usuario mira, tanto en la habitación como en las pantallas. Desde el lanzamiento, el usuario puede compartir su vista y Gemini resalta en la imagen el elemento relevante.
Los lentes también pueden duplicar la pantalla de una computadora conectada por cable USB-C, sin instalar programas. Según Google, permiten abrir varias aplicaciones a la vez y usar mini ventanas al caminar. Incluyen más de 150 aplicaciones pensadas para realidad extendida, además de las de Google Play.
Entre los contenidos figuran el canal de la NBA, que permite ver varios partidos a la vez con suscripción, y juegos como Fallout: Factions, según Android Authority. Xreal presentó además un teclado inalámbrico y un control de juegos hecho con GameSir, con un botón dedicado a Gemini.
Google Fotos sumará este año una galería espacial que rodea al usuario con sus recuerdos, según el blog de Google. Las ventas en tiendas de Google y otros comercios están previstas para 2027, según Android Authority.
Los primeros envíos a compradores de Estados Unidos, Canadá y Corea del Sur están previstos para mediados de noviembre, y en Japón las ventas comienzan el 2 de noviembre.

articles.title: Investigadores de Google y Anthropic detectaron falla de seguridad que afecta a la mayoría de centros de datos del mundo
articles.text:
Alex Matrosov, investigador de Anthropic, y Dan Holmes, de Google, descubrieron una falla en el código de arranque que utilizan la mayoría de proveedores de servidores y centros de datos del planeta, que dejó expuestos a millones de equipos frente a ataques capaces de ejecutar código malicioso antes de que cualquier sistema de defensa pueda activarse. La vulnerabilidad, identificada como CVE-2026-97631, recibió una calificación de severidad de 9,5 sobre 10 y afecta al TianoCore EDK II, el código abierto que las empresas de hardware emplean para construir el firmware UEFI que se ejecuta durante el inicio de los equipos.
El EDK2 es, según un representante del UEFI Forum, “la solución de referencia predominante” para implementar las especificaciones UEFI. Prácticamente todos los proveedores independientes de BIOS, entre ellos AMI, Insyde y Phoenix, utilizan de manera extensa este código base. También lo emplea Project Mu, la versión reforzada de EDK2 desarrollada por Microsoft, que incluye el componente vulnerable.
El fallo permite eludir el arranque seguro de los equipos
El problema reside en un componente del protocolo ICMP y consiste en una corrupción de memoria que un atacante puede aprovechar para ejecutar código antes de que el sistema operativo y el firmware puedan aplicar mecanismos de defensa como el Secure Boot. Esta función establece una cadena de confianza para todo el código que se carga durante el arranque, incluido el que corresponde al Trusted Platform Module (TPM).
Los ataques que exploten esta falla no logran persistencia, es decir, el código malicioso corre una sola vez. Sin embargo, esa única ejecución puede bastar para abrir la puerta a otros programas maliciosos que sí se instalen de forma permanente y se activen en cada arranque posterior del equipo.
Un fallo de 16 años en el controlador de arranque por red
CVE-2026-97631 corresponde a un desbordamiento de búfer presente desde hace 16 años en el controlador PXE-Base Code (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), responsable de que servidores, equipos de almacenamiento y otros dispositivos puedan iniciarse con código descargado desde una red local. Durante ese proceso, conocido como entorno de pre-ejecución de arranque, el controlador mantiene un escucha de red para detectar mensajes de error ICMP.
El defecto radica en que el controlador no impone un límite de copia de memoria de 504 bytes, por lo que los datos adyacentes pueden sobrescribirse. Un atacante con acceso de bajo nivel a una red local, o un usuario malicioso dentro de esa red, puede enviar un mensaje de error que agregue código más allá de ese límite, lo que corrompe el módulo UEFI que corre en el procesador.
El aviso oficial del proyecto explica que el controlador PXE Base Code mantiene abierta una solicitud de recepción para mensajes de error ICMP y copia cada mensaje recibido en un campo fijo de 504 bytes dentro de su estructura de contexto privada.
Tanto en el manejador de IPv4 como en el de IPv6, el control de límites está mal implementado: si el mensaje supera los 504 bytes, el sistema igual copia los bytes excedentes, y el puntero de destino avanza según la longitud acumulada en lugar de la longitud de cada fragmento, lo cual permite que un mensaje de tamaño excesivo escriba datos controlados por el atacante fuera del campo previsto. Nada en el camino de recepción anterior restringe la longitud del mensaje.
Un ataque que puede ejecutarse con un simple envío unicast
El error malicioso puede entregarse mediante un envío unicast simple desde cualquier distancia de red hacia la dirección IP del dispositivo objetivo, siempre que se transmita durante la secuencia de arranque PXE. Un atacante puede provocar una denegación de servicio con solo hacer que la secuencia de arranque se bloquee. Si además conoce la versión específica del firmware del objetivo, puede introducir lo que el aviso describe como un “evento falsificado” que ejecuta código malicioso directamente sobre el procesador dentro de su entorno de firmware UEFI.
Ese código corre en el anillo 0 (ring 0), el nivel de ejecución más privilegiado de un procesador. Según explicó HD Moore, creador de Metasploit y director de investigación en la firma de seguridad Dragos, esta falla en el analizador ICMP de la pila de red de EDK2 resulta relevante por su efecto sobre la cadena de confianza y el ecosistema en general.
Moore señaló que un atacante interesado en comprometer un terminal o servidor cercano podría usar este error para secuestrar el flujo del programa en un punto donde el proceso de arranque todavía tiene acceso a componentes sensibles, como el TPM del dispositivo, lo que podría emplearse para romper el cifrado de disco en escenarios donde el atacante cuenta con acceso de red de corto plazo, una situación aún más sencilla en un caso de robo físico del equipo.
Los exploits que aprovechan esta vulnerabilidad logran además eludir los procesos de verificación diseñados para demostrar de forma criptográfica a servidores remotos que el hardware es seguro, lo que representa una vía concreta para escalar privilegios limitados.
La divulgación se adelantó al plazo previsto
Matrosov y Holmes habían acordado mantener la falla en reserva hasta una divulgación coordinada prevista para enero. Sin embargo, AMI publicó el mes pasado una solicitud de incorporación de código que detallaba la vulnerabilidad e incluía una corrección. Una vez que esa publicación llegó a conocimiento de los descubridores originales, los miembros del proyecto TianoCore emitieron un aviso público la semana pasada.
Con el código de parche ya disponible públicamente, resultará sencillo para atacantes con conocimientos avanzados comprender cómo se activa la vulnerabilidad y construir exploits funcionales. La urgencia se agrava porque corregir fallas de código UEFI en millones de dispositivos finales, vendidos y utilizados por miles de fabricantes de hardware y proveedores de nube, es un proceso lento y complejo. Esta revelación se produjo seis días después de otra divulgación igualmente apresurada, en ese caso sobre una vulnerabilidad crítica de ejecución de código en el lenguaje de programación PHP.

articles.title: The Sony Bravia Theater Trio ‘matches the cinematic scale of even the very biggest TVs’ — I was blown away by how well this three-bar system creates huge, spatial sound
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Although it’s tricky to say exactly which home audio pigeonhole Sony’s Trio speaker package belongs in, we can at least confidently file it under ‘brilliant’.
Reasons to buy
- + Exceptional sound quality for both films and music
- + Excellent adaptation to any room layout
- + It’s a perfect partner for really big TVs
- + Good expansion options
Reasons to avoid
- - It’s… reassuringly expensive
- - Needs optional rear speakers for a proper surround sound effect
- - Rather limited listening ‘sweet spot’
- - Limited physical connectivity
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8) review
The Sony Bravia Theater Trio is hard to define, but easy to love. Hard to define because its three-speaker (Trio, geddit?) package doesn’t feel quite like either a soundbar or a home theatre separates system; easy to love because it sounds amazing.
Sony’s own story of how the Trio came to be states that it was borne from frustration in its audio department about the inability of regular soundbar solutions — even high-end ones — to deliver sound with enough power and scale to convincingly partner with really big TVs. It was deemed that rather than creating a mammoth uber-long single soundbar to solve this problem, a much more practical solution would be to create a three-piece centre, left, right speaker package instead.
While the left and right speakers of the Trio system are larger and heavier than the sort of satellite speakers usually sold with or as options for regular soundbar systems, the package overall still looks startlingly compact overall for a system designed for king-sized TVs. The center speaker only measures in at 23.19 x 2.52 x 6.5 inches / 589 x 64 x 165mm, in fact. But you can, of course, place the wireless left and right speakers pretty much as far apart as your room allows, to help create a soundstage commensurate in scale with a monster TV.
I would quickly add at this point, though, that I personally don’t see the Trio as only worth getting if you have a huge TV. It’s actually so good and, as I’ll explain, so flexible with its sound that it’s worth considering by really any home theater fan who’s able to afford it.
Just throwing a trio of speakers at the big TV audio problem won’t in itself guarantee a satisfying home theater audio solution, of course. Especially when those three speakers only deliver dedicated left, right, centre and up-firing channels, rather than the many more channels that even some single bar soundbars can manage these days. The thing is, though, the Bravia Theater Trio’s channel count isn’t actually restricted to the the handful we’ve just mentioned. The brand’s revolutionary 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system is capable of adding up to 24 ‘virtual’ (created by psychoacoustic processing) extra channels of sound to the system’s ‘physical’ ones.
The 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system’s calculation process for figuring out where to place the sound from these extra virtual speakers uses a supplied, high-quality mic dongle that plugs into your phone to tailor the sound to your room layout. This works so well that you’ll be able to still enjoy a totally coherent, balanced, symmetrical soundstage from your Trio system no matter how awkward your room layout might be.
This room adaptation part of the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system becomes even more useful if you add a pair of Sony’s new Rear 9 optional surround sound speakers. Even when I deliberately set the the two front and Rear 9 speakers in the most unhelpful positions I could manage, the processing still somehow manages to put me at the heart of a colossal 360-degree soundstage.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I’ve let the Trio’s cleverest trick, though, lead me into discussing the system’s performance before I’ve finished going through every feature it has to offer. So let’s quickly get back to that.
While the Trio’s centre speaker’s long, slim design suits simple placement on a desktop under your TV, the left and right speakers sneak a narrow straight bit into their otherwise cylindrical shape to allow them to be wall mounted if that suits your set up.
Connectivity is passable. The highlight is an HDMI loop through that supports 4K/120Hz gaming feeds — as you’d hope with a sound system from the brand responsible for the PlayStation 5 — as well as the HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision HDR formats, but not HDR10+. And the HDMI output also supports the eARC system for taking in sound from your TV.
Unfortunately, the only other port is a USB slot that’s apparently only for software updates. A second HDMI input and an optical digital audio input would have been nice on a £1,999 home cinema system these days perhaps, but the Trio’s support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth (6.0) alongside the HDMIs will likely deliver everything most modern households will need.
These wireless options support direct streaming from Spotify Connect and Apple Airplay 2. On top of this, the system can also utilize Hi-Res Audio files and carries Sony’s redoubtable DSEE Ultimate AI upscaling system for making compressed audio sound better.
The latest Bravia Connect app for iOS and Android helps you set the system up, as well as providing an attractive and useful visual interface as a back up to the fairly basic remote control the system ships with. And it's particularly handy, given the Trio doesn’t carry an LED display.
Finally in the feature department, the Trio can play both the Dolby Atmos and DTS:X surround sound formats. In fact, it doesn’t just play them; it eats them for breakfast.
Any doubts about the Trio’s $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999 price evaporate in an irresistible bombardment of almost impossibly massive sound staging, levels of power, detail and impact that seem to go far beyond the system’s claimed 405W of confirmed power. It also serves up mesmerizing detailing and precision, and an immaculate tone that has more in common with a premium full separates system than a minimalistic three-speaker package.
The system’s remarkable drivers and even more remarkable 360 Spatial Sound Mapping processing create a soundstage that fills at least the front half of even very large rooms, with the physical existence of the Trio’s three speakers essentially completely disappearing. As well as being capable of creating an epic sense of space for big movie locations, the size of sound the Trio can produce means it's effortlessly able to ‘fill’ the screen area and match the cinematic scale of even the very biggest TVs.
Despite its immense and immersive size, though, the Trio’s sound doesn’t forget the small things in home cinema and music life. It can pull in the boundaries of its sound superbly when a soundtrack wants to portray a tight space, for starters. Also, every detail in a movie sound mix is beautifully rendered, no matter how small, and produced with exactly the correct weight relative to other mix elements.
There’s no hint of harshness or brittleness to any sound the Trio makes, no matter how high pitched or deep it might be. In fact, despite the center speaker’s small size, the system gives the impression of having no ceiling for treble sounds to butt up against and turn harsh, and no low-frequency floor for bass sounds to flatten off against.
The relatively hefty left and right speakers do most of the heavy low-frequency lifting without making deep sounds feel trapped in, hard edged or distorted. They’re reactive enough to serve sudden bass hits with impeccable timing, too, and have enough range in the low frequencies they can produce to stop rumbles becoming overwhelming or coarse.
This excellent bass performance is particularly welcome, given that bass has been a weakness of some of Sony’s current soundbars, and that the system is quite compact. Perhaps an even bigger worry is that Sony sells Sub 8 and Sub 9 external wireless subwoofer upgrades for the package, which always makes me wonder if there’s a weakness in the core system that such an add-on is required to fix.
The Trio can deliver hard, sudden impact sounds with proper venom and propulsion, while the soundstage remains balanced and authoritative even at high volumes, no matter how dense the content might be.
Sound systems that go as big and dynamic with film soundtracks as the Trio can aren’t always able to turn their hands effectively to music. The Trio, though, is at least as engaging with music as it is movies.
Even in native stereo mode, without any of Sony’s remarkable virtual surround processing in play, the trio of speakers deliver excellent stereo separation and vocal placement. Nothing sounds at all strained, no matter what type of music you’re playing or how dense a track gets. It retains its genuinely hi-fi feel, too, at higher volumes than you’ve probably ever heard your favorite albums before. And yet, at the same time, people with neighbors will be pleased to hear that its speakers are sensitive enough to deliver music compellingly even at low volumes, something many soundbars struggle with.
Dolby Atmos music sounds similarly refined. It's detailed without being forensic, but also enjoys a more three-dimensional presentation that includes height elements. And if you’re happy to take off your purist music hat, I’d also recommend you try stereo tracks — or, at least, relatively poppy or ambient stereo tracks — through its 360 Spatial Sound Mapping processing, which gives it a more spacious and surround sound feel. Certainly Sony’s ‘upmixing’ with this effect is much superior to similar modes attempted by most other home audio packages.
It’s a tough ask to find things I don’t love about Sony’s Trio system. But I’m paid to try, so here goes. First, for all its virtual speaker creating talents, it only creates a quite limited sense of sound coming from behind your seating position. This can be solved extremely well by adding Sony’s new Rear 9 extra wireless surround speakers — though, at $749.99 / £699 / $ 1,299 a pair, this upgrade isn’t cheap.
The left/right spread of stereo music strangely narrows slightly when playing music through the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping despite expanding in every other way. And finally — and possibly most frustratingly depending on how big your household is — the area you need to sit in after calibrating the Trio for the optimal 360 Spatial Sound Mapping effect is quite small. Though even outside of this sweet spot, it’s still gloriously easy to appreciate just how good the Trio’s overall sound is.
Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8) review: Price and release date
- Released: July 2026 (UK and Australia), May 2026 (US)
- $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999
At first glance the Trio’s $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999 price looks substantial for a three-piece speaker package. Samsung gives you a full surround soundbar package, the HW-Q990H, for just $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$1,499, after all. Once you’ve placed the Trio’s speakers wherever you want them to go, though, and run the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system setup, the system reveals itself to be a pretty much separates-grade performer capable of partnering with a huge screen and even filling a big room.
Hitting almost $2,750 / £2,700 / AU$4,300 if you add the admittedly impressive Rear 9 speakers starts to look a bit of a stretch, but you could always add the rears later as funds allow. The out-of-the-box Trio won’t let you down in the mean time.
Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8): Specs
| Dimensions | Main bar: 23.19 x 2.52 x 6.50 inches / 589 x 64 x 165mm; left/right speakers: 6.3 x 13.27 x 6.5 inches / 160 x 337 x 165mm | 
| Speaker channels | 3.0.2 | 
| Connections | One HDMI input (with eARC), one HDMI output (4K/120Hz), USB service port | 
| Dolby Atmos / DTS:X | Yes/Yes | 
| Sub included | Optional extra | 
| Rear speakers included | No | 
Should I buy the Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8)?
| Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8) Scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | The system’s three-front-speaker approach enables it to deliver a sound appropriate to really any screen size, even really huge ones. Its processing and audio format support is excellent too. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | Despite the fairly compact size of its three speakers, the Trio package often manages to sound like a premium separates system | 5 / 5 | 
| Design | From the surprisingly compact shape of the center speaker to the gorgeously well-built cylindrical stance of the left and rights, the Theater Trio is an elegantly understated addition to your room. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Setup & usability | The speakers all connected with each other automatically during my tests, and provided you plug the provided mic into your phone and run the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping set up procedure, its speakers are extremely flexible when it comes to where you put them. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Value | The Theater Trio package’s price puts it above the vast majority of regular soundbars — but its sound is a cut above any regular soundbar, too | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You have a very big TV
The Trio’s package of separate center, front left and front right speakers was expressly designed to solve the issue where regular soundbars just don’t create a sound stage big enough to match the size of the pictures made by massive TVs (especially those of 85 inches and more).
You want fantastic movie and music sound quality
The Trio throws off the shackles of some of Sony’s current soundbars, using hi-fi grade speaker designs and up to 24 virtual speakers created by Sony’s amazing 360 Spatial Sound Mapping to craft one of the most powerful but also most refined, balanced and immersive soundstages I’ve heard from a one-box speaker package.
You have an awkwardly shaped room
A key part of the Trio’s 360 Spatial Sound Mapping involves adapting the sound of its real and virtual speakers to your room layout — and this process is so flexible that it can deliver a convincing sound stage no matter how awkward your speaker placement might be.
Don't buy it if...
You can’t afford it
There are some very good soundbars around for much less than the Trio’s $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999 asking price - which rises to nearly $2,750 / £2,700 / AU$4,300 if you add the Rear 9 surround speakers. But if you can afford it, the scale and finesse of the Trio’s sound is a cut above those cheaper soundbar alternatives.
The small sweet spot is a problem
The Trio optimizes the sound stage created by its real and virtual speakers around what turns out to be a rather compact sweet spot. So if you have a big household to cater for, you’ll have to accept that not everyone will get the perfect experience — unless you all huddle up.
You want a sound system that can work as a switch box
The Trio’s limited connectivity prevents you from attaching more than one hard-wired source to it at a time.
Sony Bravia Theatre Trio (HT-A8) review: Also consider
Samsung HW-Q990H
If you can’t quite stretch your finances to accommodate the Sony Trio package, Samsung’s HW-Q990H soundbar system delivers a powerful and detailed full surround sound solution for $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$1,499. The Q990H crafts a remarkably full hemisphere of sound for Dolby Atmos and DTS:X soundtracks, but the Trio’s sound is more refined and flexible — and only requires you to house three speakers. Read our full Samsung HW-Q990H review.
Sennheiser Ambeo Max
Sennheiser’s most powerful soundbar delivers a remarkably large sound stage for a single-bar device, courtesy of the fearsome array of ultra-robust and punchy drivers it squeezes into its uncompromising chassis. This helps it get nearer than any other remotely mainstream single-bar soundbar to supporting really big screens like the Trio does. While it used to cost $2,999.95 / £2,199 / AU$3,999, too, it’s now widely available for $1,699.99 / £1,599 / AU$2,999. It still can’t ultimately match the scale of the Trio, though, due to the latter’s separate left and right speakers.
How I tested the Sony Bravia Theatre Trio (HT-A8)
- I used the Sony Trio as my main living room audio system for 11 days.
- Also tested in a second room with a different size and layout, and with a pair of optional Rear 9 surround speakers.
- Tested with 4K Blu-rays, CDs, streamed audio, and games, using all direct HDMI connection, eARC and wireless connection options
I tested the Trio as my main living room audio system for 11 days overall, as well as using it in a second room with a different layout for two further days. I also moved the left and right speakers (and the optional rears) to all sorts of awkward places to test the flexibility of the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping processing.
During the testing period, I fed the Trio system audio content from a wide range of sources, including movie soundtracks from streaming boxes and 4K Blu-ray players over HDMI; music from a CD player and the various music streaming services the system supports; and game soundtracks from an Xbox Series X. Key movies used were Blade Runner 2049, It Chapter One, Civil War, and Sinners.
- First reviewed: October 2026
- Read TechRadar's review guarantee
John has been writing about home entertainment technology for more than two decades - an especially impressive feat considering he still claims to only be 35 years old (yeah, right). In that time he’s reviewed hundreds if not thousands of TVs, projectors and speakers, and spent frankly far too long sitting by himself in a dark room.

articles.title: “Esperamos que muy pocos opten por esta oferta”: Microsoft proyecta que menos de 3.000 empleados aceptarán el retiro voluntario
articles.text:
Microsoft calcula que 3.000 trabajadores o menos pedirán acogerse al programa de salida voluntaria que la compañía lanzó esta semana para más de una cuarta parte de su plantilla, según declaró un portavoz a Business Insider. La directora financiera, Amy Hood, confirmó esa proyección en un memorando interno en el que respondió a las dudas que generó la iniciativa entre los empleados.
“Sé que ha habido algunas preguntas sobre la justificación de la oferta de salida voluntaria que anunciamos esta semana”, escribió Hood.
“Nuestra intención es ofrecer a los empleados la posibilidad de decidir si quieren dejar la empresa por su propia voluntad. Esperamos que muy pocos opten por esta oferta debido a las oportunidades de crecimiento que ofrece Microsoft”, agregó.
Por qué Microsoft espera baja adhesión al plan de salidas
La explicación de Hood apunta a un argumento concreto: la compañía confía en que las oportunidades internas de desarrollo profesional disuadirán a la mayoría de los empleados elegibles de abandonar la empresa.
La ejecutiva planteó el programa como una decisión individual y no como una herramienta pensada para vaciar áreas específicas de la organización.
Ese mensaje buscó despejar las dudas que surgieron apenas se conoció el alcance de la medida. Al tratarse de una oferta dirigida a decenas de miles de trabajadores, incluidos cargos de alta responsabilidad, parte del personal cuestionó qué lógica de negocio había detrás de una convocatoria tan amplia.
La proyección de menos de 3.000 salidas equivale a una fracción mínima del universo de empleados elegibles. Microsoft ofreció un retiro voluntario a unos 60.000 empleados de Estados Unidos, Canadá, India y el Reino Unido: la cifra, confirmada por Business Insider y Bloomberg, convierte a la expectativa oficial de la empresa en un porcentaje reducido frente al total convocado.
Cómo funciona la oferta de salida voluntaria de Microsoft
La propuesta se llama Voluntary Exit Offer y fue comunicada el 26 de octubre a través de un mensaje interno de la directora de personal de la compañía, Amy Coleman, publicado también en el blog corporativo de Microsoft. Según detalló Coleman, el programa está dirigido a empleados de nivel 70 o inferior que integren equipos participantes.
Business Insider precisó que ese umbral incluye a altos directivos, mientras que TechCrunch describió el rango alcanzado como el que va desde la posición de vicepresidente hacia abajo en la estructura jerárquica. Esto significa que la oferta no quedó limitada a puestos operativos, sino que contempló también a mandos con responsabilidad de gestión.
No todas las áreas de la empresa quedaron incluidas. Coleman explicó que algunas organizaciones ofrecen el retiro y otras no, en función de sus prioridades internas, los compromisos asumidos con clientes y las necesidades de personal de cada equipo. La aplicación del programa, entonces, varía según el sector dentro de la compañía.
Los trabajadores considerados elegibles debían recibir ese mismo 26 de octubre un correo con los detalles individuales de su oferta. Microsoft definió el programa como voluntario y por tiempo limitado, y precisó que incluye apoyo económico y recursos de planificación de carrera para quienes decidan marcharse.
Qué datos no reveló Microsoft sobre el programa
El comunicado de la compañía dejó varios puntos sin precisar: no se detalló cuánto dinero recibirá cada empleado que acepte la salida, el número oficial de renuncias que espera la empresa, ni el plazo del que disponen los trabajadores para tomar una decisión.
Los reportes de prensa consultados señalan que los beneficios económicos serían similares a los de un paquete de indemnización estándar, aunque sin cifras concretas confirmadas por la empresa.

articles.title: Mozilla apela a la nostalgia con memes clásicos de internet para recuperar usuarios de Firefox
articles.text:
Mozilla apela a la nostalgia con memes clásicos de internet para recuperar usuarios de Firefox. La compañía lanzó un video publicitario que reúne a varias de las figuras más reconocibles de la cultura viral de los años 2000, con un tono cómico que esconde un mensaje sobre la privacidad digital.
El anuncio, de aproximadamente un minuto de duración, plantea una pregunta que funciona como eje de toda la campaña: “¿Cómo es que internet es menos privado que en 2006, cuando toda la familia compartía un solo ordenador?”.
Qué memes aparecen en el anuncio de Firefox
Entre los protagonistas del video figuran el cantante Tay Zonday, conocido por su canción Chocolate Rain, y Chuck Testa, otro de los rostros recurrentes de la era dorada de los memes.
También aparecen la Novia psicópata, Annoying Orange y el protagonista de Numa Numa, que con una cámara de baja resolución popularizó su particular parodia de Dragostea din tei, del grupo O-Zone.
El listado se completa con figuras que no surgieron en YouTube, como Bad Luck Brian y Apparently Kid, el niño conocido como Noah Ritter que se hizo viral por una entrevista espontánea frente a las cámaras.
Todos ellos representan una etapa en la que el contenido viral se construía con imágenes de baja resolución, texto plano y composiciones caseras que, pese a su simpleza técnica, lograban alcance global.
Por qué Firefox usa la nostalgia como estrategia publicitaria
El mensaje central del video busca contraponer dos momentos de internet. Por un lado, una época en la que la red se percibía como un espacio más personal y espontáneo, incluso cuando los equipos de cómputo eran compartidos por toda una familia.
Por otro lado, un presente en el que los datos de los usuarios circulan de forma constante y las empresas destinan sumas de dinero considerables para acceder a esa información.
Con ese contraste, Mozilla busca posicionar a Firefox como una alternativa para proteger los datos personales, tanto en dispositivos móviles como en computadoras, frente a navegadores como Edge.
Cómo reaccionaron los usuarios al video de los memes
Aunque la campaña incluye una reflexión explícita sobre la privacidad, buena parte de la recepción del público se enfocó en el componente nostálgico del video, dejando en segundo plano el mensaje original de la marca.
Muchos usuarios compararon la pieza con los antiguos YouTube Rewind, aquellos resúmenes anuales que Google producía para reunir lo más relevante y viral de cada año en la plataforma.
También se señaló que algunos de los memes seleccionados tienen un carácter muy específico dentro de la cultura de internet estadounidense y que, en otros países, no alcanzaron la misma repercusión en su momento.
Google Chrome ahora utiliza tus correos de Gmail para autocompletar formularios
Google ha lanzado una versión avanzada de la función de autocompletado para Chrome que extrae información directamente de los correos de Gmail para llenar formularios en línea. Esta herramienta ya se está desplegando en Estados Unidos, tanto en computadoras de escritorio como en las aplicaciones de Gemini en Chrome para iOS y Android.
A diferencia del sistema anterior, que se limitaba a utilizar únicamente los datos almacenados de forma manual en el navegador, la nueva actualización es capaz de escanear los mensajes recibidos para sugerir información específica.
Entre los datos que puede extraer automáticamente se encuentran números de confirmación de vuelos, códigos de seguimiento de envíos, números de pedidos, credenciales de socios, direcciones, teléfonos y tarjetas de crédito.
Esta función es una extensión de Personal Intelligence, un sistema que conecta las diversas aplicaciones de Google con el asistente Gemini para gestionar datos y resolver consultas complejas.
El uso de esta herramienta es completamente opcional, permitiendo a los usuarios activarla o desactivarla desde la configuración de Chrome, y Google garantiza que toda la información sensible se procesa bajo protocolos de cifrado.

articles.title: SpaceX AI in talks with Mississippi regulators over data center issues
articles.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI hit with multi-million dollar fine for building Mississippi data centers without the right permits
SpaceXAI faces massive daily fines over unpermitted data center constructions
- Mississippi regulators say three SpaceXAI sites began work without required stormwater permits
- SpaceXAI could face $6.1 million in penalties across three Mississippi sites
- State officials are seeking daily penalties of up to $25,000
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI faces potential penalties reaching $6.1 million after Mississippi regulators identified alleged construction permit violations involving three data center facilities in the state.
State environmental authorities claim construction activities began before the company obtained the necessary stormwater authorization, exposing its subsidiary to substantial financial penalties.
It is now seeking penalties of up to $25,000 daily, with the company's preliminary financial exposure calculated across all three affected facilities.
Three Mississippi data centers face regulatory scrutiny
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality issued the enforcement notice to MZX Tech LLC, a subsidiary responsible for the company's local infrastructure.
The affected facilities include Macrohard and Macroharder, both already operational, while construction continues at a third computing complex known as Minihard.
Although the three facilities support operations around Memphis, Tennessee, their locations across the state boundary place them under Mississippi's environmental regulations.
A fourth computing facility sits within Memphis itself, where the company began developing its artificial intelligence infrastructure during 2024.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The alleged violations were disclosed through a regulatory filing submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission as part of the company's financial reporting.
SpaceXAI confirmed that it is cooperating with state environmental officials and discussing a possible settlement covering the alleged violations at all three locations.
The proposed arrangement would consolidate the regulatory matters into one agreement, although the company has not disclosed any finalized settlement terms.
Separate lawsuit challenges gas turbine operations
Beyond the construction allegations, SpaceXAI faces another legal challenge concerning gas turbines used to generate electricity at its Southaven facility in Mississippi.
The NAACP alleges that the company constructed and operated the power generation installation without securing environmental permits required under federal and state regulations.
The organization is seeking financial penalties and an injunction restricting turbine operations, arguing that the company's activities violated federal air pollution legislation.
Federal government lawyers attempted to dismiss the lawsuit, maintaining that the requested penalties and operational restrictions could threaten economic and national security interests.
However, US District Judge Debra Brown rejected that intervention, determining that federal enforcement responsibilities did not grant unrestricted authority over environmental litigation.
"The EPA’s role as a primary enforcer of the Clean Air Act does not mean that the federal government retains complete control over all Clean Air Act litigation," said Brown.
The decision permits the NAACP's lawsuit to continue without establishing whether the company's turbine operations breached the environmental requirements cited by the organization.
Mississippi has previously penalized developers for construction without stormwater permits, including Complete Oil Field Disposal, which received a $4,200 sanction in August 2024.
In February 2025, JS LLC was fined $10,200 after regulators identified unauthorized construction affecting approximately 10.44 acres.
SpaceXAI has faced separate environmental scrutiny over its Memphis power generation, removing 20 generators and obtaining permits for another 15 following complaints about unauthorized operations.
The company's potential $6.1 million liability across three Mississippi sites remains unresolved, with regulators still discussing a possible settlement.
Via DCD

articles.title: Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: tiny, fun earbuds only let down by their unfortunate software situation
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Huawei FreeBuds Neo are perhaps the ideal small and affordable earbuds, offering you a tiny carry case and light buds without skimping on sound quality or ANC — which is good enough, for the money. However, software issues really hold them back and the stamina isn't too impressive either. Still, as small earbuds go, they're some of the best out there.
Reasons to buy
- + Small, light buds
- + Tiny carry case
- + Great value for money
Reasons to avoid
- - Borderline-unusable app
- - ANC good, not great
- - Battery life not amazing
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Huawei FreeBuds Neo: Two-minute review
Storied Chinese company Huawei may still be struggling to win friends in the phone and tablet worlds, with its lack of access to the Play Store still making the company's hand-held products impossible to recommend, but the brand's been a surprisingly reliable maker of admirable earbuds.
We gave the Huawei FreeBuds 5 Pro a perfect score earlier this year, and I maintain that the Huawei FreeArc are the best hook-style open earbuds I've ever tested. But now, instead of doing something better than everyone else, Huawei is doing something different.
The Huawei FreeBuds Neo seem to be the result of someone thinking the AirPods Pro 3 are perfect except for being too big; the brand continues its mission of all-but imitating Apple, while slyly improving the formula. That is to say, these are wireless in-ear buds which are ice-white (note: other finishes are available) but really small.
We've seen small earbuds before (see the JLab JBuds Mini for something really diddy) but they often tend to be cheap and feature-light. Not the FreeBuds Neo, which don't ask you to make compromises and are still affordable, compared to the FreeBuds 5 Pro or AirPods.
The carry case is a slender pill, which was second to none when it came to how easy it was to slip into my pocket and forget about. The buds are light, with shortened stems which make them look truncated.
It's not all about the design. These buds sound fun and energetic, with a V-shaped sound profile that adds some zest to your music. They're not the best-sounding buds I've tested, even at the price, but only audiophiles will be let down by what you're getting.
Now for the let-down, and it's a common one for Huawei: software. You see, the brand's app isn't on the Play Store, and you have to download it through its own app store, which you have to side-load on your phone. A complicated process which literally didn't work for me. Throughout my testing process, I couldn't access the app, and I know from past experience that this isn't an unheard-of occurrence.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Admittedly the app isn't that useful if you don't want EQ — a problem in and of itself — but if features are locked behind the roll of the dice that is 'will the app download?', it's not great.
Add to that the knowledge that the battery life and ANC are both good, but not particularly stellar and you'll see compromises — but these are all more understandable when you bear in mind the small size.
Despite the setbacks, these are still the best small earbuds you can buy — the best of a small bunch, if you'll pardon the pun — but they might not be mighty enough to sway people who don't care all that much about the compact and oh-so-portable size of their earbuds.
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Price and release date
- Released in September 2026, sold October
- Goes for £119.99 / AU$290 (about AU$160)
- Don't get excited though; there is unlikely to be a US release
The Huawei FreeBuds Neo were unveiled on September 2, 2026, ahead of a release later in the month.
The buds cost £119.99 / AU$290 (about $160, but Huawei doesn’t officially sell them in the States). So they’re about a third cheaper than the brand’s top buds, including the FreeBuds Pro 5, which go for £179.99 (about $240, AU$360).
It’s a smart price, for buds which feel like a ‘Lite’ alternative to the Pro model, as you can consider them a streamlined pick.
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Specs
| Drivers | 11mm | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | 
| Battery life | 6 hours (ANC on), 9 hours (ANC off) | 
| Weight | 4.8g (buds) 31.4g (case) | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Frequency response | 20-40kHz | 
| Waterproofing | IP55 | 
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Features
- Significant app download problems
- Unimpressive 6-hour battery life
- ANC is fine, not great
Installing Huawei’s Audio Connect is a real challenge for Android users like me. It’s not on the Play Store, so you have to side load the Huawei AppGallery, and use that to download it. (If you have an iPhone, you’ll find Audio Connect on the App Store, easy peasy).
Not only does that mean you’re downloading an unwanted app just to get to another one, but the process is fraught with difficulty. Case in point, I simply couldn’t install the AppGallery onto my Samsung phone, despite trying multiple times and diving into the settings. The APK wouldn’t take, and so I couldn’t use Audio Connect.
I’ve had troubles with the process before, and I’m ready to declare the app unusable for some people. Every time I need to use it on a pair of buds, it feels like I’m tossing a coin to see if it’ll work out this time.
If you do download it, you’re offered the bare bones of such an app, including the ability to change the touch control functions, tweak ANC strength, adjust EQ, use multipoint connections and turn on spatial audio. I used the FreeBuds Neo just fine without Audio Connect, though if I’d paid money for the buds, I’d be irked that I wasn’t getting all of these tools.
The buds have a 6-hour battery life with ANC on and 9 hours with it turned off (not 6.5 and 10 hours, as Huawei advertises loudly — the small text on its website reveals that this is just for lower-quality music such as MP3s, which I really hope you don’t listen to).
Using the case, you get up to 22 hours with ANC on, or 33 hours with it turned off. Again, those stats are for higher-resolution music streaming, but you'll get more if you listen to low-res tunes. Don't do that to yourself, though.
It’s not an especially competitive battery life, but in my testing, it often felt like I’d eke an extra half hour or so out of the buds. And it’s hard to be too annoyed with the limited battery life with small buds: where would a chunkier battery pack go?
ANC isn’t ground-breaking either, but it’s absolutely fine. I used it on planes, trains and buses; it removed the engine rumble from the last two and lessened it on the former, but didn’t do as much to silence people around me with all their unreliable or sporadic sounds.
- Features score: 3/5
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Design
- Tiny 31.4g lozenge case
- Light short-stem buds
- Reliable in-ear fit
The FreeBuds Neo’s entire pitch rests on their design: they’re the JLab JBuds Mini meets the AirPods Pro 3. They’re small earbuds, both in terms of the carry case and the buds themselves.
As soon as I removed the lozenge-shaped charging case from the box, I was surprised by how small it was. It’s just shy of 7cm wide and 3cm deep, and weighs just 31.4g. It disappeared into my trouser pockets enough that I kept losing them, only to discover that what I thought was a rolled tissue was in fact the charging case.
Like the earbuds, the case comes in white, black, silver or pink. The case basically just has enough space for the earbuds, along with a USB-C charging port and color-changing status indicator LED, which was useful for letting me know if the buds were at full charge.
Those earbuds don’t take up much space either, because like the case, they’re minuscule. Unlike those other baby buds from JLab, the FreeBuds Neo are ostensibly stem-toting earbuds, but with the tiniest stem I’ve ever seen. They look a lot like imitation AirPods Pro, but if Huawei changed its mind half-way through making the stem.
True to the pint-sized promise, the FreeBuds Neo only weigh 4.8g, and the weight isn’t just useful for comfort. Tip-toting earbuds can be rather hit-or-miss when it comes to in-ear stability, but not once in my testing did the Huawei’s wobble or fall.
Despite the small size, Huawei found space in the Neo to add touch controls — if you can set them up in the app. The buds also have an IP55 protection, ensuring they’re safe against limited dust ingress and gentle jets of water (including rain).
- Design score: 4.5/5
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Sound quality
- 11mm driver per bud.
- Has V-shaped sound: focus on bass and treble
- Supports LDAC playback on supported phones
Huawei hasn't returned the FreeBuds 5 Pro's dual-driver system in the FreeBuds Neo, and I don't blame it; the whole point is for them to be nice and small.
Instead, you're getting a sole 11mm driver per bud, which acts as a jack of all trades across the audio spectrum.
Don't expect audiophile-level sound, then, but I see these being pleasing for the average listener. They offer a V-shaped sound profile, which means the bass is hearty and the treble sharp.
As is always the case with V-shaped sounds, it means that you'll sometimes find mids are lacking. For example in Mipso's Talking in My Sleep, you get lovely textured strings and vocals, and the bass is controlled and full, but it's hard to tell where the acoustic guitars begin and other instruments end. Likewise in What About Flamingos? by Lake Street Dive, you get lovely resonant low-end and articulate treble, but only the faint hint of all the other instruments making up the composition.
Of course, in plenty of songs, all you want is low-end and top-end. I enjoyed listening to pop and electronic music without feeling like I was missing out on anything. There's a reason this kind of sound profile is chosen by earbud manufacturers; it's a crowd-pleaser.
Perhaps a symptom of the small size or driver configuration, but I didn't hear as prominent or pronounced a sound stage as you often do in earbuds like this. Sometimes instruments sounded a little more squished together than I'd like, but it was only an issue in songs with a complex instrumentation.
If you perked up at my earlier mention of high-res and low-res playback, in the battery section, then you'll be happy to know that the buds do support the LDAC codec (as long as you're on Android, because iPhones somehow still don't support it).
- Sound quality: 4/5
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Value
- Cut the costs from premium alternatives
- Cost more than alternative small buds
Is size all you care about when it comes to your earbuds? Then as a super-small option, you're likely going to find these poor value for money. Buy the JLabs — the JLab JBuds Mini ANC even have noise-nixing!
For everyone else, though, these are a good get. They look like premium earbuds, they feel like premium earbuds, and they sound like them... However, they cost a fair bit less than you'd expect.
I'd happily recommend the FreeBuds Neo at their retail price. Obviously, discounts are always great, but you shouldn't wait for one before buying them if you're interested.
- Value: 4/5
Should I buy the Huawei FreeBuds Neo?
| Huawei FreeBuds Neo score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | The battery life and ANC won't wow you, but the app problems make the features worth ignoring. | 3/5 | 
| Design | They're lovely and compact, and I never had comfort or fit issues | 4.5/5 | 
| Sound quality | A charming V-shaped sound will be a crowd-pleaser, but not ideal for audiophiles. | 4/5 | 
| Value | You're getting some solid ANC headphones for a smaller price. | 4/5 | 
Buy them if…
You want small-form earbuds
That's the main appeal of these, right? If you want something smaller than the average earbuds, these are the best ones to look at.
You want premium-feeling earbuds
I kept forgetting that the Huawei cost what they do, because they feel like buds which cost 50% more.
You want a charging indicator
It's a small feature, but many brands do it poorly; the Huawei's LED is great so you know as soon as your buds are charged.
Don’t buy them if…
You're a frequent app user
Always using your earbud app to tweak with settings? Fine if you're an iOS user, a bit risky if you're on Android. 
You need top-tier ANC
The FreeBuds Neo are fine for noise cancellation, but you can do better, and you don't need to pay that much more for it either.
Huawei FreeBuds Neo review: Also consider
Looking for alternative over-ears? Here are a few small-sized ones we would recommend.
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Huawei FreeBuds Neo | JLab JBuds Mini ANC | Sony WF-C710N | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Drivers | 11mm | 6mm | 40mm | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Battery life (ANC on) | 6 hours (buds) 22 hours (case) | 7 hours (buds) 25 hours (case) | 8.5 hours (buds) / 30 hours (case) | 
| Weight | 4.8g (buds) 31.4g (case) | 3.4g (buds) 20.7g (case) | 5.2g (bud) 38g (case) | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | Bluetooth 6.0 | Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Waterproofing | IP55 | IP55 | IPX4 | 
JLab JBuds Mini ANC
These are small and, more importantly, roughly half the price of the Huawei. You won't get the same audio quality, but the even-smaller case and buds will please those who just want something tiny. 
Read our hands-on with the JLab JBuds Mini ANC 
Sony WF-C710N
Another tiny premium option comes from Sony, so you know they're good. They have fantastic ANC and sound great, but they don't support LDAC and don't have great touch controls.
Read our full Sony WF-C710N review
How I tested the Huawei FreeBuds Neo
- Tested for a month
- Paired with Android phone for Bluetooth playback
- Used on multiple holidays as well as use at home and around neighborhood.
The Huawei FreeBuds Neo got the pleasure of an entire month of use before I wrote this review, which gave me time to fully appreciate how they work.
That time included multiple holidays, so I brought the buds to various countries and tested them on flights, train journeys and coach trips. Of course, I also used them at home, at the gym, and on walks around my neighborhood.
During the testing process, the buds were connected to my Android phone. I listened primarily on Spotify and to my own music library of WAV tracks, but also conducted calls, played games and streamed lots of TV on Prime Video.
I've been reviewing tech for TechRadar since early 2019, and in that time have tested many other pairs of earbuds, as well as countless Huawei products.
- First reviewed in October 2026
Tom Bedford is a freelance contributor covering tech, entertainment and gaming. Beyond TechRadar, he has bylines on sites including GamesRadar, Digital Trends, Android Police, TechAdvisor, WhattoWatch and BGR. From 2019 to 2022 he was on the TechRadar team as the staff writer and then deputy editor for the mobile team.

articles.title: Volt Typhoon Used Covert Silent Train Network in Four Zero-Day Exploitation Campaigns
articles.text:
The China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Volt Typhoon has been attributed to a now-disrupted covert access network dubbed Silent Train that has been put to use for zero-day exploitation and strategic access.
"First identified in late 2023, Silent Train uses rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise infrastructure," Lumen Technologies Black Lotus Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It employs anti-forensic techniques, compartmentalized operations, and post-operation cleanup to minimize detection and attribution."
Its main purpose is to facilitate critical attack phases like vulnerability exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration, and to maintain continued access to victim environments. The activity stands out for two main reasons -
- It singled out entities that could provide scalable access to downstream customers, sensitive networks, or strategic programs.
- It targeted endpoint management platforms, network management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators, and control plane technologies that play a crucial role within enterprise environments.
Hundreds of victims have been identified across telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms, and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, and emergency services.
Volt Typhoon (aka Bronze Silhouette, Insidious Taurus, UNC3236, Vanguard Panda, and Voltzite) is the moniker assigned to a China-linked state-sponsored group known for its targeting of critical infrastructure networks, particularly communications, energy, transportation, and water and wastewater systems sectors.
Known to be active since at least 2021, the threat actor was previously observed exploiting a file upload vulnerability in Versa Director as a zero-day (CVE-2024-39717) to deliver a bespoke web shell called VersaMem designed to harvest credentials and enable access to downstream customers.
The latest findings from Black Lotus Labs show that the security flaw was one among four confirmed zero-day campaigns the threat actor has conducted through Silent Train. The remaining three vulnerabilities are listed below -
- CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 - A set of insecure deserialization and command injection vulnerabilities in N-able N-central.
- CVE-2026-20127 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller
- CVE-2026-16812 - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator
Separately, Volt Typhoon is also suspected to have taken advantage of a likely zero-day vulnerability in Quest KACE before it was patched in October 2025. The campaign is estimated to have impacted more than 30 victims.
"Silent Train is built around rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation, and continuously refreshed," Black Lotus Labs said.
"This model has enabled Volt Typhoon to conduct exploitation and post-exploitation operations with exceptional operational security while minimizing opportunities for detection, attribution, and disruption."
A defining characteristic of these attacks is the repeated targeting of systems that can open the door to broad visibility, control, and access across large enterprise environments of strategic value to the U.S.
What's interesting is that the covert access capability began to take shape sometime around November 2023, just weeks before the first round of disruption targeting KV-botnet, an IoT botnet linked to multiple China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors, including Volt Typhoon.
Silent Train's operational activity is said to have surged in the wake of the botnet's second disruption in late January 2024, while simultaneously shifting to an ephemeral infrastructure comprising diverse device types and across geographies.
"Rather than continue using persistent infrastructure, Volt Typhoon shifted to a model using one-time-use chains of compromised devices that it could rebuild as needed," Black Lotus Labs said. "Volt Typhoon rapidly assembled and dismantled transient infrastructure, creating a resilient, secure, and compartmentalized framework that protected valuable access."
Described as a "layered, multi-hop framework," Silent Train is designed to let Volt Typhoon operators relay malicious traffic through several devices before it reaches the targets so as to obscure its origins from both victims and defenders. Each link in the chain serves a specific purpose -
- Virtual private servers (VPS) that function as a temporary staging area and allow threat actors to provision and discard them after each session. The sessions begin from VPS infrastructure located outside the U.S.
- Compromised non-U.S. SOHO and IoT devices located across different countries, providers, and hardware that conceal the starting point of the attack.
- U.S.-based compromised devices that function as an exit node before reaching the domestic victim and help evade geofencing and IP reputation blocklists.
No less than 27 device classes, ranging from SOHO and IoT devices (e.g., TP-Link, Intelbras, Ruckus Wireless, SATO, NETGEAR, Zyxel, and Cambium) to enterprise platforms (e.g., Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect, and CyberPanel), have been exploited and enrolled into the covert network.
"Silent Train stands out for its operational discipline, focusing on short-lived, selfmanaged sessions rather than persistent relays or C2 infrastructure," Black Lotus Labs said. "To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node."
"This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and 'live off the land' utilities. At the end of operational sessions, they removed every artifact and dismantled the operational chain in their wake. Silent Train sessions lasted about four hours on average, with some lasting only minutes."
Another notable aspect is the designation of certain device types to specific positions within Silent Train. For instance, Intelbras modems have been found to only appear as relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi and Fortinet FortiGate appliances served as U.S.-based intermediary and exit points responsible for interacting with the victim.
Put differently, the infrastructure points to deliberate compartmentalization across layers, confining some device types to certain roles that remain constant while the underlying infrastructure itself changes over time so as to complicate attribution efforts.
By early 2025, however, Silent Train is believed to have evolved from a completely ephemeral relay network to a hybrid architecture that retained enterprise-grade devices for an average of one to three months instead of changing them after each engagement.
Subsequent maturation of the platform introduced reverse-tunnel variants that used open-source proxies like Chisel and FRP to send traffic from infected devices to upstream infrastructure.
Within the U.S., Hawaii, California, and Texas have emerged as the focus areas of Silent Train operations, which boils down to the fact that these states host major military installations, telecommunications infrastructure, defense contractors, satellite communications providers, and critical logistics networks.
"Victimology indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region," Black Lotus Labs said.
"The resulting picture is one of a highly structured framework built to acquire, protect, and sustain strategic access at scale. Through repeated targeting of centralized management platforms and control plane technologies, Silent Train shows how Volt Typhoon systematically pursues and preserves access to some of the most consequential networks in the United States."

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Carbon, una IA tan potente que por ahora está vetada al público general
articles.text:
Google presentó este miércoles Gemini 4 Carbon, su nuevo modelo de inteligencia artificial, que encabeza con 59 puntos el índice de la firma independiente Artificial Analysis. Por ahora solo lo usará un grupo reducido de especialistas en ciberseguridad; desarrolladores, empresas y público general deberán esperar, sin fecha confirmada.
El anuncio lo firmó Koray Kavukcuoglu, vicepresidente sénior de Google DeepMind y arquitecto jefe de inteligencia artificial de la empresa. Según Google, Carbon lidera tres pruebas públicas de seguridad informática: 88,2% en SEC-bench Pro, que mide la capacidad de encontrar fallas en programas reales; 54,8% en ExploitGym, que comprueba si una falla puede aprovecharse, y 71,0% en CWE-bench, que evalúa si el modelo la corrige.
En el índice de Artificial Analysis, versión 5.0, Carbon supera a Claude Opus 5.5, de Anthropic, con 58 puntos, y a GPT-6 Astra, de OpenAI, con 57, según VentureBeat. Argon, el modelo anterior de Google, obtuvo 50. En la tabla de Google, Carbon logra el mejor resultado en 15 de 17 pruebas.
Argon se presentó el 30 de septiembre para socios de ciberseguridad y se abrió de forma más amplia el 13 de octubre, según VentureBeat. Carbon sigue el mismo camino, 15 días después de esa ampliación. Google no publicó un informe técnico ni la cantidad de parámetros del modelo.
Solo especialistas en ciberseguridad tendrán acceso por ahora
Google dijo que esta semana dará acceso a “un subconjunto de defensores cibernéticos” y que lo ampliará por etapas a más socios de confianza mediante su Programa Fairwind, que tiene más de 650 socios, exige verificación de antecedentes y prohíbe compartir o revender el acceso, según WebProNews, que cita la página del programa.
El resto de los usuarios no tiene plazo. La empresa afirmó que lo ofrecerá a desarrolladores, empresas y consumidores “lo antes posible”, tras reunir comentarios y ajustar las salvaguardas del modelo. También participa en el proceso voluntario del gobierno de Estados Unidos para probar modelos antes de su lanzamiento.
Cuando llegue a los desarrolladores, el precio inicial será de USD 2 por cada millón de tokens de entrada y de USD 10 por cada millón de salida; después subirá a USD 4 y USD 20. Google no precisó cuándo termina ese período introductorio; el de Argon vence el 30 de noviembre.
Las pruebas de seguridad se midieron sin restricciones
Google aclaró que las evaluaciones externas de ciberseguridad se hicieron sin salvaguardas. VentureBeat señaló que, por eso, el anuncio no demuestra que los clientes obtendrán los mismos resultados con las restricciones que acompañen al modelo cuando se comercialice.
La empresa también afirmó que el equipo de Chrome halló que Carbon generó correcciones de mayor calidad con una ventaja superior a 10 veces frente al modelo de otro laboratorio. Google no nombró al rival ni publicó los datos de esa comparación, según VentureBeat.
Las pruebas independientes mostraron matices: Carbon mejora de forma notable sobre Argon en programación y trabajo con conocimiento, pero queda detrás de varios rivales en tareas profesionales y registra más alucinaciones que Argon en una prueba de datos factuales, informó VentureBeat. OpenAI conserva ventaja en una prueba de ingeniería de software y Anthropic en una de uso de la computadora.
Google describió además mejoras en la conducta del modelo: las alertas graves de desvío de conducta bajaron casi 80% en sus equipos internos y, en un banco de pruebas de inyección de instrucciones —ataques que ocultan órdenes en el contenido que lee el modelo—, el índice de éxito de los ataques fue de 0,0%. Todas son mediciones de la propia compañía.
Carbon puede trabajar durante días para encontrar y corregir errores sutiles en grandes bases de código, según observaciones de los equipos internos de Google.

articles.title: Egypt's Tanmiya Capital closes $130 million fund backed by EIB, IFC and EBRD
articles.text: Egypt-based private equity firm Tanmiya Capital Ventures (TCV) has announced the final close of its second fund at $130 million, exceeding its $120 million target, following a $37.5 million commitment from the European Investment Bank (EIB) through its development arm, EIB Global. The fund is backed by international and local institutional investors, including the Egyptian-American Enterprise Fund (EAEF), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), International Finance Corporation (IFC) and Egypt's Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise Development Agency (MSMEDA). Founded in 2016, Tanmiya Capital Ventures focuses on growth equity and private equity investments in established mid-market Egyptian businesses. Fund II will target companies operating in healthcare, training, fintech, consumer goods, logistics and transport, providing capital and operational support to facilitate expansion. The fund is expected to build a portfolio of six to eight companies, supporting business growth, corporate governance improvements and job creation. At least 30% of its portfolio companies are expected to meet one or more of the EIB's gender equality financing criteria. Press release: The European Investment Bank (EIB), through its development arm EIB Global, invested $37.5 million in Tanmiya Capital Fund II to expand access to growth capital for established small and medium-sized companies in Egypt. The investment was announced today at a ceremony in Cairo attended by EIB Vice-President Gelsomina Vigliotti and Tanmiya Capital Ventures Managing Partners Ahmed El Guindy, Youssef Ahmed Ayoub and Mohamed Mohsen Mahgoub. The EIB commitment helped Tanmiya Capital Fund II reach a final close of $130 million, exceeding its $120 million target. The fund is supported by a diversified group of international and local investors, including the Egyptian-American Enterprise Fund (EAEF), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and Egypt’s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise Development Agency (MSMEDA). Managed by the independent Egyptian investment firm Tanmiya Capital, the fund will invest in a diversified portfolio of established, high-growth companies in Egypt. It will focus on businesses seeking strategic capital to expand, professionalise their operations and strengthen their competitiveness, with investments expected across healthcare, training, financial technology, consumer goods, logistics and transport. The investment addresses the limited availability of long-term equity finance for small and medium-sized companies in Egypt. By combining capital with strategic and managerial support, the fund is expected to help portfolio companies scale up, improve governance and create jobs. At least 30% of portfolio companies are expected to meet one or more of the EIB’s criteria for financing that supports gender equality. “Egypt’s private sector has enormous potential to drive sustainable growth, create quality jobs and deepen economic ties with Europe. Our investment in Tanmiya Capital Fund II will provide ambitious local companies with the growth capital and expertise they need to expand. It also reflects the European Union’s commitment, through Global Gateway and the new Agenda for the Mediterranean, to supporting a more competitive, inclusive and resilient Egyptian economy,” said EIB Vice-President Gelsomina Vigliotti. “The successful closing of Tanmiya Capital Fund II above its target reflects strong investor confidence in our strategy and in the potential of Egypt’s private sector. The EIB’s commitment brings not only capital, but also valuable international expertise and a shared focus on sustainable growth, strong governance and long-term value creation. Together, we will support ambitious Egyptian companies as they scale up, become more competitive and expand their links with regional and European markets,” said Tanmiya Capital Managing Partner Ahmed El Guindy. “Our investment in Tanmiya Capital Ventures Fund II reflects IFC’s commitment to strengthening Egypt’s private sector by expanding access to the long-term growth capital businesses need to grow and create jobs," said Ary Naïm, IFC's Division Director for North Africa and the Horn of Africa. "By partnering with experienced local fund managers, we can help promising Egyptian companies, including family-owned businesses, strengthen their operations, become more competitive, and scale. This is an important part of our broader work to mobilize private investment and support sustainable, inclusive growth in Egypt.” “Our investment in Tanmiya Capital Fund II reinforces MSMEDA’s Fund of Funds program mandate, through which we partner with experienced private equity and venture capital managers and support emerging ones to crowd in private and international capital into promising Egyptian companies. We believe TCVII will channel much-needed growth capital and expertise to businesses with real potential to expand and create jobs, in line with the Egypt’s strategy to empower the private sector and Vision 2030,” said Mostafa Ismail Hassan, CEO of the Egypt’s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise Development Agency (MSMEDA). “We are proud to continue our long-standing partnership with TCV, a team that has consistently demonstrated its ability to invest in and build growing businesses in Egypt. The fund’s oversubscribed close is a strong signal of investor confidence, and our commitment reflects our firm belief in the long-term fundamentals of the Egyptian economy and the central role of its private sector in driving growth and job creation,” said Yasmine Ghobrial, Chief Investment Officer of the Egyptian-American Enterprise Fund (EAEF). The operation follows a Team Europe approach and supports the EU-Africa Global Gateway Investment Package. It is also expected to strengthen commercial links between Egypt and Europe, as portfolio companies may source equipment, technology and services from European suppliers or develop partnerships with European businesses. At its target scale, the fund is expected to build a portfolio of six to eight companies and support thousands of jobs across Egypt. The EIB will also contribute its experience in environmental, social and governance standards and international private equity best practice through its participation in the fund’s advisory committee.

articles.title: I chose the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro as the best health and fitness gadget of the year in our awards — here's why
articles.text:
Why the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro's outstanding construction, new stamina metrics and Apple Watch-rivaling accuracy make it my Fitness Device of the Year award winner
The Fenix rises once again
The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro is Garmin's latest — and greatest — watch. The Fenix series always occupies a flagship position in Garmin's lineup: while the company does make more expensive watches, most of those are specialist pieces of gear, such as the Tactix for soldiers, the Descent for professional divers, and the Marq series as an ultra-premium option for fashion-forward Garmin users.
The Garmin Fenix series is its top-tier 'generalist' watch, and considering it only comes out once every few years, anticipation is always high. Fortunately, the Fenix 9 Pro lives up to the hype, and is my Fitness Devices of the Year at the TechRadar Product of the Year Awards 2026.
It's a powerhouse of a watch, from construction and performance, and has coped with every test we have thrown at it, from hikes in Chamonix, to comparison tests against the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and an electrical heart rate monitor, the Frontier X2.
Let's start with construction. The Fenix 9 Pro's entire case is now made of titanium, rather than a titanium bezel and fiber-reinforced polymer (that's plastic, to you and me) elsewhere.
It's thinner, and the lack of visible screws (aside from the back plate) make for a refined, sleek aesthetic. The display is sapphire crystal as standard, too, protecting the super-bright AMOLED touchscreen display, with the usual MIP Power Glass solar charging options as an additional extra.
The construction makes for an amazing watch, and these upgrades make the Fenix 9 Pro really feel just that, Pro — more like a Marq. I'm wearing the 43mm version, and it really doesn't feel like an ultra-chunky Fenix. In fact, it feels far more like wearing an upmarket metal dive watch.
This sealed unit design necessitated a redesign in the buttons, according to Garmin's promotional material, in order to make sure it remained waterproof up to 40m deep, but Garmin cracked it and the watch retains Garmin's distinctive five-button design.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It's even revamped the LED light, with an introduction of a third green option to add to its black and red tones. The green light offers improved visibility compared to the red option, without sacrificing your night-eyes.
Software-wise, the UX is familiar to Garmin watch users, as everything is innately customizable, from the widget stack to workout views to watch faces. New features include Garmin Epic, which allows you to string several workouts together into one mega-event, such as multiple ski runs over one long weekend, for example. You can start it from the watch, and view or share it in the app. Rucking also got a useful redesign, while Maps has been updated to provide an angled POV option.
In our performance test, I was expecting accuracy — after all, the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro retains Garmin's Elevate V5 heart rate sensor array from previous years — but I wasn't expecting it to cleave so close to the heart rate monitor and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 (which Apple claims is the most accurate wearable to date) during my test workouts.
Rerouting course directions has proven to be responsive and speedy, while the battery performs as described, lasting for a week, and the watch is comfortable to wear during sleep, workouts and every day.
There wasn't really any doubt that the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro was going to be a good watch, or even a great one. Like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, it builds on everything Garmin has done before to create a worthy successor to the ever-popular Fenix line. When the Fenix 10 comes out in a few years, this one will come down in price just like the Fenix 8 before it, and we'll see far more adopters take it on and have fun with it.
I suppose I could have chosen something like the cheap Google Fitbit Air, the Garmin Cirqa, or the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to be our Fitness Device of the Year. But when I thought about what was going to dominate my limited wrist real estate if I sign up for a race, there was only ever going to be a handful of options, and the 43mm Garmin Fenix 9 Pro was first on the list.
It's smart enough not to look out of place in the office, it's got everything I need for training, it's got all the complications I need from the Connect IQ score, like Spotify and Komoot, and a week-long battery life (sorry Apple) that cinches it for me over the Ultra 4.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Matt is TechRadar's expert on all things fitness, wellness and wearable tech.
A former staffer at Men's Health, he holds a Master's Degree in journalism from Cardiff and has written for brands like Runner's World, Women's Health, Men's Fitness, LiveScience and Fit&Well on everything fitness tech, exercise, nutrition and mental wellbeing.
He is the author of the upcoming book The Health Data Heist, set to be published by Bloomsbury in 2027. When he’s not training or writing about health and fitness, he can be found reading doorstop-thick fantasy books with lots of fictional maps in them.
