articles.title: OpenAI asegura que un modelo sin publicar refutó una hipótesis matemática vigente desde los noventa
articles.text:
OpenAI afirma que uno de sus modelos de inteligencia artificial, todavía sin publicar, logró refutar la hipótesis del tiempo exponencial, una conjetura de finales de los noventa que sostenía cientos de artículos de informática teórica, desde la teoría de grafos hasta la biología computacional.
La compañía atribuye a ese mismo sistema otros dos hallazgos matemáticos: la demostración de una conjetura sobre ondas abierta desde 1991 y la prueba de que la teoría de Yang-Mills, uno de los pilares de la física de partículas, existe en sentido matemático.
OpenAI presenta los tres resultados como “datos de investigación en bruto” y pidió a especialistas externos que formen grupos independientes para verificarlos.
Cualquiera de estos tres hallazgos, de confirmarse, alcanzaría para sostener una carrera académica completa y para aspirar a varios premios internacionales.
El de la hipótesis del tiempo exponencial, en particular, roza uno de los Problemas del Milenio, los siete desafíos matemáticos dotados con un millón de dólares cada uno, de los cuales solo uno ha sido resuelto hasta ahora.
Qué dice la hipótesis del tiempo exponencial y por qué su refutación es relevante
La hipótesis del tiempo exponencial está vinculada al problema P frente a NP, formulado de manera independiente por Stephen Cook y Leonid Levin en 1971.
Esa pregunta busca determinar si todo problema cuya solución puede comprobarse con rapidez puede también resolverse con la misma rapidez. La hipótesis va más allá: no solo asume que la respuesta es negativa, sino que sostiene que el costo de resolver los casos más difíciles crece de forma exponencial.
El problema concreto sobre el que se apoya es sencillo de enunciar. Dada una fórmula lógica cuyas variables solo pueden ser verdaderas o falsas, se trata de determinar si existe alguna combinación que la haga verdadera. Cada variable adicional duplica las combinaciones posibles: con 100 variables, por ejemplo, existen unos 1,27 quintillones de posibilidades.
Existen métodos para evitar probar todas las combinaciones, pero la hipótesis sostenía que, incluso en el peor de los casos, el tiempo de cálculo seguiría disparándose de forma exponencial con cada variable que se sumara.
La hipótesis del tiempo exponencial es la conjetura informática que afirmaba que ciertos problemas lógicos no pueden resolverse más rápido que de forma exponencial en el peor de los casos; su eventual refutación obligaría a revisar buena parte de los fundamentos teóricos que daban por válida esa barrera de dificultad.
Según OpenAI, su modelo encontró la refutación el 16 de octubre y, un día después, ya estaba traducida a Lean, un lenguaje que permite a una máquina verificar cada paso de una demostración matemática. La empresa publicó además un algoritmo capaz de contar las soluciones de este tipo de fórmulas más rápido de lo que la hipótesis consideraba posible.
La revisión de este resultado quedó en manos de Russell Impagliazzo y Ramamohan Paturi, de la Universidad de California en San Diego, dos de los autores originales de la hipótesis hace más de dos décadas, junto con Ryan Williams, investigador del Instituto Tecnológico de Massachusetts (MIT).
El avance sobre ondas que conecta con la conjetura de Kakeya
El segundo resultado que reivindica OpenAI es la demostración de la conjetura del suavizado local, planteada en 1991 por el matemático Christopher Sogge.
Esta conjetura estudia cómo se suavizan las ondas cuando se promedian en el tiempo. La compañía sostiene haberla probado en todas las dimensiones, lo que arrastraría consigo otras dos conjeturas célebres del análisis armónico: la de restricción de Stein y la de Kakeya.
La conjetura de Kakeya nació en 1917 como un acertijo planteado por el matemático japonés Soichi Kakeya, quien se preguntaba cuál es la superficie más pequeña en la que puede darse la vuelta a una aguja. La respuesta conocida es que esa superficie puede ser tan pequeña como se quiera.
Una versión más moderna de la pregunta afina el planteamiento: si una figura capaz de alojar la aguja en todas las direcciones puede no ocupar ningún volumen, cabe preguntarse si de todos modos llena siempre todas las dimensiones del espacio en que se encuentra.
Hong Wang y Joshua Zahl ya habían demostrado esta conjetura para espacios de tres dimensiones el año anterior, un trabajo que le valió a Wang la Medalla Fields en julio.
OpenAI asegura haber extendido ahora la solución a cualquier número de dimensiones. Alex Iosevich, especialista en análisis armónico de la Universidad de Rochester, calificó el hallazgo como un “desarrollo histórico” en declaraciones recogidas por Al Jazeera.
El vínculo con la teoría de Yang-Mills y la física de partículas
El tercer hallazgo que reclama OpenAI pertenece al terreno de la teoría cuántica de campos. La compañía sostiene haber demostrado que existen, en cuatro dimensiones, la teoría de Yang-Mills pura, la cromodinámica cuántica (que describe la fuerza que mantiene unidos a los quarks dentro de protones y neutrones) y la versión más sencilla de la teoría de gran unificación.
Probar que la teoría de Yang-Mills existe equivale a resolver la mitad de otro de los Problemas del Milenio. La otra mitad corresponde a la llamada “brecha de masa”, que explicaría por qué la fuerza nuclear fuerte solo actúa a distancias minúsculas. Esa segunda parte del problema, según el propio anuncio, OpenAI no logró demostrarla.
La verificación de este resultado quedó a cargo de un grupo liderado por David Gross, premio Nobel de Física en 2004 por el descubrimiento de la libertad asintótica, la propiedad en la que se apoya la demostración. Entre los integrantes de ese grupo figura Arthur Jaffe, quien redactó junto a Edward Witten el enunciado oficial del problema.
A diferencia de los otros dos hallazgos, este tercer resultado no se hizo público. El grupo de revisión optó por no difundir el material por el momento y encargarse de redactar el resultado por su cuenta.

articles.title: Gartner says only 3% of organizations are getting AI cost savings from productivity, yet 85% plan to spend more
articles.text:
Facepalm: Ever since it started making its way into the workplace, we've been told that AI will skyrocket productivity and cut costs – promises that have also been used to justify layoffs. So, how many organizations are actually exceeding their cost-saving targets through productivity gains? According to Gartner, a massive 3%.
The figure comes from Gartner's HR Symposium in Orlando. In a finding that perfectly sums up the blind faith so many executives have in AI, 77% of board members expect the technology will deliver value in the form of productivity and cost savings. This is despite 97% of organizations being unable to achieve cost savings through productivity alone.
CV Viverito, senior director analyst for Gartner's HR practice, said that organizations will not generate cost savings from AI at this point. "The greater opportunity is to use AI to do things that weren't possible before, such as shifting employee time into new capabilities, outcomes, and sources of growth," Viverito added.
Another entirely unsurprising finding is that almost four in ten companies are now over budget on their AI spending. But when has overspending on something that isn't bringing the promised cost-reduction gains discouraged execs? Despite everything, 85% of companies say they are planning on spending even more next year.
None of this should come as a shock to anyone paying attention to similar surveys. In January, PwC's latest Global CEO survey, completed by 4,454 chief executive officers across 95 countries, revealed that 56% of CEOs had seen no cost or revenue benefits since introducing AI to their businesses.
There was also a 2025 MIT report that said 95% of AI implementations don't increase profits, while a 2024 survey found generative AI could actually be harming productivity at work.
So, what does Gartner recommend companies actually do? For starters, agree on what they're trying to achieve. Its survey of 297 chief HR officers found that 78% reported no agreement among leaders on where AI creates value. Apparently, that discussion can wait until after the money has been spent.
Gartner wants businesses to focus investment where AI can make a difference, help managers redesign work, and use their existing AI expertise. It also recommends doing something useful with the time employees save. Just 21% of the time freed up by AI went toward more innovative work. Meta's CTO would probably have a lot to say about that part.

articles.title: Airbnb Cuts Recommendation Staleness from 2 Days to Seconds with Chronon
articles.text:
Airbnb has extended its open source Chronon feature platform with Push Mode and Near Real Time (NRT) Model Transform to update sequence based recommendation embeddings within seconds of guest activity. The change reduced embedding staleness from nearly two days to less than a minute, with typical updates arriving within 10 to 30 seconds. Airbnb also reported a 1.67% improvement in offline NDCG and an approximately 0.33% increase in uncancelled bookings in online A/B testing.
The work builds on Airbnb’s JourneyFormer based sequence recommender, which uses a Transformer encoder to represent a guest’s booking, review and browsing history. Previously, the encoder ran as a daily batch job, generating embeddings that were stored in a low latency store. During a search, the ranking system retrieved the latest embedding and combined it with the live query, keeping the Transformer outside the latency sensitive serving path. However, activity occurring after the daily batch could remain absent from the embedding until the following run, with processing delays bringing effective staleness close to two days.
Airbnb’s initial architecture showing the daily batch sequence encoder, embedding store and online ranking path. (Source : Airbnb Blog Post)
Airbnb addressed the freshness problem by adding two capabilities to Chronon. Push Mode causes a streaming job to publish a notification when a feature value is committed, allowing downstream processing to react to updated guest activity rather than polling or waiting for a scheduled job. NRT Model Transform allows an already deployed model to run inside that streaming pipeline. Airbnb uses the same Transformer sequence encoder for the near real time path, avoiding a separate inference implementation for the streaming workflow.
The resulting pipeline captures events such as searches and listing views, combines them with the guest’s existing short and long-term sequence data, and triggers model inference when the updated feature state is available. The generated embedding is then written to the same low-latency store used by the batch system. Consequently, the online ranking path remains largely unchanged while the representation it retrieves becomes more current.
Pengyu Hou, Senior Software Engineer, Infrastructure at Airbnb, described the platform change as addressing the gap between event-driven data and model inference:
NRT Model Transform lets Chronon call an already deployed model ... directly from within the streaming flow.
The approach follows a broader feature serving pattern in which predictions can be updated when underlying features change rather than computed on every user request. Feast, another open-source feature platform, documents cached prediction architectures where inference is triggered by feature updates, trading additional writes and pipeline complexity for lower serving latency. Chronon instead integrates streaming computation and model transformation into its feature platform and emphasizes consistency between offline and online computation.
Airbnb’s near real-time Chronon architecture (Source: Airbnb Blog Post)
Airbnb has contributed Push Mode and NRT Model Transform to the public Chronon repository. Chronon supports both batch and streaming computation and provides online feature serving designed to maintain consistency between training and production inference.

articles.title: This open-source keyboard lets you snap keys together in any layout
articles.text:
The takeaway: Custom keyboard builders can swap out switches, keycaps, plates, and firmware these days, but the layout is usually locked in once the PCB is made. Now, a new open-source project called Keybytes is trying to get around that limitation by giving each key its own tiny circuit board and microcontroller. The keys snap together with magnets and connect to a small hub, allowing a keyboard to start out as a single key and grow into pretty much any shape.
The project comes from Nathan Alspaugh, an MIT freshman studying aerospace engineering, who said he has spent around 100 hours working on it since March. When he posted the project to Hacker News this week, he said the idea came from his frustration that nobody sold triangle- or circle-shaped keyboards.
Each key, called a Keybit, consists of a 19.05mm-square circuit board fitted with a Cherry MX switch and an inexpensive CH32V003 RISC-V chip. The neighboring module, whether another key or the hub, receives power and I2C data through spring-loaded pogo pins along all four edges.
The hub, called the Keyword, occupies the same 1u footprint but stacks two PCBs. An STM32WB55 on the upper board handles Bluetooth and stores firmware for every key. Meanwhile, the lower board houses the charging circuitry for an optional LiPo battery and the USB-C port.
Rather than sharing a single bus, each Keybit bit-bangs a separate I2C connection along each of its four sides. Alspaugh explained in the Hacker News thread that this approach reduces parasitic capacitance and allows the software to determine the physical position of each key. In theory, that means a chain of keys could extend indefinitely.
Getting the magnets right took considerably more trial and error. According to his build journal, the first magnetic cases couldn't hold the modules together against the force exerted by the pogo pins. Rather than redesigning the boards to accommodate weaker pins, Alspaugh opted for stronger magnets and printed case after case in resin at a makerspace. The hub's case alone went through 12 iterations. His first working build finally came together on October 24.
Even so, the current demo features just two keys attached to the hub, as Alspaugh is still building additional modules and finishing the firmware. Layout options are also limited to a flat grid for now.
Scaling up would get expensive quickly, too. Alspaugh estimates that a fully assembled, full-size keyboard with two hubs and roughly 110 keys would cost around $900. Almost half that amount would go toward the pogo pins, so he plans to buy and solder them himself if he ever builds one.
Anyone who wants to try the project can find the schematics, case STEP files, and bill of materials on its GitHub page, which is published under an MIT license. The PCB design files are available there, too – something Keychron held back when it opened up its case and plate designs earlier this year.

articles.title: Robôs de limpeza fazem bonito durante feira em São Paulo • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Resumo
- A Redroad, marca de soluções inteligentes de limpeza, apresentou três robôs de limpeza durante a HigiExpo 2026, feira em São Paulo.
- Os robôs RD10 Pro, RD55 e RD70 Pro atendem a diferentes portes de espaços, desde pequenos ambientes até grandes áreas.
- Os preços sugeridos são de US$ 14.900, US$ 32.900 e US$ 41.900, respectivamente.
A marca de soluções inteligentes de limpeza Redroad demonstrou três robôs durante a HigiExpo 2026, feira voltada ao setor de limpeza que ocorreu em São Paulo, na última semana. A companhia garante não apenas produtos com altíssima tecnologia, mas também uma solução completa para os clientes – em sua essência, pessoas jurídicas – que optarem por implementá-los em suas localidades nos próximos meses.
O responsável pela marca, Danny Cui, conta ao Tecnoblog quais são os pilares das novidades reveladas na capital paulista:
- Linha para diferentes portes: os três modelos atendem desde espaços pequenos, como academias e casas de repouso, a grandes áreas, como aeroportos e fábricas. “Como na limpeza comercial existem muitos setores diferentes, precisamos oferecer uma linha ampla de produtos”, disse Cui.
- Operação local: a empresa montou um escritório em São Paulo com central de atendimento em português, um centro de serviço e um estoque de peças de reposição. Os planos incluem, no futuro, uma unidade de montagem em Jacareí, no interior de São Paulo, que vai trabalhar com componentes principais importados.
- IA física: o termo delimita os algoritmos que permitem ao robô perceber o ambiente e se adaptar quando algo muda no caminho. Na prática, a equipe escaneia o local do cliente com um aparelho portátil com o objetivo de criar mapas e rotinas de limpeza antes mesmo de enviar o robô.
- Pós-venda em três camadas: a Redroad explica que os clientes obtêm atendimento via telefone, acesso remoto ou com técnicos de campo que visitam a localidade para fazer os reparos. “Respondemos à dúvida em até duas horas, encontramos a causa e a solução em até 24 horas e consertamos em até 48. Se não conseguirmos consertar, fornecemos máquinas substitutas”, afirmou o executivo.
A Redroad aproveitou a feira em São Paulo para reforçar que quer ser mais do que um fornecedor capaz de entregar dispositivos de limpeza comercial; ela se posiciona como uma parceria que estará junto do cliente desde a detecção das necessidades até o fornecimento dos equipamentos e o posterior pós-venda, inclusive com visitas de manutenção preventiva – ou seja, revisões programadas antes que surjam problemas.
“No fim das contas, o cliente final não precisa do equipamento, ele precisa garantir que o piso esteja limpo todos os dias”, disse Cui ao Tecnoblog. O executivo revelou que os contratos com os clientes costumam durar de 12 meses a cinco anos.
Conheça os produtos
Os três modelos demonstrados pela Redroad funcionam em pisos rígidos de vários tipos – mármore, madeira, granito, cimento, epóxi, cerâmica e piso plástico – e podem ser acompanhados à distância por aplicativo, segundo a fabricante. A ideia é que o cliente escolha o robô pelo tamanho e pelas características do espaço, em vez de adaptar o local ao equipamento.
Os dispositivos compartilham o mesmo software e a mesma estrutura de serviço, o que permite combiná-los num mesmo espaço. Cui dá o exemplo de um supermercado: o robô maior poderia cuidar dos corredores largos com eficiência, enquanto o menor chegaria perto das bordas e garantiria a limpeza embaixo das prateleiras. “Isso sim é uma solução”, resumiu o executivo.
RD10 Pro
O RD10 Pro é o modelo compacto da linha atual, pensado para espaços apertados, como os corredores entre prateleiras de lojas de conveniência. Ele mede 52 cm de comprimento, 42 cm de largura e 49 cm de altura, e pesa 26 kg. A Redroad afirma que o corpo de 42 cm é o mais estreito da categoria. O tamanho reduzido também facilita a entrada em elevadores e a passagem por catracas.
O robô tem dois modos de trabalho: lavagem de piso, com até 3 horas de autonomia, e varrição, com até 8 horas. Ele limpa uma faixa de 350 mm a 0,6 m/s, o que rende de 756 a 1.008 m² por hora, e sobe rampas com até 10% de inclinação. Duas escovas de rolo fazem a lavagem com alta pressão, e o sistema separa os resíduos secos dos molhados. A limpeza chega rente a paredes e pilares, pontos que costumam ficar para trás. Os tanques de água limpa e de água suja têm 10 litros cada, com um reservatório auxiliar de 4 litros.
O RD10 Pro combina visão e laser para se orientar melhor no ambiente. Ele usa câmera de profundidade 3D, sensores ultrassônicos, LiDAR – o sensor que mede distâncias com laser, também presente em carros autônomos e tablets de ponta – e um sensor de movimento (IMU), e desvia de obstáculos em 360°. O ruído fica abaixo de 65 dB, e o robô volta sozinho à base para recarregar a bateria de 20 Ah. A estrutura aberta, de desmontagem rápida, simplifica a manutenção diária. A autolimpeza do sistema de sucção vem de série; a do tanque de água suja é opcional.
A fabricante recomenda o modelo para hospitais, escritórios, shoppings, escolas, hotéis, restaurantes, academias e casas de repouso. O preço sugerido é de US$ 14.900, cerca de R$ 80,5 mil na cotação de hoje (26/10).
RD55
O RD55 é o produto intermediário, para áreas médias e grandes. Mede 82 cm de comprimento, 68 cm de largura e 113 cm de altura, e pesa 170 kg. O principal diferencial é a integração com os sistemas de elevadores e de controle de acesso dos prédios, o que permite ao robô trabalhar em vários setores de edifícios comerciais e escritórios.
O aparelho limpa uma faixa de 550 mm e rende até 1.980 m² por hora. Duas escovas de rolo lavam o piso e também recolhem pequenos resíduos secos. O rodo de sucção tem câmara dupla, recurso que, segundo a Redroad, reduz a água que sobra nas frestas do piso. Os tanques têm 45 litros para água limpa e 45 litros para água suja. O próprio robô faz a própria limpeza de tanque, com remoção de 95% dos detritos, e o ventilador do sistema de sucção tem vida útil estimada de 10 mil horas. O modelo pode trabalhar com uma estação-base que faz a recarga, reabastece a água e limpa o tanque.
A navegação combina laser e visão computacional: o robô monta o mapa do ambiente e se localiza nele ao mesmo tempo, com LiDAR, câmeras e sensores de deslocamento das rodas. Para desviar de obstáculos, cruza informações de vários quadros captados pela frente e por trás. O controle pode ser feito no próprio robô, pela nuvem ou pelo celular.
A bateria suporta 8.000 ciclos de recarga e garante cerca de 3 horas de operação. O ruído fica abaixo de 68 dB, e a garantia é de um ano para o equipamento completo. Os cenários indicados são shoppings, hospitais, supermercados, escritórios e fábricas. O preço sugerido é de US$ 32.900, cerca de R$ 177,8 mil.
RD70 Pro
O RD70 Pro é o maior produto da linha, voltado a aeroportos, grandes armazéns e supermercados. Ele tem bastante apelo para “grandes espaços públicos”, segundo Danny Cui. Para se ter uma ideia de sua robustez, o robô pesa 199 kg sem água. Na versão com escovas circulares, usa discos de 20 polegadas, que, segundo a Redroad, cobrem o dobro da área por passada de produtos concorrentes. A pressão de 27 kg sobre o piso ajuda a remover sujeira incrustada.
O robô limpa uma faixa de 560 mm, anda a até 4 km/h e rende até 2.040 m² por hora. Também sobe rampas com até 6% de inclinação. Os tanques têm 70 litros para água limpa e 50 litros para água suja – somados, são os 120 litros. A bateria de lítio de 100 Ah, que pesa 25 kg, dá cerca de 4 horas de operação e pode ser trocada em um minuto, o que evita esperar a recarga para continuar o trabalho. O robô também volta sozinho para recarregar.
O sistema de navegação NeverLost 360° reúne câmera panorâmica, LiDAR, câmera de profundidade, sensores ultrassônicos, sensor de movimento e para-choques, para que o robô se desloque sozinho e desvie de obstáculos. As limpezas podem ser agendadas conforme a rotina de cada estabelecimento, e o equipamento também pode ser operado manualmente, alternando entre os modos de trabalho.
O RD70 Pro gera relatórios automáticos que servem para inspeção de qualidade, comprovação do serviço feito e rastreabilidade das operações. O ruído fica entre 75 e 80 dB. O modelo segue normas da União Europeia e tem garantia de um ano para o equipamento completo. O preço sugerido é de US$ 41.900, cerca de R$ 226,4 mil.
Robô humanoide vista estande
Além dos três robôs de limpeza, o estande da Redroad na HigiExpo recebeu um robô humanoide, que proporcionou experiências interativas aos visitantes durante os três dias de feira, de 20 a 22 de outubro.
O espaço também teve demonstrações ao vivo dos robôs de limpeza, com limpeza rente às bordas, passagem por corredores estreitos, deslocamento entre andares, integração com sistemas de controle de acesso e retorno automático à base para recarga.
Distribuidores, empresas de serviços de limpeza, equipes de gestão predial e grandes redes varejistas puderam conversar com a equipe da Redroad sobre a escolha de equipamentos, condições para projetos-piloto – as chamadas provas de conceito, em que o cliente testa o robô no próprio ambiente antes de fechar contrato –, aplicações práticas e parcerias comerciais. Segundo a empresa, essas conversas levam em conta as características de cada ambiente e as necessidades específicas de cada projeto.
A companhia aproveitou o momento para anunciar sua chegada ao Instagram, por meio do perfil @redroadbrazil.

articles.title: Monte Carlo Data launches Bayes, an AI agent for autonomously monitoring and fixing autonomous agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Monte Carlo Data launches Bayes, an AI agent for autonomously monitoring and fixing autonomous agents
Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence agents is at an all-time high and many enterprises have gotten so carried away that they’re deploying them faster than they keep up.
Their human AI engineers only have the capacity to watch over a handful of AI agents at any one time, so they’re in desperate need of help. What better solution could there be than more AI agents?
That’s what the big data observability company Monte Carlo Data Inc. seems to think anyway. Today it announced a new offering called Bayes, described as an “AI teammate” to differentiate it from the autonomous agents it’s designed to watch. Bayes is really an agent itself, but rather than do work itself, it’s tasked with observing the ones that do get work done.
It watches for signs of unreliability and if it spots something, it troubleshoots the problem, whether that’s with the agent itself or the data being fed into it, implements a fix autonomously and then verifies that the agent is now functioning as it’s supposed to.
Bayes is the culmination of Monte Carlo’s evolution from big data observability to AI. The company borrowed the observability concept from the world of software applications, pioneering tools to help humans keep tabs on their structured data environments. It later expanded to cover unstructured data too, before pivoting last year to embrace generative AI, launching tools for monitoring both inputs and outputs.
The company says there’s an urgent need for Bayes. The average human engineer struggles to monitor more than two or three AI agents and their associated data pipelines at a time, but many organizations have deployed many more than this. With each new agentic deployment, there’s a need to evaluate its work constantly and ensure that its outputs don’t start going astray later on. Clearly, it’s time to automate that task too.
Monte Carlo’s pitch has resonated with customers such as Axios Media Inc., the technology news website that uses AI agents for research, drafting, localization, managing news feeds and other tasks. Shreye Saxena, senior data scientist at Axios, explained that the nature of media work means it cannot compromise on its agent’s accuracy. “If the injected data is incorrect or the trajectory is wrong and it produces a response without checking the database, then we’re not going to get the outcomes we need from our agents,” he said.
Bayes works by scanning a company’s technology environment to discover the agents they’ve deployed and the data environments that power them. It can be given as much or as little responsibility as the customer feels comfortable with, performing tasks like monitoring agent’s outputs, triaging issues and executing fixes in the background.
When it spots a problem, it will trace that failure all the way back to the developmental decisions made pre-deployment, studying both the model that powers it and the data pipelines it relies on. To do that, it integrates with third-party coding assistants and software deployment pipelines.
Gartner Inc. analyst Sanjeev Mohan said Monte Carlo is effectively going after the Holy Grail of AI, giving enterprises a way to build self-improving AI agents. “The idea isn’t new, but pulling it off has been elusive,” he said. “You have to see what agents actually do at runtime and trace it back through the system all the way to the data.”
Monte Carlo says Bayes has already had a profound impact on early adopters. A South American financial services institution reported that Bayes detected 200% more incidents than its internal monitoring systems, while also reducing the number of false positives by 80%. The cloud data warehouse giant Snowflake Inc. is using Bayes to help its own customers build and run more reliable Cortex-based agents.
The goal, according to Monte Carlo co-founder and Chief Executive Barr Moses, is to make customers feel as if they can trust their AI agents. “There aren’t enough engineers to keep those agents trustworthy, but Bayes changes the math,” he said. “It understands your agents and your data together, fixes what breaks and gets better at your environment every day, so teams can spend less time firefighting and more time shipping.”

articles.title: 'The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute': Oracle deal means Google TPUs are coming to a rival cloud for the first time
articles.text:
'The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute': Oracle deal means Google TPUs are coming to a rival cloud for the first time
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) set to launch Google's TPUs in 2027
- Oracle becomes the first cloud vendor (outside of Google) to sell TPUs
- TPU 8t and 8i, launched earlier this year, will be added to the platform
- Google's TPUs are specifically optimized for AI workloads
Oracle has confirmed it will be making Google Cloud's TPUs available through its own OCI platform in a bid to expand the range of AI accelerators available to customers. In doing so, customers will be able to choose which hardware they use to train and run AI models.
Announced at the company's annual AI World conference, the partnership gives Oracle's customers access to Google's purpose-built AI accelerators without them having to go through Google Cloud, while also offering another option instead of Nvidia's GPUs.
It marks an important development for Google's hardware, because it's the first time a hyperscaler other than Google Cloud has sold its TPUs.
Oracle becomes the first third-party cloud vendor to sell Google's TPUs
Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) are custom-designed chips designed to accelerate machine learning workloads, spanning both model training and AI inference, but unlike general-purpose GPUs, they've been optimized specifically for artificial intelligence.
While Nvidia remains the dominant supplier of AI accelerators, helping it to maintain its position as the world's most valuable company with a market cap of $5.265 trillion, its facing increasing pressure from hyperscalers' own hardware and custom silicon endeavours.
OCI President Mahesh Thiagarajan explained that "different AI workloads have different compute needs," hence the decision to offer another option to customers.
"The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute," Google AI & Infrastructure SVP and Chief Technologist Amin Vahdat added.

articles.title: Smart TVs spy on you, even when you opt out: study
articles.text:
A new study has shown that your smart TV might be tracking you and what you watch, even when you opt out of tracking.
The study, named Watching the Watchers, was conducted by researchers affiliated with Northeastern University in Boston, Massachusetts.
- Essentially, it examines automatic content recognition (ACR) features, which the study noted are built into most available smart TVs—and whether turning ACR off actually stops TVs from sending whatever is on your screen to providers.
The researchers tested TVs running Tizen OS (Samsung), Roku OS (Roku, TCL), webOS (LG), SmartCast OS (Vizio), Google TV OS (Sony, Hisense, TCL), Fire TV OS, and others like VIDAA and Xumo.
To add some context, here is how ACR works: essentially, the TV takes short audio or video snapshots of what is on screen, and those snapshots (or the digital fingerprints made from them) are then sent to the internet or ACR provider. From there, the provider compares what was sent to a library of known content to determine exactly what you are watching. The data can reveal your viewing habits and can be used for targeted ads or sold to other companies.
Interestingly, the researchers found out that antenna broadcasts were almost always tracked on every analyzed system. On the streaming side, no TV tracked YouTube or Netflix, but free ad-supported streaming platform Tubi was tracked on Tizen OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS.
The researchers also noted that most operating systems tracked their own streaming services, except Fire TV OS and Google TV on Sony.
Outside of antenna and streaming services, the researchers said that devices on HDMI ports were tracked on five screen systems, but not on Roku OS or SmartCast OS. Interestingly, screen mirroring was only tracked on one of the tested brands: VIDAA OS. Even more concerning, Vizio’s SmartCast OS sent ACR-pattern traffic back to its provider, even when the TV sat idle.
The researchers also said turning these features off didn’t always work. After running each scenario more than 30 times across each operating system, only four (webOS, Google TV on Sony, VIDAA OS, and Fire TV OS) were found to actually shut off the feature if the user opted out of ACR. Interestingly, another recent report that dove into LG’s smart TVs found other concerning practices, like capturing data when offline or in standby mode, recording people, scanning Wi-Fi networks, and more.
Samsung’s built-in streaming service still showed ACR-consistent traffic, and the same thing happened with Vizio, where traffic was sent to its Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint.
If you own a smart TV, Watching the Watchers also shared some tips for what to do if you don’t like being spied on. Turning ACR off is the first step, especially if you have a TV that actually lets you turn it off. Further, you can disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device that doesn’t use ACR. Finally, for those using TVs that don’t respect the ACR toggle, the researchers also shared a blocklist that you can use to prevent the TV from communicating with the ACR endpoints.
Source: Watching the Watchers

articles.title: Microsoft hits 10 quarters of record-breaking revenue in a row | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Whatever the future of AI might be, the current situation is still very good for Microsoft. The tech giant reported yet another quarterly revenue record on Wednesday: $92.3 billion, a 19% increase over the year-ago quarter.
Microsoft has now reported record-breaking revenue for 10 quarters in a row.
This is profitable revenue, too. Microsoft reported that net income reached $36.6 billion, an increase of 32% on a GAAP basis, over the year-ago quarter.
The record-breaking income was largely driven on the strength of Microsoft Cloud, which reached $63.9 billion in revenue this quarter, an increase of 30% over the year-ago quarter, Microsoft said.
Microsoft has reorganized its business reporting into two basic segments: 1) Agents and Infra and 2) Devices and Consumer. On the flip side, revenue in Devices and Consumer was $15.5 billion, decreased of 3%, with Windows OEM and devices revenue falling 22% from the year-ago quarter.
True, not all of Microsoft’s healthy cloud revenue can be attributed to AI. Microsoft 365 accounted for nearly $28 billion. But Azure brought in the most, at $33.2 billion. And again, not all of that is necessarily AI-related. Enterprises run all sorts of the traditional software and SaaS applications on Azure.
Still, a good chunk of the revenue was from AI, because Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI. Despite branching out to AWS, Oracle, and others, OpenAI still runs a lot of its services on Microsoft’s cloud. (Anthropic runs on Azure as well.) Microsoft also said its “commercial remaining performance obligation increased 73% to $677 billion.” That represents future revenue committed under existing contracts of the AI labs.
But, like all the big cloud providers, Microsoft is also spending big to prepare to deliver on those commitments. Capital expenditures topped $45.2 billion, another all-time quarterly record.

articles.title: Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV
articles.text:
“Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about.
Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030. It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the GMC Sierra EV, and of course the divisive Hummer EVs. And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category.
So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. Yes, you did read that right, it does weigh 4 tons. And yes, the electric Escalade does weigh a third more than the last gas-powered one we tested.
The Escalade IQ holds its own among the medium-duty trucks.
Jonathan Gitlin

Jonathan Gitlin

Jonathan Gitlin
Behind the wheel
However, it drives better. Like many a modern luxury EV, the Escalade IQ is held up by air suspension. Controlled by computers, air suspension is remarkably effective at concealing a car’s mass, although here it has been tuned for a rather floaty ride. In lesser electric SUVs—ones that weigh a mere 3 tons or less—you can often forget that curb weight entirely until it’s time to brake. Here, you just need to drive over something, like a recessed utility hole cover on the road, for the transient shock that makes its way into the cabin to remind you.
From behind the wheel, I find it slightly sobering, perhaps no bad thing when taking responsibility on the road. It’s easier to drive than one might expect, particularly at low speeds where the rear-wheel steering gives the car a shorter effective wheelbase than its actual 136.2 inches (3,460 mm). It might fill a parking space, but it’s not hard work getting it in or out. Forward visibility is good, but I found the passenger mirror less than completely effective and was glad for the blindspot monitoring camera that appeared when I used the turn signals, even if the camera quality was just the right side of potato.
At highway speeds, the rear wheels steer with the front wheels to effectively lengthen the wheelbase and thus increase straight-line stability. Nominal power and torque are 680 hp (505 kW) and 615 lb-ft (834 Nm), which you can increase to 750 hp (560 KW) and 785 lb-ft (1,064 Nm) with the V button on the steering wheel—this engages Velocity Max mode. It’s not ever going to ripple the tarmac like that electric Porsche Cayenne, but you can still hit 60 mph (97 km/h) from a standstill in less than 5 seconds should you need to.
Super Cruise works well.
Jonathan Gitlin

Jonathan Gitlin

Jonathan Gitlin

Jonathan Gitlin

Jonathan Gitlin
Super Cruise is standard and works well on its premapped roads. The one-pedal driving calibration is, as always on GM EVs, very well-calibrated on its highest setting. It’s very effective for city driving, as you quickly adjust to its rate of deceleration to judge stops perfectly. There’s also a paddle on the steering wheel that will add regenerative braking on demand, should you wish to slow more but don’t feel like using the brake pedal.
The 460-mile range estimate is entirely believable, even with little attention given to driving efficiently. As you’ll note from the photos, on shorter trips the Escalade IQ reported efficiencies that wouldn’t be out of place in something like an Ioniq 5. But at highway speeds, you don’t get to recuperate nearly as much energy, and once it all averages out, the answer is close to 2.1 miles/kWh (29.6 kWh/100 km). Cadillac doesn’t provide a 10–80 percent fast charging time for the Escalade IQ—only that it can add 100 miles in 10 minutes—and by the end of the week, I was still at 65 percent state of charge, so a full DC fast-charge time remains a mystery. (But at least the car had plenty of range when it was collected.)
A tech-filled experience
Even if the Escalade IQ isn’t Cadillac’s flagship EV—that’s the hand-built $300,000 Celestiq sedan—the automaker has still packed in as much technology as it could. In front of the driver is a 55-inch display that encompasses touch-sensitive panels either side of the main instrument display and stretches across the width of the dash. On the left are the trip computer and lights, and to the right of the instrument display is the main infotainment touchscreen, which runs Android Automotive OS.

Jonathan Gitlin
The dial controller on the center console allows you to interact with the infotainment, so you don’t need to use the touchscreen or try voice commands, something that worked here with moderate success. I would expect a slightly better scroll action considering the $153,490 sticker price for our Escalade IQ Premium Sport, but like the 55-inch display, the hardware is shared across the Cadillac EVrange. Climate controls are on a separate touchscreen, this one ahead of the center console and below the infotainment.
Another touchscreen serves the front-seat passenger, plus a pair for the middle row (the optional $1,995 rear-seat entertainment system). These stream video from a wide range of platforms—the industry mostly adopting Android Automotive OS has meant plenty of app support—and the screen for the front passenger has a filter that prevents the driver from seeing what’s being displayed while the vehicle is in motion. You can use your phone as an input controller, either as a keyboard or to play games, although it’s a little kludgy.
It is roomy in the back, and the middle row moves fore and aft. This can give the third row more than enough legroom for long journeys, although the lack of vertical space to put legs means that sitting back there involves knees next to faces.
I can see the appeal of the Escalade IQ as an alternative to the traditionally powered Escalade. It might not be very efficient for an EV, but 2.1 miles/kWh is still the equivalent of more than 70 mpg (3.3 L/100 km), whereas a standard V8 version only manages 16 mpg (14.7 L/100 km) combined. And you have to stop and fill that one up with gas almost 80 miles (129 km) before the electric one runs out of range.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

articles.title: It's the end of the aisle for smart AI trolleys at Morrisons — tech partner Instacart winds down the experiment after finding 'adoption has not scaled quickly enough'
articles.text:
Morrisons AI smart trolley trial is over, as partner Instacart winds down its cart operations — but supermarkets seem intent on automating the wrong tech
Goodbye, Caper Carts
- Morrisons is shutting down its smart AI trolley trial
- Partner Instacart will no longer develop the Caper Carts being used
- AI tech is better used behind the scenes at stores
Farewell then, smart AI trolleys: after first being introduced in July, Morrisons' trial of grocery carts that total up your shopping expenses as you go is being wound down, as partner Instacart is now abandoning the Caper Carts tech that powered the scheme.
As The Grocer reports, Instacart has decided that "retailer adoption has not scaled quickly enough to justify our continued investment" in Caper Carts. The trolleys will also be withdrawn from US stores, where they were a little more well established at retailers including Schnucks and Wegmans.
"The trial has given us greater insight into the continued evolution of our customers' shopping habits and we will continue to pilot and develop solutions to meet those needs," a spokesperson for Morrisons told The Grocer. The trial was only run at a single Morrisons store, in Ashton-on-Ribble in Preston.
Via cameras and scales built into the carts, shoppers were able to log all of their purchases as they made their way around the store, with an integrated touchscreen displaying information on the trolley contents. At checkout, a dedicated lane enabled smart trolley shoppers to pay for their items with a barcode scan.
Let the customers decide
Clearly, both Instacart and Morrisons weren't seeing enough uptake for the AI-powered trolleys, and it's a sign that supermarkets don't necessarily know what's in our best interests. Piloting a smart cart around a store puts the onus on shoppers to learn another way of scanning items and paying for them at a checkout.
People will usually prefer the familiar, and at the same time it's not really clear how much faster scan-as-you-go would be compared to scan-at-the-till anyway. Having a camera scan something and use AI to recognize it is a relatively speedy process nowadays (you can do it on your phone), but obviously not speedy enough.
Where AI innovations can be successful is behind the scenes at retailers. For example, AI cameras on the shelves at Morrisons have been much more successful (and won awards) — these cameras watch stock levels, put in orders for anything that's running low, and give staff a heads-up on any potential problems.

We've also seen AI schemes that can predict demand and reduce shortages and waste on a large scale, and it would seem that shoppers would rather see the items they need in stock than have an intelligent trolley.

articles.title: Elle utilise l’IA pour contester ses impôts : le tribunal la sanctionne avec une amende
articles.text:
Le 4 décembre 2025, Marie-Line X a introduit une requête pour contester un redressement fiscal datant de 2023. Autant dire que cette requête n’a pas été bien reçue. En fait, le tribunal administratif de Rennes (Ille-et-Vilaine) lui a infligé une amende de 500 euros pour recours abusif, comme le rapporte Franceinfo. Parmi tous les éléments qui ont abouti à cette amende, le tribunal a constaté « une requête manifestement écrite à l’aide d’un outil d’intelligence artificielle ».
Une amende de 500 euros pour recours abusif
Pourquoi le tribunal a-t-il infligé à Marie-Line X une amende de 500 euros ? Tout d’abord, la contribuable bretonne avait déjà déposé une requête similaire, qui avait été rejetée. Ensuite, elle a saisi le tribunal administratif de Rennes sans avoir préalablement adressé de réclamation à l’administration fiscale, une démarche obligatoire dans ce type de litige. Marie-Line X assure de son côté être « de bonne foi », avoir « suivi les indications écrites » du Service des impôts des entreprises (SIE) et n’avoir « jamais été informée d’une dette en 2023 jusqu’à la notification ». Enfin, et non des moindres, le tribunal a relevé un manque de précision dans ses arguments.
Concernant ce dernier point, le magistrat explique : « les moyens de la requête – laquelle a au demeurant été manifestement écrite à l’aide d’un outil d’intelligence artificielle – ne sont pas assortis des précisions les plus élémentaires permettant au juge d’en apprécier la portée et le bien-fondé ».
Le recours à l’IA pointé du doigt par le tribunal
Le tribunal administratif de Rennes semble avoir été quelque peu agacé par le fait que Marie-Line X ait eu recours à l’intelligence artificielle pour élaborer sa requête, et ce principalement pour deux raisons. D’une part, le recours à l’IA entraînerait une multiplication notable des requêtes judiciaires. La juridiction explique à ce titre : « Dans un contexte marqué par une hausse particulièrement forte du nombre de requêtes (…) devant tous les tribunaux administratifs depuis deux ans, on constate l’usage de plus en plus décomplexé des outils d’intelligence artificielle pour générer des “requêtes” ».
D’autre part, l’IA générerait des requêtes creuses, qui manquent de détails. La juridiction explique qu’ « aux yeux de bien des justiciables, les requêtes “fabriquées par l’IA” ont toutes les apparences de leur côté : un vocabulaire juridique y est employé et le propos paraît structuré ». Cependant : « aux yeux du professionnel du droit, ces requêtes ont souvent un vilain défaut : elles sont creuses et fourmillent de références fallacieuses ».
En fin de compte, le tribunal administratif de Rennes a principalement sanctionné le caractère abusif de la requête de Marie-Line X, et le recours à l’intelligence artificielle ne l’a clairement pas aidé dans cette affaire. Il semble que la juridiction veuille aussi lancer un avertissement pour limiter le nombre de requêtes élaborées à l’aide de l’IA. La présidence du tribunal invite d’ailleurs les justiciables bretons à « utiliser avec tact, discernement et mesure » les outils d’intelligence artificielle. Prudence donc la prochaine fois que vous devrez élaborer ce type de requête, même si, rappelons-le, le recours à l’IA n’est pas le seul élément qui a mené à une amende dans cette affaire.

articles.title: Apple annonce son premier MacBook tactile : comment suivre la conférence en direct ?
articles.text:
John Ternus veut aller vite, très vite. Apple organise aujourd’hui son troisième rendez-vous presse depuis septembre après la keynote des iPhone le 9 septembre et l’événement consacré à la maison connectée le 13 octobre. Il ne devrait pas s’agir d’une grande keynote de deux heures mais d’une « expérience » plus courte, avec la présentation de nouveaux produits et la possibilité pour les médias invités, dont Numerama pour la France, de les essayer en avant-première. En un peu plus d’un mois, Apple aura renouvelé ses iPhone, ses Watch, ses AirPods, son Apple TV, son HomePod mini, son iPad mini, la quasi-totalité de ses Mac et lancé l’écran domotique HomeView.
Le 28 octobre, les rumeurs s’accordent sur l’annonce d’un MacBook Pro tactile avec un écran OLED : une première pour Apple, qui a toujours critiqué publiquement les écrans tactiles des concurrents. Après l’iPad mini lundi et les MacBook Pro et iMac M6 mardi, la rentrée d’Apple pourrait se conclure avec une refonte majeure de son ordinateur portable haut de gamme (et un aperçu du futur des Mac dans les prochaines années).
À quelle heure est l’annonce d’Apple et comment la suivre en direct ?
Lundi et mardi, Apple a publié des communiqués de presse à 14 heures.
L’annonce de mercredi aura lieu plus tard : le carton d’invitation d’Apple parle de 10 heures en Californie, soit 18 heures en France. Le changement d’heure raccourcit l’écart entre le Pacifique et la France : il n’y a plus que huit heures de décalage.
Combien de temps durera la présentation ? Apple semble trahir le secret sur son site : les précommandes pour les nouveaux Mac et iPad ouvrent mercredi à 18h10, soit dix minutes après l’heure du rendez-vous donné aux médias. On peut en déduire que la keynote, quelle que soit sa forme, ne sera pas très longue. Apple devrait présenter le MacBook Pro pendant 10 minutes, puis mettre à jour son site avec les annonces du jour. On ne sait pas encore si John Ternus orchestrera la conférence en personne ou s’il s’agira d’une vidéo préenregistrée.
Y aura-t-il un livestream ?
Apple n’a annoncé aucune retransmission publique sur son site. La logique voudrait que son site soit mis à jour à 18h10 avec les nouveaux produits et une vidéo de présentation. La « retransmission vidéo » pourrait être réservée aux journalistes sur place.
Pour ne rien rater dès 18 heures (et possiblement avant, dès notre arrivée sur place), Numerama vous proposera des images en direct des annonces sur les réseaux sociaux. Suivez-nous sur X ou Instagram pour ne rien rater. Nous ajouterons les tweets les plus importants à cet article. Nous publierons des extraits de la keynote réservée à la presse.
Nos articles et vidéos sur le MacBook Pro tactile à suivre dans la foulée
Numerama est un des rares médias européens invités à Los Angeles. Nous vous proposerons une prise en main et une analyse de la nouvelle stratégie d’Apple après avoir discuté avec la marque et essayé les nouveaux Mac. Nous prévoyons un reportage vidéo sur YouTube et des vidéos courtes sur X, Instagram et TikTok. Abonnez-vous et activez les alertes pour ne rien rater.
Le défi est de taille pour Apple. En 2010, Steve Jobs expliquait qu’un écran tactile vertical était « ergonomiquement terrible ». Après avoir passé des années à nous expliquer que les ordinateurs tactiles sont inutilisables, Apple devra trouver une explication convaincante pour justifier ce changement de stratégie.

articles.title: Jedify formally launches Data Agents for building AI analysts in plain language - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Jedify formally launches Data Agents for building AI analysts in plain language
Enterprise artificial intelligence context startup Jedify Inc. today formally launched Data Agents, a product that lets business teams set up autonomous AI analysts by describing the work they want done in plain language.
Data Agents takes on a longstanding limit of business intelligence software, where analysts have to build dashboards ahead of time around the questions they expect people to ask. Generic AI assistants have tried to fill that gap. In Jedify’s telling, those tools end up guessing at what a business means from its raw tables and schemas.
The company’s core product is a context graph that pulls structured data and documents into a single model of how a business works, down to metric definitions and record-level permissions. Data Agents runs on top of it. Because joins and schema mapping are already worked out inside the graph, building an agent comes down to describing the question.
Users decide when an agent runs, whether on request, on a schedule or when a condition they have defined is met. A market that starts to underperform is the kind of anomaly an agent is meant to catch on its own, and Jedify’s deep research engine then works out what most likely drove the change.
Data access is tied to the person asking the question. Anything that user is barred from seeing, even a single row in a table, stays out of the agent’s results. On cost, Jedify claims its agents burn far fewer tokens per question than ones that have to explore raw schema at query time.
Teams can also work with the agents outside Jedify’s own interface. Under the Model Context Protocol, each one appears as a tool that can be called from Claude, ChatGPT, Slack or any agent platform a company runs. Results can go straight to email or Slack too.
Jedify is pitching the product at data teams and the business staff they support, arguing that analysts who keep fielding the same dashboard request can hand it off to an agent. On the business side, people in finance, revenue operations and sales can set up their own agents.
Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Adi Elimelech said enterprises are moving analytics “from answering questions to doing meaningful work.” The goal, he said, is for teams to build “an analytical workforce” matched to how their business operates and reach those agents from the tools employees already use.
Online casino game developer RubyPlay Ltd. is already using the product. Its team set an agent up once and scheduled it to run every day, and the report now arrives without anyone asking for it.
“It even flagged us on its own that not all of our target markets were covered yet, which told us it was reasoning through the task rather than just running a script,” said Avi Baruch, vice president of data and business applications at RubyPlay.
Data Agents is available now through Jedify’s Agents Hub, and companies can start on it for free. Jedify is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $33 million, including a $24 million Series A round led by Norwest in June.

articles.title: Police seize Virtualine bulletproof service tied to ransowmare, cybercrime
articles.text:
U.S. law enforcement has seized the primary domain of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service advertised on cybercrime forums for facilitating illegal activities.
The service also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, and promised to shield customers from legal complaints and requests from law enforcement and other authorities.
The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed that Virtualine marketed services that permitted “illegal/black hat activities” ranging from phishing, spamming, and carding to port scanning.
The FBI seized the primary domain of the service, virtualine[.net], following an investigation that involved Germany’s Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands’ Politie Midden-Nederland, the U.K.’s National Crime Agency, as well as private partners OverRIPE and Lumen.
Although Virtualine drew an apparent line at child content, authorities say that the operator knowingly hosted an online forum promoting child abuse material and ignored repeated notices from law enforcement, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and a victim’s attorney.
Authorities allege that after legal pressure against the forum increased, Virtualine worked with the administrators to set up a new site.
"Virtualine hosts this new website to this day, and it has already received at least one abuse complaint about sexually explicit images of children found on that website," the DoJ said.
The administrator of the Virtualine rejected the allegation in an open letter to authorities published on a new website, virtualine[.]org, captured by cybersecurity company Silent Push.
The operator said that while claims about the service's illegal activities and customers "deserve a fair investigation," they regarded "sexual exploitation of children as a crime against humanity."
Cybercrime ecosystem
Virtualine also accepted direct Bitcoin payments from customers, helping cybercriminals launder proceeds stolen elsewhere.
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, which provided intelligence support to law enforcement, linked Virtualine’s payment addresses directly to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, scams, and phishing platforms.
“Virtualine accepted direct bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without flagging their funds through hosted exchange compliance programs,” Chainalysis notes.
“Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added.
In a report published today, blockchain intelligence firm TRM said ransomware groups were responsible for 5% of Virtualine’s financial flows, while a Russian drug marketplace made up approximately 44%.
"A large sextortion scheme and a mixer were also major sources of funds," the company said.
TRM says that Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer this year, with transactions indicating a constant financial relationship.
A press release from the Dutch police notes that dozens of physical servers were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline.
Politie also said its investigators recovered data from more than 3,000 Virtualine customers, and follow-up action against them is underway.
According to the authorities in the Netherlands, the illegal platform was facilitating cybercrime operations since at least 2022, including ransomware, botnets, infostealers, phishing, and distribution of child abuse material.
Although the bulletproof hosting provider remains partially online, researchers observed that its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, suggesting that much of its infrastructure may no longer be reachable.

articles.title: Google dégaine Gemini 4 Carbon, le plus puissant modèle d'IA actuellement — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sundar Pichai, CEO de Google, s’est offert un petit « je vous l’avais dit » sur X ce mercredi 28 octobre : il avait bien promis de sortir de nouveaux modèles à intervalles réguliers.
Gemini 4 Carbon arrive donc deux semaines après l’ouverture de Gemini 4 Argon aux abonnés payants, et Google le présente comme son modèle le plus puissant dans un billet de blog signé Koray Kavukcuoglu, vice-président de Google DeepMind et architecte en chef de l’IA chez Google.
En revanche, pas d’inquiétude, vous pouvez toujours jouer avec Argon parce que personne ne peut encore l’essayer dans l’application Gemini. Carbon est d’abord réservé à une poignée d’experts en cybersécurité.
Carbon, Top 1 des modèles du moment
Carbon obtient 59 points sur l’Intelligence Index d’Artificial Analysis, un classement indépendant qui compile plusieurs tests. Dans le tableau publié par Google, Claude Opus 5.5 d’Anthropic obtient 58 points, GPT-6 Astra d’OpenAI 57 et Argon 50. Carbon prend neuf points à son prédécesseur, mais un seul à son premier rival.
Ajoutons que Carbon ne domine pas toutes les lignes de son propre tableau. Il devance GPT-6 Astra et Opus 5.5 sur la majorité des tests publiés, mais se classe seulement quatrième sur WebDev Arena, un classement de développement web, malgré un gain de 89 points Elo (le système de points hérité des échecs). Côté sécurité du modèle lui-même, Google revendique 0 % d’attaques réussies par injection de prompt, contre 0,7 % pour Argon sur le test de Gray Swan.
Un modèle pour les longues et lourdes tâches
Google le conçoit surtout pour les tâches longues, celles que doivent mener seuls des agents comme Spark, qui exécute des tâches en arrière-plan dans Gemini. En interne, ses équipes ont vu Carbon travailler plusieurs jours d’affilée pour remonter à l’origine de bugs dans de grosses bases de code, puis les corriger.
Google met surtout en avant la cybersécurité, avec trois tests où Carbon arrive en tête :
- 88,2 % sur SEC-bench Pro, qui consiste à dénicher des failles dans de vrais logiciels ;
- 54,8 % sur ExploitGym, qui vérifie si une faille peut réellement être exploitée ;
- 71 % sur CWE-bench, qui mesure la capacité à écrire le correctif.
Tous ces chiffres viennent de Google. L’entreprise précise que les trois tests de cybersécurité ont été passés « sans garde-fous », c’est-à-dire sans les filtres censés bloquer les demandes malveillantes. Or une IA qui sait trouver une faille, l’exploiter et la corriger intéresse autant les défenseurs que les pirates.
C’est pour cela que Google n’ouvre Carbon qu’à une sélection de défenseurs, puis l’étendra à d’autres partenaires de confiance via son programme Fairwind.
Un prix déjà fixé, mais aucune date
Google affiche déjà un tarif pour les développeurs, identique au prix de lancement d’Argon : 2 dollars par million de tokens envoyés au modèle (environ 1,80 euro HT) et 10 dollars par million de tokens générés (environ 9 euros HT).
Rappelons qu’un token est un fragment de mot, et un million de tokens représente donc plusieurs centaines de milliers de mots. Une fois la période de lancement terminée, ces prix doubleront à 4 et 20 dollars (environ 3,60 et 18 euros HT). Google ne donne aucune date d’ouverture aux développeurs, aux entreprises et au grand public, et promet seulement de le faire « dès que possible ».
Argon avait mis à peine deux semaines entre son annonce, le 30 septembre, et son ouverture aux abonnés Google AI Pro et Ultra.

articles.title: Core Ultra 9, double Ethernet et USB4 : le mini-PC GEEKOM GT1 Mega est à 806,55 €

Le mini-PC GEEKOM GT1 Mega avec Core Ultra 9, 16 Go et 1 To est à 806,55 € (-5 %)
Le GEEKOM GT1 Mega réunit un processeur Intel Core Ultra 9, 16 Go de mémoire vive et une connectique adaptée à plusieurs écrans.
Amazon propose le mini-PC GEEKOM GT1 Mega à 806,55 €, contre un ancien prix de 849 €, également indiqué comme le plus bas des 30 derniers jours. L’économie atteint 42,45 €, soit 5 %. L’ordinateur est vendu par GEEKOM Mini PC FR et expédié par Amazon, avec la livraison gratuite proposée.
Un Core Ultra 9 dans un format compact

La connectique comprend deux ports USB4, deux sorties HDMI, des ports USB-A et un lecteur de cartes SD. Le constructeur annonce la prise en charge de quatre écrans 4K simultanément, selon les connexions utilisées.
Deux ports Ethernet 2,5 Gbit/s complètent le Wi-Fi 7. Le mini-PC affiche une note de 4,2/5 sur 13 évaluations Amazon, un nombre encore limité pour apprécier les retours des acheteurs.

articles.title: Ukrainian Hive and Nefilim Ransomware Affiliate Gets 70 Months in US Prison
articles.text:
A 36-year-old Ukrainian national was sentenced to prison in the US for his role in Nefilim ransomware attacks.
The man, Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak, who had been living in Barcelona, was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the US in April 2025. He pleaded guilty in December 2025.
According to court documents, Stryzhak joined the Nefilim ransomware operation as an affiliate in June 2021 and used the malware in attacks against organizations in the US and abroad.
Stryzhak agreed with Nefilim administrator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk to pay the Nefilim administrators 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims.
The defendant operated as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate between June 2021 and October 2021. One of his victims was an unnamed company in the oil and gas transportation industry.
Documents presented in court also show that Stryzhak was one of the early affiliates to join the Hive ransomware group, which hit over 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023.
The documents show that Stryzhak used the Hive ransomware against seven victim organizations, including a dental office, a healthcare provider, and law firms. Some of the victims paid a ransom, and the cybercriminals provided a decryption key to recover the encrypted files.
Stryzhak was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud.
“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals. These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses,” FBI operations director Brett Leatherman said.
The US State Department is offering up to $10 million for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, and up to $1 million for information on other leaders of the ransomware groups he ran.

articles.title: Taiwan working on autonomous drone swarms to counter China’s increasingly aggressive grey-zone military tactics — island has already completed flight simulations, now working towards flight trials over maritime areas
articles.text:
Taiwan working on autonomous drone swarms to counter China’s increasingly aggressive grey-zone military tactics — island has already completed flight simulations, now working towards flight trials over maritime areas
Taipei has also received its first shipment of U.S.-made V-BAT drones.
Taiwan’s Ocean Affairs Council is working on an autonomous system that would allow drone fleets to coordinate and execute missions without human intervention in response to "grey-zone" activities carried out by China. According to the South China Morning Post, the council is working with the National Cheng Kung University, which has already completed simultaneous flight simulations of two drone fleets, with each fleet comprising 10 units. This is already the second step of the process, which has shifted from individual aircraft control to the coordination of two drone detachments.
This project is designed to help Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA) to counter Beijing’s grey-zone tactics in the waters surrounding the island nation. There have already been instances of civilian Chinese ships damaging undersea cables that Taipei relies on, with the CGA increasing its defensive patrols around 24 undersea cables and closely monitoring nearly a hundred China-linked boats. Despite that, Chinese “research vessels” continue to loiter over Taiwan-U.S. undersea cables, mimicking the activities of Russian trawlers in the Atlantic.
“The next stage will involve hardware-in-the-loop testing, prototype integration and flight trials over actual maritime areas to assess reliability under different sea and weather conditions,” the council said. The researchers programmed the drones to have a minimum separation of 100 feet in 3D space, and they’re also incorporating leader-follower formation flying and dynamic obstacle avoidance. This should allow them to respond to quickly changing conditions out in the open sea and even deal with unexpected hazards.
More than that, the autonomous system Taipei is working on would let different types of drones coordinate their movements, divide tasks, and plan routes, primarily for maritime surveillance. This is especially important as it would allow them to use different types of drones to accomplish various missions, much like how different air forces use different aircraft types. 
The project is currently focusing on three Western-made drones — the Jump 20, V-BAT, and Flexrotor. In fact, the Ocean Affairs Council just received the V-BAT, a VTOL drone built by U.S. defense firm Shield AI. This unit can take off vertically from the relatively constrained deck space of non-aircraft carrier ships and offers an endurance of over 12 hours for extended missions, making it ideal for the CGA, as it would not need to make major renovations to its ships to accommodate these drones while extending their reach.

articles.title: Tus mensajes de Discord podrían aparecer en Google si no haces este ajuste
articles.text:
Discord implementará un cambio que podría poner en riesgo la privacidad de sus usuarios. La plataforma anunció que parte del contenido publicado en sus servidores públicos comenzará a ser visible en los buscadores web, incluyendo tus mensajes. Si piensas publicar en alguno de ellos, tus conversaciones podrían aparecer en Google a menos que realices un ajuste.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, Discord intentará recuperar el papel de los viejos foros de la web, esos lugares en donde las personas publicaban y comentaban sobre algún tema en específico. La popularidad de la plataforma terminó por enterrar esa práctica, migrando las conversaciones a lugares cerrados en los que necesitabas una invitación para mirar el contenido. Ahora Discord quiere abrirse al mundo y robarle un pedazo de mercado a Reddit, que domina en las búsquedas.
La novedad afecta solamente a los Canales Descubribles, que son comunidades públicas con al menos 1.000 miembros y que aparecen en el sistema de descubrimiento de Discord. Según la empresa, estos espacios recibirán una mayor presencia en la web para que cualquier usuario encuentre respuestas a preguntas sin necesidad de navegar dentro de la aplicación. Todos los servidores contarán con una página pública en internet, que mostrará información sobre la comunidad y resúmenes automáticos de las conversaciones de los canales públicos.
Las páginas públicas se mostrarán a partir del 16 de noviembre de 2026, aunque semanas después la medida se extenderá a los mensajes. Discord confirmó que mostrará mensajes de canales públicos en los resultados de búsqueda de la web a mediados de diciembre de 2026. La compañía afirma que hay miles de respuestas útiles dentro de sus comunidades, las cuales permanecen ocultas para quienes buscan información en internet.
Cómo evitar que tus mensajes de Discord aparezcan en las búsquedas de Google
La decisión ya prendió las alertas entre los defensores de la privacidad, aunque la compañía dejó claro que no hay nada que temer. Los mensajes no incluirán nombre de usuario ni la fotografía de perfil de la persona que lo escribió y solo se considerarán aquellos que se hayan publicado antes del 16 de noviembre. Aquellos enviados antes de la entrada en vigor de esta función no se indexarán en los motores de búsqueda.
Si eres usuario de Discord y no deseas que tus publicaciones se muestren en Google, existe un modo de evitarlo. Solo basta entrar en los ajustes de tu cuenta y elegir la opción Datos y Privacidad, ubicada en el menú lateral. Ahí encontrarás una opción llamada "Mostrar el contenido de mis mensajes de los canales descubribles en la web", la cual tendrás que deshabilitar. Aprovechando que te encuentras en esa sección, también puedes desactivar el resto de funciones que aprovechan tus datos para que Discord te espíe y muestre contenido patrocinado.
Una vez que deshabilites la función, los mensajes que publiques en los canales públicos no aparecerán en Google. Es probable que las conversaciones publicadas mientras la opción estaba activa permanezcan visibles si ya se indexaron por el buscador, siempre y cuando el administrador no las haya eliminado manualmente.
Por último, los administradores tendrán la última palabra sobre el contenido de sus comunidades, ya que podrán elegir qué canales participan en la indexación o desactivar la exposición del servidor.

articles.title: Anatel ordena que clientes de telefonia móvel façam biometria • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Anatel ordena que clientes de telefonia móvel façam biometria
Reconhecimento facial será usado em ativações, troca de chip, portabilidade e mudanças contratuais. Linhas sem cadastro poderão ser suspensas em 2029.
A Anatel tornou obrigatória a validação biométrica para ativar e manter linhas de celular. A nova regra, aprovada pela Superintendência de Planejamento e Regulamentação e divulgada nesta quarta-feira (28/10), vale para pessoas físicas e microempreendedores individuais (MEI) e será implantada gradualmente até o fim de 2028.
Segundo a documentação, o reconhecimento facial será exigido para clientes em novas ativações, portabilidade, troca de chip e alterações cadastrais ou contratuais solicitadas pelo consumidor. Quem já tem uma linha também precisará passar pelo procedimento até 31 de dezembro de 2028. Pessoas jurídicas que não sejam MEI ficam fora da exigência.
O objetivo é dificultar a abertura e a transferência de linhas usando dados falsos ou de terceiros. Uma das fraudes mais conhecidas é o SIM swap, em que criminosos conseguem transferir o número da vítima para outro chip e passam a receber ligações e códigos de autenticação enviados por SMS.
A biometria é mais uma barreira nesse processo. A Anatel já tornou obrigatória a confirmação por SMS nas portabilidades e anunciou o Anatel Protege, ferramenta para impedir a abertura de linhas vinculadas ao CPF do usuário.
O uso de biometria no setor, no entanto, não é novidade. Desde 2021, operadoras já adotam o chamado ID Digital na ativação de algumas linhas pré-pagas, com envio de selfie e documento para validar o cadastro. A nova norma amplia esse tipo de verificação para outras operações.
A norma técnica da Anatel prevê validação do CPF, captura do rosto e uma prova de vida para confirmar que há uma pessoa real diante da câmera. Depois, a imagem será comparada com uma base biométrica já existente, pública ou privada.
Se o reconhecimento não funcionar, haverá alternativas, incluindo nova tentativa, atendimento presencial ou comparação da selfie com a fotografia de um documento oficial.
A Vivo, por exemplo, já utiliza um processo similar em alguns atendimentos. Em solicitações feitas por telefone ou WhatsApp, a operadora pode enviar um SMS com um link para confirmar a identidade. O cliente precisa mostrar o rosto e aguardar alguns segundos pela validação antes que uma alteração de plano, por exemplo, possa prosseguir.
A medida busca dificultar fraudes, mas também cria mais uma situação em que consumidores terão de fornecer dados biométricos para acessar um serviço. As prestadoras também poderão acrescentar outras verificações para identificar fraudes.
A norma determina que a coleta seja limitada ao necessário, exige cumprimento da LGPD e proíbe o compartilhamento irregular com terceiros. Os sistemas também deverão manter registros auditáveis das verificações.
