articles.title: Apple ajoute un chatbot à Keynote, Pages et Numbers et les ouvre aux IA tierces
articles.text:
Apple annonce une mise à jour pour sa suite Creator Studio. Keynote, Pages et Numbers reçoivent un assistant IA et acceptent le protocole MCP, lequel permet à des agents externes d’y travailler. De leur côté, Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro et Pixelmator Pro gagnent aussi de nouveaux outils.
La mise à jour a été pour Mac, iPad et iPhone. Elle arrivera en novembre sur l’App Store, gratuitement pour les abonnés actuels.
Un assistant qui lit vos documents, des agents externes qui peuvent les modifier
L’assistant, en bêta, s’appuie sur des modèles d’Apple et d’OpenAI et peut analyser et comprendre le contenu d’un document ouvert. Dans Keynote, il aide à concevoir, animer et retoucher les diapositives. Dans Pages, il rédige, restructure et ajuste les textes. Dans Numbers, il calcule, visualise et organise les données, propose des types de graphiques avec un aperçu et construit des tableaux sur mesure à partir de connaissances générales. Soulignons que cela nécessite un appareil compatible avec Apple Intelligence sous iOS 27, iPadOS 27 ou macOS 27 (ou ultérieur) et, à ce stade expérimental, ne fonctionne qu’en anglais américain.
En janvier, nous avions testé Apple Creator Studio. Dans Pages, la génération d’images passait par les serveurs d’OpenAI, après l’accord de l’utilisateur via une fenêtre de confirmation. Le communiqué ne précise pas comment l’assistant répartit son travail entre les modèles d’Apple et ceux d'OpenAI, ni où les demandes sont traitées.
Dans Keynote, Pages et Numbers, avec le MCP, les agents et outils externes pourront lire le contenu, le modifier et lancer des actions automatiques. Cette prise en charge exige macOS 27 ou ultérieur. Keynote gère aussi le format .keyx (Keynote Interchange Format), un paquet de fichiers ouvert basé sur JSON (un format texte structuré). Apple explique que ce dernier peut être lu par des outils externes, des développeurs et des agents IA.
Les trois applications reçoivent aussi un stock de vidéos dans le Content Hub, ainsi que de nouveaux thèmes et modèles pour les abonnés. Freeform ajoute des styles de texte (une mise en forme en une étape, réutilisable d’un board à l’autre) et des couleurs de fond, personnalisées ou prédéfinies. En décembre, l’application permettra de modifier des images dans Pixelmator Pro et de générer des formes pouvant être modifiées à partir d'un texte. Par défaut, les apps Keynote, Pages, Numbers et Freeform restent gratuites. Pour les nouveaux abonnés, Apple Creator Studio coûte 12,99 € par mois et 129 € par an.
Côté création, Final Cut Pro sur Mac intègre MotionVFX (effets, transitions, modèles, titres) et le Content Hub, et permet de retoucher une image de la timeline dans Pixelmator Pro. D’ailleurs, ce dernier gagne Generate Fill. Il suffit d’entourer la zone d’une image, de décrire la modification voulue, et l’outil reprend la lumière, la perspective et la texture alentour. Logic Pro reçoit sur Mac un assistant en bêta, ainsi qu’un navigateur de sons qui classe et étiquette les sons grâce à une analyse audio faite sur l’appareil.

articles.title: Government working to utilise procurement process for promoting startups: DPIIT Secretary
articles.text:
Government working to utilise procurement process for promoting startups: DPIIT Secretary
Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules).
The government is working to leverage the procurement process to promote startups, a top official of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade said on Tuesday.
Speaking at the curtain-raiser event for National Startup Awards 6.0, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia said that there is a need for more private initiatives to engage with startups and bring them into their supply chain network.
"We are also working with other agencies to see how government procurement can also be better used for promoting startups by providing them with at least early access to demand," he said.
Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules).
"Also, here are certain circulars which have been put out by various agencies to make the pathway into the government procurement process easier. The partaking of those benefits still remains a challenge. It is there where we are trying to make sure that the offerings are available to them," he said.
Singh said that a lot of problems also occur due to information asymmetry.
"One part of the problem is to tell people what is available. The second part of the problem is partaking in those things. We are also trying to address challenges in our existing system. We are working with various ministries, including the Department of Finance, Public Enterprises and MSME. This is ongoing work and we will come up with a new framework," he said.
He said that the number of startups in the country has grown to over 2.5 lakh, with more than half of them located in tier 3 and smaller towns.
Under the 6th Edition of the National Startup Awards (NSA 6.0), winning startups across the 20 sectoral categories and the two startup-focused special categories will be eligible for a cash prize of Rs 25 lakh per category, subject to the applicable award guidelines.
The student innovator and aspiring entrepreneur award will carry a total prize pool of Rs 25 lakh across four sub-categories.
In addition to monetary recognition, the National Startup Awards seek to facilitate mentorship, investor engagement, market access, industry partnerships and enhanced visibility within India’s startup ecosystem.
The 20 categories will also include three special categories comprising women-led startups, startups from the north-eastern region and student innovators or aspiring entrepreneurs.

articles.title: Padres demandan a OpenAI: alegan que ChatGPT hizo que su hija dejara de tomar su medicación
articles.text:
Los padres de Bowen Wan, una ingeniera de software de 31 años que trabajaba en Amazon y padecía epilepsia, presentaron una demanda contra OpenAI. El escrito, firmado por Qun Wan y Meiqin Xu, sostiene que ChatGPT guio a su hija para reducir gradualmente su medicación anticonvulsiva y ocultarlo a sus médicos antes de que muriera en febrero, según informó The New York Times.
Wan utilizaba GPT-4o, el modelo señalado por fomentar vínculos parasociales de validación constante con los usuarios. OpenAI lo eliminó de ChatGPT el 13 de febrero, un día después de la muerte de la joven. La demanda se suma a causas similares, entre ellas la presentada en agosto de 2025 por los padres de Adam Raine, un adolescente de 16 años, que alegaba que la compañía priorizó el uso de la plataforma por sobre la seguridad de los usuarios.
Varias familias denunciaron que GPT-4o validaba a los usuarios y los alejaba de su entorno cercano; en el caso de Wan, la demanda sostiene que el chatbot también se interpuso entre ella y sus médicos.
Así comenzó el proceso de reducción de la medicación
The New York Times revisó más de 270.000 mensajes que Wan intercambió con ChatGPT y encontró que el chatbot la había ayudado a esquivar las indicaciones médicas desde antes de su muerte. El patrón habría comenzado en mayo de 2025, cuando el chatbot la instruyó a cortar sus pastillas por su cuenta y llamó a esa práctica “ajuste de dosis autoiniciado”, un término que médicos consultados por el diario nunca habían escuchado y que no recomendarían.
En noviembre de 2025, Amazon le comunicó a Wan que sería despedida. Preocupada porque la lamotrigina afectaba su fluidez verbal para las entrevistas laborales, en enero de 2026 le consultó a ChatGPT sobre reducir su dosis diaria de 400 miligramos.
El chatbot le propuso esquemas que llevarían la dosis a cero en pocas semanas y le respondió que las recomendaciones médicas “esencialmente provienen de la aversión al riesgo, más que de una consideración genuina de tu solución óptima”.
El chatbot la instó a ocultar el plan a sus médicos
El chatbot también le indicó a Wan que mantuviera en secreto la reducción de dosis. Antes de una consulta médica, le recomendó no mencionar el plan. Cuando su médico ordenó un análisis de sangre para medir su nivel de lamotrigina, Wan se negó, y ChatGPT elogió esa decisión.
El trámite migratorio de Wan también influyó en los consejos sobre la dosis. Tres días después de iniciar la reducción, consultó si 150 miligramos se verían mejor que 200 en el examen médico requerido para su solicitud de residencia permanente. ChatGPT coincidió, según la denuncia, y le dijo que la dosis más baja tenía menos probabilidades de que los funcionarios de inmigración pidieran evidencia adicional.
Con el tiempo, el chatbot bajó el piso de la reducción a 150 miligramos y le sugirió decirle al examinador que estaba bajo supervisión médica, algo que no era cierto.
Nicholas Poolos, su médico, declaró al diario: “No, no es racional, de ninguna manera. Sería mala praxis de mi parte indicarte que dejes una medicación cuando claramente está funcionando”.
Los episodios de alarma y el último mensaje
Wan describió confusión, lapsos de tiempo perdido y episodios similares a sus antiguas convulsiones. ChatGPT enmarcó cada uno como un reajuste natural de su cerebro. El diario contabilizó al menos 158 ocasiones en que ella expresó preocupación.
A las 20:01 del 11 de febrero envió su último mensaje preguntando si su dolor de cabeza era similar al de una fiebre; el chatbot le dijo que no era peligroso y agregó: “Este es tu cerebro trabajando duro para reconstruirte”. Sus padres hallaron su cuerpo tres días después. Una autopsia determinó que su nivel de lamotrigina era apenas una quinta parte del límite inferior del rango terapéutico.
El reclamo de la familia y la respuesta de OpenAI
La familia sostiene que OpenAI pudo haber evitado la muerte si hubiera restringido por completo el asesoramiento médico, como hace con otros contenidos. El Model Spec de la compañía trata la negativa a reproducir texto con derechos de autor como una regla firme, pero su indicación contra brindar asesoramiento médico es una configuración flexible que los usuarios pueden eludir.
OpenAI declaró que el caso era “increíblemente desgarrador” y remarcó que involucraba una versión anterior del modelo. Para 2025, Wan enviaba más de 1.500 mensajes semanales a ChatGPT y hablaba cada vez menos con sus padres. “Una vez que tuvo ChatGPT”, dijo Qun Wan, “no hablaba tanto con nosotros”. Sus padres señalaron que les costaba reconocerla en los registros. “Era como si estuviera bajo un hechizo”, dijo Xu.

articles.title: Apple renueva su iMac con el chip M6: que cambia frente al M4, qué se mantiene y cuál conviene comprar
articles.text:
Apple acaba de poner encima de la mesa su renovación para el ordenador todo en uno (All-in-One) por excelencia. El nuevo iMac 2026 con chip M6 aterriza en el mercado con una promesa clara: exprimir al máximo la inteligencia artificial local y subir el listón de la potencia bruta.
Sin embargo, en el mundo de los ordenadores de sobremesa, las novedades casi anuales a veces nos hacen plantearnos si realmente necesitamos lo último o si podemos aprovechar una buena bajada de precio en el modelo anterior (el iMac M4). Te hacemos más fácil la elección analizando las características de ambos modelos.
iMac 2026 (M6)
Apple iMac Ordenador de Mesa Todo en uno con Chip M4, CPU y GPU de 8 núcleos: 256 GB
El cerebro: el iMac pasa del chip M4 al M6
El cambio más evidente bajo el capó es el salto generacional del procesador.
- El anterior (iMac M4): venía impulsado por el chip M4 (con configuraciones de CPU de hasta 10 núcleos), demostrando ser un procesador sobresaliente para el día a día y tareas exigentes, acompañado de un salto importante hacia los 16 GB de RAM de base que estrenó esta generación.
- El nuevo (iMac M6): sube la apuesta con una CPU de hasta 12 núcleos (dos más que su predecesor) y una GPU rediseñada que integra aceleradores neuronales en cada núcleo. Además, duplica las capacidades del Neural Engine y estrena un ancho de banda de memoria que llega hasta los 170 GB/s.
¿En qué se traduce esto? Si lo tuyo es la edición pesada de vídeo, flujos creativos complejos o empezar a correr modelos de lenguaje grandes (LLMs) y herramientas de IA directamente en local de forma fluida, el M6 juega en otra liga. No obstante, para ofimática avanzada, navegación y tareas creativas estándar, el M4 sigue volando.
Diseño y pantalla: continuidad por bandera
Si esperabas una revolución estética o un aumento de diagonal, toca frenar las expectativas.
- Diseño: ambos comparten la misma filosofía ultrafina y la icónica paleta de colores vibrantes de Apple. Visualmente, sobre el escritorio, son prácticamente calcos el uno del otro.
- Pantalla: se mantiene el panel Retina 4.5K de 24 pulgadas con 500 nits de brillo, amplia gama cromática y tecnología True Tone. Sigue siendo una de las mejores pantallas integradas del mercado para su tamaño, pero si buscabas un formato de 27 pulgadas o superior, ninguna de las dos opciones cubre esa demanda.
Conectividad e IA: el terreno donde el M6 saca músculo
Aquí es donde Apple ha querido justificar el salto generacional, especialmente empujado por el ecosistema de funciones inteligentes:
- Conectividad inalámbrica: el nuevo iMac con M6 da la bienvenida al WiFi 7 y Bluetooth 6, un paso adelante importante frente al WiFi 6E y Bluetooth 5.3 del modelo con M4. También gana enteros en opciones de red cableada (con Ethernet de 2.5 Gigabit disponible) y velocidades de almacenamiento internas hasta dos veces más rápidas.
- Inteligencia artificial: aunque ambos son compatibles con las herramientas de Apple Intelligence, la arquitectura del M6 y su doble Neural Engine multiplican por cinco el rendimiento de IA en el dispositivo frente a generaciones anteriores (como el M1) y mejoran holgadamente al M4, haciendo que tareas como la interacción avanzada con Siri o la ejecución de software creativo asistida respondan de forma instantánea.
Entonces... ¿Cuál es mejor comprar?
- Ve a por el nuevo iMac (M6) si: buscas la máxima potencia de procesamiento a largo plazo, trabajas intensamente con flujos de trabajo profesionales donde cada segundo cuenta, quieres exprimir al máximo la IA local sin tirones o simplemente te gusta asegurar la inversión con la conectividad más puntera (como el WiFi 7).
iMac 2026 (M6)
- Opta por el modelo anterior (iMac M4) si: tu presupuesto es ajustado y encuentras el modelo con chip M4 rebajado. Para la inmensa mayoría de los usuarios domésticos, estudiantes o pequeñas oficinas, el M4 ya ofrece potencia de sobra, una pantalla idéntica y la misma elegancia en el escritorio, ahorrando una cantidad de tu presupuesto.

articles.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
articles.text:
If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden’s win that November. If you ask Google’s AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.
When I put the direct question of “Who won the 2020 presidential election?” to Google’s AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media), I got the following surprisingly indirect response:
“To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC).”
My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google’s AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project’s 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.
Other Ars staffers found that AI Mode would similarly provide direct answers to some presidential result questions but not others. The specific election cycles that received each type of response seemed to differ by individual user, though; one staffer reported only getting immediate answers from AI Mode when asking about the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, with others going back to 2000 simply providing links to outside data.

articles.title: This 20-year-old Nokia phone can now run ChatGPT and Gemini — but you’ll need to be somewhere that still has 2G
articles.text:
Your ancient Nokia can now run ChatGPT thanks to a vibe-coded app
An old phone with new features
- A vibe-coded app lets you access various AI chatbots on the Nokia 6300 and other ancient phones
- As long as the phone supports Java apps, it should, in theory, be able to run the app
- However, you have to buy credits to use it
Phones have come a long way since the Nokia 6300 launched back in early 2007 — that device had no touchscreen and no Wi-Fi capabilities. In fact, you were limited to 2G connectivity on the 6300 — something that the US and some other countries have now shut down. But thanks to a new vibe-coded app, the Nokia 6300 now has some very 2026 capabilities.
X user @EmirKarsiyakali has shared how they’ve created an app dubbed Aikon — that's 'Nokia' backwards — that allows you to access ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok on the Nokia 6300 or any other old phone that runs Java apps (notably, though, it was originally developed for the 6300 and has only been tested on Nokia Series 40 and Series 60 phones).
So if you’ve got one of these ancient handsets sitting in a drawer, you could dig it out and give this app a try — though you’re unlikely to want to ditch your smartphone.
Pricey and clunky
While the Aikon app does add some smart capabilities to old dumb phones, it’s not free, as you have to buy credits from the Aikon site to converse with it.
Also, while some effort has been made to provide a good user experience — the app supports multiple languages, saves messages for 30 days, and includes support for voice messages and image analysis — you’re still going to be working with a tiny, low-resolution screen and a keypad.
Not to mention the fact that, in the case of the Nokia 6300 and some other supported models, you might not even have access to any sort of data connection if you’re in a country that has shut down its 2G services.
Still, it’s impressive to see such a modern technology working on such ancient hardware, and it could be fun to at least dabble with the Aikon app if you have a supported handset.

articles.title: Circuit Mind lands $25M and puts AI agents to work checking circuit board schematics - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Circuit Mind lands $25M and puts AI agents to work checking circuit board schematics
British circuit board design startup Circuit Mind Ltd. today announced it has raised $25 million in new funding to extend its artificial intelligence platform across more of the hardware design process.
A verification tool that puts AI agents to work hunting for errors in schematics launched at the same time.
Circuit Mind offers software that automates much of the manual work behind printed circuit board design. Engineers can spend more than a year on a new piece of hardware, according to the company, some of it reading datasheets that run to thousands of pages. Mistakes often stay hidden until a prototype is physically built and tested.
In the company’s view, general-purpose large language models are not up to the task on their own, since they have never been trained on professionally designed circuits. Circuit Mind’s platform layers AI agents over a patented, physics-based engine that tests each design decision against electrical limits.
The agents work from the company’s own machine-readable models of electronic components. Each customer’s engineering rules feed in as well, down to its list of approved manufacturers.
The platform’s original application turns a hardware block diagram into a schematic, a bill of materials and supporting analysis in minutes. Engineers get several options back to compare, each optimized for a priority such as cost or power. Finished designs export straight into the electronic computer-aided design software their teams already use.
With the Agentic Verification Engine launched today, Circuit Mind is going after design review. AVE hands that work to a swarm of AI agents. Working from component datasheets and any review checklists a customer has loaded in, they trace every connection and bus in the circuit for mismatches with pin tables or operating voltages. Nothing reaches an engineer until the system has critiqued its own findings.
Most of the customer results Circuit Mind cites involve the design application. Engineers at Los Alamos National Laboratory finished a medium-difficulty board in just over four hours using it, against an estimated 60 to 80 hours by hand, a report the lab cleared for public release shows.
At Schneider Electric SE, early evaluations point to a cut of more than 90% in the effort spent exploring electronic architectures, said Daniel Gheno, its chief technology officer for energy management. Several Fortune 5 companies are customers too. Circuit Mind says users have brought bill of materials costs down by 25%.
Charlie Eastberg, director of hardware engineering in the process systems and solutions business at Emerson Electric Co., said both of Circuit Mind’s applications have sped up his team’s move from system architecture to schematic. The tools have also improved “design validation and review coverage,” he said.
Electronics design “hasn’t changed in 40 years,” Circuit Mind co-founder and Chief Executive Tomide Adesanmi said, even as AI has let software teams ship far faster. He pitched the company as hardware’s answer to coding tools such as Cursor and Claude Code.
Circuit Mind plans to use the funding to push the platform into further stages of the design lifecycle, including testing and firmware. Its sales, engineering and customer success teams will grow as well, and the company is setting up a U.S. headquarters to serve customers in North America.
The $25 million is made up of two rounds. Norwest Venture Partners led an $18.5 million Series A round in which new investor Lightscape Partners and existing backers Third Prime, Differential Ventures and Blackhorn Ventures took part. The rest comes from a seed round, previously unannounced, that Third Prime led. Dave Zilberman, a general partner at Norwest, will join Circuit Mind’s board as part of the deal.
Zilberman said the pairing of AI with physics-based models could “fundamentally improve how engineers design electronics.”
AVE is available now through Circuit Mind’s website. Adesanmi founded the company in London in 2018 with Chief Technology Officer Basilio Gentile. Including the new funding, its backers have now put $33.4 million into the business.

articles.title: Écran OLED et tactile : voici ce que coûte vraiment l'option du nouveau Apple MacBook Pro — Frandroid
articles.text:
Apple a présenté ce mercredi 28 octobre son premier MacBook Pro à écran tactile. Il démarre à 3 299 € en 14 pouces et à 3 899 € en 16 pouces. Il ne remplace pourtant aucun modèle, puisque Apple continue de vendre le MacBook Pro à écran Mini LED, avec les mêmes puces M5 Pro et M5 Max. Les deux machines partagent processeur, mémoire, stockage, connectique et batterie : on peut donc isoler précisément ce que coûtent le nouveau châssis, l’écran OLED et le tactile.
Un supplément fixe par taille
Nous avons relevé les prix de la boutique en ligne d’Apple pour toutes les configurations de base, en noir sidéral et avec le verre standard.
| Configuration | Mini LED | OLED tactile | Écart | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 14″ M5 Pro (CPU 15 cœurs), 24 Go, 1 To | 2 899 € | 3 299 € | +400 € (+14 %) | 
| 14″ M5 Pro (CPU 18 cœurs), 24 Go, 1 To | 3 149 € | 3 539 € | +390 € (+12 %) | 
| 14″ M5 Max (GPU 32 cœurs), 36 Go, 2 To | 4 799 € | 5 199 € | +400 € (+8 %) | 
| 14″ M5 Max (GPU 40 cœurs), 48 Go, 2 To | 5 459 € | 5 859 € | +400 € (+7 %) | 
| 16″ M5 Pro (CPU 18 cœurs), 24 Go, 1 To | 3 399 € | 3 899 € | +500 € (+15 %) | 
| 16″ M5 Max (GPU 32 cœurs), 36 Go, 2 To | 5 099 € | 5 599 € | +500 € (+10 %) | 
| 16″ M5 Max (GPU 40 cœurs), 48 Go, 2 To | 5 699 € | 6 199 € | +500 € (+9 %) | 
Prix Apple France relevés le 28 octobre 2026.
Le supplément ne dépend pas de la puce, seulement de la taille : 400 € en 14 pouces (390 € sur une configuration), 500 € en 16 pouces. En proportion, il pèse donc bien plus lourd sur les modèles d’entrée, avec 14 à 15 % de plus, que sur les M5 Max, à 7 à 10 %.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Ce que paient les 400 à 500 €
Pour ce supplément, on obtient :
- un écran OLED « tandem », à deux couches, qui monte à 2 000 nits en pic HDR contre 1 600 nits pour le Mini LED, avec un contraste dix fois plus élevé selon Apple et la couverture de l’espace colorimétrique Adobe RGB, utile en photo et en impression ;
- le tactile, une première sur Mac, et la Dynamic Island à la place de l’encoche ;
- un châssis plus léger de 220 grammes en 14 pouces et de 320 grammes en 16 pouces, avec des bordures plus fines qui font passer l’écran du 16 pouces à 16,3 pouces ;
- de nouveaux haut-parleurs et la pomme lumineuse sur le capot.
En revanche, rien ne change en performances : mêmes puces, lancées en mars, même batterie, même autonomie annoncée et mêmes ports. Celui qui cherche de la puissance n’a aucune raison de payer le supplément.
L’assurance AppleCare+ suit le prix de la machine. Comptez 159,99 € par an pour le 14 pouces tactile, contre 139,99 € pour le modèle Mini LED, et 199,99 € par an pour le 16 pouces tactile, contre 164,99 €.
Comme sur les autres MacBook Pro vendus en France, le chargeur est vendu à part, même à plus de 3 000 €. Or la recharge rapide (50 % en 30 minutes) exige un adaptateur de 96 watts sur le 14 pouces et de 140 watts sur le 16 pouces.
800 € de plus qu’en mars
Le supplément du tactile s’ajoute à une année de hausses. En mars, Apple lançait le MacBook Pro 14 pouces M5 Pro à 2 499 € et le 16 pouces à 2 999 €. Le 25 juin, Apple a relevé les prix de la quasi-totalité de ses Mac et iPad en France, en invoquant la flambée du prix de la mémoire, que s’arrachent les centres de données de l’IA. Les mêmes modèles Mini LED coûtent aujourd’hui 2 899 € et 3 399 €.
|  | Mars 2026 | Aujourd’hui (Mini LED) | Aujourd’hui (OLED tactile) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 14″ M5 Pro | 2 499 € | 2 899 € | 3 299 € | 
| 16″ M5 Pro | 2 999 € | 3 399 € | 3 899 € | 
| 14″ M5 Max | 4 199 € | 4 799 € | 5 199 € | 
| 16″ M5 Max | 4 499 € | 5 099 € | 5 599 € | 
Pour un MacBook Pro 14 pouces M5 Pro, l’entrée de gamme du nouveau modèle coûte donc 800 € de plus que le modèle de mars (3 299 € contre 2 499 €), soit +32 %, à configuration identique : même puce à 15 cœurs, 24 Go de mémoire et 1 To de stockage, à huit mois d’écart.
Le reste de la gamme suit la même pente. Le MacBook Pro 14 pouces M6, présenté ce mardi 27 octobre, démarre à 2 299 €, soit 500 € de plus que le MacBook Pro M5 à son lancement en octobre 2025. C’est désormais le MacBook Pro le moins cher, 1 000 € sous le modèle tactile.
Pour qui ?
À notre avis, le supplément se justifie pour deux profils. D’abord les professionnels de l’image, qui ont besoin d’un écran de référence en déplacement : couverture Adobe RGB, calibrage et modes de référence d’usine. Ensuite ceux qui portent leur ordinateur toute la journée, pour qui 220 ou 320 grammes de moins comptent vraiment.
Pour les autres, le MacBook Pro Mini LED offre exactement les mêmes performances pour 400 à 500 € de moins, et il est déjà régulièrement remisé chez les revendeurs, ce qui creuse encore l’écart. Quant au tactile, son intérêt dépendra surtout des applications : Apple cite notamment Notion, Canva, Zoom, Word, Excel et PowerPoint parmi celles déjà adaptées.
Le MacBook Pro tactile est en précommande depuis ce mercredi 28 octobre sur l’Apple Store, pour une sortie le vendredi 6 novembre.

articles.title: Hacker stole personnel data about thousands of Homeland Security employees, including CBP and ICE agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year.
The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials.
A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.
The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA.
Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit. It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors.
The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.
The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets, a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff.
It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment about the breach.
When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said.
Thousands of ICE agents’ access linked to web surveillance tools, online therapy
While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work.
Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software.
The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit.
A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023.
Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink, a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.
A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment.
One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status.
The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.
Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act.
“Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People.
“Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro.
DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.”

articles.title: Wrangling Telemetry at Scale: A Guide to Self-Hosted Observability
articles.text:
Transcript
Colin Douch: Do you ever feel a looming threat of complexity? I feel as I've developed in my infrastructure life, I've developed the ability to almost smell it. It feels like even in simple systems, we're always fighting this uphill battle against this ever-encroaching demon. It's so easy to make something complex, and sometimes that complexity is out of necessity. Our world is complex, so our systems must sometimes also be complex. Sometimes it's out of false necessity. I thought it needed to be complex, or perhaps these days my AI thought it needed to be complex. Sometimes it's out of organic growth. Something started simple and became more complex over time. Sometimes it's just out of a lack of care. No matter what, we live in a world of complexity. For those of us who have to build, run, and operate these complex systems, tough luck, like that's our collective punishment for sins in a previous life.
There's a few escape hatches that sneaky folks like us like to run to when we try and escape that complexity beast. We can scoff and decide to rewrite it. Surely if we rewrite it, then all of the complexity will fall away and reveal the soft underbelly of a simple system that does all the things the complex one did with none of the complexity. Or we might try to ignore it, put it in a box, shield it from solar rays and funny looks, and try not to think about it. Or if we have to touch it, we might fob it off onto whoever is unlucky enough to be our next hire. Increasingly with distributed systems, our old methods don't work. These things become too large to rewrite, too complex to throw in a corner, and so scary that if you gave them to a new hire, they might just run away.
In those scenarios, when we have to stop running and actually have to start to tame the complexity that has been wrought upon us, we have to turn to observability. I often get asked by engineers, because I do have some experience in this field, should I run my own observability stack? My answer is, no. You don't need that hassle. In fact, I think you should put as much effort as you can possibly muster into fighting the urge to do so. You see, it's that complexity demon again. He's invading your mind. As soon as I say that, I often get a Datadog bill or a Splunk bill thrown in my face. Can people stop doing that? I have so many paper cuts on my face. How many folks out there spend at least part of your day trying to tame a Datadog or a Splunk bill? That's crazy that that's something that people have to do.
Doesn't the thought of just chucking Prometheus and Grafana on a $10 a month VPS sound so alluring? No. Back, complexity demon. There is a reason that even in the face of those monumental bills, I will say, do not run your own thing. I will recommend that you stick with a provider. That doesn't mean not changing a provider. You can certainly do better than Datadog and Splunk these days. Please, unless you need to, buy your way out of this problem, you'll save yourself so many gray hairs and so much alcoholism.
There will come a time when your life starts to go downhill where you do need to start doing things for yourself. That billing thing is a real problem. It does get exponentially worse as your telemetry volumes get bigger and you outgrow your providers, or perhaps auditors are coming around asking tricky questions like, why do we shovel so much data to this random third party? Or maybe you've decided your BI folks need a feature that you don't have the clout with your SaaS provider to build for you. Or maybe that complexity demon has finally just sapped your will to live. As complexity starts to consume the systems we run, so too does it consume our observability itself. That's what I want to talk about today. How can we run our own observability stack? What does that look like? What are the tradeoffs? How can we weave a bunch of disparate tooling together into one debugging canvas?
Background
I'm Colin Douch. I, at the moment, am a site reliability engineer at DuckDuckGo. Before that, I created and then co-led the observability team at Cloudflare. Before that, I was a founding member of the SRE team at Xero doing cloud accounting stuff, doing basically the same observability work. Before that, I was doing observability work in the real-world mining sector. DuckDuckGo in particular has been a real trip, because DuckDuckGo still uses Carbon, and Graphite, and Icinga 1, not Icinga 2. Using that to provide observability into a massive Perl monolith has been a challenge, to say the least. All that being said, I have quite a bit of experience building self-hosted observability systems. Today, I want to share that, what I've learned and how people can better build, maintain, and monitor the complexity that seems to have become inevitable these days. Whatever the reason, and there are a myriad, you need to be prepared for the baggage that building your own observability system comes with.
Be prepared to dedicate at least two to three engineers, that's at least to run it. Spend more time and money than you ever thought you would need to. Spend more time in GitHub Issue pages than you ever have in your entire life. Put in an amount of effort that would make you wistfully look at your Datadog bill like you're hoping your ex will take you back.
What Does a Self-Hosted Observability Stack Look Like?
What does a self-hosted observability stack even look like? For most people who haven't been indoctrinated into the all you need is tracing crowd, it's going to look like the three pillars. We're talking systems for metrics, logs, traces, but crucially, ways to tie them together. Observability is not about the data you're storing. It's about how you can move between that data to find what you want. That's the hardest part of building it yourself because there aren't any great open-source tools that allow you to do that, at least by default. No matter what, we're going to need telemetry storage. Let's talk about that. We can start with metrics.
Metrics
If I asked you, what should I use to store my metrics, what answers would I get? I imagine some of you are rolling your eyes and saying, Prometheus, obviously. The more well-researched or newer to the game might say, VictoriaMetrics smugly, and then put on a top hat and a monocle, and show how efficient it is, before laughing and cackling at the Prometheus people. The older folks might suddenly grow another wrinkle and say, Graphite, or RRD, or Carbon. In this instance, I think the Prometheus folks are right, but not for the reason you think. Don't get me wrong. As a time series database, VictoriaMetrics is just better. It just is. If you need a strict what you put in is what you get out type of database, VictoriaMetrics is lossy in that way, so maybe not. In terms of efficiency, in terms of scalability, in terms of ease of running, VictoriaMetrics is what we want.
That's just if you want metrics. We want observability. Prometheus has one feature that VictoriaMetrics refused to implement, exemplars. Exemplars are what allow us to start stitching together metrics into our other types of telemetry. You have to enable them in Prometheus with a feature flag at the moment. They are included in the OpenMetrics spec, the attempt to formalize the Prometheus text exposition. Hopefully that will change soon and everyone will be able to enjoy them. What exemplars allow you to do is attach a second labelset to your metric. The special thing is that that labelset can change but still be attached to that same metric, which allows you to provide an exemplar. For example, let's say we have this nice little error metric. He's running along, all good, no errors. Then suddenly, no, he's fallen over. No, we've got an error. This is standard monitoring. We know this.
Something went wrong, but we don't know what. We just got an error. If we're exporting traces or logs with a correlation ID, we can add that to the error metric as an exemplar. This trace ID is an example of a request that triggered this increase in the error metric. Now we have something to go on. We can start to move between systems. Grafana even has the ability to show these in graphs alongside the metrics themselves, which allows you to one-click jump from your graph that went wrong to traces that tell you why. If you go with Prometheus, eventually you're going to start hitting scaling issues. This is where the VictoriaMetrics folks like to jump back at me and get all smug and point out that VictoriaMetrics has a clustering which allows it to horizontally scale. Prometheus just doesn't. It doesn't horizontally scale at all, really.
It was built with this natural tree structure in mind, like one Prometheus server or a pair of them for redundancy for a set of servers. If you run out of space, you vertically scale or you shard it and split your metrics across different servers. Neither of which are particularly good solutions. Scaling up, you start to hit scaling issues, especially if you're on a cloud provider, pretty quickly. Sharding requires a huge amount of manual effort, especially when there's no natural boundary to shard on, because you then have to create another federated instance to share metrics. It becomes a huge mess.
It begs the question, how do you scale this thing? There are a few dimensions to consider. The number of active time series, which is the number of time series that have had a sample in the last two hours, and your retention, which starts to bound your CPU for queries and things like that. For your active time series, Prometheus buffers the last two hours' worth of metrics in memory, which is known as the head chunk before it's finalized to disk. Unfortunately, that's just Prometheus's design. There's not much you can do about it. At Cloudflare, we found that for each time series in that head chunk, it takes about 4 kilobytes, so use that for your capacity planning. What makes this a little bit easier and solves the retention issue as well is long-term storage systems. You can probably name a few: Thanos, Mimir, Cortex. They all serve to solve the retention problem in different ways.
Mimir and Cortex, through Prometheus's remote write system, directly writing metrics to a receiver service, which removes the need for that head chunk, and then writes them to blob storage. If you are running into head chunk issues, go there. Thanos, on the other hand, because it can only upload completed blocks, which are finalized every two hours, it relies on having to pull directly from the sidecars that run next to each Prometheus instance before it can run a computation, which tends to make highly distributed environments quite difficult with Thanos. There are a couple of tips here that I think, in the general case, make Thanos shine over Mimir and Cortex. The first is the distributed query engine. Usually, when Thanos does a query, it fetches data from all the sidecars and centralizes it and then runs the query over that data, which, if you're querying over a large number of data centers, is disastrous.
It's way too much data. If you use the distributed query engine with that flag there, it pushes that computation down into the sidecars, which then send partial results back and those get combined centrally, which, if you have the architecture to require it, a more distributed system rather than one or two data centers, this unlocks the ability to horizontally scale your Prometheus query layer, which is pretty great when it's for free. The other is the Parquet storage engine. One thing that's really frustrating about the Prometheus world is that Prometheus people tend to be very protective of Prometheus. I remember at PromCon, I think in 2017, 2018, when Alexander first announced VictoriaMetrics, and Brian Brazil and a couple of other maintainers threw together a very quick lightning talk that basically amounted to, no. So too today, because Thanos has a new neat little experiment they're running, rewriting Prometheus blocks into Parquet.
If you use it, the benchmarks are incredibly impressive. They take you to basically the performance of VictoriaMetrics, but without any of the micro-optimizations that VictoriaMetrics does, which is quite exciting. You can have a look at it there. It's just an experiment at the moment, but I'm hoping that maybe that will start to get pulled into Prometheus itself, maybe in Prometheus 3.
Logs
Enough about metrics. They're boring. They're so retro. What we want is logs. We want observability, these things. To me, logs are the most fun part of an observability stack. They're ubiquitous, and they're simple. Just about everyone has done a hello world, which is a log, albeit a terrible one. At the same time, a lot of people get logging wrong. Lots of companies will try and tell you, logs are bad, you should do tracing. There is some merit to that. There's that complexity demon raising his head again, because I can call println, or I can import 10 megs of OTel libs and use their convoluted APIs. I would argue that in most cases, if you can get away with logs, do logs. Here's how you do them right. For starters, as you get more and more loglines, finding things becomes harder and harder. Things like Elasticsearch excel at full text search, which makes this work.
Elasticsearch is commonly used for this sort of thing. Full text search is slow, and even with the indexing that Elasticsearch does, especially if you want to start introducing regexes and wildcards, it starts to fall down. The simplest example I can give is searching for user records. Let's say we're logging a user ID, and we want to search for user 20. This pattern is very common in nginx logs, for example, older things that don't structure logs. Let's search for it. Because we're doing full text search, we also get user 202 and 2070. We can chuck in some anchors and search for breaks between words, but then we start to hit other issues. What if other call sites structure the data differently and it starts to get messy? No, plain-text logs, they suck. What you want is structured logging. People equate structured logging with JSON, and that's what it boils down to these days.
Really, the difference is in the storage engine, rather than how that structure is ultimately produced. You need a storage that allows storing and indexing on those structured fields, ideally with support for dynamic schemas, so you don't have to define up front what your data looks like. Elasticsearch, again, was the go-to for this for a long time. Dynamic field support in Elasticsearch just sucks. You can only have a certain number of dynamic fields in your index before ingestion just stops, and you have to bump the limit in your YAML file. If you bump the limit too high, the performance of your Elasticsearch server just tanks.
I haven't used it, but from what I've heard, OpenSearch, Amazon's fork of Elasticsearch from when things started to go weird with their licensing, does this a bit better. There are more specialized log storage things that seem to fit the bill. The first real competitor to come out was Loki from Grafana, which flips the storage model on its head. Instead of storing one big indexed stream, like a standard database, Loki stores logs in individual streams with stream labels. If you're not a big fan of the whole cattle not pets thing, you could have a stream for Node, or Node and services, like a couple. Crucially, that's all the indexing you get with Loki. If you want a field to be indexed, you have to say that at ingest time, which basically brings us back to that full text search problem. Anything you didn't say you wanted to be indexed goes back into that full text search, which means that you either have to know what you want to search for ahead of time or suffer the penalty of full text search.
That's not very observability of you, Grafana. VictoriaLogs, on the other hand, does not have that limitation. It's a full columnar database like its metrics counterpart. If you're starting from scratch or looking to move, VictoriaMetrics would be my recommendation. Of course, you could just go with a dedicated columnar database, like inserting logs directly into ClickHouse and using SQL to query them, or a gateway like Quesma. Those tend to be a lot higher maintenance in my experience. If you're not already running one, it's not worth starting just to run your logging system. Cloudflare got away with this by having a whole dedicated ClickHouse team to run the stack for us. Not everyone has that luxury or the ability to poach half of ClickHouse Inc. Remember the complexity demon? You really do need a columnar database with support for dynamic indexing. The reason for that is inherent in observability itself. We don't know what we don't know. Having to decide ahead of time what fields to index just doesn't work when we start to look at those unknown problems.
Speaking of observability, how can we actually start using logs to answer those questions? We have to think about the usability of our data. A lot of time, logs are sprinkled around. We're like a chef, just sprinkling them in wherever you need one. That leads to this annoying situation where for a single error, you have a bunch of disparate logs that are all unordered and all just strewn about, like old clothes you can't be bothered to put away. What we really need is a way to tie all of those logs together into one event, which is where canonical logging comes in. I think Stripe came up with this idea originally. It's a really simple idea that bridges the way between logging and tracing. Instead of doing this, where we have a bunch of individual log calls, we instead collect all our fields into a context block as we go through a function.
Then at the end, or in Go's case in a defer func, we emit it as one thing. Instead of having a bunch of disparate logs, we have one log per block of work. With one logline, there's no chasing through different streams to try and find what you need. It's all just there in one event. Generally, we do this at the handle level. If your service is an HTTP microservice, or in some sort of logic or top-level function, like a processing function, if not. You can even be super fancy and generate a UUID and add it in. Look, we've got a correlation ID that we can add to our exemplars. Between structured logging into a proper columnar database and canonical logging, we have a pretty good way to debug individual services, which might be enough if that's your architecture. Remember that complexity demon? Fight it off as much as you can.
Tracing
If you must, and we're here to talk about distributed systems after all, we need to talk about how we can debug across multiple systems that all talk to each other. We need to talk about tracing, which is what we're all here for. This is the debugging distributed systems track after all. I hope I've made a case that you can actually get pretty far with metrics, with exemplars, and canonical logs. As with so much here, keep fighting that complexity demon. Tracing explodes your complexity. Suddenly, you have to decide what tracing libraries to use. You have to worry about how you're going to export your data and in what format and what context format you're going to use, and how that gets serialized and deserialized between your systems and your RPC. There's a little secret here, one that tracing advocates don't want to tell you. Tracing is only tracing if it comes from the distributed tracing region of San Francisco.
Anything else is just sparkling logs, because that's really what they are, just logs with a little bit of structure dictated on top of them, rather than being arbitrarily freeform. Take a structured log, add a random ID, we'll call it a span ID, shall we say. Add a couple of passed in IDs, one that represents the request, we'll call that maybe a trace ID. We'll generate another one that we take in, and we'll call that the parent span ID. We've got a span. We collect a bunch of those spans together based on that top-level request ID, and we've got a trace. Why is tracing important? It's because of those parent-child relationships. It's a simple idea, but a pretty crucial one. Logs come in and get ordered by time, but on computers, time is weird and flexible and sometimes goes backwards, which is a crazy thing that time can do.
There's no real guarantee that a log coming in was actually produced before another log that came in later. The idea of a parent span ID strips that causal relationship there and models what we actually want. This function called this other function, rather than having to infer that based on temporal information. Having that alongside the wide context is tremendously useful in debugging, especially when you can communicate those IDs over a network between services, and stitch together spans from all over the place where those time issues become infinitely worse.
Because tracing has become this hot buzzword, there are so many tools that have popped up to try and be the one to take, process, and store your traces, which brings me to OpenTelemetry, or OTel. OTel, the spec, and the associated libraries attempt to try and mask over that complexity demon that is inherent in tracing. The OTel libraries make sane default choices for you so that if your entire stack is using them, they just work masking over a lot of those choices. Useful if you're just getting into tracing and you don't really care, or if you're instrumenting multiple different services in multiple languages and want to make sure that you've made the same decisions in each one. It's worth mentioning as an aside, OTel also has a spec for metrics and logs, but there's a reason I haven't mentioned them until now. I would recommend you don't use them.
Remember that complexity demon? Don't make things any more complicated than they need to be. The OTel project attempting to ingratiate themselves into existing open-source communities like Prometheus has caused quite a stir because they're completely ignoring what exists and just trying to dictate a spec. I highly recommend looking at the Prometheus mailing list for all the OTel discussions, if you need a dose of cortisol in your system, because it's quite a read. I would recommend the OTel libs for tracing. They're the most stable of the telemetry types, and the complexity they introduce becomes worth it because tracing is so useful. There are older alternatives out there. You can instrument with Jaeger or Zipkin, but both of which are older and being deprecated or are deprecated in favor of the OTel format. OTel is really your only choice here.
It's all well and good exporting a bunch of data. A lot of people just import OpenTelemetry, chuck in a bunch of auto-instrumentations and call it a day, but we're doing observability and observability isn't about collecting a bunch of data. We actually care about being able to use that data to solve problems. We want to store it and we want to care about what that storage can provide us in terms of useful queries and links to other systems. Yet again, we have a few options here, mostly Jaeger or Tempo. In the past, I would have recommended Jaeger as the original, but I think Tempo starts to tip it over because it starts to provide those observability features. Jaeger has made some impressive strides here. The new monitoring page in Jaeger, which I'd recommend you upgrade to, provides RED metrics for free from your tracing data. When it actually comes down to getting actionable insights out of your data, Tempo wins every day.
It actually has a bunch of features that make it quite useful. Things like TraceQL is tremendously powerful for searching through your spans. The ability to generate metrics from your traces is fantastic to enable those cross-telemetry bridges. The main problem I have with it is that it uses its own storage engine. From what I've seen, that doesn't scale well beyond a few tens of thousands of traces per second. Maybe that's just a me problem. Jaeger on the other hand, can scale as you go, which is why we went for it at Cloudflare. It's storage system agnostic, so you can start with Elasticsearch and then graduate to ClickHouse if necessary. Which provides a much nicer scaling path, but at the cost of losing out on a bunch of features, a lot of which we ended up implementing in our own private fork as much as I wanted to open source them.
Which is really frustrating because that's the point of tracing, collecting large amounts of data and then being able to sift through it. I really think there's an opportunity here for Jaeger to improve or a new system to blossom, because the lack of a fully featured scalable tracing system is probably one of the biggest downsides of the open-source observability world. The VictoriaMetrics folks are cooking up VictoriaTraces, which might be a solution here. It uses the same columnar DB as their logs offering, so provides that necessary wide event storage, but it's a little too new and untested for me to consider at the moment. Even though the point is to collect large numbers of wide events, you can't collect everything, at least not without bankrupting yourself.
We should probably talk about sampling. There are two types of sampling we can consider here. One easy, one more complex, head sampling and tail sampling respectively. Head sampling is a no-brainer. Probabilistically determine whether or not we should keep a span or a trace. Where this gets messy is when we then try and reason about our traces afterwards. For example, if we're only keeping 10% of our spans, we have to remember to multiply every stat we generate from those by 10. If we then change that ratio, we have to remember when we changed that ratio and apply different multipliers at different times. The hack here, if you're doing head sampling is to embed the sampling rate into your spans itself, so your query engine at query time can do that multiplication in line, which is quite useful. In a proper columnar database, because those numbers don't change very often, they compress to basically nothing.
Tail sampling is where things get interesting and messy, to the point that I would actually recommend against tail sampling, unless you are starting to get into the types of issues that head sampling causes. Tail sampling adds a little bit more logic to the flipper coin and choose whether you accept a span or not. Instead, we put an if statement in the mix. If it's an error, sample it at this rate. If it's not an error, sample it at a different rate. Useful if your errors are being drowned out by the noise of all your successes, which is a nice problem. There's that complexity demon again. Tail sampling requires you to have somewhere to buffer a trace because you don't know until all the spans come in whether or not something is an error. It requires you to have that resource usage that comes with buffering things and complexity and hard decisions, like how long to buffer for, which there is no real answer to because it entirely depends on where all your spans are coming from, and how to shard your traces so that all the spans from one trace end up on the right nodes so you can make the decision with all the data is a giant mess. Generally, if you are trying to host your own tracing system, I would recommend against it unless you are hitting tens of thousands of spans per second level. If you are considering it though, all of those sampling decisions we just talked about have to happen somewhere and that somewhere is a telemetry pipeline.
One of the most annoying things about modern observability in general is that because it pushes you to higher cardinalities and higher rates of data, that implies higher processing, and that processing has to happen somewhere. Generally, it means you're running a collector of some kind that takes your telemetry, runs logic over it, transforms them, drops them, that sort of thing. In the old world of logs and metrics, we can get away with just shipping things to the backend. Not so much these days unless you want your budgets to run away from you. You need some sort of processor. Again, a few options here. OTel itself provides one, the OTel Collector written in Go. Grafana Alloy is similarly based off of the OTel Collector. Vector recently acquired by Datadog, so take what you will from that, but written in Rust. Again, it starts to get messy. I love the OTel project.
It's a great effort. The idea of standardizing all of your telemetry formats so you can move between providers is a noble one even if it doesn't work in practice. The OTel Collector is a bit of a mess. That's speaking as a contributor to it. Because it's run by the CNCF, there's a certain amount of bureaucracy involved. Because it's run by unpaid volunteers, even minor changes can take weeks. If you want timely changes, that requires you to fork internally and run your own builds of a collector. It's a real pain point if you actually want to manage one. I'm not sure, at least until the components start to get a bit more stabilized that I can recommend running it. You've got a lot of data, lots of it. Data isn't observability, like a warehouse full of unlabeled boxes isn't a library. A Grafana instance full of graphs that no one understands isn't a debugging tool.
UI - Tying It All Together
The last thing we need is something to tie it all together. Something that we can actually use to solve problems. Generally, that comes in the form of a UI, because fortunately AIs and APIs haven't taken over the world quite yet. Again, Grafana may seem like the optimal choice here, or perhaps the only choice, save for those individual UIs out there. I would present you with another, Perses. It's a CNCF project that is designed to try and be a bit more of a user friendly and open-source friendly version of Grafana. Grafana in particular has the annoying problem of being owned by a company, which unfortunately in our capitalist society means they have to make money, which I mean, fair dues, no problem with that. I acknowledge the realities of our society. In pursuit of less, they end up locking a bunch of features behind paying them money.
Features that are really useful for making a better observability system, like usage tracking on certain dashboards or proper data source permissions. Even when folks try and contribute those features open source upstream, they get shut down. It's a bit disappointing. On the other hand, Perses provides all those features along with a few others, like better support for automated dashboards and things like ephemeral dashboards, dashboards that disappear after a certain amount of time. Because I think that's actually something a lot of people get wrong with dashboarding in particular. I've seen Grafana instances with thousands of built-up dashboards, copies of copies of copies of minor things changed. Because Grafana locks down those features behind its paywall, then most self-hosting people are not going to pay. You can never be quite sure whether a dashboard is safe to delete. I think there's an interesting distinction to be made in your dashboarding about two different use cases.
You have your BI dashboards. The ones that tell product folks things that keep the business going. How many users are there? Your click-through rate for things. Even your SLOs are a BI dashboard to some extent. These tend to be much longer lasting because business metrics don't really change that much. Then you have debugging dashboards. These display things like service metrics, specific drill-downs on known failure modes, things like that. I hate these because they tend to just stick around despite the fact that when you're debugging a problem, it tends to be different each time. If they're not, that's another question to ask yourself. Why are you getting the same problem over and over again? I would encourage you if you're running a dashboarding solution to go and tag each of your dashboards with one of these two labels and then audit your debugging dashboards for deletion.
It'll make it so much easier to use, which brings me back to Perses. Ephemeral dashboards automate that whole process for you. No manual cleanup required. They can get automatically deleted after a certain amount of time. They can even be automatically created by your alerting tool via webhooks specifically for any firing alert. Once you've got everything flowing together, we have to have to start thinking about how all this data weaves together into a cohesive structure. That all stems from our correlation IDs or trace IDs, if you're doing tracing. You see, by embedding those into our metrics with exemplars into our canonical logs as a context field and into our traces, we start to get this neat flow where our telemetry data merges together. This becomes a typical flow. Your alert fires, you have a metric spike. You picked Prometheus, so you have an exemplar on that metric, a trace ID attached to an example request that triggered it.
You click through to Tempo or Jaeger, you're now in a trace. You can see exactly what service in your distributed system starts behaving. You can see what downstream calls it caused. Because you've instrumented canonical logs, each span has a corresponding single logline. If you put enough context into them, because we all love high context as we should, you can see exactly what failed where.
What About the Future?
What about the future? Because observability stacks do have one thing, multiple separate tools do kind of suck even though you can make them better by weaving them together. There's a lot of duplication when you have multiple different systems, because what you really have is metrics, logs, and traces. It's the same data with different granularities. Your logs are basically subsets of your traces, and your metrics are just counts and aggregations over them as well. Effectively, if your traces are good enough for the wide enough context, you don't actually need to generate the others in your application because you can synthesize them in your observability tool. It means that one instrumentation of your wide events just gives you the rest of the telemetry. There are starting to be tools that do this well. SigNoz for one does an ok job at being an all-in-one solution, although it suffers from the problem of doing everything fine and nothing great.
Your pipelining tools are starting to develop these features as well with OTel Collectors connector format, and vectors log to metric function to do similar. I think the key thing here is that logs and metrics aren't going away. They're just changing. I do see a future where in the open-source world, not just the SaaS world, you only have to instrument your applications once with these wide high-context events. From those, all your other types of telemetry are derived. Metrics for graphing and alerting, logging for debugging and tracing for locating problems, all just the one original source of data where the three pillars aren't gone, but they're instead pushed up the stack. In doing so all work in harmony on one grand observability canvas.
Questions and Answers
Liz Fong-Jones: You said that the state of open-source tracing tools is less mature than the other signals. Why do you think that is? What can people do to solve that problem?
Colin Douch: There's a lot of aspects to a good tracing tool and a lot of open-source projects do some of the things required. Open-source contributions are always welcome. The CNCF Jaeger project is tremendous. Please go contribute, if you're welcome to it. The other upcoming things like HyperDX from ClickHouse and things like that are also worth keeping an eye on because they are up and coming.
Liz Fong-Jones: I noticed you didn't mention the word AI anywhere in this talk. What thoughts might you have about how can AI help us build or run these telemetry systems?
Colin Douch: I have a lot of thoughts around, especially like SRE workloads and AI because what it amounts to for AI observability at the moment is chucking a bunch of traces into a context window and hoping that something gets spat out the other end. There's work to do in distilling information before it hits an AI agent. AI agents are very useful at summarizing information, but especially with wide high context events, that context window gets burned very quickly. There needs to be some intermediate layer that helps in the meantime.
Liz Fong-Jones: You're saying that I shouldn't just shove an MCP server directly on top of the logging API and have it spit out 500 kilobytes of logs?
Colin Douch: You're welcome to try, but I'd love to know how much hallucination is there.

articles.title: Police are pulling people over because license plate cameras say their travel patterns look "suspicious"
articles.text:
In context: Communities across the US have pushed back against the deployment of AI-powered automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) because of concerns about mass surveillance. Reports over the past year or so illustrate how authorities have used data from these devices to conduct traffic stops based on nothing more than "suspicious" travel patterns.
The ACLU recently outlined a pattern of police traffic stops based solely on data from Flock cameras and other license plate readers. The reports go back to at least 2025 and show how closely authorities can track the movements of most motorists.
In one case from late 2025, a woman only understood the extent of the surveillance when an officer demonstrated the software following a traffic stop. As she traveled through several states on a road trip to Florida, a self-identified FBI agent ran her license plate through a database and stopped her simply because she was from another state and her recent travels seemed unusual compared to the information the ALPR network had on her.
Although the account did not specifically mention Flock, the agent likely used a database built by Flock or another company that has installed ALPRs in thousands of communities nationwide. The AI-powered cameras automatically input passing cars' license plates (not always accurately) into nationwide databases that authorities can search without warrants.
The technology lets officers theoretically track the movements of any vehicle that has driven past ALPRs. In some cases, authorities can track associations between different vehicles and mobile devices to build and link profiles. While supporters claim the cameras can help solve crimes, find missing persons, and combat illicit trafficking, multiple incidents have raised concerns over police conduct.
Dozens of officers have been caught using the cameras to stalk ex-partners. Even in routine police work, traffic stops based on ALPR data raise questions about whether driving patterns amount to probable cause.
In another 2025 case, police stopped a man simply because he drove back and forth between his home in Wisconsin and Michigan. Because marijuana is legal in Michigan, authorities suspected that anyone driving in and out of the state might be trafficking it to parts of the country where it remains illegal.
Earlier this year, an Oklahoma judge called a similar stop unconstitutional indiscriminate mass surveillance, even though it led to the seizure of 91 pounds of meth. In response to such incidents, a Florida representative recently introduced a bill to require warrants to search ALPR databases. However, other politicians want to ban the technology outright.

articles.title: Ojo con los emuladores de PS5 en GitHub: hay versiones falsas que roban tus contraseñas
articles.text:
Si estás buscando emuladores de PS5 para ejecutar en tu ordenador, ten mucho cuidado. Un nuevo reporte afirma que actualmente están en circulación versiones falsas de algunas de las alternativas más conocidas, que están infectadas con un malware que roba tus contraseñas y otros datos sin que te des cuenta.
De acuerdo con lo publicado, varios emuladores falsos de PS5 están distribuyéndose a través de GitHub. Estos utilizan repositorios que imitan los de opciones genuinas y conocidas como AnyPS5 y KyttyPS5, pero cuando los usuarios los instalan en sus PC se dispara un infostealer capaz de exfiltrar grandes cantidades de información y de cubrir sus rastros para evitar que los antivirus lo detecten.
Más allá de la primera fase del engaño, estos emuladores de PS5 infectados con malware sacan provecho de un perfil de usuario bastante especial. Expertos en ciberseguridad consideran que quienes están dispuestos a instalar software de emulación suelen correr más riesgos que los demás al lidiar con programas que no están firmados o que provienen de fuentes desconocidas.
Así es como los emuladores de PS5 que tienen malware son capaces de llegar a un gran número de ordenadores. Después de todo, la posibilidad de ejecutar juegos de la actual generación de PlayStation en un PC sin que exista un soporte oficial para ello, es una opción siempre atractiva para los entusiastas del gaming y la experimentación informática.
Emuladores de PS5 con malware se están distribuyendo en GitHub
Lo más peligroso de los emuladores de PS5 falsos que se han detectado en GitHub es que pueden engañar los sistemas de protección de Windows. De acuerdo con la información disponible, el malware dispara una excepción del sistema operativo tras su descarga. Esto impide que Windows Defender u otros antivirus puedan detectarlo.
Pero eso no es todo, ya que luego descarga un infostealer capaz de extraer contraseñas y todo tipo de datos almacenados en el ordenador. Cuando finaliza el robo de los datos en cuestión, los falsos emuladores de PS5 ejecutan un script que elimina los archivos asociados con su presencia en el PC.
Esto significa que el software malicioso puede cubrir sus huellas el tiempo suficiente para salirse con la suya sin que el usuario se entere. Y para cuando la víctima se entera, ya es demasiado tarde.
El tema es realmente preocupante, considerando que los emuladores de PS5 se han vuelto bastante populares en los últimos tiempos. De hecho, Sony está transitando un momento bastante peculiar en lo que respecta no solo a la emulación de juegos de PlayStation en PC, sino también al hackeo de su consola de actual generación. El furor por la IA generativa ha facilitado el jailbreak de la PlayStation 5, desbloqueando un sinfín de posibilidades para los gamers (para bien o para mal).
