articles.title: « Un bug éternel » : cette faille critique se cache dans le démarrage de la plupart des serveurs du monde, et la corriger relève du casse-tête
articles.text:
C’est une faille notée 9,5 sur 10 en gravité, qui pourrait survivre indéfiniment tant elle est enfouie profondément dans les machines.
Son doux nom ? CVE-2026-97631. Révélée le 22 octobre 2026, elle se loge dans le firmware de la plupart des serveurs, sous le système d’exploitation, dans des couches logicielles que personne ne voit jamais.
Interrogé par le site américain Ars Technica, HD Moore, directeur de la recherche chez Dragos, une entreprise spécialisée dans la sécurité des infrastructures industrielles, la qualifie déjà de « bug éternel ».
Le logiciel qui démarre avant tout le reste
L’attaque se joue dans un laps de temps très réduit, pratiquement à l’instant où notre doigt lâche le bouton d’allumage. Quand on allume un serveur, le système d’exploitation n’est pas le premier programme à se lancer. Avant lui s’exécute le firmware, un logiciel stocké sur une puce de la carte mère, qui vérifie le matériel puis passe la main au système.
Sur les machines modernes, ce firmware suit une norme appelée UEFI. La plupart des fabricants le construisent à partir d’une même base de code open source, EDK2, que les grands fournisseurs du secteur comme AMI, Insyde ou Phoenix utilisent abondamment. Jusque-là, rien de compliqué.
Sauf que dans les centres de données, les serveurs ne démarrent pas toujours depuis leur disque. Pour installer des centaines de machines sans intervenir sur chacune, les administrateurs utilisent le démarrage réseau, ou PXE, qui permet à un serveur de récupérer sur le réseau local le code dont il a besoin. Et c’est dans ce mécanisme, activé par défaut, que se loge la faille.
Pendant ce démarrage réseau, le firmware range les messages d’erreur qu’il reçoit dans un espace mémoire de 504 octets. Le code chargé de cette copie ne vérifie pas correctement leur taille, si bien qu’un message trop long déborde et écrase les données voisines.
En envoyant un message forgé au bon moment, un attaquant peut ainsi faire exécuter ses propres instructions avec le plus haut niveau de privilège du processeur. Ce code s’exécute avant Secure Boot, le mécanisme censé vérifier la légitimité de tout ce qui se charge au démarrage. Or, comme le souligne HD Moore, la machine a encore accès à ce stade à des composants sensibles comme la puce TPM, qui conserve notamment les clés de chiffrement des disques.
Une menace réelle, mais circonscrite
Si le code injecté ne survit pas à un redémarrage, il peut toutefois servir à installer d’autres programmes malveillants qui, eux, se relanceront à chaque démarrage.
Reste que l’attaque suppose d’avoir déjà accès au réseau local de la cible, ce qui la réserve à un employé malveillant ou à un attaquant déjà infiltré cherchant à étendre ses droits. Elle doit en outre être ajustée à chaque modèle et à chaque version de firmware.
Le correctif disponible tient en quelques lignes, mais c’est bien son déploiement qui risque de poser problème. Il devra passer des fournisseurs de firmware aux fabricants de serveurs, puis à chaque administrateur, chargé de mettre à jour le BIOS de ses machines.
Les entreprises sont invitées à interroger le fabricant de leur firmware et, si possible, à désactiver le démarrage réseau. Sur les serveurs qui ne recevront plus jamais de mise à jour, la faille restera ouverte, d’où ce « bug éternel ».

articles.title: Australia advierte sobre el uso de la IA por gobiernos extranjeros para hackear infraestructura crítica
articles.text:
La Dirección Australiana de Señales advirtió que la inteligencia artificial constituye una amenaza “sin precedentes” para la ciberseguridad del país, ya que gobiernos extranjeros recurren a esta tecnología para atacar redes informáticas e infraestructura crítica.
El organismo detalló que, en el último año, delincuentes y hackers patrocinados por Estados han utilizado modelos de IA para lanzar ofensivas a una escala mayor que en cualquier período anterior.
Cómo la inteligencia artificial potencia los ciberataques a infraestructura crítica
El informe anual de la ASD sobre amenazas cibernéticas identifica a la inteligencia artificial como el factor que más ha transformado el panorama de riesgos digitales durante los últimos doce meses. Según el documento, esta tecnología permite a los actores maliciosos detectar vulnerabilidades con mayor rapidez y explotarlas con una sofisticación inédita hasta ahora.
“La IA ha sido la fuerza determinante en el panorama de las amenazas cibernéticas durante el último año, permitiendo a los actores maliciosos encontrar vulnerabilidades más rápido y explotarlas a una escala, velocidad y sofisticación sin precedentes”, señala el reporte de la agencia.
El organismo reconoció, sin embargo, que los modelos de IA no representan únicamente un riesgo. La propia ASD utilizó herramientas de esta tecnología para la elaboración de su informe anual, lo que evidencia el potencial beneficioso de estos sistemas cuando se emplean con fines legítimos.
La inquietud por el poder de las herramientas avanzadas de inteligencia artificial no se limita a Australia. A nivel global, la preocupación ha crecido tras una serie de incidentes de piratería que involucraron modelos desarrollados por compañías líderes del sector, entre ellas OpenAI y Anthropic.
Aumento de advertencias de ciberseguridad en Australia
Los datos recopilados por la agencia reflejan un incremento sustancial en la actividad maliciosa registrada en el país. La ASD emitió más de 4.400 advertencias sobre posibles ataques durante el último año, una cifra que representa un aumento del 80% respecto al período anterior.
Este salto en las alertas confirma la tendencia señalada por el organismo: la masificación de herramientas de inteligencia artificial ha facilitado que un mayor número de actores, tanto criminales como estatales, identifiquen puntos débiles en los sistemas informáticos con menor esfuerzo y en menos tiempo.
Hackers vinculados a China, Rusia y Corea del Norte apuntan a Australia
El reporte de la agencia también identificó el origen de buena parte de las amenazas detectadas. Hackers vinculados a China, Rusia y Corea del Norte han dirigido ataques contra Australia o contra sus aliados en los últimos meses, de acuerdo con lo documentado por la ASD.
Esta información se enmarca dentro de un contexto más amplio de tensión cibernética entre potencias globales, donde el uso de inteligencia artificial se suma como una herramienta adicional al arsenal de los grupos de hackers patrocinados por Estados.
Vulnerabilidad crítica en PHP detectada mediante inteligencia artificial
Uno de los episodios más recientes citados en el informe ocurrió este mes, cuando gobiernos y empresas debieron corregir con urgencia fallas críticas detectadas en PHP, el lenguaje de programación que da soporte a una gran parte de los sitios web del mundo.
La particularidad de este caso radica en el método empleado para hallar la falla: la vulnerabilidad se detectó mediante el uso de un modelo avanzado de OpenAI, lo que ilustra la doble naturaleza de la inteligencia artificial en el terreno de la ciberseguridad, capaz tanto de exponer riesgos como de ser utilizada para explotarlos.

articles.title: Jio Platforms gains 27% on day one of listing, becomes second most valued company in India
articles.text:
Jio Platforms gains 27% on day one of listing, becomes second most valued company in India
Jio Platforms exceeded market expectations with a 26.81% gain on day one of listing and a market capitalisation of Rs 13 lakh crore.
After making a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange today, the shares of Jio Platforms closed at Rs 1,419, at a gain of 26.81%.
Jio Platforms achieved a market capitalisation of Rs 13,06,761.47 crore on its first day of trading, making it the second most valued company on the Indian stock markets, next only only to its parent firm Reliance Industries.
The top five Indian companies in terms of market capitalisation now are: Reliance Industries (Rs 16 lakh crore), Jio Platforms (Rs 13 lakh crore), Bharti Airtel (Rs 12 lakh crore), HDFC Bank (Rs 10.57 lakh crore), and ICICI Bank (Rs 9.89 lakh crore). Tata Consultancy Services has moved to the sixth place (Rs 8.90 lakh crore).
Jio Platforms' share opened at Rs 1,358 today, gaining 21.3% over the issue price of Rs 1,119 apiece.
The company's Rs 30,213-crore IPO received an overwhelming response from investors last week. It was oversubscribed in less than two hours on opening day, and closed with a 22X oversubscription.
As it positions itself as a technology firm, Jio Platforms is betting on digital services, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing to drive growth beyond telecom.
"There is no either-or at Jio: the network is our technology," said Akash Ambani, Managing Director of Jio Platforms, highlighting the company's in-house 5G core, cloud-native radio access network, and software platform serving 533.3 million customers.
“Connectivity was the first product we built on that platform. Digital services, AI and cloud are what we are layering on top of it now," he said.
Meanwhile, brokerage houses are bullish on the prospects of Jio Platforms.
Motilal Oswal, in its note, said scaling up digital platforms (cloud, enterprise communications, IoT, and managed services, along with international tie-ups for 5G/UBR technology) will offer Jio Platforms the next leg of growth beyond the connectivity business.
The brokerage house has set a bull-case target price of Rs 1,690 crore and a bear-case target price of Rs 1,035.

articles.title: Ce moteur invisible de l'IPTV pirate alimentait des dizaines de sites : il ferme sans explication
articles.text:
Peu connu du grand public, Streamed alimentait pourtant des dizaines de sites pirates, dont la fréquentation cumulée atteignait plusieurs centaines de millions de visites mensuelles. Ce "moteur invisible" vient de mettre fin à ses activités ; une disparition qui révèle la dépendance de ces plateformes illicites à quelques infrastructures communes.
Un message d'adieu et fin du spectacle ! Depuis le 27 octobre, Streamed annonce avoir cessé ses activités, sans fournir la moindre explication. En effet, plusieurs domaines associés au service affichent désormais ce message. Pour les sites qui utilisaient ses lecteurs vidéo, cette fermeture peut avoir des conséquences immédiates.
Un fournisseur presque invisible derrière des dizaines de sites pirates
Streamed n'était pas seulement un site permettant de regarder du sport gratuitement. Il fournissait surtout une infrastructure de diffusion que d'autres plateformes pouvaient intégrer directement à leurs pages, sans avoir à héberger elles-mêmes les retransmissions.
Ce modèle, appelé Piracy-as-a-Service, permet à un site pirate de proposer des matchs en direct en s'appuyant sur un fournisseur extérieur. Plusieurs plateformes peuvent ainsi afficher des lecteurs différents en apparence, tout en dépendant des mêmes serveurs pour acheminer les images.
L'ampleur du réseau apparaît dans un document transmis début octobre au gouvernement américain par la Motion Picture Association (MPA). Selon les données Similarweb citées par l'organisation, une trentaine de sites utilisaient Streamed en juillet 2026, pour un total de 463 millions de visites cumulées sur le mois, contre 134 millions un an plus tôt. Attention toutefois : ces chiffres correspondent à la fréquentation des sites utilisant Streamed, et non à celle du fournisseur lui-même.
Parmi les plateformes concernées figurait notamment Mapple, dont certaines retransmissions renvoyaient déjà une erreur 404 au moment des vérifications menées par TorrentFreak. La disparition d'un seul intermédiaire peut donc perturber simultanément plusieurs services.
Une fermeture mystérieuse, mais pas forcément une victoire des ayants droit
Pourquoi Streamed a-t-il cessé ses activités ? Pour l'instant, personne ne le sait. Ses opérateurs se contentent de remercier leurs utilisateurs et les orientent vers plusieurs plateformes concurrentes.
La fermeture intervient quelques semaines après que la MPA a désigné Streamed comme une menace importante dans son rapport annuel sur les marchés du piratage. Mais aucune saisie judiciaire n'a été annoncée et ni la MPA ni l'Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE) n'ont revendiqué d'intervention. Il serait donc prématuré de présenter cette disparition comme le résultat d'une opération antipiratage.
L'affaire illustre néanmoins une fragilité de l'écosystème du streaming illégal. Derrière la multiplication des adresses et des sites accessibles gratuitement, les infrastructures de diffusion peuvent être beaucoup plus concentrées qu'il n'y paraît.
Fermer un fournisseur commun peut ainsi affecter davantage de plateformes que le blocage d'un seul domaine. Mais l'inverse est également vrai : les sites concernés peuvent chercher d'autres sources pour rétablir leurs retransmissions. La disparition de Streamed perturbe donc une partie du réseau, sans démontrer que le piratage sportif recule durablement.

articles.title: MacBook Neo 2 : on a une bonne et une mauvaise nouvelle sur le futur PC abordable d'Apple
articles.text:
Apple devrait présenter ce mercredi 28 octobre son premier MacBook Pro avec un écran tactile. Mais ce jour, c’est aussi le MacBook Neo 2 qui fait parler de lui, alors qu’il n’est pas attendu avant plusieurs mois. Au programme : quelques améliorations, mais aussi quelques inquiétudes sur le prix du MacBook le moins cher d’Apple.
En 2027, il devrait y avoir un deuxième MacBook Neo
Comme souvent, c’est le journaliste de Bloomberg Mark Gurman qui nous informe des projets d’Apple. Cette fois-ci, il explique qu’Apple préparerait des versions améliorées des MacBook Air (avec la puce M6) et MacBook Neo. Arrivée prévue « pour le premier semestre de l’année prochaine », écrit-il. Un renouvellement pas surprenant, puisque cette machine a rencontré un énorme succès à sa sortie, au point de connaître des ruptures de stocks.
Aujourd’hui, le MacBook Neo est équipé de 8 Go de RAM. Une quantité de mémoire vive qui commence à ne plus suffire : les fonctions d’IA les plus avancées de macOS 27 demandent 12 Go de RAM minimum (et une puce M3 minimum). Avec sa puce d’iPhone 16 Pro, le MacBook Neo fait pâle figure, alors même que la gamme Air commence à 16 Go. C’est pourquoi Apple chercherait à faire passer le Neo 2 à 12 Go de RAM. Le tout grâce à une puce A19 Pro, qu’on trouve dans les iPhone 17 Pro, Pro Max et iPhone Air.
Pour le moment, on ignore quels seraient les autres changements à venir sur cette deuxième itération du Neo. On sait seulement qu’il pourrait être décliné dans de nouveaux coloris ; actuellement il existe en argent, rose, jaune et bleu.
Attention au prix du MacBook Neo 2
C’est là que l’épineuse question du prix arrive. À sa sortie, le MacBook Neo était vendu à 699 euros (et même 599 euros avec la réduction étudiante !), du jamais vu pour un ordinateur portable de la marque. Mais patatras en juin dernier : le prix augmente de 100 euros, avec en cause, la hausse du prix des composants et principalement de la mémoire vive. Et ce n’était pas le seul produit Apple à voir son prix augmenter ce jour-là.
Apple voudrait donc passer à 12 Go de RAM, ce qui aura un impact évident sur le prix. Si le MacBook Neo 2 sort durant la première moitié de 2027 (peut-être en mars comme le premier), difficile de penser que le prix serait maintenu à 799 euros. Une augmentation qui irait à l’encontre même de la raison d’être du modèle Neo : un ordinateur portable « simple », conçu pour la bureautique légère, endurant, qu’on transporte partout, mais surtout qui est abordable en termes de prix.

articles.title: Discord to let search engines index public server messages
articles.text:
Discord will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation.
The goal is to surface useful information to the wider internet community instead of keeping it buried in Discord conversations.
“Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord,” the messaging platform explains.
The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers, publicly listed communities with at least 1,000 members. The platform says it hosts approximately 63,000 such servers.
This decision excludes private servers, direct messages between users, and group announcements on servers that don’t meet the requirements.
According to the company's schedule, the rollout will happen in two stages:
- On November 16, every Discoverable Server will get a public Server Web Page which will display automatically generated summaries of active conversations from that date onward.
- Starting mid-December, every eligible message posted on Discoverable Servers will appear on the Server Web Page and may be indexed by web search engines.
Server Web Pages will be automatically created on November 16 if admins haven’t created them by then, and the only way to avoid them is to change the server type to private before the cutoff date.
Discord has been piloting Community Messages and Server Web Pages in the NBA 2K, Rust, and Dead by Daylight gaming groups.
The December rollout will be gradual, and Discord says messages posted before the release date will be excluded.
Channel administrators can choose to exclude individual channels or turn off all channel content sharing entirely using controls available under Server Settings > Web Presence.
Community members can also control if their messages appear on the Server Web Page through User Settings > Data and Privacy. However, changing that setting only affects future messages, and past messages that became public cannot be retracted.
If admins and users leave the settings at their defaults, their content will automatically be included in the new sharing scheme.
However, message sharing will stay off by default in all EU countries, the UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea. In those places, members must explicitly enable it in their privacy settings.
Underage users are automatically excluded and cannot activate the feature until they turn 18.

articles.title: Discord quiere que los mensajes de sus servidores públicos se puedan buscar en Google, con todo lo que eso conlleva
articles.text:
Discord ha anunciado que los servidores que sean públicos podrán configurarse para ser localizables por los motores de búsqueda. La empresa afirma que el objetivo es rescatar respuestas útiles que ahora se encuentran enterradas en los chat. Una especie de acercamiento a Reddit que puede ayudar a mucha gente a encontrar respuestas útiles, pero que algunos usuarios ven también un problema de privacidad.
Qué pasa. El cambio se aplica únicamente a los "Servidores descubribles" (Discoverable Servers), que es básicamente el nivel más público de Discord. Se trata de servidores con al menos 1.000 miembros, y que los administradores han elegido listar en el directorio de descubrimiento de Discord para que cualquiera pueda unirse sin un enlace de invitación.
Discord afirma que hay más de 63.000 de ellos. La compañía recalca que los servidores privados, los mensajes directos y los mensajes directos grupales no se ven afectados por esta medida. Ni siquiera los servidores comunitarios más pequeños que requieren invitación.
Por qué lo hace Discord. En su anuncio, Discord argumenta que muchas conversaciones que antes vivían en foros se han trasladado a sus servidores, dejando información valiosa "bloqueada en las conversaciones de Discord, inaccesible para el resto de internet". Y la empresa afirma ahora que quiere ponerle solución.
Qué cambia y cuándo. Discord ha establecido el despliegue en dos fases, siendo el próximo 16 de noviembre el día en el que todos los servidores descubribles obtendrán una página web pública. La compañía afirma que, los servidores que no hayan configurado una recibirán una página predeterminada creada a partir de su perfil de servidor. Estas páginas también mostrarán resúmenes automatizados de las conversaciones activas.
Por otra parte, a mediados de diciembre, los mensajes de los canales públicos podrán empezar a aparecer en esas páginas y en las búsquedas web. Discord afirma que el despliegue será gradual, por lo que es posible que tarden unas semanas en aparecer los primeros mensajes. La compañía afirma que los nombres de usuario y los avatares no aparecerán junto a los mensajes publicados, y que los mensajes enviados antes de mediados de diciembre tampoco se incluirán.
Qué pueden controlar los usuarios y los admins. Discord afirma que los controles ya están disponibles, antes de que nada entre en funcionamiento. Los administradores pueden elegir qué canales participan, o excluir todos ellos. Y si no cambian nada, los canales públicos se mantendrán incluidos por defecto. Además, los miembros pueden desactivar la visibilidad de sus mensajes. Según Discord, existe un único interruptor para hacer que dejen de ser visibles esos mensajes en todos los servidores públicos a los que pertenecen.
Por otra parte, la empresa señala que los resúmenes de los canales se generan por separado de los mensajes individuales. Según Discord, seguirán apareciendo en las páginas de los servidores a menos que los administradores los desactiven. Y también está el tema de las etiquetas, pues los canales cuyo contenido pueda aparecer en la web estarán marcados, para que los miembros lo sepan antes de publicar, al igual que ocurre en Reddit.
División. Tal y como cuentan algunos usuarios en Reddit, publicar en un servidor público de Discord no significa aceptar ser encontrado en todo internet, ya que la gente escribe para una comunidad y un contexto específicos. Otros plantean que las conversaciones indexadas públicamente puedan terminar utilizándose como datos de entrenamiento para modelos de IA.
Discord terminó de matar a los foros en internet, pero es cierto que la gran mayoría de las conversaciones pueden ser útiles para usuarios ajenos a la aplicación. Si ya filtrabas en Google por respuestas solamente de Reddit, ahora con esta medida podrás hacer lo mismo para Discord, o al menos en sus servidores públicos.
Exponer chats a internet, y a la IA. El problema en términos de privacidad no es poco, y precisamente fue también el tema de debate principal durante la polémica sobre los acuerdos para compartir datos en Reddit. En la información de Discord no se aborda directamente el tema de la IA, pero poco se les escapa a estos sistemas automatizados una vez algo es público.
Otra cuestión que provoca discordia (hehe) es que, fuera de un puñado de regiones, los miembros se inscriben a estos cambios por defecto a menos que lo desactiven. En la UE, el Reino Unido, Canadá, Brasil, Australia y Corea del Sur, la configuración está desactivada por defecto debido, por lo que los mensajes solo aparecen si los usuarios la activan. Además, los usuarios que no hayan especificado ser mayores de edad no pueden activarla.
Hasta ahora, Discord ha probado la función de forma limitada en las comunidades de juegos como NBA 2K, Rust y Dead by Daylight, donde, según la empresa, solo se mostraban posts de administradores y moderadores. Queda ver cómo se encaja esta medida una vez entre en vigor.

articles.title: Statt Spielfiguren jetzt Server: Playmobil-Mutter baut Stammwerk zum Rechenzentrum um
articles.text:
Statt Spielfiguren jetzt Server: Playmobil-Mutter baut Stammwerk zum Rechenzentrum um
Wo noch bis vor kurzem Playmobil-Spielwaren produziert wurden, entsteht jetzt ein Hochleistungs-Rechenzentrum: Die Playmobil-Mutter Horst-Brandstätter-Group baut auf dem Gelände ihres Werks in Dietenhofen einen Rechen-Campus, der auf eine Leistung von 100 Megawatt ausgelegt sei und Potenzial darüber hinaus habe, wie das Unternehmen mitteilte.
Modulares System für Rechenzentrum geplant
Brandstätter stellt die Infrastruktur, Partner sollen die jeweiligen Anwendungen teils in Eigenregie bewerkstelligen. Die Angebote reichen vom bloßen Bereitstellen der Flächen mit entsprechender Netzanbindung bis zur fertigen Rechenleistung.
Die Sparte Playmobil digital sei ein neuer, eigenständiger Zweig in der Unternehmensgruppe. Bau und Betrieb des Campus werden von einem Team verantwortet, das mehr als 25 Jahre Erfahrung in den Bereichen Rechenzentren und IT aufweise.
Günstige Netzanbindung
Der Standort in Dietenhofen biete gute Voraussetzungen für ein Rechenzentrum. Auf dem Playmobil-Areal bestehe bereits eine Anbindung an eine 110-Kilovolt-Leitung. Der Netzbetreiber N-ERGIE in Nürnberg habe die entsprechenden Netzkapazitäten zugesichert.
„Wo über Jahrzehnte Playmobil produziert wurde, wollen wir künftig eine der wichtigsten Infrastrukturen der digitalen Zukunft ermöglichen“, sagte Brandstätter-Vorstand Matthias Fauser. Große Rechnerleistungen sind vor allem für Anwendungen der Künstlichen Intelligenz in Zukunft mehr und mehr von Bedeutung.
Spielwaren-Produktion geschlossen
Das Gelände in Dietenhofen war bis zum Sommer das einzige deutsche Werk, in dem Playmobil Spielwaren produziert hatte. Es wurde Ende Juni geschlossen, die Produktion wurde ins Ausland verlagert. 350 Mitarbeitende verloren ihren Arbeitsplatz. Die Marke Playmobil steht bereits seit längerer Zeit wirtschaftlich unter Druck.

articles.title: Assez puissant pour un MacBook Pro, ce chargeur Ugreen 100W ultra-compact perd 24 % de son prix — Frandroid
articles.text:
Un chargeur de 100 W, c’est d’ordinaire un bloc qui prend toute la place sur la multiprise. Avec sa gamme Nexode Air, Ugreen mise sur un format ultra-compact. Ce modèle a beau uniquement intégrer un seul port USB-C, il charge aussi bien un iPhone 18 Pro ou un Galaxy S26 qu’un MacBook Pro. En ce moment, ce petit accessoire profite de 24 % de réduction sur Amazon.
Pourquoi choisir l’Ugreen Nexode Air 100W ?
- Une puissance de 100 W sur un unique port USB-C
- Un format ultra-compact
- Un câble USB-C de 1 mètre compatible 100 W fourni
Habituellement affiché à 49,99 euros, le Nexode Air 100W est aujourd’hui en promotion à 37,99 euros sur Amazon.
Un 100 W qui ne monopolise pas la multiprise
C’est sans doute son plus grand atout : le chargeur Ugreen Nexode Air 100W brille par un gabarit ultra-compact qui permet de l’emporter partout, qu’il soit glissé au fond d’une poche ou dans la housse de votre ordinateur portable.
Pour réussir ce tour de force, la marque s’appuie sur la technologie au nitrure de gallium (GaN II), qui permet de réduire l’encombrement de 74 % par rapport à un bloc secteur classique de même puissance, tout en limitant la chauffe et en optimisant le rendement énergétique. Une surveillance de la température ajuste la chauffe pendant la charge. En revanche, il n’y a qu’un seul port USB-C. Il ne sera donc possible de recharger qu’un seul appareil à la fois.
De quoi recharger un smartphone comme un MacBook
Avec son unique port USB-C, le Nexode Air est capable de délivrer une puissance de 100 W. D’après la marque, il recharge un iPhone 18 Pro ou iPhone 18 Pro Max à 50 % en 15 minutes, et à 80 % en 30 minutes. Il doit cette vitesse au protocole AVS, qu’Apple exige (avec au moins 60 W) pour charger ses iPhone 18 Pro au plus vite. Un MacBook Pro 14 pouces grimpe à 55 % en 30 minutes. Sur les MacBook Pro 16 pouces, qui acceptent jusqu’à 140 W, la charge sera plus lente qu’avec le bloc d’origine.
Côté compatibilité, il gère la norme USB Power Delivery et le protocole PPS (en 45 et 60 W), ce qui lui permet notamment de délivrer la charge la plus rapide sur les smartphones Samsung Galaxy. Il alimente tout aussi facilement un iPad, un Google Pixel ou encore une console portable comme le Steam Deck. Gardez en tête qu’aucun smartphone n’utilise les 100 W : cette marge sert surtout aux ordinateurs portables et aux tablettes.

articles.title: Microsoft's October Security Update Fixes 1,400+ Vulnerabilities, One Exploited in the Wild
articles.text:
Microsoft's latest monthly security update addresses 1415 vulnerabilities across multiple products. One vulnerability affecting Windows Shell has been exploited in the wild, while 85 are classified as critical. Affected products include Windows OS, Office, Exchange, .NET, Edge, as well as potentially Hyper-V and Azure components.
CVE-2026-96951 enables to inject special elements into Windows Shell, "allowing an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network", specifically the Mark of the Web (MOTW) defenses. Microsoft notes that a potential attack vector is an email or instant message containing a maliciously crafted file designed to exploit the vulnerability. However,
In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action. For example, an attacker could entice a user to either click a link that directs the user to the attacker's site or send a malicious attachment.
Reddit user falconupkid, a moderator of the r/SecOpsDaily community, warned that
With this volume, expect a high number of "wormable" or pre-auth RCEs that will require immediate prioritization. The sheer noise will make it easy to miss the critical few.
They also pointed out that, given the scale of the patch, the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation should be considered "effectively zero". They recommends prioritizing all CVEs with a severity higher than 9.0 and planning remediation accordingly, including against potential regressions.
Security expert Brian Krebs highlighted a vulnerability in the .NET Framework allowing a security feature bypass; CVE-2026-108398 "was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug". However, Microsoft reported no evidence of exploitation to date.
Reddit user Odd_Round9576 shared their negative experience after applying one of the patches, confirming the importance of deploying updates in stages, rather than all at once, and monitoring for potential regressions:
Be careful with KB5127648 - it broke our WPA-Enterprise Wifi. After installing and rebooting, clients were no longer able to join a WPA-Enterprise network. Uninstalling the update resolves the issue
On a similar note, Appropriate-Pipeline6575 reported that the update broke their IPSec VPN on some laptops, preventing coworkers from connecting.
While the growing number of vulnerabilities identified in recent months, potentially driven in part by the use of AI agents, may ultimately improve security, it also places an additional burden on security teams, Krebs notes:
Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
For a complete review of the patched vulnerabilities check Patch Tuesday and the Internet Storm Center

articles.title: Upwind Security Raises $400 Million at $3.8 Billion Valuation
articles.text:
Upwind Security Raises $400 Million at $3.8 Billion Valuation
The massive funding round comes just days after reports emerged that Upwind had attracted acquisition interest from several companies, including Datadog
Upwind Security today announced a $400 million Series C funding round at a $3.8 billion valuation. Coming just nine months after the company announced a $250 funding round at $1.5 billion valuation, the investment brings the total amount raised by the company to over $800 million.
Upwind offers a runtime-native cloud security platform that provides organizations with increased visibility into networks, APIs, and data flows, which the company says is used by hundreds of organizations, including Siemens, Roku, and Nubank.
Upwind explains that its platform “uses runtime intelligence to help security, development, and DevOps teams identify their most critical exposures, remediate risks proactively, and detect attacks in real time.”
Headquartered in San Francisco, California, Upwind was founded in 2022 by Amiram Shachar, who previously founded Spot.io, which was acquired by NetApp for $450 million.
The latest funding round was led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Canapi Ventures and existing investors including TCV, Greylock Partners, Salesforce Ventures.
The massive funding round comes just days after reports emerged that Upwind had attracted acquisition interest from several companies, including Datadog. According to The Information, Datadog had offered nearly $4 billion to acquire the cybersecurity security startup, while other potential buyers had also expressed interest. However, Israeli technology publication CTechquestioned the report, citing information indicating that Datadog had not made the alleged offer.

articles.title: Amazon anuncia os novos Echo Dot, Echo Time e Echo Studio; veja preços • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Amazon anuncia os novos Echo Dot, Echo Time e Echo Studio; veja preços
Amazon Echo Time é destaque por funcionar como um despertador inteligente. Todos foram anunciados para o mercado brasileiro.
A Amazon atualizou a linha Echo com três dispositivos. Estamos falando dos novos Echo Dot, Echo Time e Echo Studio com Câmera. Todos são compatíveis com a Alexa, obviamente, sendo também capazes de funcionar com a Alexa+.
As novidades foram anunciadas para vários países, incluindo o Brasil. Por aqui, os preços começam em R$ 819.
O Echo Dot continua sendo um alto-falante portátil e com corpo arredondado. Mas, agora, o gadget pode funcionar como um “hub de casa inteligente”, que não depende de um aparelho externo para gerenciar outros dispositivos inteligentes do lar. Para quem prioriza o aspecto sonoro, a novidade está na acústica aprimorada para permitir que o alto-falante reproduza graves 50% mais intensos.
O Echo Time não é uma atualização, mas um dispositivo novo. Na primeira olhada, ele remete a um Echo Dot, só que com tela. A sua principal função é atuar como um despertador inteligente. Nesse sentido, o destaque fica para a tecnologia Omnisense, que monitora parâmetros específicos para despertar o usuário em momentos de sono leve. A tela fica mais escura à noite e aumenta o brilho gradualmente conforme o nascer do Sol.
O Echo Studio já existia, mas, agora, traz câmera integrada, como o nome deixa claro. O componente tem sensor de 13 megapixels e traz o recurso Visão Inteligente, que “permite que a Alexa+ veja e entenda o que está à sua frente e ajude em tempo real”, segundo a Amazon. Outro destaque é a função Live View (Vídeo ao Vivo), que monitora a casa na sua ausência. Quanto ao aspecto sonoro, um dos atributos é a tecnologia Áudio Espacial Imersivo.
No Brasil, o novo Echo Dot e o Echo Time já estão em pré-venda no site da Amazon, embora o lançamento oficial esteja previsto somente para 11 de novembro de 2026. Já o Echo Studio com Câmera chegará “em breve”, de acordo com a companhia.

articles.title: Palit says the Galax factory isn't closing, despite a report blaming Nvidia chip shortages
articles.text:
What just happened? For the second time this year, the Galax graphics card brand has been forced to deny that it's in trouble. This time, brand owner Palit confirmed that its Galax factory wasn't closing down due to Nvidia not supplying enough RTX 5000 chips, something that had been rumored.
Palit's official statement says it is aware of recent reports and speculation regarding Galax's business operations. It adds that the brand continues to operate as usual, no manufacturing facilities have been shut down, and Galax products remain available in both domestic and international markets.
The statement also notes that Galax and Palit share the same manufacturing facilities, with production and business operations continuing as normal.
The rumors stemmed from an "exclusive" news report by a Spanish outlet, which claimed industry sources had confirmed Palit was closing the Galax factory as Nvidia couldn't provide enough RTX 5000 chips to keep it running.
 – 포시포시 (@harukaze5719) October 28, 2026
This would have been an especially surprising turn of events, given that Galax launched the GeForce RTX 5080 HOF Extreme - the world's first RTX 5080 with two 16-pin connectors - only last week.
It's easy to understand why people might have believed this report. There have long been rumors that Nvidia is prioritizing the GB202 chip used in the RTX 5090 for the more lucrative RTX Pro Blackwell-based models. It had even been claimed that the flagship was being discontinued, though Nvidia denied it.
Then there's the whole Palit/Galax situation. In April, Galax was rumored to be doing an EVGA and shutting down entirely. However, Palit, which has owned Galax since 2007, confirmed that it was undergoing a restructuring that brought Galax's operations directly under Palit Group headquarters in Taiwan, sparking the rumors.
The company said at the time that it would continue to develop, produce, and support the Galax, KFA2, and HOF brands to strengthen its presence in the discrete GPU market.
Ultimately, the rumor was just another effect of the AI-driven memory chip crisis that has pushed the price of graphics cards to astronomical levels. The RTX 5090, for example, is hard to find for less than $9,000 these days – and we complained when it arrived with a $2,000 MSRP.

articles.title: Northstar launches with $7M to give AI agents the context to act on security risks - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Northstar launches with $7M to give AI agents the context to act on security risks
Cybersecurity startup Northstar Security AI Inc. launched today with $7 million in new funding to give artificial intelligence agents the context they need to act on security risks.
Northstar offers a platform that feeds data from a company’s existing security and information technology tools into a real-time Security Context Graph. A known vulnerability, an unmanaged device or an overprivileged account can look manageable on its own.
Put together, the same issues can leave a critical business system exposed. Those toxic combinations are what the graph is meant to find, since the underlying data usually sits in tools that don’t share it.
A company laptop with no endpoint protection is the example Northstar uses to illustrate the problem. Working out whether that one device poses a meaningful risk can mean going through six different tools. An analyst on the platform can type that question in plain language.
In that scenario, the reply shows the laptop belongs to a privileged user who can reach the payroll system. Fixing it then falls to Northstar’s AI agents, which can kick off a remediation workflow to push endpoint protection onto the machine. Humans can supervise those steps where appropriate.
The graph is also open to outside AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, so customers can build their own security workflows on Anthropic PBC’s Claude and other AI tools. Northstar currently integrates with more than 70 security and IT systems, including those from Okta Inc., GitHub Inc. and Workday Inc.
Amer Deeba (pictured), Northstar’s co-founder and chief executive, said security teams are “drowning in data but starving for context.” Decades of spending on tools that find problems have left the follow-up work largely manual, he said.
Randy Barr, chief information security officer at Cequence Security Inc., said his team uses Northstar’s agentic workflows to continuously remediate security issues. Security teams don’t need “another dashboard generating more findings,” he said.
Deeba started Northstar with Ed Rowe, its chief technology officer, whom he first worked with at Adobe Inc. in the late 1990s. After senior leadership roles at Qualys Inc., Deeba co-founded Normalyze Inc., a data security posture management startup that Proofpoint Inc. acquired in 2024. Rowe was chief technology officer at Farmers Business Network Inc. AppDynamics Inc. is also on his resume, from a stint as senior vice president of engineering.
MVP Ventures and Outliers Venture Capital joined the seed round, which Wing Venture Capital led. Cybersecurity industry veterans Gerhard Eschelbeck, Renaud Deraison and Justin Somaini invested as individuals.

articles.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026.
Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend.
Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results.
This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending.
Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI.
Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost.
“Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.”
Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers.
“It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own — this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.”
It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. These new reporting tools can be seen as a kind of FDE-lite, a lighter version of that hands-on help, for Anthropic customers.
“We’re at a point now where it’s mature enough, where once you’re in, it’s going to be harder and harder to switch because you’ve spent the effort,” he said. “Even if they’re all mostly the same, they’re all going to be slightly different, have their own slight quirks of how they handle agent.md files, etc., and so that cost to switch is not zero.”

articles.title: Nvidia and Oracle bring Vera CPU instances online in multi-gigawatt deployment
articles.text:
Standalone Nvidia Vera CPUs land in Oracle Cloud's multi-gigawatt deployment — our independent benchmarking of a local server reveals Vera's massive memory bandwidth lead over dual Xeon 6 server
Standalone Vera is generally available on OCI Superclusters now.
Nvidia and Oracle have announced general availability of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Superclusters at Oracle AI World on Tuesday. The announcement comes hot on the heels of Google Cloud announcing general availability for Vera Rubin last week, putting two major hyperscaler feathers in Nvidia’s cap. However, Oracle’s announcement is interesting, specifically calling out standalone Vera instances on OCI Superclusters. We've included a few benchmarks we've performed on a Vera server for a forthcoming review to highlight some of the chip's performance characteristics, but do note that these tests were not conducted on OCI infrastructure.
Neoclouds have been banging the drum of Vera for the past several weeks, with instances under way at Nscale, CoreWeave, and Nebius, among others, so it makes sense to see Vera in the GPU-dominant and AI-focused neoclouds. A standalone deployment at a hyperscaler like Oracle sends a different signal, however.
Although hyperscalers maintain large fleets of hardware, sometimes even renting from the neoclouds, the CPU focus is primarily on x86, with OCI Superclusters otherwise offering the Ampere Altra for an Arm-based instance. It’s Nvidia’s first standalone CPU push into the hyperscale data center, placing Vera alongside the x86 competition regardless of the GPU compute.
Vera is not meant to upend the x86 guard, at least in isolation. Ian Buck, Nvidia’s mind behind CUDA and the face of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure buildout, said in March — when the chip was revealed — that the world couldn’t be served by a single, 88-core SKU. However, Vera is opening the door at hyperscalers like Oracle to expand in future CPU generations.
AMD and Intel maintain the lead when it comes to single-socket density, which is only set to expand in the next generation, as AMD’s upcoming EPYC Venice CPUs can pack up to 512 threads in a single socket. However, Vera offers some distinct advantages due to its topology depending on the workload, many of which are becoming increasingly relevant in the agentic AI era.
Memory bandwidth, for instance, is one of Vera’s strong suits, and that’s not just a marketing claim. Nvidia has said the memory system is capable of 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, but we can see Nvidia’s lead outside of theoretical numbers in our testing below.
Take the industry-standard Stream benchmark as an example. Nvidia’s use of LPDDR5X-9600, along with a monolithic die and distributed mesh for caching, allows it to more than double the bandwidth available on a dual Intel Xeon 6980P system, even when it’s paired with MRDIMMs sporting speeds of 8,800 MT/s. We’re showing triad here, as it’s the most “demanding” of Stream’s operations, but the leads for Vera are similar across add, copy, and scale as well.
This bandwidth is critical for some types of agentic loops, particularly those dealing with large database queries or extensive documentation. You can see the OpenMP “spread” policy offers a massive boost to Vera’s memory bandwidth, as well. Both AMD and Intel maintain centralized memory control and system-level cache, while Vera distributes it in a mesh across the die. The result, at least in OpenMP set properly, is much higher memory bandwidth by binding processes as far away from each other as possible.
Another critical performance vector for agentic AI is Python. The agentic world is expanding, but much of the foundation of the AI software ecosystem is built on Python. Common agentic frameworks like CrewAI and LangGraph are written in Python, and although we’re seeing more frameworks built in languages like Rust and TypeScript, Python performance is still critical to agentic loops.
And, unsurprisingly, it’s an area where Vera is also strong, beating out CPUs that are much more powerful on paper. Popular agentic harnesses are built on Python, but so are many of the applications that also run on Python, including foundational AI libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow.
Nvidia’s focus on agentic AI makes sense given the times we’re living in, but it can miss the forest for the trees. Oracle bringing Vera standalone instances online shifts the focus onto the broader implications of Vera’s entrance into the data center. There are some aspects of performance that characterize agentic AI workloads, but many agent workloads are regular data center workloads in the first place, just under high concurrency.
For instance, SQLite performance is important for any server querying a large database, regardless of its written by logic, a person, or an AI agent. Nvidia’s second-gen Scalable Coherency Fabric (SCF), which we saw at play in Stream, shows up in a real workload here, with these database queries largely bound by data movement across the system.
And that is what makes Vera so interesting in the context of Oracle’s announcement. It’s a CPU built for agentic AI, says Nvidia, but the crosstalk with general data center workloads is strong. It’s not just a CPU to use because you need access to Nvidia’s accelerators. Depending on the workload, it may even be a better choice than the x86 guard.
Ultimately, we have to see how customers of these hyperscalers use (or don’t use) Vera in production. It’s demonstrated its usefulness in agentic AI loops, but it’s also showing early promise in certain general-purpose workloads. Oracle’s standalone deployment is a sign that there’s some demand for Vera that isn't exclusively tied at the hip of a Rubin GPU.
Oracle is approaching cautiously, however, as any hyperscaler should be when bringing up a multi-gigawatt deployment. The company said it will also offer Nvidia’s HGX NVL8, bringing eight Rubin GPUs together in a cluster, connected to a dual, 64-core Intel Xeon 6 host with 4TB of DDR5 memory.
Our testing of Vera shared in this article is part of a larger benchmarking session we had with the chip, and we'll share the technical details of the test setup in our forthcoming review. We’ll be publishing our full results shortly on Tom’s Hardware.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Japanese internet giant GMO tells customers to shut down and disconnect PCs from the internet following data breach and ransomware threat
articles.text:
Japanese internet giant GMO tells customers to shut down and disconnect PCs from the internet following data breach and ransomware threat
Hackers threatened to install ransomware on user devices
- GMO warned customers to back up data, disconnect devices, and shut down systems after a cyberattack
- Attackers allegedly stole customer data, leaked information, and threatened ransomware deployment
- Compromised trading-platform credentials and reports of unauthorized transactions raised concerns for affected users
Japanese internet giant GMO Group has told its customers to scan their computers for viruses, back up all of their data, disconnect the devices from the internet and then shut them down.
The announcement, which literally told customers, “unplug any cords connected to your PC," was made in response to a cyberattack it recently suffered, as well as the threats then made by the malicious actors.
GMO Group gets hit
GMO Internet Group is a large Japanese technology conglomerate whose business spans internet infrastructure, cybersecurity, online advertising, financial services, and more. It brings in billions of dollars every year, and operates a broad portfolio of subsidiaries, among which is Onamae Desktop Cloud, a popular VPS service provider.
Its main customers seem to be individual retail forex (FX) traders in Japan who run automated trading software. It provides a rented Windows desktop hosted on GMO’s servers, allowing customers to keep trading applications running, while being able to shut down their own computers.
On October 20, 2026, the company disclosed having suffered a cyberattack in which threat actors installed malware on some customer environments. Apparently, up to 26,739 servers were at risk, and the company responded by progressively shutting them down, launching an investigation, and cleaning them up.
“We have confirmed that unauthorized access by a third party occurred against Onamae.com Desktop Cloud and that unauthorized programs were installed in some customers’ server environments,” the company said at the time.
The investigation determined that the attackers walked away with sensitive customer data, although it wasn’t said how many customers were compromised, or what types of information were taken. It was also later reported that the unnamed attackers were demanding roughly $50 million in ransom, in exchange for deleting the data. They threatened to release the data on the dark web if the demands aren’t met. Onamae said it wouldn’t pay the attackers, and the data eventually did leak.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Despite the data leaking, no known entities claimed responsibility for the attack.
Condolences money
The attackers also threatened to install ransomware on devices belonging to Onamae customers, triggering the warning and the call for everyone to shut down and unplug their devices:
“1. Request for a full scan of your own device for virus checks 2. Request for backup 3. Request to disconnect network and power from customer PC. Before 12:00 PM on Tuesday, October 27make sure to back up, disconnect the network, turn off the power, and unplug any cords connected to your PC,” the warning, machine-translated from Japanese, reads.
It seems the attackers never acted on their threat, since no ransomware was found on customer servers.
Onamae said it would not pay the attackers, but would instead compensate each customer $30 for their troubles, regardless or not if they actually suffered any damage or not. Those that suffered more meaningful damage will be compensated separately, it was said. Replacement computers were also offered, BleepingComputer reports.
The company has continued its investigation of the attack and is currently analyzing the leaked data to see how many customers were affected, and what is at risk. It also warned the public and the media not to share the leaked information, threatening legal information against those who do.
In one of the updates, Onamae said login credentials and some account details from users of trading platforms MetaTrader 4 and MetaTrader 5 were compromised. “Some customers have reported transactions in their trading accounts that they do not recognize,” it added, before urging customers to reset their passwords and terminate all active sessions.
The full scope of the attack, as well as material damages (which might be substantial), are yet to be seen.

articles.title: Florida county won’t investigate sketchy Flock cameras removed by mystery owners
articles.text:
A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared.
On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents “remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned to get Flock cameras removed, told the Post that she was worried “that data could be anywhere.”
Of the 12 cameras found, five were eventually claimed by city law enforcement, the Post reported. Apparently, a police department mistakenly issued guidance claiming that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit, a Flock spokesperson told the Post, even though the county required individual permits. However, neither Flock nor the city police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce that claimed the sketchy cameras will confirm who gave the guidance.
Over three years, the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s Flock contract ballooned from $22,000 to $470,000 in 2025, the year before the county mandated removals on county roads. However, Erick Gill, a St. Lucie County spokesperson, told the Post that despite ending that nearly half-million-dollar contract, the county lacks resources to investigate who owned the seven other unpermitted cameras found.
“It sounds like when you do something wrong, and you don’t want to get caught, and you kind of just want to sweep it under the rug,” Galindo told the Post.
According to Gill, the county’s goal was to remove the cameras, not to identify owners, which is why the county gave owners 30 days to take the cameras down without facing any questions.
“Our goal was to get the cameras out of the right-of-way within 30 days,” Gill said. “We accomplished that goal.”
Asked for comment, Gill did not address the cameras of unknown origin, only reiterating that the directive was to remove the cameras.
The Post reported that Flock “did not respond to emailed questions about who operated and removed the cameras or the apparent confusion over permitting requirements.” However, a Flock spokesperson told Ars that Flock knows who owned them and simply won’t disclose it to St. Lucie County residents.
“The cameras have been removed and belonged to several different customers,” Flock’s spokesperson said. “Flock does not share specifics regarding individual agency contracts, camera counts, locations, or deployments.”
Flock CEO said protests aren’t “real”
In St. Lucie County, Galindo’s petition makes it clear that some residents were already concerned about the lack of transparency around Flock cameras, and that was before they learned several unpermitted cameras were also collecting their data.
“These high-tech surveillance devices have been installed without clear, publicized consent or adequate discussion with the people they affect—us, the citizens who cherish their privacy and value transparency,” the petition said. Most concerning, the petition emphasized, studies have shown that Flock’s cameras “often lead to invasions of privacy, data misuse, and can even disproportionately affect marginalized communities.”
But Flock has downplayed the mass backlash, as its camera network continues to grow. On Monday, 404 Media shared leaked audio from a private police conference in which Flock CEO Garrett Langley claimed nationwide anti-Flock protests like Galindo’s “are not real” and repeated a disproven conspiracy theory that Russian bots supposedly fueled viral anti-Flock social media posts.
“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley reportedly said. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like, ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things.’”
Seemingly hoping to reassure police facing protests in their own communities, Langley insisted that “it’s anonymous bots, and so it is not real. Inorganic activity has led to organic activity, but when I look at protests across the country, it is the same people with the same signs and the same message. That’s not normal. That’s not organic at all.”
Flock’s line to police ignores that the ACLU has created a toolkit to help communities “DeFlock,” citing genuine concerns that “creepy cameras make it possible to track everyone’s movements” without a warrant. On the day 404 Media leaked Langley’s statements, the ACLU updated its resource providing instructions on how to “Get the Flock out,” while warning about lack of oversight for Flock’s huge camera database.
Flock fights to obscure 100,000 cameras
For Flock protesters, cases like the one in Florida are disturbing, since Flock appears to take great pains to obscure who owns cameras where and how large its camera network is. Talking to the Texas Tribune in August, Flock estimated there are about 120,000 cameras used by law enforcement nationwide, but cybersecurity researcher Joshua Michael recently discovered that the network is nearly twice as large and has since faced legal threats from Flock for sharing his findings publicly.
In a research paper this September, Michael explained how he found a Flock access token that let him retrieve device locations without logging in. He notified Flock of the vulnerability, but he also created a map tracking all the devices. Analyzing that map, Matt Busel, founder of a software studio called Tensorust, noted that Michael exposed a network of 214,073 devices, not 120,000. Most likely, the nearly 100,000 difference represents Flock’s private camera network, which Busel warned is operated without regulatory oversight.
“It is bigger than anything Flock says out loud,” Busel wrote.
Busel told Ars that “it’s concerning” that St. Lucie County isn’t investigating ownership, since Michael’s map and his analysis show how many holes there are in the public’s understanding of how much their movements are tracked by Flock. The company’s statements do not appear to sympathize with residents who fear their data may have been misused by unknown Flock owners.
“Flock’s lack of transparency is a recurring pattern; they seem to prioritize obscuring the network’s footprint over public accountability,” Busel said. “My analysis suggests this isn’t just about localized camera placement but a broader effort to limit visibility into their total operating capacity.”
Instead of increasing transparency as public criticism swells, Flock has moved to protect private camera owners, including seemingly the ones in St. Lucie County. After Michael published the map, Flock sent a cease-and-desist letter, accusing Michael of violating laws by openly encouraging others to download its confidential data.
“An inadvertently exposed credential is not an invitation to access private systems or data,” Flock said.
Flock has demanded that Michael pull down the map, the data file, and his research paper. They’ve also asked Michael to name anyone who received the data. Otherwise, Flock has threatened to sue for injunctive relief, as well as statutory and punitive damages, since they said Michael knew the data was confidential and proprietary.
Michael has no plans to yank the data. On his site, he posted an update noting that “Flock Safety has responded to my research with a cease-and-desist letter threatening litigation. In an email to its customers, the company branded me a malicious actor, announcing it had notified law enforcement. That same email concedes Flock found no indication of unauthorized access to its data when it closed the issue in December, which is precisely the monitoring failure my research warns about. I’m not backing down.”
Asked for comment, Michael sent a statement to Ars, arguing that his research has national security implications. He confirmed that he is currently self-funding his legal defense and accepting donations from supporters on his website.
“Our nation is not protected by ignorance of a risk,” Michael said, adding:
My research on FlockSurveillance.orgdocuments cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences. There is an extremely deep irony in slandering me as a malicious actor, and confirming my thesis in the same email. My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people. Flock Safety has threatened me with litigation, notified law enforcement, and promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline. These actions against my good faith cybersecurity research covering national security should be considered a betrayal to our nation and sovereignty.
“I will not put Flock’s quarterly profits ahead of the security of the United States,” Michael continued. “Today I fund my legal defense myself and I am grateful beyond imagination that Proton is taking a stand to host a mirror of my research map. This is not a problem that will just disappear and the people of our country are rightfully concerned.”
This story was updated on Wednesday to include Michael’s statement.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Carbon, una IA que puede detectar fallos antes que los hackers
articles.text:
A unas semanas del lanzamiento de Gemini 4 Argon, Google ha presentado un nuevo modelo de IA que la compañía describe como el más potente a la fecha. Conocido como Gemini 4 Carbon, esta variante cuenta con capacidades de programación y razonamiento avanzado, así como funciones especializadas en ciberseguridad. Según la tecnológica, Carbon es eficaz para encontrar y corregir fallos de seguridad.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, Gemini 4 Carbon toma el relevo de Argon, que se anunció hace apenas unas semanas. Google ya no quiere dejar pasar mucho tiempo entre un lanzamiento y otro, por lo que agilizó los tiempos de desarrollo para cerrar la brecha con Anthropic y OpenAI. Otro factor para el despliegue de este modelo es la oleada de hackeos por parte de agentes autónomos, los cuales vulneraron múltiples empresas y gobiernos en los últimos meses.
Es aquí donde entra Gemini 4 Carbon, que ofrece un salto considerable con respecto a su predecesor en todas las fases del ciclo de defensa. El modelo se entrenó para identificar fallos en el código, analizar si una vulnerabilidad puede explotarse en condiciones reales y generar correcciones que mitiguen el problema. Google afirma que la ciberseguridad es uno de los campos más importantes para el futuro inmediato de la IA, por lo que ha construido su modelo con este objetivo en mente.
Gemini 4 Carbon es la IA más poderosa de Google para ciberseguridad
En términos de benchmarks, Gemini 4 Carbon obtuvo un 88,2% en SEC-bench Pro, una prueba especializada en detección de vulnerabilidades. En ExploitGym, que se enfoca en validar la explotabilidad de fallos, la IA de Google alcanzó un 54,8%, mientras que en CWE-bench, una referencia para evaluar la capacidad de generar parches efectivos, Carbon logró un 71,1%.
Google menciona que sus ingenieros ya utilizan Gemini 4 Carbon para encontrar errores en bases de código de gran tamaño. La IA puede mantener procesos de análisis durante periodos prolongados, lo cual le otorga una ventaja en auditorías de seguridad a gran escala. En el caso de la generación de código seguro, Carbon duplica la tasa de éxito obtenida por Argon y el equipo de Chrome ya lo usa para corregir vulnerabilidades reales.
La seguridad también se extiende al comportamiento del modelo, donde existen protecciones contra prompt injection. En las pruebas internas, el modelo consiguió bloquear intentos de manipulación indirecta, mientras que en la resistencia frente a ataques, Carbon consigue una reducción cercana al 50%.
El modelo también brilla en desarrollo de software y conocimiento general
Aunque el enfoque de Google y otras empresas está en la ciberseguridad, los modelos también han mejorado en razonamiento y tareas con agentes. En el caso de Gemini 4 Carbon, la IA puede llevar a cabo proyectos de ingeniería de larga duración, ya que el modelo se optimizó para que los agentes puedan trabajar por días manteniendo el contexto necesario para resolver problemas difíciles.
En desarrollo, el nuevo modelo de Google alcanza una puntuación de 1.769 Elo en la clasificación de WebDev Arena, una referencia para evaluar qué tan buena es creando aplicaciones web. Por otro lado, Carbon lidera la versión 5.0 del índice de inteligencia de Artificial Analysis, lo que lo coloca como uno de los modelos más avanzados de propósito general.
Todo lo anterior suena muy bien, excepto porque Gemini 4 Carbon todavía no está disponible para el público general. Google confirmó que ofrecerá un acceso limitado a profesionales de ciberseguridad y socios del programa Fairwind en una primera etapa. Posteriormente, el acceso se ampliará a desarrolladores, empresas y consumidores, por lo que deberemos esperar algunas semanas para poder usarlo.

articles.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
articles.text:
Sponsored
Creating AI value with enterprise context
How establishing a company brain can support more accurate, cost-effective AI and autonomous agents.
In association withAtlan
Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.
An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.
Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.
“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”
The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.
This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
