articles.title: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’
articles.text:
Asked about AI and the trend of college students booing tech CEOs at graduation ceremonies, Instagram head Adam Mosseri acknowledged in an interview that a lot of people really don’t like AI, and it’s not just young people and creatives. Appearing on the Colin and Samir podcast to talk about the launch of widescreen and long-form video for Instagram, Mosseri said he thinks there’s a trend of “more anxiety and more frustration and more anger about AI,” particularly in creative industries:
Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’
The Instagram boss said that worries about AI come down to ‘a fear of being left behind in some way.’
It’s not only getting worse, it’s going to continue to get worse. I think we’re going to see more frustration and anger, some of it founded, some of it unfounded, over the next couple of years, and that’s going to make it hard for a lot of people, not just in the industry.
Mosseri claimed Instagram doesn’t rank AI creators differently, but raised the question of ranking quality, saying, “There’s a lot of great AI content out there, there’s also a lot of AI slop. Do we rank AI content as well as we rank non-AI content? Probably not.” Talking about AI slop again after previously bringing it up in a New Year’s slideshow dump, he said he thinks the term AI “slop” is used “too liberally.”
Instagram began cracking down on AI-generated profiles in August, after launching a label for AI accounts earlier this year, but misleading AI content like celebrity deepfakes remains an issue. Earlier this month, Mosseri said Instagram is “actively working out what to do” about AI fakes, but he noted, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform.”
Mosseri said Instagram is “now starting to require AI accounts to label themselves, because we think it’s important that people know if what they’re looking at is real or not real.” He also acknowledged there are fears around AI, including from creators:
I think people are concerned about a lot of things. I think they’re concerned about owning their content and models getting trained on their content. I think they’re concerned— there’s people who are concerned about safety. They’re concerned about job displacement, having AI displace whatever it is they do, if you’re a content creator or an engineer or a mathematician. I think there’s concerns about— I mean, fundamentally what I think it comes down to when you really have, like, a heart-to-heart with someone is a fear of being left behind in some way.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Echo Time wants to be the smartest thing on your nightstand
articles.text:
Amazon’s new Echo Time wants to be the smartest thing on your nightstand
The Time is an intriguing smart display
- Amazon’s Echo Time is a smart clock with Alexa+ and a 3.2-inch display
- A camera-free design and customizable clock faces set it apart
- Sensors and adaptive lighting aim to improve your wake-up routine
Amazon has long offered a wide variety of smart speakers and smart displays, all powered by Alexa, and more recently, many have gotten the upgrade to Alexa+. Now, after several new devices, from Kindles to tablets with a glare-free Nano Matte coating, Amazon has five more, and the most intriguing is the $199 / £184.99 / AU$379 Echo Time.
A device that earns a spot on your bedside table needs to clear a high bar, and the devices team at Amazon, led by Panos Panay, thinks they’ve cracked it with this one. Speaking to press and creators, Panos called the Echo Time the ‘smartest clock in the world,’ and, first and foremost, it's meant to show you the time in a range of ways.
It really presents itself as a more well-thought-out Echo Spot. Rather than a half-circle display, the Echo Time offers a 3.2-inch screen wrapped in what looks like the body of an Echo Dot Max, with woven mesh on the rear, top, and sides. Controls sit at the top, just above the woven mesh, for volume up, volume down, and microphone mute. It does have microphones you can mute, but the Time notably doesn’t have a camera.
That’s a refreshing admission for a device designed for your nightstand and will likely make the Time more popular than the Spot.
Instead, Echo Time aims to mix clock skills with Alexa+. Like the previous Echo Spot and the forthcoming Apple HomeView, you can customize it with a range of clock faces and even add mini widgets. I saw several designs that look like traditional clocks, with or without hands or numbers, as well as digital ones and others that use photos.
There are some collaborative designs pulling from famous characters like Harry Potter or the Powerpuff Girls — I am hoping for some Disney, Star Wars, or Marvel ones one day. You can swipe left or right to adjust the clock face and long-press to swipe between and customize them.
It can, as you might suspect, function as an alarm clock, but Amazon takes this a step further, as it can raise or lower the brightness of the display and glow light at the bottom to help with your wind-down or wake-up routine. For instance, rather than blaring a loud horn as your alarm, it can intelligently raise the display brightness and work with connected smart home gadgets, like a smart bulb, to help ease your wake-up. It can gradually raise the brightness like a sunrise, and at night, it could start to dim things and even cut blue light from the display. At night, the display can drop to as low as 0.3 nits, meaning that the glow won’t keep you up and the screen can be viewed without burning your retinas.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It will also utilize Omnisense to find the best time to wake you up if you opt in, which is different from Soli on, say, the Google Nest Hub or the Hatch Sleep Clock with sleep tracking. Echo Time isn’t looking to track your sleep but is using these sensors — room temperature, presence detection, ultrasound for breathing, and proximity — to figure out when you’re in a state of lighter sleep and start to wake you up. From there, when an alarm is set, Alexa and the Echo Time can make the call to sound it earlier.
And since it’s running Alexa+, you don’t need to be precise with your asks. You could tell Alexa you have an important meeting at 9 AM, so you need to be up by 7:30 or 7:45 AM, and have it figure out the best routine, potentially setting an alarm but also cueing the lights and hopefully easing you into your day.
With its built-in speakers and screen, you can ask Alexa topical questions and even request music playback, and the Echo Time will happily oblige. It seems like a fully capable Alexa smart display, but it’s unlike the rest of the Echo Show or the standard Echo lineup. Echo Time is squarely built around being a digital clock with Alexa capabilities. And that's a good thing.
Instead of trying to be another smart display that does a little bit of everything, it offers a camera-free design, customizable clock faces, and smart features designed to help you start your day or ease into slumber. It's a more purpose-built Echo, and that could be exactly what makes it worth the space on your nightstand.
At $199.99, it is the same price as the Echo Show 8 and more than the Echo Spot at $109.99. That puts it in an interesting spot in the lineup, and I'm looking forward to spending more time with it soon. Its price puts it firmly in premium smart-clock, smart display territory, so it’ll be interesting to see whether its added features justify the cost over other Echo devices.
Amazon’s also dropping the Amazon Kids Echo Time at $209.99 / £194.99 in Galactic Grape — my favorite — or Cosmic Lime, and it comes bundled with a year of Amazon Kids+. The standard Echo Time comes in Graphite, Glacier White, and Coral Pink for $199.99. Both are available to order now and are shipping now.

articles.title: 'We analyzed 119 million ear data points' — how Samsung builtGalaxy Buds On, its first open-type earbuds
articles.text:
'We analyzed 119 million ear data points' — how Samsung built Galaxy Buds On, its first open-type earbuds
Finding the fit that balances audio and awareness
- Samsung unveils its first open-ear buds
- Galaxy Buds On feature twin drivers for open adaptive listening
- 9.5 hours of battery life
Staying connected to the real world is the hot new thing, or so it seems if you've been paying attention to the parade of new clip-on (or cuff-style) open earbuds arriving from Sony, Anker, and Bose, to name a few. The solution is so good when done well that you'll regularly see these buds occupying a healthy chunk of our best open earbuds buying guide. And now Samsung is joining the trend with its first pair: Galaxy Buds Open.
Unlike over-the-ear headphones or in-ear buds, open-ear options must deliver quality sound without the benefit of an audio seal betwixt your ear canal and the buds' driver housings, and all while not making you feel like you're wearing too-heavy ear cuffs (each earpiece here weighs 6.65g). As a Samsung exec told us, "Designing these buds is a complex challenge because of the unique anatomy of ears and the difficulty to find the perfect balance between a secure fit and a comfortable fit."
Part of that is acknowledging that every ear is different. Samsung told us it used AI and "analyzed 119 million ear data points to find the optimal fit for the widest range of users possible." Engineers used that information to optimize the components, including wire length, weight, bridge length, battery, speaker placement, and to select an alloy that flexes for the clip-on components but also stays secure. Samsung claims you could almost forget you're wearing them.
The sound of things
Samsung sounds confident in the fit, but it also had to do some fairly complex audio engineering to make these open earbuds capable of delivering high-quality audio that doesn't leak out to the person next to you.
One of the most interesting aspects of this audio design is the TwinBoost drivers that can be used to both enhance the open-ear audio quality and cut down on audio leakage. The way it works is the open earbuds project "matching reverse soundwaves" from the rear of the speaker, which could cancel out some of the escaping audio. It's a claim we obviously can't confirm until we test the Galaxy Buds On. This is essentially like active noise cancellation, which these buds lack, but instead of the buds creating antiphase sound waves to counteract the noise leaking into your ears, it uses counteracting sounds to cut down on noise leaking from the speakers near your ears.
Galaxy Buds On can't seal you off from outside sounds; in fact, they're designed not to, but they can help keep your calls clear. To manage call quality, the earbuds include three mics and a "voice pickup unit". Samsung claims the Galaxy Buds On capture your voice through the mics and even "jaw movement" to help isolate your voice from other external noises. For those sounds that are not blocked by these audio features, Samsung added some machine learning to automatically cancel out recognized noises such as car horns and construction work.
The buds also support head gestures for accepting and rejecting calls, Gemini access, and Quick Voice Memos. More impressively, Samsung is rating the Galaxy Buds On for 9.5 hours of audio playback and, with the charge case, a total of 38 hours of battery life. Battery life with calls is 5.5 hours and 25 hours with the charging cradle.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Galaxy Buds On, which are only available in black, list for $229 (AU and UK pricing were unavailable at the time of writing) and in early November. That price puts them a touch cheaper than the excellent (and also noise-reducing) Shokz Openfit Pro, at $249, and makes them quite a bit more affordable than Bose Ultra Open ($299).
We'll have more to say about the actual fit, audio quality, external noise cancellation, and battery life when we get a chance to test out the new Galaxy Buds On. But things are looking good on paper.
Correction 10-28-2026: An earlier version of this story mistakenly called the new Samsung earbuds "Galaxy Buds Open". The formal name is "Samsung Galaxy Buds On".

articles.title: Intel Wants a Quantum Business, Classiq Could Help Build One - EE Times
articles.text:
Intel has spent more than a decade developing the components of a quantum computer, from silicon spin-qubit chips to control electronics and software. Now, with its proposed acquisition of Classiq, the company is looking to turn that research effort into a business.
Classiq develops software that helps users design quantum algorithms and run them across different hardware platforms. For Intel, the company adds a layer at the top of the quantum computing stack, along with relationships with enterprises that are preparing for a time when quantum computers can solve commercially valuable problems.
Intel expects the transaction, which is subject to regulatory approvals, to close in the first half of 2027. The company did not disclose the purchase price.
“We haven’t really done much by way of customer engagement or trying to commercialize our technology,” Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade said on a media call. “We believe we have most of the elements of the quantum computing stack except for the very top platform layer,” which Classiq provides.
The acquisition would allow Intel to offer capabilities extending from quantum chips and control electronics to the software used to develop applications, Ranade said. It would also mark a change in the way Intel views its quantum work.
“This is not going to be a high-margin business from day one,” he said. “This is really a bet on the future.”
That future depends not only on Intel’s ability to scale its own spin-qubit technology, but also on its ability to serve an industry pursuing several competing approaches. Intel said it intends to maintain Classiq’s support for other quantum hardware platforms.
From gates to applications
Classiq was founded on the premise that software would become a bottleneck as quantum hardware advanced, said co-founder and CEO Nir Minerbi.
Early quantum software development was largely limited to gate-level programming, a process he compared to designing a chip at the transistor level. Classiq set out to raise the level of abstraction, allowing developers to describe what they want a quantum program to do while its software synthesizes a circuit.
“We embraced many of the technologies that allowed scaling up in classical computing, like EDA technologies, modeling, synthesis, compilation,” Minerbi said on the media call.
That approach, he said, has allowed enterprises, academic institutions, and governments to begin building quantum teams without requiring every member to be a quantum computing expert. Specialists in a particular industry can contribute knowledge of their own problems while working with people who understand quantum algorithms.
Minerbi said companies using Classiq include BMW, Lufthansa, Comcast, Wells Fargo, and Merck. They are developing applications, building teams, and creating intellectual property as they prepare for more capable quantum hardware.
“All of them are preparing for the day when commercial value could be extracted from this hardware,” he said.
The distinction matters: Customers can use the software to explore and prepare applications today, but Minerbi’s description does not mean those applications are already delivering a commercial advantage on Intel quantum processors.
Intel’s existing software will sit below Classiq’s platform. Classiq synthesizes algorithmic quantum circuits, which then flow into Intel’s hybrid quantum-classical compiler and runtime, according to Anne Matsuura, Intel’s senior director of quantum software and system architecture.
“Our compiler deals with both the quantum and classical parts of a quantum program, and it separates them and optimizes them separately,” Matsuura said on the media call.
Matsuura also clarified that Classiq’s algorithmic circuits are different from the physical circuits and wiring in a quantum computer. Its software operates several layers above the hardware. That division of work reflects a broader challenge in quantum computing: connecting an end user’s problem to hardware whose characteristics vary from one system to another.
Izhar Medalsy, co-founder and CEO of quantum software startup Quantum Elements, sees the two companies as bringing complementary capabilities. In his view, Classiq focuses on translating end-user problems into quantum circuits, while hardware providers must address the characteristics of their particular systems.
“Classiq has done a strong job of understanding enterprise needs,” Medalsy told EE Times. “The acquisition is a signal that Intel wants to engage more directly with end users and their applications.”
Quantum Elements approaches the stack from closer to the hardware, using digital representations of quantum processors to help develop software for different systems. Medalsy described its work and Classiq’s as complementary.
Intel’s spin-qubit bet
Intel has chosen silicon spin qubits as the basis for its own quantum hardware. Unlike some competing approaches, spin qubits can be made using processes related to those used in semiconductor manufacturing—a potential advantage for a company with Intel’s fabrication experience.
Ranade said Intel makes qubit chips and control electronics at its fab in Hillsboro, Oregon. The company calls the respective processes 18AQ, with the Q standing for quantum, and 18AC, with the C standing for cryogenic.
The qubit process uses interconnect geometry and design rules based on Intel’s 18A technology, Ranade said, although the process used to make the qubit device itself is distinct and requires some specialized equipment. He said more than 90% of the process equipment is the same.
Owen Lozman, managing partner of Copenhagen-based quantum investment fund 55 North, sees Intel’s semiconductor manufacturing and packaging capabilities as strengths. The company has also demonstrated an ability to run development and testing cycles quickly, he said. But even with those advantages, Intel faces challenges in scaling spin qubits into a useful quantum computer.
“There are a lot of engineering challenges to overcome, even if you get the physics right,” Lozman told EE Times.
Among them are achieving uniformity across spin qubits and managing the wiring and control signals needed as systems grow. Lozman’s fund has invested in Groove, another company developing spin-qubit technology; he said 55 North does not hold a position in Classiq.
While that hardware development continues, Lozman sees value in giving developers software to prepare applications and understand the resources their algorithms will require. He said the acquisition brings Intel an experienced team working on a layer of software it did not previously own.
“I think you have to kind of move early,” he said. “I think they get an early mover advantage.”
The neutrality question
Intel’s commitment to spin qubits gives it a clear direction for its own hardware. Classiq, however, has built its platform to work across a broader field, where companies are pursuing different approaches and the eventual leaders are not yet clear.
That creates a question for Intel: Can it use Classiq to strengthen its own quantum offering while maintaining the confidence of customers and hardware providers that rely on the software to work across platforms?
For Medalsy, independence matters. His company also works with multiple hardware partners, and he said customers pay close attention to whether a software provider is tied to a particular system. “I think keeping yourself independent and not coupled to any specific hardware provider is extremely important,” he said.
Intel said it intends to continue supporting Classiq’s existing integrations and maintain a hardware-agnostic platform. Medalsy believes the company will have to manage the concerns that come with changing ownership. “Time will tell if the industry will accept that as a neutral play or maybe more of a fully integrated approach,” he said.
Asked what commitments or safeguards would maintain partners’ confidence, Minerbi said the reaction so far had been positive. He argued that hardware vendors need access to end users and that Classiq can help provide it. He did not identify specific safeguards during the call.
Intel’s explanation for keeping the platform open rests on a broader view of its role in the industry. Although its own qubit development will remain focused on spin qubits, Ranade said Intel is open to providing foundry services, photonics, and advanced packaging to companies pursuing other modalities.
“We are completely agnostic to the modality” when it comes to the Classiq platform, he said. “Our intent is to have Classiq continue to support all modalities.”
According to Minerbi, the combination could allow Intel to engage with other hardware providers as well as end users. Those relationships could give Intel customers for its manufacturing capabilities while extending the reach of Classiq’s software.
Lozman said he believes Intel has good reasons to preserve that breadth. Supporting other platforms can give the company visibility across the ecosystem, he said, while helping it recover the value of its investment. But Intel will need to manage those relationships carefully, he said, balancing the advantage of ownership against the value of a platform used by others.
“It’s not easy,” Lozman said. “It will take a lot of discipline.”

articles.title: Payer sans déverrouiller son smartphone ? Google Wallet prépare une nouveauté pour aller plus vite
articles.text:
Payer avec son smartphone est très pratique, mais cela demande quelques préalables, comme le fait de vérifier son identité avec votre empreinte digitale ou un code par exemple avant de valider une transaction. Cette validation reste alors active quelques minutes seulement avant d’expirer. Mais Google Wallet pourrait changer cela pour coller à un système proche de ce qui existe déjà dans l’application pour valider les paiements de titres de transport en commun.
De nouveaux indices dans le code de l’application
C’est dans les paramètres de la version 26.42.1003171897 de l’application Wallet que l’on retrouve une option baptisée « Tap to Pay » (« Payer d’un simple geste »), qui fonctionne notamment grâce au NFC. Actuellement, il est déjà possible de désactiver cette option pour les réseaux de transport en commun pris en charge, ce qui permet de valider un trajet sans déverrouiller son appareil. L’arrivée potentielle de cette option pour les paiements de tous les jours offrirait donc un fonctionnement similaire.
Dans l’onglet « Sécurité », « Tap to Pay » apparaît désormais à côté du paiement de titres de transport en commun. – Source : Android Authority
Bien qu’elle soit visible dans le code en dessous de la mention « Indiquez si vous souhaitez valider votre identité lorsque vous utilisez vos éléments stockés dans Wallet », cette option n’est pas encore opérationnelle. En sélectionnant l’option « Tap to pay », l’application se ferme brutalement à cause d’un bug, ce qui rend pour l’instant impossible l’accès aux éventuels réglages ou détails prévus par Google.
La question de la sécurité
Supprimer l’obligation de déverrouiller son smartphone pour régler des achats pose forcément des questions sur la protection des données et la sécurité de vos comptes bancaires. Si un tiers venait à s’emparer du téléphone, l’absence de vérification préalable vous exposerait immédiatement à des risques de paiements frauduleux.
À lire : Google Wallet change complètement l’affichage de vos cartes de paiement, voici à quoi ça ressemble
L’analyse du code ne permet pas encore de savoir si Google prévoit d’ajouter des garde-fous spécifiques pour encadrer cette nouveauté. Dans la mesure où il s’agit d’une option trouvée dans le code, mais pas encore activée, impossible de savoir si Google se décidera à la déployer ou non et dans quelles conditions. En attendant, dites-nous si vous seriez prêt ou non à sacrifier de la sécurité contre de la praticité.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raphael Gruber, Jan Rothörl, Simon M. Fröhlich, Maarten A. Brems, Fabian Kammerbauer, Maria-Andromachi Syskaki, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Sachin Krishnia, Asle Sudbø, Peter Virnau, Mathias Kläui. articles.title: Sony ISP subsidiary data breach exposes 2.5 million customer records
articles.text:
Sony Network Communications has confirmed a data breach that compromised approximately 2.5 million records containing current and former customers’ personal information.
A Sony Group Corporation subsidiary, the company provides telecommunications and technology services, acting as an internet service provider (ISP) in Japan.
The breach occurred on October 19 and was detected four days later, when the company shut down the compromised servers and blocked external communication.
In an announcement yesterday, the company said that its So-net member database, supporting its internet access service, was accessed by an unauthorized party.
The investigation confirmed that a total of 2,585,481 customer records had been exposed, including the following types of information:
- Full names
- Phone numbers
- Email addresses
- User IDs
- Dates of birth
- Gender
- Internet Connection IDs
No banking, payment card, or other account details were exposed.
An additional 54,401 email addresses from several email services were also exposed along with account passwords. The company advises users to change their passwords.
In the breakdown of exposed records, Sony Network Communications says there are 2,141,986 So-net entries and 443,495 plala (S Course) records. The latter impacts another internet service provider, NTT Docomo, which contracts Sony Network Communications to provide its Docomo Hikari services.
NTT Docomo also notified customers about the breach and warned of phishing emails and fake websites impersonating its d POINT Club and a Universal Studios Japan (USJ) campaign, falsely claiming that recipients had won and prompting them to enter personal information to claim tickets.
Docomo says the incident affects all current Hikari service clients and those who canceled within the preceding six months.
Sony reported the incident to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission and is investigating its cause and scope.
As of October 27, neither company had confirmed misuse of the exposed data in the wild.
Since the start of the year, multiple cyberattacks have targeted high-value companies and providers in Japan.
One of the most recent is the incident at GMO Internet Group and its Onamae Desktop Cloud service, which suffered a widespread malware attack on customer servers.
Telecommunications giant KDDI suffered a breach affecting 12 million customers, and IDC Frontier was targeted by ransomware.
Previously, NTT was hit in early 2025 by hackers who gained access to its systems and stole the data of 18,000 corporate customers.
The recent rate of data breaches is so unprecedented and threatening that the Japanese government held urgent meetings on Monday to plan its response.

articles.title: iPhone 18e : deux nouveautés majeures se précisent, mais Apple refuse toujours de corriger son plus gros défaut
articles.text:
iPhone 18e : deux nouveautés majeures se précisent, mais Apple refuse toujours de corriger son plus gros défaut
Attendu pour le printemps 2027, l’iPhone 18e n’a presque plus de secrets grâce à une nouvelle fuite. Malgré deux évolutions matérielles bienvenues, Apple maintiendrait une concession technique majeure du côté de l’affichage.
Après les iPhone 18 Pro et iPhone Duo, Apple prévoirait de revenir au printemps pour annoncer de nouveaux modèles. Outre les iPhone 18 et Air 2, l’iPhone 18e ferait son apparition, avec deux changements bien précis par rapport à son prédécesseur, l’iPhone 17e. Cependant, son plus gros défaut face aux autres smartphones milieu de gamme ne serait pas gommé, délivrant un écran figé dans le passé malgré une tarification élevée.
De la puissance à n’en plus finir sur l’iPhone 18e, mais à quel prix ?
Pour séduire les acheteurs au premier trimestre 2027, aux alentours de mars, Apple miserait sur deux améliorations ciblées pour l’iPhone 18e selon l’informateur Digital Chat Station. La première concernerait l’intégration de la puce A20, gravée en 2 nanomètres. De quoi offrir un gain notable en performances et en efficacité énergétique par rapport à la puce A19 de 3 nm embarquée sur l’iPhone 17e, le tout possiblement épaulé par 9 Go de RAM au lieu de 8 Go actuellement.
La seconde évolution toucherait la caméra frontale, qui abandonnerait enfin son vieux capteur de 12 Mpx. Bien que la fuite évoque un passage à 24 Mpx, Apple devrait logiquement opter pour l’objectif de 18 Mpx des iPhone 17, déjà réutilisé sur les iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max et Duo.
Vient ensuite le point qui fâche. La source souligne en effet que l’iPhone 18e conserverait son vieillissant taux de rafraîchissement de 60 Hz, toujours associé à une dalle Oled compacte de 6,12 pouces. Un choix qui priverait de nouveau l’appareil du 120 Hz, pourtant généralisé sur les smartphones d’entrée de gamme de nos jours. Pour espérer un affichage plus fluide sur cette déclinaison, il faudrait patienter jusqu’à l’hypothétique iPhone 19e en 2028, qui adopterait au passage la technologie ProMotion, faisant varier la fréquence d’affichage de manière dynamique en fonction du contenu à l’écran.
Pour le module photo arrière, le statu quo dominerait, avec toujours un seul et unique capteur de 48 Mpx, identique aux iPhone 16e et 17e, là où des rivaux multiplient les optiques polyvalentes entre ultra grand-angle et téléobjectif. Une façon pour Apple de contenir la hausse du coût des composants tout en évitant de cannibaliser l’iPhone 18 standard.

articles.title: Le studio Arkane Lyon joue sa survie avec Xbox : un mois de sursis pour éviter la fermeture
articles.text:
Le studio lyonnais derrière Dishonored et le très attendu Marvel’s Blade a obtenu un mois supplémentaire pour trouver un repreneur. Un délai qui pourrait être décisif pour les quelque 217 salariés, alors que Microsoft n’écarte toujours pas une fermeture.
La menace plane toujours sur Arkane Lyon. Après plusieurs mois d’incertitude, le studio français, propriété de Bethesda et de Microsoft, bénéficie d’un sursis supplémentaire pour tenter de sauver son avenir. Mais derrière cette prolongation se cache une réalité préoccupante, puisque sans solution viable, l’un des noms emblématiques du jeu vidéo français pourrait bien disparaître.
Xbox accorde un mois supplémentaire à Arkane Lyon
L’information, rapportée notamment par PC Gamer, confirme que Microsoft a accepté de prolonger d’un mois la période de consultation autour de l’avenir du studio. L’échéance initiale, fixée au 13 novembre 2026, devait permettre de rechercher un éventuel repreneur. Le calendrier est désormais repoussé, mais sans que cela garantisse une issue favorable.
« Nous explorons les différentes options possibles, notamment la recherche d’un partenaire pour accompagner le studio dans la suite du développement », explique un porte-parole de Microsoft.
Une piste particulièrement importante pour Marvel’s Blade, le jeu d’action annoncé en 2023 et toujours en production. Selon des sources citées par le média américain, le projet nécessiterait encore plusieurs années de développement, et le fait de trouver un partenaire capable de reprendre le studio et de financer la suite du projet apparaît donc comme un enjeu majeur.
Microsoft précise que les documents évoquant une fermeture ne constituent pas une décision définitive, mais relèvent de la procédure de consultation. Pour les 217 salariés concernés, le répit reste néanmoins très fragile.
Arkane, énième victime de la restructuration de Microsoft ?
Une situation qui s’inscrit dans une très vaste réorganisation chez Xbox, marquée par des suppressions de postes et des changements profonds au sein de ses studios. En juillet, Microsoft a annoncé une nouvelle vague de réductions d’effectifs, avec environ 3 200 postes concernés à terme dans sa division jeux vidéo.
Le groupe poursuit également ses efforts pour réduire ses coûts. Comme nous l’évoquions récemment, Microsoft a proposé à quelque 60 000 salariés un dispositif de départ volontaire indemnisé, signe que la rationalisation dépasse largement le seul périmètre de Xbox.
En septembre dernier, Satya Nadella défendait cette restructuration et affichait sa confiance dans la capacité de la branche gaming à retrouver la croissance. Mais pour Arkane Lyon, les ambitions financières du groupe se heurtent à une question immédiate, à savoir l’avenir des équipes et de leurs projets.
Le mois supplémentaire pourrait permettre de débloquer une solution. À défaut, la fermeture du studio resterait une possibilité bien réelle, et avec elle, la perspective de voir disparaître un savoir-faire français reconnu, avec un studio fondé à la toute fin des années 90, et dont le tout premier projet était un certain Arx Fatalis.

articles.title: Mehr als 1.000 Mathematiker verpflichten sich, komplett auf KI zu verzichten – das steckt dahinter
articles.text:
Verband gegen KI: Über 1.000 Mathematiker verpflichten sich zum kompletten Verzicht
Manche mathematischen Probleme haben Wissenschaftler:innen jahrzehntelang vor eine scheinbar unlösbare Herausforderung gestellt. KI-Unternehmen setzen ihre Modelle aber immer öfter ein, um diese Rätsel zu lösen. So veröffentlichte OpenAI Anfang des Monats auf einen Schlag 722 Fachartikel, die eine ganze Reihe mathematischer Probleme beweisen oder widerlegen. Einige Wissenschaftler:innen sind davon beeindruckt, viele lehnen diese Vorgehensweise allerdings strikt ab und formieren sich zu einer Gegenbewegung. Mehr als 1.000 von ihnen haben sich jetzt in der Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) darauf verständigt, KI in ihrer Forschung zu meiden.
Mathematik müsse menschlich bleiben
Auf seiner Website erklärt der AHM, er wolle „die Mathematik als menschliches Unterfangen vor der Bedrohung durch Künstliche Intelligenz“ schützen. Ziel sei es dabei auch, die Unabhängigkeit der mathematischen Gemeinschaft vor dem Vordringen unternehmerischer Interessen zu bewahren. „Angesichts der schwerwiegenden gesellschaftlichen, ökologischen und wirtschaftlichen Auswirkungen der KI-Industrie und der Gefahr eines ungebremsten Wachstums der KI bemühen wir uns, uns nicht mitschuldig zu machen“, heißt es weiter.
Nach dem Verständnis der AHM stelle KI eine grundlegende Bedrohung für die wissenschaftliche Praxis und das mathematische Verständnis dar. Mathematischer Fortschritt erfordere menschliches Fachwissen, das durch Schreiben und sorgfältiges Denken entwickelt werde. Die automatisierte Produktion und Rezeption von Mathematik untergrabe daher die intellektuellen Grundlagen des Fachgebiets.
Gegen den Willen der Forschungsgemeinschaft
Unternehmen wie OpenAI hätten laut dem AHM mathematische Probleme ausgewählt, um für die Fähigkeiten ihrer Produkte zu werben, ohne die Folgen für die mathematische Gemeinschaft zu bedenken. In einer Stellungnahme zu den veröffentlichten Fachartikeln verweist der Verband auch auf die zahlreichen Klagen gegen OpenAI, die dem Unternehmen unter anderem Urheberrechtsverletzungen vorwerfen.
Die mathematische Gemeinschaft habe OpenAI nicht gebeten, bestehende Rätsel zu lösen, und weise jeden angeblichen Mehrwert zurück. „Die Veröffentlichung von über 700 Dateien auf einmal ist kein Beweis für wissenschaftliche Seriosität, sondern eine Demonstration von Macht”, so der Verband. Er wolle mit seinen Mitgliedern deshalb für eine Mathematik einstehen, die „vertrauenswürdig bleibt, ethisch erforscht wird und im öffentlichen Interesse liegt“.
Wozu sich die Forscher:innen verpflichten
„Mathematiker:innen haben daher die Pflicht, Maßnahmen zu ergreifen“, so der Verband auf seiner Website weiter. „Sowohl individuelles Handeln als auch eine groß angelegte Koordination sind erforderlich, um sicherzustellen, dass sich Mathematiker:innen kritisch mit KI-Unternehmen und deren Produkten auseinandersetzen.“ In diesem Zuge fordert der AHM Wissenschaftler:innen nachdrücklich auf, ihre Zusammenarbeit mit OpenAI einzustellen und zu einer Wissenschaft zurückzukehren, in deren Mittelpunkt das menschliche Verständnis stehe.
Wer dem Verband beitritt, verpflichtet sich laut Richtlinien dazu, keine KI-generierten mathematischen Texte zu veröffentlichen und auch zu Forschungszwecken keine KI-Modelle zu nutzen. Mehr als 1.000 Mathematiker:innen weltweit haben sich dem erst vor wenigen Wochen gegründeten Verband bisher angeschlossen. Die gesamte Liste ist online einsehbar. Darunter sind namhafte Wissenschaftler:innen vom MIT, vom California Institute of Technology sowie von der Technischen Universität München.

articles.title: 1 147 pages d'une complexité « redoutable » : les physiciens refusent de publier trop tôt la preuve d'OpenAI malgré l'appel des mathématiciens
articles.text:
Une preuve scientifique d’une longueur et d’une complexité remarquables. C’est ainsi qu’ont réagi les cinq physiciens à la lecture de la démonstration écrite par un modèle d’intelligence artificielle de la société américaine OpenAI, au sujet de l’un des sept grands problèmes du prix du millénaire : la théorie de Yang-Mills.
OpenAI affirme que son modèle a prouvé l’existence de la théorie quantique de Yang-Mills sur le plan mathématique.
Cette théorie est la base de la chromodynamique quantique, qui décrit l’interaction nucléaire forte. C’est elle qui colle les quarks entre eux. Les quarks sont les briques des protons et des neutrons, au cœur des noyaux atomiques.
Ces cinq scientifiques, sollicités par OpenAI pour analyser les travaux de ce modèle d’IA, ne se prononcent pas à ce stade sur la véracité de la preuve. Dans leur communiqué commun, publié ce mardi 27 octobre 2026, ils se contentent d’en noter les contours : on parle d’un document long de 1 147 pages et d’une technicité manifeste. D’où leur réaction initiale.
« La longueur et la complexité des manuscrits d’OpenAI sont redoutables, et il faudra du temps pour en assimiler la méthodologie et la portée, aussi bien en physique qu’en mathématiques », préviennent-ils. « Notre groupe de travail mènera les efforts pour y parvenir. » À l’issue de ce travail, le groupe prévoit bien de publier la preuve, accompagnée de son analyse.
Vérifier d’abord que la preuve est correcte
Mais cela ne se fera manifestement pas à brève échéance. Pas question de céder à la précipitation : « Avant de la rendre publique, nous voulons être convaincus qu’elle est correcte », prévient le groupe de travail. Les neuf mathématiciens de l’AGMAI, qui réclamaient la veille une publication « sans délai », vont donc devoir patienter.
Ces neuf mathématiciens, parmi lesquels Edward Witten, Timothy Gowers et Martin Hairer, siègent à l’AGMAI (Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence), un groupe consultatif indépendant hébergé par l’Institute for Advanced Study de Princeton, qui conseille les entreprises d’IA sur la diffusion de leurs résultats mathématiques. Ils appelaient OpenAI à partager immédiatement la preuve, en faisant observer que la démonstration, bien que rattachée à la physique, a aussi des implications majeures en maths.
La publication complète n’interviendra qu’au moment où les physiciens « seront satisfaits de la qualité et de la justesse des preuves ». L’occasion, par ailleurs, de mener « une expérience sur la façon dont la communauté académique peut gérer le développement rapide de nouvelles connaissances par l’IA ». Aussi ont-ils l’intention « d’avancer très prudemment ».
Les cinq physiciens vont s’appuyer sur la formalisation de la preuve en Lean, que leur fournit OpenAI. Lean est un logiciel de vérification de preuves : il contrôle mécaniquement chaque étape d’une démonstration. Première étape : est-ce que l’énoncé et les définitions traduits dans Lean correspondent bien aux standards de la physique et des mathématiques, sans la moindre erreur ? Si c’est le cas, le groupe publiera la preuve formalisée en Lean, puis lancera un travail d’évaluation plus large.
Cette phase impliquera d’autres chercheurs de la communauté scientifique.
Qui sont les cinq physiciens qui étudient la preuve ?
En attendant, les cinq physiciens retenus pour l’étape initiale ne sont pas des bleus : ce sont des scientifiques de très haut niveau, et des experts de la physique des particules. Le collectif est présidé par David Gross, colauréat du prix Nobel de physique 2004 pour ses travaux sur la liberté asymptotique, une propriété des théories de Yang-Mills (l’interaction forte s’affaiblit à très courte distance).
Arthur Jaffe a cosigné l’énoncé du problème autour de la théorie de Yang-Mills. Michael Douglas a publié début 2026, dans la revue Nature Reviews Physics, un état des lieux de la recherche sur ce problème. Nikita Nekrasov, ancien doctorant de David Gross à Princeton, a reçu en 2023 le prix Dannie Heineman de physique mathématique. Igor Klebanov, enfin, est un spécialiste du confinement des quarks.
Même à supposer que tout soit exact, la preuve avancée par OpenAI ne résout que la moitié du problème du millénaire.
L’énoncé de l’institut Clay demande aussi de démontrer l’existence d’un « écart de masse », c’est-à-dire que les particules décrites par la théorie ne peuvent pas avoir une masse arbitrairement proche de zéro. OpenAI ne revendique rien sur ce second volet de l’énigme. Le communiqué des physiciens range d’ailleurs l’écart de masse, comme le confinement des quarks, parmi les grands défis encore ouverts.
Le prix de l’institut Clay n’est donc pas en jeu à ce stade.

articles.title: Google just handed its rivals the keys to Android
articles.text:
Google just handed its rivals the keys to Android
Google is giving coding agents like Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex deeper access to its Android development tools, including devices, performance profilers and production crash reports; now, agents can now investigate bugs, test changes, and verify their own fixes.
The push spans Android Studio and the terminal-based Android CLI, with Google opening both to third-party agents rather than steering developers toward Gemini. Matthew McCullough, vice president of product for Android, has emphasized giving developers the freedom to choose their own models and coding agents.
In a Wednesday post, Adarsh Fernando, senior product manager for Android developer tools, describes the goal as giving developers and their agents “the tools and knowledge to build high-quality Android apps faster.” The updates were announced Wednesday at Android Dev Summit.
Bring your own agent
The company’s Bring Your Own Agent feature now supports more than 40 coding agents that speak the open Agent Client Protocol, among them Anthropic’s Claude Agent, OpenAI’s Codex, and Google’s own Antigravity, and Google says the feature is now stable in Wednesday’s release of Android Studio Rabbit 2.
A developer can install several and switch between them without leaving the IDE, and connected agents inherit the IDE’s own read on a project — its structure, build configuration, symbols, and tools such as Compose Preview, the emulator, and Logcat — context they would otherwise have to rebuild through code searches and terminal guesswork.
Alongside it, a new Change Review feature scans an agent’s pending changes for common issues and can walk a developer through a large set of modifications before anything is applied, and Google is pushing the same reach beyond the IDE with official Android CLI plugins for Claude Code, and Codex that cover project creation, emulator management, UI inspection, and its Android documentation.
Compose previews from the terminal
Another announcement includes the new android preview command that lets coding agents render Jetpack Compose previews directly in the terminal without launching an IDE or emulator.
The company says agents using it completed UI tasks 77% faster while using up to three times fewer tokens, though it shared little about how it measured those results. The CLI also adds android device remote, giving agents access to physical devices in Google’s lab for testing.
agents using it completed UI tasks 77% faster while using up to three times fewer tokens, though it shared little about how it measured those results.
Finding memory leaks with Claude
Google is also giving agents more ways to investigate problems after an app is built, including performance issues, production crashes and memory leaks. In one demo, Claude Code worked with LeakCanary, an open source leak-detection library, to check critical user journeys for memory leaks using a single instruction from the developer.
Claude Code ran the journeys across multiple devices in parallel, analyzed heap dumps through the CLI’s LeakCanary integration, and traced the leaks back to the offending code. It then made the fixes and reran the tests to confirm they worked. Google says the tooling helped capable models complete these investigations nearly twice as fast while using up to 25% fewer tokens.
autonomous bug-finding can outrun autonomous bug-fixing — an Anthropic scanner flagged some 29,000 possible vulnerabilities in open-source code while only a few hundred were ever fixed.
The demo is very impressive, and it also runs against a record that counsels patience, since autonomous bug-finding can outrun autonomous bug-fixing — an Anthropic scanner flagged some 29,000 possible vulnerabilities in open-source code while only a few hundred were ever fixed.
A companion android signals command now pipes Android vitals and Firebase Crashlytics data into the same terminal workflow, which gives agents a direct line to production crashes, ANRs, and memory problems, but none of this retires the human in the loop, as developers who watched Claude Code land a Linux kernel fix only for reviewers to catch a race condition can attest.
A companion android signals command now pipes Android vitals and Firebase Crashlytics data into the same terminal workflow
Benchmarking agents with Android Bench
Google is also introducing Android Bench 2.0 to evaluate how models and agent harnesses perform on more complex Android development tasks. It tests whether completed apps actually run with assignments ranging from building an app from mockups to migrating an existing interface. Some tasks are modeled on work that would take an Android engineer several days, and the benchmark also measures completion time and cost.

articles.title: Apple lance un Mac à plus de 16 000 euros — Frandroid
articles.text:
Apple a présenté ce mercredi 28 octobre un MacBook Pro plus fin, plus léger et doté pour la première fois d’un écran OLED tactile. Sur l’Apple Store français, sa version 16 pouces configurée au maximum (puce M5 Max avec GPU 40 cœurs, 128 gigaoctets de mémoire, 16 téraoctets de stockage et verre d’écran nano-texturé) s’affiche à 16 383 euros. Aucun MacBook n’était jamais monté aussi haut.
Presque toute la note vient du stockage, puisqu’Apple permet désormais de monter à 16 téraoctets, le double du maximum de la génération M4 Max. La marque annonce un SSD jusqu’à deux fois plus rapide, selon ses propres mesures face à un MacBook Pro M1 Max, associé aux puces M5 Pro et M5 Max déjà vues au printemps dans le MacBook Pro 14 M5 Pro.

Les 14 téraoctets supplémentaires coûtent donc 7 700 euros, soit 550 euros le téraoctet. Et comme sur tous les Mac à puce Apple, ce stockage ne s’ajoute pas après coup : il faut le payer le jour de l’achat.
Face au MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+, 683 euros d’écart

Pour le reste, sa fiche technique ressemble beaucoup à celle du Mac : 128 gigaoctets de mémoire unifiée, 2 téraoctets de stockage, écran 16 pouces OLED tandem tactile de 30 à 120 Hz, 1,9 kg. Il coûte donc 683 euros de moins, et son SSD, monté sur un port M.2, peut se remplacer plus tard.

articles.title: Anthropic compra empresa de una sola persona que usó Claude para desarrollar tratamientos médicos
articles.text:
Anthropic informó el 27 de octubre que compró Mithril Medicine, una empresa de una sola persona que desarrollaba tratamientos para dos formas raras de distrofia muscular. Su fundador, Cody Tranbarger, usó el chatbot Claude para organizar contratos, logística y experimentos con 11 laboratorios externos.
Según el anuncio de la compañía, Mithril llevó un posible tratamiento desde la idea hasta resultados prometedores en ratones en menos de 18 meses. Tranbarger ahora trabaja en Anthropic, donde continúa la investigación y planea abrir varios programas nuevos.
La empresa de inteligencia artificial calcula que, si los candidatos a medicamento se sostienen, uno podría estar listo para empezar ensayos clínicos en humanos a fines de 2028. El sitio especializado R&D World precisó que Anthropic adquirió Mithril en julio y que sus programas son los primeros de desarrollo de fármacos propios de la compañía.
Un empleado, ocho asesores y laboratorios por contrato
Mithril, con sede en Cambridge, Massachusetts, tenía un único empleado de tiempo completo, según R&D World. Detrás había ocho consultores y asesores con experiencia en biología, ingeniería de anticuerpos y planificación de investigación. Los laboratorios contratados producían los anticuerpos, medían su unión a los blancos y hacían los ensayos con células y con ratones.
Tranbarger se graduó en 2025 del programa conjunto de maestría en ciencias y en administración de empresas en biotecnología de Harvard. Trabajó antes en Prime Medicine, una empresa de edición genética, y en Casdin Capital, un fondo de inversión en ciencias de la vida. También fue emprendedor residente en Atlas Venture, una firma de capital de riesgo.
El primer programa apunta a la distrofia muscular congénita ligada al gen LAMA2. Mithril desarrolló anticuerpos biespecíficos, que se unen a dos blancos para formar un puente molecular entre el músculo y su tejido de sostén. El segundo programa, contra la alfa-distroglicanopatía, busca llegar a ensayos en humanos en 2029 como pronto.
Anthropic llama a este esquema “Pipeline-in-a-Person” y prevé probarlo en otros programas de enfermedades raras. Mithril apunta a elegir sus candidatos formales a fármaco en 2027.
Resultados en ratones con límites y errores de Claude
El informe técnico que acompaña el anuncio, que aún no pasó por revisión de pares, describe moléculas de investigación en etapa temprana. A las seis semanas de vida, siete ratones tratados con un formato de anticuerpo mostraron cerca del doble de fuerza de agarre y de fuerza máxima del tríceps que cuatro ratones que recibieron una solución de control, según R&D World.
El mismo informe reconoce límites. Los investigadores asignaron el tratamiento por camada, sin azar, y probaron el grupo con anticuerpo entre 126 y 161 días después del grupo de control, con una mudanza de la colonia de por medio. Esas diferencias complican atribuir la mejora al tratamiento, y el documento pide una réplica simultánea y a ciegas.
Sobre el trabajo con Claude, el informe cita una semana elegida como el mejor ejemplo reciente: el chatbot sintetizó en menos de ocho minutos un reporte de producción de 341 páginas sobre 113 construcciones de anticuerpos. Un integrante del equipo rechazó su recomendación de medir la velocidad de unión de las 113. Claude rehízo el plan para cubrir 89, en menos de cuatro minutos.
El equipo también analizó seis errores de Claude. Al menos tres llegaron a laboratorios externos en correos que personas habían editado y enviado. En uno, el chatbot pedía menos material por tubo del que necesitaba el laboratorio; el equipo lo corrigió antes del llenado. Dos errores en la revisión de datos de producción pasaron inadvertidos durante más de cuatro días.
Anthropic presentó la compra junto con alianzas con seis organizaciones: BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers Squibb, Divergence Labs, Enveda, Generate Biomedicines y The Column Group, según Silicon Report. La compañía no divulgó el precio de la adquisición de Mithril, y la fecha más cercana que fija es 2027, cuando Mithril pretende elegir sus candidatos formales a medicamento.

articles.title: Chrome Opens Trial for the Email Verification API: Letting Sites Verify Without Sending Emails
articles.text:
Google has opened a Chrome origin trial for the Email Verification API, a WICG proposal that lets a browser confirm a visitor owns the email address they typed, without sending a single message. The trial began in Chrome 150 on desktop, with Gmail taking part as the first participating provider.
The idea replaces the familiar one-time code or magic link. Today a user enters an email, leaves for their inbox, copies a code, and returns, a context switch that often loses them. The proposal uses a three-party model where the browser sits between the site (the "verifier") and the mailbox provider (the "issuer"). If the user is already signed in to their provider, the browser quietly fetches a signed token and drops it into the form, and the server validates that token on submission. Google notes the issuer never learns which site made the request.
For developers the front end implementation is fairly straightforward. The email field needs an autocomplete hint, plus a hidden input carrying a session-bound nonce:
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="hidden" name="token" nonce={nonce} autocomplete="email-verification-token">
The heavier work sits on the server side, where the token's signature is checked against the provider's keys. Resend's Phil Nash, who wrote a walkthrough of the flow, published an npm package and a Next.js example to handle that parsing and validation.
On Hacker News a developer said there is "literally no worse context switch" than hopping to an inbox mid sign-up, and that email verification had cost them "dozens, maybe hundreds" of registrations they never finished. Another pointed out that verification mail is frequently blocked or filtered to spam, with no visible difference between delayed and lost messages, so removing it is a genuine win.
One commenter argued the privacy claim is thin:
Make everything what works complicated.
There is no advantage.
"User privacy is enhanced as the issuer does not learn which web application is making the request as the request is mediated by the browser." Every web application nowadays send you a welcome, onboarding, reminder after the verification. (No user privacy enhancement)
So we get a new process that solves nothing, but makes everything complicated. (And complicated helps the big and hurt the little in th long run)
Not verified but feels like a Google draft that closes the web.
Another called the issuer's blindness to the requesting site a "functional liability" rather than a feature. Developers who rely on per-recipient addresses, such as name+site@example.com, noted the flow still forces a fallback whenever the provider cannot attest those aliases. Others likened it to FedCM, folding identity primitives into the browser as password managers once did.
Outside Chrome with a signed-in Gmail account, sites drop back to the classic confirmation email, and the established syntax, MX, and SMTP checking services still cover the addresses this API cannot.
Teams already testing should track breaking changes. Chrome's October update added Android and third-party origin trials in Chrome 154, renamed the Sec-Fetch-Dest issuance value to email-verification, and from Chrome 156 returns the email exactly as submitted. The verifier and issuer guides track the current contract.
The Email Verification API remains an experimental proposal, best used today as a progressive enhancement while the WICG gathers feedback from sites, providers, and users.

articles.title: Chrome and Firefox Updates Patch Over 200 Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Google and Mozilla on Tuesday rolled out fresh Chrome and Firefox updates that resolve more than 200 vulnerabilities in the popular browsers.
The Chrome 156 update arrives with patches for 52 security defects, including four critical-severity flaws: memory corruption in FileSystem, improper input validation in FileAPI and Skia, and use-after-free in Layout.
CVE-2026-118306, the FileSystem bug, could allow arbitrary code execution outside the sandbox through a crafted HTML page.
Patches were also released for 46 high-severity bugs, most of which are memory corruption, improper input validation, and use-after-free issues.
Google has not determined any of the bug bounty rewards to be paid out to the reporting researchers. No reward will be handed out for the remaining 39 vulnerabilities, most of which were found internally or with the aid of AI.
The new Chrome release is now rolling out to users as versions 156.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and macOS, and as version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux.
Mozilla announced the release of Firefox 159 with patches for 167 security defects, including 108 high-severity flaws.
Most of the fixes resolve use-after-free issues in the browser. Multiple sandbox escape, privilege escalation, incorrect boundary, and same-origin policy bypass issues were also patched.
On Tuesday, Mozilla also released Thunderbird 159 and 153.6, and Firefox ESR 153.6 and 115.44 with patches for many of these vulnerabilities.
Google and Mozilla make no mention of any of these security bugs being exploited in the wild, but users are advised to update their browsers as soon as possible.

articles.title: Nova dona da Telecom Italia diz que Brasil não é prioritário • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nova dona da Telecom Italia diz que Brasil não é prioritário
Poste Italiane afirma que operação brasileira é lucrativa e não está à venda, mas será usada "taticamente".
A Poste Italiane, nova controladora da Telecom Italia e, indiretamente, da TIM Brasil, indicou que a operação brasileira não é considerada estratégica para seus planos futuros. A declaração marca uma mudança de tom pouco mais de um mês após a companhia assumir o controle da matriz italiana.
O CEO da Poste Italiane, Matteo Del Fante, disse que a TIM Brasil é lucrativa e gera bastante caixa, mas não é essencial para o projeto que a empresa pretende desenvolver com a Telecom Italia. Ao mesmo tempo, afirmou que a operação não está à venda.
Essa é a pergunta que continua sem resposta. Durante uma conferência econômica em Roma, Del Fante afirmou apenas que a Poste pretende usar a operação brasileira “de maneira tática” nos próximos meses, mas não explicou o que isso significa na prática. O executivo foi mais direto ao dizer que a TIM Brasil “não está à venda”.
A agência Reuters avalia que a fala pode abrir espaço para uma eventual separação da operação brasileira no futuro. Até agora, não há busca por comprador nem processo formal de venda. O significado desse “uso tático” pode ficar mais claro no primeiro trimestre de 2027, quando Del Fante pretende apresentar um novo plano de negócios para Poste Italiane e Telecom Italia.
A prioridade está na Itália. O grupo quer aproveitar a aquisição da Telecom Italia para ampliar sua atuação em serviços digitais e transformação tecnológica, combinando os clientes corporativos da operadora com a estrutura da estatal italiana. Nesse desenho, a operação brasileira gera resultado financeiro, mas não ocupa o mesmo papel estratégico.
A situação contrasta com o discurso adotado antes da conclusão da aquisição. Em julho, o CEO da TIM Brasil, Alberto Griselli, disse que o fortalecimento da nova controladora poderia beneficiar a filial e lembrou que a Poste havia tratado a operação brasileira como uma “joia”. A mudança também recoloca um tema antigo no radar. Em 2022, integrantes do atual governo italiano chegaram a defender a venda da TIM Brasil para direcionar recursos à operação europeia.
Por enquanto, nada foi anunciado para a operação local. A Telecom Italia controla cerca de 67% da TIM Brasil. A companhia é a única subsidiária estrangeira do grupo e, segundo a Reuters, responde por quase metade de seus lucros operacionais principais. A participação está avaliada em aproximadamente R$ 31,8 bilhões.
No Brasil, a TIM continua entre as três grandes operadoras de telefonia móvel, ao lado de Vivo e Claro. Também atua em banda larga fixa, embora tenha sido ultrapassada pela Starlink em número de acessos.

articles.title: German startups are betting big on Japan. Should the rest of Europe follow? | EU-Startups
articles.text:
German startups are increasingly looking towards Japan as a destination for international expansion, industrial partnerships and technological cooperation.
From DefenceTech and nuclear fusion to quantum computing and space infrastructure, recent developments suggest that Tokyo is becoming an important partner for some of Europe’s most ambitious technology companies.
This momentum became particularly visible today, during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Japan. Munich-based Proxima Fusion announced two Japanese partnerships, while drone manufacturer Quantum Systems unveiled agreements with Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic, alongside plans to establish a permanent presence in Tokyo.
The announcements form part of a wider diplomatic push. According to Japanese news agency Jiji Press, Germany and Japan were expected to sign 33 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) spanning AI, nuclear fusion and other advanced technologies.
However, the more interesting story for Europe’s startup ecosystem extends beyond a single diplomatic visit.
More than handshakes
For Quantum Systems, the visit marks a step towards becoming an established player in Japan’s DefenceTech market.
Founded in 2015 in Gilching by Florian Seibel, Michael Kriegel, Tobias Kloss and Armin Busse, Quantum Systems develops unmanned aerial systems and software for defence, security and civilian applications.
The company announced the establishment of Quantum Systems Japan K.K., including a Tokyo office, alongside MoUs with Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic. The agreements aim to combine Japanese manufacturing capabilities with German drone technology, strengthening local supply chains and bringing Quantum Systems closer to Japanese customers.
Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said: “Japan has understood where defence is heading: unmanned systems, rapid innovation and the industrial capacity to deliver at scale. Ukraine has shown why this matters. When personnel are scarce and threats evolve fast, technological advantage is decisive. Japan’s manufacturing strength and our operational experience are a powerful combination. We are proud to put down roots in Japan and honoured to help strengthen its defence industrial base.”
Meanwhile, Munich-based Proxima Fusion, founded in 2023 as a spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, announced two separate agreements involving fusion energy.
As EU-Startups reported earlier today, its agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering focuses on plasma-heating systems and fuel-cycle technologies. A separate agreement with Fujikura explores industrial-scale manufacturing of superconducting tape in Lower Saxony, building on a previously announced €140 million manufacturing initiative.
The cooperation also extends into space. Established German aerospace group OHB signed an MoU with Japanese space-tech company Astroscale, founded in 2013, to explore opportunities in orbital servicing, surveillance and space security. Astroscale, on the same day, also announced a €17 million (£15 million) MOD Contract from the UK Government.
Tokyo was already calling
The latest announcements are part of a broader trend we’v seen here at EU-Startups.
Munich-based defence AI startup Helsing, founded in 2021, has already been pursuing opportunities in Japan. In August 2026, Reuters reported that Japanese conglomerate Rakuten was helping Helsing pursue a potential contract to supply unmanned systems to Japan’s military. Its HX-2 strike drone was undergoing testing by Japan’s Ground Self-Defence Forces.
Industrial cooperation has also attracted Japanese capital into Germany. In March 2025, Panasonic announced a €30 million equity investment in Munich-based tado°, founded in 2011, expanding an existing partnership combining Panasonic’s heat pumps with tado°’s smart heating controls and energy management software.
Quantum computing provides another example. Braunschweig-based QUDORA Technologies, founded in 2021, established a Japanese subsidiary and partnered with Fixstars in May 2026 to make its quantum computing tools accessible through a cloud platform.
By October, QUDORA Japan had been selected for a government-backed research project alongside Kyocera and Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology.
Even outside DeepTech, German companies have recognised the opportunity. Cologne-based translation technology company DeepL, founded in 2017, established a Japanese subsidiary in 2023 to strengthen its local commercial operations.
These developments suggest that Japanese partnerships are becoming an increasingly deliberate part of German startups’ international strategies.
Why Japan, why now?
Japan’s strengths in electronics, robotics, precision engineering, advanced materials and industrial manufacturing offer European startups capabilities that can be difficult and expensive to develop independently.
For companies building fusion reactors, quantum computers or advanced robotics, access to established manufacturers and specialised suppliers may be just as valuable as attracting new customers.
Japan has also been working to strengthen its startup ecosystem. Its five-year startup development plan, introduced in 2022, set an ambitious objective of increasing annual startup investment to approximately €56 billion (¥10 trillion) by the 2027 financial year.
Meanwhile, cooperation between Brussels and Tokyo is expanding. In May 2026, the EU and Japan agreed to deepen collaboration in AI, quantum technology, semiconductors, digital infrastructure and cross-border data flows.
The Tokyo test
Despite the momentum, Japan is not necessarily an easy market to enter.
Language barriers, different business practices, complex procurement processes and the importance of long-term corporate relationships can make expansion challenging, particularly for startups with limited resources.
The experiences of Quantum Systems, Helsing and QUDORA highlight one possible solution: finding established Japanese partners rather than attempting to navigate the market independently.
German startups appear to have recognised the opportunity Japan offers foreign tech and talent. The question now is whether the rest of Europe will follow.

articles.title: Cloud security startup Upwind raises $400M at $3.8B valuation as revenue quadruples - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cloud security startup Upwind raises $400M at $3.8B valuation as revenue quadruples
Cloud and artificial intelligence security startup Upwind Security Inc. today revealed that it has raised $400 million in new funding at a valuation of $3.8 billion.
Reports in early September had the round at $300 million. By the time it closed, Upwind had taken in an additional $100 million, and the company used the announcement to disclose that its revenue has quadrupled so far in 2026.
Upwind’s platform works from runtime data gathered across cloud workloads, application programming interfaces and AI agents. Co-founder and Chief Executive Amiram Shachar said Upwind was built to “unify those signals,” so security, development and DevOps teams share one view of their cloud and AI systems, including which data each can reach. Developers can follow any finding back to the code behind it.
The company argues that a patchwork of separate tools leaves teams with alerts that lack context, such as a warning about an AI agent’s activity with no hint of what the agent was after. Sorting through those alerts is the job Upwind has handed to specialized AI agents built into its platform. Those agents can investigate an alert, confirm it and carry out the fix, Upwind says, leaving human staff to focus on judgment and response.
Shachar said the AI agents companies now deploy can change cloud environments faster than human teams can keep up with on their own, so security tools have to show how workloads, APIs and agents interact as it happens. With that view in place, he said, customers can move “beyond alert management.”
Hundreds of organizations use Upwind, according to the company, and the customers it names include Siemens AG, Roku Inc. and Carvana Co. Amazon Web Services Inc. customers can open Upwind from inside the AWS console through an integration with AWS Security Hub, and billing runs through their AWS account. The platform also runs on Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
Upwind plans to put the new funding toward product development and a broader go-to-market push.
The close comes days after Israeli business daily Globes cited a report by The Information saying Upwind had turned down a $4 billion takeover offer from Datadog Inc. Today’s announcement does not mention it.
Shachar co-founded Upwind in 2022 with former colleagues from Spot, a cloud infrastructure optimization startup that NetApp Inc. reportedly bought for $450 million in 2020.
Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series C round. Canapi Ventures came in as a new investor, while Cyberstarts, Greylock Partners, Craft Ventures Management, Salesforce Ventures and Picture Capital all returned. In January, a $250 million Series B round led by Bessemer valued Upwind at $1.5 billion. Investors have now put about $830 million into the company.

articles.title: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming 'vulnpocalypse' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched. According to researchers who found the bugs, this is only the beginning, as AI changes how quickly novel vulnerabilities can be uncovered and exploited.
On this episode of TechCrunch’sEquity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Tomer Schwartz, CTO of Exposure Management & AppSec at Google-owned Wiz, who was part of the scramble — alongside OpenAI, research group Calif, and the PHP team — to fix the bugs. On the show, Schwartz and Bellan get into what the race looked like from the inside, how early-stage startups can build with security in mind, and why patching by hand won’t scale.
