articles.title: Cloudflare Opens Quicksilver to Customers as Workers KV Instant, Inside a 1 MB Envelope
articles.text:
Cloudflare recently made Quicksilver available to customers for the first time, as a new mode for Workers KV called KV Instant. Reads resolve in 1.62 ms at the 99th percentile, compared with 287 ms for classic KV. What determines whether a team can use it isn't the latency, but the envelope around it.
Quicksilver is Cloudflare’s own configuration store, introduced in 2020. Nearly every request to Cloudflare looks up at least one key in it, Rob Sutter writes, and it has never been a customer-facing product. Brendan Irvine-Broque, who works on Cloudflare’s developer platform, announced the change on X:
we have this crazy key-value store at Cloudflare called Quicksilver
instantly updates keys across our whole network. microsecond reads from every location. stupid fast
our customers have asked us for years to make it available
we finally did – in a way we think is quite simple - as a new mode for Workers KV
The published figures, measured to over 300 edge locations:
| Mode | p99 reads (all) | median write replication | p99 write replication | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Instant | 1.62 ms | 107 ms | 256 ms | 
| Classic | 287 ms | under 1 s | 4.38 s | 
Cloudflare notes it has no sub-second fidelity for replication lag in classic mode, so the classic median and p95 figures are upper bounds rather than measurements. p95 reads in Instant mode are reported in microseconds.
The API is the Workers KV one, with three differences. Mode is set at namespace creation with a "mode": "instant" attribute, and cannot be changed afterward. Metadata is unsupported, so getWithMetadata always returns null. And list returns every matching key with no pagination.
Then the limits. A namespace holds at most 10,000 key-value pairs and one megabyte in total, with keys up to 300 bytes. Writes are capped at one per namespace per second, which Cloudflare contrasts with classic KV’s one write per key per second, on the grounds that a single system of record "makes it easier for you to reason about update order in your application." That difference is the one most likely to catch a team migrating: a pattern classic KV permits across many keys concurrently becomes a single serialised queue.
Pricing points the same direction, and Cloudflare says so plainly: "storage and Class A operations are significantly more expensive than Workers KV."
|  | Reads (Class B) | Writes, deletes, lists (Class A) | Storage | 
|---|---|---|---|
| KV Instant | $0.20 per million | $0.10 per operation | $100 per MB, per month | 
| Classic KV | $0.50 per million | $5.00 per million | $0.50 per GB, per month | 
Reads cost 60% less. A write costs ten cents, against five dollars per million in classic mode. Storage runs $100 per megabyte per month, and since a namespace tops out at one megabyte, that is also the ceiling. Multi-key reads bill per key, so requesting three keys in one get costs the same three Class B operations as three separate calls.
Irvine-Broque set out the reasoning in the same thread:
just like how we use Quicksilver ourselves, it’s for small data that is read often and updated infrequently
pricing reflects this - reads actually cost 60% less than even Workers KV
Writes cost what they cost, he added, because writing a key replicates it to hundreds of locations. This is a store priced so that you read from it constantly and write to it rarely.
Benjie Malinao, also on X, read the fit the same way:
This is the config store agents actually need. Sub-2ms p99 reads and global writes landing in about a quarter second at p99, on the same KV API. Feature flags and agent settings without waiting on a TTL. I’d move hot-path config over first.
Feature flags, routing tables and agent settings fit that shape. Session state, user records and anything with a write path do not.
The comparison practitioners reached for was Vercel. Developer Shawn Mclean asked Irvine-Broque directly:
I’m looking into using Vercel Global Config for a middleware read. They claim 15ms. If I move my workloads to CF, are you saying I can read from middleware for a platform tenant domain mapping in 2ms?
The answer did not quite confirm it:
even p50 of Workers KV (non-instant) from 2 years ago was ~5ms. KV Instant is even faster than that (see numbers in the post)
Cloudflare’s own worked example is a launch flag read on every request and flipped at a keynote, which is precisely the workload: one key, one write, read everywhere immediately.
Classic Workers KV, which launched during Birthday Week in 2018, remains the recommendation for large or frequently updated data. The two modes now sit under one API with opposite economics.
KV Instant is in private beta with a sign-up form, and Cloudflare says it plans to open it up more widely. No general availability date is given.

articles.title: 10 ans après, Apple ressuscite l'un des détails les plus emblématiques du MacBook — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les MacBook ont perdu leur logo Apple lumineux en 2015, avec le MacBook 12 pouces. La pomme n’avait pas de LED à elle. Elle était découpée dans la coque et laissait passer la lumière du rétroéclairage, c’est-à-dire les LED qui éclairent la dalle LCD par l’arrière.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Apple n’a jamais expliqué pourquoi elle l’a retirée. L’explication la plus probable tient à son écran Retina de 0,88 millimètre d’épaisseur. Avec une dalle aussi fine, la lumière qui traverse la pomme aurait pu créer une zone plus claire au milieu de l’image. Le MacBook Pro a suivi en 2016, puis le MacBook Air en 2018. Depuis, la pomme est en métal poli et elle reflète la lumière sans en produire.
Alors que les nouveaux MacBook Pro avec écran Oled tactile viennent enfin d’être dévoilés ce mercredi 28 octobre, la marque confirme le retour de ce logo lumineux.
La pomme s’allume de nouveau sur le MacBook Pro
John Ternus, qui a succédé à Tim Cook à la tête d’Apple, l’avait laissé entrevoir le matin même dans une courte vidéo sans légende publiée sur X. Sur le nouveau MacBook Pro, la pomme au dos de l’écran s’allume bien. Il s’agit pour beaucoup d’utilisateurs d’un argument indéniable et, on peut le dire, un brin nostalgique.
En revanche, l’ancienne méthode des MacBook Pro et MacBook Air ne fonctionne plus ici. Un écran Oled n’a pas de rétroéclairage, puisque chaque pixel produit sa propre lumière. Apple n’a pas détaillé sa solution, mais la pomme dispose forcément de son propre éclairage.

articles.title: Congress is questioning Delaware's plan to let AI agents run companies
articles.text:
WTF?! The idea of an entire business being run by an AI agent sounds like a nightmare, but it's a scenario that Delaware is pushing for. Now, the state's plan is facing pushback from a senior lawmaker who says having an AI in charge could protect owners and investors from liability for harmful actions.
House Oversight Committee chairman James Comer wrote to Governor Matt Meyer on October 26, requesting documents about the proposed Artificial Intelligence Company, or AIC.
The Kentucky Republican wants details of safety assessments and industry involvement, warning that the investigation could lead to federal legislation restricting state AI initiatives.
Under the draft bill, Delaware would establish a 30-month regulatory sandbox to test the concept. An AIC could pursue any lawful purpose except banking, with an AI agent handling business decisions without routine human supervision. The company itself could sue and be sued.
Each AIC would have one member, either a person or an entity, responsible for keeping it adequately funded. That member would generally be protected from the company's liabilities. However, the draft includes exceptions for fraud, willful lawbreaking, and allowing activities the member knew, or should have known, fell outside the company's stated purpose.
The proposal would not make every AI-related disaster somebody else's problem. But critics question whether those exceptions offer enough protection when software makes the decisions and humans collect the profits.
UC Berkeley law professor Andrew Baker told the Financial Times that the proposed liability shield appeared excessively generous and lacked a sufficiently developed justification.
Supporters argue that giving autonomous systems a legal identity would make their actions traceable and provide a target for liability. Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez outlined the proposal with Norm Ai CEO John Nay in Fortune.
There's also a financial incentive, naturally. Spotlight Delaware reports that Patibanda-Sanchez highlighted the formation fees these companies could generate. Corporate taxes and fees already contribute more than $2 billion annually to Delaware's budget, roughly a third of its revenue.
The idea of putting AI in charge of a company isn't new. In October 2025, Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber called for AI agents in every board meeting. A month later, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said he wants his company to become the first big firm run by an AI.
For now, this remains a proposal. Spotlight Delaware reported that the bill was likely to be introduced next year, while Meyer's office told Ars it was reviewing Comer's letter.
Given the many recent incidents in which AI agents have gone rogue and hacked other companies, putting the technology in charge of a company seems like a rash move. That's without mentioning the repeated warnings from experts about an AI apocalypse. Or maybe it's exactly what the sneaky AI wants?

articles.title: London’s AP Ventures closes €269.62 million third fund to back early-stage industrial and energy tech startups | EU-Startups
articles.text:
AP Ventures, a London-based independent VC firm investing in early-stage industrial and energy technologies, today announced the final close of AP Ventures Fund III LP (Fund III).
The VC firm has raised €269.62 million ($300 million) in commitments for Fund III from a “diverse group” of existing and new institutional investors, including sovereign wealth funds, corporates, pension funds, and family offices. Since its initial close in 2024, Fund III has backed 13 portfolio companies developing technologies focused on industrial and energy systems. 
“This final close reflects the confidence our existing and new investors place in AP Ventures’ ability to identify and support exceptional technology companies. Strong support from returning investors, alongside new institutional partners, allows us to keep backing the technologies industry needs to operate more productively and securely, from the materials it depends on to the processes and data that run it,” said Andrew Hinkly, Founder and Managing Partner at AP Ventures.
AP Ventures began as part of Anglo American Platinum’s PGM (Platinum Group Metal) Investment Programme, and in 2018 it launched as an independent venture capital fund to invest in PGM applications. As cornerstone investors, Anglo American Platinum and South Africa’s Public Investment Corporation (PIC) each committed $100 million to AP Ventures.
Anglo American Platinum Limited is a member of the Anglo American plc Group and is the world’s leading primary producer of platinum group metals, whereas the Public Investment Corporation (PIC) is a public asset management firm wholly owned by the South African government, with the Minister of Finance as the sole shareholder representative of the government.
Led by Hinkly and Kevin Eggers, AP Ventures invests globally in early-stage technologies reshaping the industrial economy, including advanced materials, industrial processes, and energy systems.
According to the firm, this fundraise comes as demand accelerates for high-performing infrastructure across energy and industry. It notes that development and operations of industrial and energy systems are being reshaped by rising power demand, tightening supply chains for critical minerals and materials, and the growing role of AI, data and automation in industrial operations. This creates a growing opportunity for technologies that boost productivity and strengthen supply security, AP Ventures says. 
Fund III invests in early-stage technology companies and works alongside founders through commercialisation, industrial deployment and scale-up.  Its strategic focus spans low-carbon molecules, including hydrogen, across production, storage, transport and end use; carbon capture and utilisation; and circularity and advanced recycling, with applications in energy-intensive, hard-to-abate sectors such as chemicals, steel, aviation and heavy mobility. 
Its present portfolio of 13 companies includes:
Teragen Energy: a Southborough-based startup that develops metal-supported solid oxide fuel cells that can provide clean, on-site power for data centres and other critical infrastructure. 
Aether Fuels: a Chicago-based startup that converts industrial waste gases, biogas and waste biomass into drop-in liquid fuels, giving aviation and shipping a new, locally sourced fuel supply.
CREW Carbon: a US-based startup whose mineral-based process replaces conventional wastewater treatment chemicals, cutting operating costs and supply-chain exposure for water utilities while generating high-quality carbon removal credits.
Rosy Soil: a US-based sustainable soil company which sells patented, peat-free potting soils from biochar, replacing a finite, increasingly restricted raw material while improving plant health and sequestering carbon. 
Reclinker: a Cardiff-based startup which harnesses the Electric Arc Furnace process used in steel production and recycling to convert used cement into on-specification Ordinary Portland Cement. 
Lydian Labs: a Boston-based startup which uses modular, load-following reactors to convert electricity, water and carbon dioxide into synthetic fuels, enabling flexible, distributed fuel production that tracks variable power supply. 
Rubi Laboratories: a San Francisco-based startup which converts carbon dioxide into high-purity cellulose for textile fibres such as viscose and lyocell, giving brands a feedstock independent of forestry and agricultural supply chains.
“We focus on backing technically differentiated companies that solve real operational problems across the industries and value chains in which we invest. Whether improving energy efficiency, resource productivity, safety, environmental performance or supply-chain resilience, this combination of technical rigour and commercial pull is what continues to define AP Ventures’ approach,” said Eggers, founder and Partner at AP Ventures.
Headquartered in London, with offices in Johannesburg and San Francisco, AP Ventures initially invests at Seed and Series A stages and works closely with founders to help them navigate technical and commercial milestones and connect them with a global network of financial and industrial partners.
The firm connects its Limited Partners and portfolio companies to a specialised network that draws on the collective expertise of its team, investors, and broader industrial community.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO filing lists a Canada-based risk
articles.text:
Anthropic is preparing for the world’s largest IPO, and it’s citing Canadian copyright battles as one of the many risks facing investors who want to participate.
The news: Nearly a third of the frontier AI giant’s IPO filing on Monday was dedicated to “Risk Factors,” such as reputational harm from misaligned AI, the need to secure more capital for compute, and litigation related to AI model harms.
A detailed list of Anthropic’s legal matters from the filing includes four copyright actions in Canada, which allege that the work of authors and news publishers was illegally copied to train the company’s AI models. It’s facing multiple similar copyright suits in the US from music publishers, plus individual suits from authors who opted out of a class-action lawsuit that Anthropic settled for $1.5 billion.
Anthropic “disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters,” the prospectus says.
From the source: “Much of Anthropic’s pitch is that a company with a single product—one it admits is dangerously uncontrollable and unpopular—can justify a $1.5-trillion (or so) price tag,” Semafor’s business reporters wrote.
The context: While the filing shows a massively capitalized company with a valuation that could eclipse the $1.5-trillion figure, it also shows one massively in debt. Anthropic owes $400 billion in future obligations for compute purchases and data centre leases and, despite 1,368-percent revenue growth, saw a net loss of $80 billion in the first half of 2026.
The business is using that debt load to rapidly accelerate its plans. This includes expansion into Canada with recent hiring sprees and data centre projects (its first is planned for Nova Scotia), all while it contends with the copyright lawsuits and an uncertain regulatory future in the country. Anthropic may be chasing a huge reward in its public offering, but its mounting legal fights only add to the sheer scale of all that risk.

Another open banking delay
Last Friday, Canada’s Competition Bureau submitted its endorsement of the country’s proposed open banking regulations, citing their “alignment with a pro-competitive regulatory framework.” However, The Logic reported this week that the long-awaited financial data-sharing system is once again held up as the feds weigh whether to adopt a US-based technical standard-setter.

A glance at China’s stock market could fill any AI bubble doomer with a sense of vindication. Mainland China’s AI-dominated STAR50 index has dropped by 40 percent in less than four months, erasing around $480 billion in market value, according to Reuters. Don’t assume this crash is a warning signal for Western markets, however, as China’s market operates under stricter government control and features outsized retail investor participation, meaning it’s more prone to drastic sentiment- or policy-driven swings.

Toronto-based Coinkite is facing a class action lawsuit after more than $140 million USD in Bitcoin was stolen from users of its offline crypto wallet storage device, Coldcard, over the summer. articles.title: China-Linked Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell to Root Firewalls
articles.text:
A China-linked threat actor has been exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to gain root access to firewalls and deploy webshells for persistent access, cybersecurity firm Dream reports.
The hackers have been chaining an exploit for the two PHP flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with another for Fragnesia, a privilege escalation bug in the Linux kernel tracked as CVE-2026-46300.
As part of the observed attacks, the hackers used the Chinese internet asset search engine FOFA to identify 19,000 internet-facing firewalls from a specific vendor, and proceeded to exploit 25 of them on October 23-24, Dream says.
After discovery, the hackers first filtered servers in the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, then filtered those running newer PHP releases, which gave them a pool of 240 potential targets.
Using an automated tool, the attackers then targeted the firewalls with the full PHP2Shell-Fragnesia exploit chain, dropping a PHP root webshell on 24 devices for persistent access.
While no post-exploitation activity was observed on 22 of the firewalls, the hackers did progress further on two servers belonging to a US government-affiliated environment.
The first rooted server crashed shortly after exploitation, on October 23. The attacker launched a second wave of attacks on October 24, which was successful.
“The attacker monitored [the first firewall] with 240 automated probes over two hours, waiting for it to recover. It didn’t. The second firewall, whose certificate data definitively linked it to the target organization, had timed out during the original batch,” Dream notes.
To maintain access to the firewall, the attackers deployed a reverse SSH tunnel and then used it to target an internal firewall management server with the PHP2Shell-Fragnesia chain, gaining access to the configurations, credentials and settings of every firewall the organization managed.
The hackers then used the management server to access and decrypt the LDAP service account password, enumerate users and groups in the domain, perform password spraying attacks, and attempt to create Active Directory backdoor accounts, among others.
Dream has not attributed the activity to a specific threat actor but believes it is part of a Chinese-nexus operation.
“Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts,” Dream notes.

articles.title: As AI agents reshape the web, Google opens Gemini and Search to more apps | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform.
Introduced in Gemini and Google Search earlier this year, connected apps let users securely link and interact with popular third-party services, then use them to take specific actions. For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist.
We’ve seen varying takes on the idea by other consumer-facing AI services like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse. The premise is that such integrations could ultimately shift consumer behavior away from launching and using individual apps to instead using their favorite services through their preferred AI provider.
However, to successfully capture and retain consumers’ attention, there have to actually be a wide range of connected apps to explore.
Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance.
The platform preview is currently available in beta to developers in the U.S., and will allow developers to build and submit apps that can be used across Google’s products.
To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains.
Essentially, this process lets devs connect their app to Google’s services so it can be used with the search giant’s AI features. Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both.
After the app is live, developers can track traffic, latency, and error rates, and maintain control over their brand identity, such as their verified logos and authenticated accounts.
Similar to how SEO allowed companies and websites to show search engine rankings, this could well be one of the initial steps for businesses that want their services to be more visible to users on the agentic web.
Google already has over 50 Connected Apps available in Gemini, including from partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, Peloton, and others, in addition to its own expansive set of services, from Workplace and Photos to YouTube Music and Google Home.
These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks. Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others.
Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search.
The new Connected Apps platform is in public preview for U.S. developers who sign up for the waitlist. Google did not share when it would become more broadly available.

articles.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
articles.text:
Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.
Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.
One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.
Mapping the risks
The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.
Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims, and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

articles.title: $4,700 audiophile-grade network hub promises a noise-free experience and music with 'emotional impact' — seven isolation stages per port were chosen with 'listening comparisons'
articles.text:
$4,700 audiophile-grade network hub promises a noise-free experience and music with 'emotional impact' — seven isolation stages per port were chosen with 'listening comparisons,' uses a $5 Realtek controller
The perfect cure for that latest bout of audiophilia nervosa?
There are a lot of salesman sayings, and, chances are, most were inspired by audiophiles. The eternal sufferers of audiophilia nervosa keep coming up with novel ways to attribute sonic and emotional characteristics to any piece of equipment — even when discussing things purely in the digital realm. One of the current fads is audiophile-grade network switches, like the Aurender NH10 Network Hub, coming in at a mere $4,700.
This piece of gear —which we presume is actually a network switch, rather than a hub — comes fitted with eight gigabit ports. Six of those are standard copper inputs, while the other two are SFP ports where audiophiles can plug in a transceiver for either fiber or copper. The product page remarks that, naturally, a fiber connection is electrically isolated. I was teeing up a joke about the existence of audiophile-grade SFP transceivers when, while proofreading, I found that life does truly imitate art. Oh, and that $4,700 doesn't even get you 10 GbE capabilities.
Four of the six copper ports on the Aurender switch have a total of seven electrical filtering stages behind them, while the remaining pair "only" has two. According to an article at Headphonesty, Aurender's designer said the team experimented with using over 10 stages, but eventually settled on seven "from listening comparisons." That's an interesting feature considering that the Ethernet standard already mandates electrical isolation for standard twisted-pair connections.
Aurender also says that it's using an OXCO (Oven-Controlled Crystal Oscillator) controlled by an FPGA for clock synchronization, and there's a BNC input on the back for an external source. From what we can tell from the board picture, the main chips include: a Realtek RT8370N switch controller ($5.5 at LCSC, an MV85 oscillator ($39 on eBay), and an AMD/Xilinx Spartan 6 FGPA ($8-15 depending on model). There are, no doubt, more manufacturing and materials costs to go from a collection of chips to an assembled switch, but presumably not enough to get anywhere close to the $4,700 asking price of the NH10.
This is all adorable, but the fact of the matter is that the hardware here cannot, by any reasonable definition, make any difference to the sound. TCP connections have built-in error correction. The Ethernet protocol includes Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC), and there are several similar layers, up to the point where the data turns into an actual analog signal.
It's also up to whichever equipment is handling the playback to electrically isolate the actual DAC output stage, not at the network or switch level. And even affordable audio interfaces have signal-to-noise ratios that 1970s recording engineers would happily give up their LSD for.
Likewise, the whole conversation about jitter is pointless, though much like any audiophile myth, it's grounded in a piece of truth — just one that's completely irrelevant in this scenario. In a recording studio, you occasionally need to sync the clock across multiple pieces of gear, just like matching tape machines back in the day. For just the one piece of playback gear, however, it's pointless, and it's downright nonsensical at the network level.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Yet logic has never stopped some self-described audiophiles. One can but wonder what folks seriously looking at these pieces of gear would feel knowing that the studios where their precious music is being made use, for example, one bog-standard Ethernet cable to carry 4 balanced analog lines. Or how their favorite guitarist's pedals and amplifier in a famous recording session were held together with lamp cord, duct tape, hopes, and dreams.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Why 'never trust, always verify - repeatably' security strategy for AI Agents, starts after login
articles.text:
Why 'never trust, always verify - repeatably' security strategy for AI Agents, starts after login
Securing AI agents requires continuous verification of actions after login
Modern digital security frameworks were originally built to correct a flawed historical assumption: the belief that if a user or system was inside the company network, they could be trusted implicitly. Over the past decade, the rapid rise of cloud storage, subscription-based business software, and remote working destroyed that network boundary.
In response, our security models shifted focus. We began verifying the identity of the person trying to log in, inspecting the hygiene of their computer, requiring multiple verification steps during login, and continuously checking that they were who they claimed to be.
Chief Information Officer and Global Chief Information Security Officer at Cato Networks.
This model works well when a human is logging in to perform a task. But with the rise of autonomous AI agents, the real security risk no centralized at the login screen. It starts after access has been granted.
An AI agent does not behave like a standard piece of software. It reads a human instruction, pulls context from company databases, utilizes multiple sets of tools, chooses its own digital tools, connects to external software communication links, and triggers complex automated workflows.
Verifying the initial login simply tells you that the agent is officially recognized by your system. It tells you absolutely nothing about whether the next action the agent plans to take is safe, ethical, or correct, focus has shifted to context.
The evolution of the machine identity problem
IT teams have already experienced a simpler, quieter version of this challenge with non-human identities. For years, companies have used automated service accounts, security tokens, and digital certificates to allow different software programs to talk to one another.
Most security leaders are all too familiar with the risks these credentials present: accounts are created for a temporary project, granted permanent access to database files, and then completely forgotten long after the project has ended. They become silent, unmonitored backdoors into the network.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
However, AI agents complicate this familiar problem by introducing the element of independent judgment.
A traditional service account follows strict, pre-written code. By contrast, an AI agent interprets a high-level goal, analyses real-time context, selects its own tools, and actively decides how to proceed.
As a result, security policies can no longer stop at the front door. We must protect every internal data or compute asset the agent can reach and monitor every single decision it makes.
Matching autonomy with executive control
To manage this risk, security leaders must separate two distinct concepts: how much independence an AI agent has, and what level of file access it holds.
The combination of these two factors dictates the level of control required. For example, a basic agent that merely summarizes long documents only needs limited reading rights and clear activity logs. However, an agent designed to update sensitive, production databases, access code repos, write new types of code, or alter business workflows requires mandatory human approval steps, strict operational boundaries, and a clear path to reverse any mistakes.
We can categorize these digital workers into 3 distinct levels of independence, applying tighter security controls as their autonomy increases:
1. First, there are Conversational AI Agents (GenAI), productivity agents usually built and managed by employees & teams as part of their productivity (e.g. managed agents, self hosted chat bots). When driving security, we must enable proper RBAC authorization, associated with the employee and team, ensuring access to non-sensitive or production-related data, enabling logging, and validating the response to ensure proper integrity.
2. Second, there are Agents Acting with Semi/Full Human Guardrails (AI Agents), such as customer support tools that draft emails or prepare database updates for review. Here, security teams must validate the parameters of the tools being used and require a human to approve any actions involving writing, deleting, spending money, or sending information externally. All above controls apply
3. Finally, there are Fully Autonomous Agents (Agentic AI), which reset passwords or trigger complex workflows on their own. These require the strictest boundaries, from visibility (agent architecture, tool usage, and more) and focus on active set of controls. The controls include strict rate limits, continuous real-time policy checks, network access restrictions, run time security controls (Public/Private Cloud) continuous identity and minimal authorization verification, and finally complete, unalterable audit trails.
The industry is leaning toward autonomous agents seeking human approval upon abnormal behavior, can that be triggered in your agent?
The need for real-time inspection
To enforce these policies, security teams need a dedicated vantage point within the network. They must be able to inspect the human prompt, the agent's response, the digital tools being used, and the movement of data while the work is actually happening.
This requires an architecture that can discover all active agent activity across the business, govern how those agents use internal tools, and maintain complete visibility over data flows and automated workflows.
The true value of this approach lies in context. When the behavior of an AI agent is viewed alongside network traffic, user activity, and cloud database logs, security teams can investigate incidents with clear evidence. They can instantly see which agent ran, who in the organization owns it, what data was moved, and which automated tool was called.
For business leaders, this means cleaner, more consistent governance across human users, software applications, and digital agents alike.
How to begin: Start with a single workflow
Securing this new landscape does not require a complete overhaul of your entire security department overnight.
Start by picking a single AI workflow that is currently in use or close to being launched. Map out its digital identity, its level of independence, the files it can access, the tools it uses, the points where a human must approve an action, and how you would undo a mistake.
This simple mapping exercise will quickly highlight where your security gaps lie. If you cannot see the agent's actions in real-time, approve its decisions, block its access, or explain its behavior after the fact, your security controls are simply too far away.
From there, build a baseline on how your secure your coding agents, AI harness (or AI orchestrator) up to utilizing of tools/skills/MCP and moving forward to data assets access and utilization of identity that will allow you to set the correct foundations and guard rails.
The core principle of a "never trust, always verify" security model must follow the agent into its daily work. The most meaningful decision is no longer who is logging in, but whether their next action should be allowed to happen, under these exact conditions, right now.

articles.title: Virgin Galactic presenta Apeiron, su nuevo "avión espacial" para vuelos comerciales
articles.text:
Virgin Galactic todavía no ha logrado poner en marcha con regularidad sus vuelos comerciales al borde del espacio, pero acaba de dar un paso crucial para por fin completarlo. La empresa fundada por Richard Branson acaba de presentar Apeiron, su primera nave de clase Delta que comenzará a operar en algún momento de 2027.
El nombre Apeiron fue elegido por el público a través de una votación que tuvo participantes de más de 80 países, según reveló Virgin Galactic. Dicha palabra proviene del griego y en inglés significa the boundless, lo que se puede traducir como "el ilimitado" o "la ilimitada".
Todavía no hay fecha definida para el inicio de los vuelos comerciales regulares del nuevo avión espacial de Virgin Galactic. La compañía indica que hoy mismo Apeiron volará hacia Spaceport America, la base de operaciones que ha montado en Nuevo México, acoplada a Eve, el avión que sirve como "nave nodriza" para sus lanzamientos en pleno vuelo.
Una vez allí, el equipo de Virgin Galactic comenzará a realizar las pruebas necesarias de cara a los vuelos de prueba. El primer paso será la validación del software que se encarga de la aviónica de la nave de clase Delta.
Cuándo volará Apeiron, la nueva nave de Virgin Galactic
A mediados de agosto, Virgin Galactic anunció que los vuelos comerciales de su nueva nave de clase Delta se postergarían hasta febrero de 2027 para resolver algunos problemas aparecidos durante la fabricación. No obstante, el primer lanzamiento se volvió a aplazar esta misma semana.
La compañía reveló que la primera unidad de Apeiron comenzaría a volar comercialmente al borde del espacio a principios del segundo trimestre de 2027. Esto da a entender que podría concretarse en el transcurso de abril del próximo año. Virgin Galactic tiene una segunda nave de clase Delta en etapa final de producción y el objetivo es que comience a operar a finales del segundo trimestre o principios del tercer trimestre de 2027.
Con la presentación de Apeiron, Virgin Galactic apuesta a revitalizar el interés por sus vuelos comerciales al borde del espacio. A pesar de las postergaciones reiteradas, la firma ha vendido todos los tickets que tenía contemplados para los primeros lanzamientos. Se estima que más de 50 asientos ya están cubiertos, con miras a lograr una rotación bien aceitada cuando las dos naves de clase Delta estén operativas.
Los viajes comerciales a la línea de Kármán siguen estando reservados para clientes de bolsillos muy profundos. Los pasajes a bordo de los aviones espaciales de Virgin Galactic cuestan unos 750.000 dólares cada uno.

articles.title: Readwise is taking on Kindle and Kobo for ebook supremacy
articles.text:
For the last several years, Readwise has been building tools for power readers. There’s the eponymous product, Readwise, which stores and categorizes your Kindle highlights to help you remember what you’ve read. There’s Readwise Reader, an app for reading newsletters, PDFs, and web articles you’ve saved for later. And now there’s Readwise Books, a full-fledged platform for buying, reading, and talking about books.
Readwise is taking on Kindle and Kobo for ebook supremacy
Taking on Kindle is hard. Beating Goodreads might be really easy.
Readwise Books is currently in beta, available through invite or to existing Readwise subscribers. I’ve been testing the app for a few days, and it’s a much bigger take on reading than most. Tristan Homsi and Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s cofounders, like to call the platform “Strava for reading” because it can track how long, how much, and how fast you read, and it can show that information to friends you make in the Readwise Books app. The app’s homepage is a feed of what other people are reading, with comments and recommendations laced throughout.
“Strava for reading” wasn’t the original goal of Readwise Books, which has been part of the Readwise plan since the beginning. “Literally, Dan and I talked about this when we first met,” Homsi says. “We feel like Kindle could be so much better. We really didn’t think it would take nine-plus years to be able to get to this point.” But it turns out, Doyon adds, that for all their ideas about innovation in books, “no one sits around wanting a better Kindle.” But there is one thing they do wish for: a better Goodreads. “Everybody hates Goodreads.”
In a sense, then, the plan for Readwise Books is to take on Kindle by first taking on Goodreads. The Readwise Books app offers a nice way to track books you want to read, are reading, and have read; it even syncs with your Kindle account to let you track books you’ve bought from Amazon by taking pictures of your starting and ending pages. You can rate and review books and see what others have said. It’s a little Strava, a little Letterboxd, and a lot nicer to look at than Goodreads.
The long-term goal, of course, is to get people to stop buying Kindle books and start buying from Readwise. Homsi and Doyon have spent the last several years working to reach deals with all five of the major US publishers in order to have a competitive library of books available. That meant endless negotiations, security reviews, DRM debates, and more — both cofounders seem exhausted just talking about the process. But eventually, by several small miracles, they got the deals done. And since those deals govern the price of books, and many things about how they’re sold and presented, they bring Readwise to a nearly even playing field almost immediately.
It all took a lot longer than expected, but Doyon and Homsi think their timing might actually be pretty good. Digital book reading continues to grow, particularly among young people; a huge amount of that reading happens on phones and tablets. Meanwhile, a new crop of E Ink devices like the tiny Xteink and the Boox Palma line have expanded the universe of available hardware for a company like Readwise.
Not long ago, Doyon says, they would have had no choice but to build an e-reader of their own. (And he says they still might.) Now, they can just make sure it runs on an E Ink-friendly flavor of Android.
After a couple of days using Readwise Books, I can say confidently I already like it better than practically all of its competition. It’s a much nicer-looking app than anything you’ll get from Kindle or Kobo; it has lots of ways to customize how books look; and at least for now, I’m finding the tracking features compel me to read more instead of annoying me. (Homsi says some early versions of the gamification features were substantially more annoying.) I’ve found a few bugs, and the half-integration with Kindle is a little confusing in spots, but it’s already a really nice place to read.
Of course, I, like millions of other people, already own a Kindle and lots of Kindle books. Switching ebook platforms is hard, and Doyon says he’s not counting on everyone to do it right away. He says he’s hopeful Readwise can persuade existing users to switch, in order to sync their notes and progress more seamlessly. He’s also hoping that the advent of AI, and the ways in which AI reliance may rot our brains, will get a lot of people back into the idea of reading more deeply again. And that a bunch of those people might be looking for a nicer, more social place to do so.

articles.title: Aïe, le prix du premier MacBook Pro tactile risque de faire (très) mal
articles.text:
Ce mercredi 28 octobre à partir de 18 heures se tient l’événement d’Apple intitulé « Pro and Tell ». Une annonce qui intervient après une semaine déjà chargée pour Apple : lundi, la marque a présenté son iPad mini Oled ; et ce mardi, elle a présenté son premier MacBook Pro équipé de la puce M6 ainsi que son iMac M6. Selon les rumeurs, la marque devrait présenter ce jour pour la première fois un MacBook équipé d’un écran tactile : il s’agirait d’un MacBook Pro OLED avec la puce M5 Pro. Mais les prix de ce nouvel ordinateur pourraient en refroidir plus d’un.
2 899 dollars pour le MacBook Pro tactile : ça pique
C’est le journaliste Mark Gurman de Bloomberg qui rapporte les propos d’une source proche d’Apple. La marque envisagerait de vendre ce MacBook Pro tactile avec une puce M5 Pro à 2 899 dollars. Quant à la version 16 pouces, son prix pourrait être de 3 399 dollars, si l’on part du principe que la version actuelle est vendue à 2 999 dollars. Interrogée par le journaliste, Apple s’est refusée à tout commentaire.
Avec cet écran tactile, ce modèle serait vendu 400 dollars plus cher que la version actuelle (avec la même puce), débarquée en mars. Rappelons que cet ordinateur a vu son prix augmenter de 400 euros en juin pour les deux versions principales : 14 et 16 pouces. Ces deux versions devraient continuer à être commercialisées selon Mark Gurman. C’est d’ailleurs le cas même avec l’arrivée hier des modèles M6. Au vu de ces tarifs, ce nouveau MacBook Pro tactile serait l’ordinateur portable le plus cher jamais commercialisé par Apple. Il devancerait même les autres constructeurs d’ordinateurs portables tactiles, comme ceux de Dell (qui ont aussi des dalles Oled).
Au regard de la différence des tarifs américains et français habituellement pratiquée par Apple, on peut supposer que les prix français seront également très chers. Pour une fourchette large, on peut estimer que le MacBook Pro tactile en version 14 pouces pourrait être vendu entre 3 200 et 3 400 euros. Quant au modèle 16 pouces, ça s’envole encore plus haut : entre 3 800 et 4 000 euros.
Qu’est-ce qui changerait sur ce nouveau MacBook Pro ?
Comme nous l’avons dit, la puce ne changerait pas : pas de puce M6 malheureusement sur ce modèle tactile. Ce serait toujours la puce M5 Pro à l’intérieur, comme sur la gamme actuelle, et le design ne devrait pas changer. Ou presque : les bordures d’écran seraient plus fines, le design global un peu plus compact et le poids serait réduit. Apple aurait par ailleurs conçu un nouveau système de charnière pour éviter de faire bouger l’écran lorsqu’on le touche (pratique sur un écran tactile). Enfin, le système de refroidissement aurait été retravaillé.
Pour la première fois sur un MacBook, cet ordinateur serait équipé d’un écran OLED XDR tactile : on pourrait utiliser macOS 27 au doigt pour faire défiler des pages, déplacer des fenêtres, etc. Sur cet écran, on trouverait d’ailleurs la Dynamic Island qu’on connaît bien sur les iPhone. Autour du poinçon de la webcam, il y aurait des animations qui se déclencheraient : elles ont déjà été aperçues dans le code du système d’exploitation.

articles.title: Les fans d'Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced risquent de replonger avec sa dernière mise à jour
articles.text:
Pour Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, remake paru le 9 juillet 2026 sur PS5, Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X et PC, il est déjà temps de rentrer au port, moins de quatre mois après sa sortie. Ubisoft a déployé ce mardi 27 octobre la mise à jour 1.0.8, la dernière grosse mise à jour de contenu du jeu, comme l’indique son communiqué. Il sera encore suivi, mais seulement par de petites mises à jour de confort.
La grosse nouveauté de la version 1.0.8 d’Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced est l’ajout du mode New Game+. Comme Assassin’s Creed Shadows, qui ne l’avait reçu que le 29 juillet 2025, quatre mois après sa sortie, le remake en était privé au lancement. Le principe est toujours le même : permettre de relancer une nouvelle partie en conservant tout ou partie de sa progression actuelle, avec un défi accru. Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced offre la possibilité de monter jusqu’à New Game+ 5.
Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced reçoit enfin son mode New Game+
Le mode New Game+ conserve l’équipement et les outils, les armes, les bibelots, les améliorations du navire Jackdaw, les animaux de compagnie, l’argent amassé, les ressources de l’inventaire, la personnalisation visuelle (tenues et apparences), la progression du repaire et celle de la flotte de Kenway. En revanche, l’histoire, les quêtes actives, les objets de quête, la découverte de la carte ou encore les forts sont réinitialisés, et les officiers doivent être recrutés de nouveau.
Outre la difficulté accrue, le New Game+ propose de nouvelles tenues et pièces de personnalisation, à acheter avec une monnaie qui lui est propre, les escudos, gagnés en relevant des défis et en pillant des coffres déjà ouverts.
Les amatrices et amateurs de défi extrême pourront se frotter à une nouvelle difficulté Cauchemar. L’idée est de pousser tous les curseurs au maximum, des dégâts reçus (quasiment doublés) à la fréquence des attaques ennemies, en passant par des fenêtres de parade et d’esquive plus courtes, des ennemis qui vous repèrent plus vite et davantage de rencontres dangereuses sur les mers. « N’importe qui peut activer la difficulté Cauchemar, quelle que soit votre progression dans l’histoire, et vous pouvez l’activer indépendamment pour le combat, l’infiltration, les batailles navales et les activités, ce qui vous permet de personnaliser encore davantage votre aventure selon votre style de jeu », indique Ubisoft.
Enfin, la mise à jour 1.0.8 d’Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced ajoute de nouvelles variantes d’assassinats, qui changent selon l’arme utilisée, ainsi que des animations reprises du Black Flag original de 2013 (lame secrète, mains nues, épée). Ubisoft précise qu’elles sont totalement aléatoires.

articles.title: L'américain Scale AI est accusé de surveiller les contractuels français
articles.text:
Scale AI est une entreprise américaine dont la plateforme Outlier fait travailler plus de 900 000 contributeurs à l’entraînement d’IA, pour des clients comme Meta, OpenAI ou Google. Cinq plaintes l’accusent de pister ces travailleurs, avec des traceurs tiers et une vérification biométrique, en violation du RGPD.
Ces plaintes ont été déposées le 27 octobre en France, en Italie, aux Pays-Bas et en Autriche par noyb, une association de défense de la vie privée, avec Intérêt à Agir, le groupe de recherche DiPLab et Reversing.Works. Derrière ChatGPT, Gemini ou Grok, il y a aussi des personnes qui vérifient et annotent les réponses des modèles, et ce sont elles que ces démarches cherchent à protéger.
Traceurs tiers et vérification biométrique : les reproches de noyb
Sur Outlier, des contributeurs présentés comme indépendants (ce que noyb conteste) rédigent des prompts, classent des réponses ou annotent des données pour Meta, OpenAI, xAI, Google, Anthropic ou le gouvernement américain. Selon l’analyse technique de noyb, des traceurs de TikTok, LinkedIn, Facebook, Sprig (une plateforme d’enquêtes) et Datadog (de l'analyse de données) se chargent sur leur appareil dès qu'ils sont sur la plateforme. Le traqueur transmettrait toutes les quelques secondes l’adresse IP, des identifiants uniques et la page consultée. Et cela concernerait aussi l’activité de l’appareil hors Outlier. Ces données peuvent donc servir au profilage et à la publicité ciblée. "Pourquoi LinkedIn ou Facebook devraient-ils savoir sur quelles tâches vous travaillez ?", s’interroge Lisa Steinfeld Leiser, juriste chez noyb.
Et puis, il y a aussi la vérification d’identité. Scale AI impose plusieurs contrôles biométriques menés par Persona. Le contributeur doit filmer son visage et envoyer une pièce d’identité. Pour l’entreprise il s’agit d’éviter l’usurpation d'identité et de vérifier les compétences. Mais pour le cabinet de noyb, le système est complètement disproportionné, d’autant que Persona peut aussi collecter adresses IP, informations sur l’appareil, géolocalisation, adresses et données de crédit. D’ailleurs, nous rapportionsen février que Discord disait avoir mis fin à son test avec Persona au Royaume-Uni, source de nombreuses critiques, et repoussait sa vérification d’âge au second semestre.
Les plaintes invoquent le RGPD et des lois nationales. Selon noyb, Scale AI n’a pas de base légale pour installer des traceurs sans consentement. Elle ne respecterait pas non plus la minimisation des données y compris pour celles de nature biométrique. L'entreprise n’aurait enfin pas répondu aux demandes d’accès des plaignants souhaitant savoir quelle informations sont conservées. Noyb réclame donc une enquête et, si besoin, une amende.
Scale AI a réagi auprès de The Register. L’entreprise affirme que les affirmations du rapport sont infondées et inexactes. Elle assure que les pratiques d’Outlier sont communiquées aux contributeurs, qui y consentent, et qu’elle utilise des outils standards pour vérifier les identités, éviter la fraude, protéger les informations confidentielles et payer correctement les travailleurs. Pour Thomas Le Bonniec, chercheur en sociologie au DiPLab, une telle surveillance serait jugée inacceptable dans tout autre emploi de l’Union européenne. Selon lui, « ce système ne prospère que grâce à son manque délibéré de transparence ».

articles.title: UEFI-Lücke: Kritischer Bug versteckt sich seit 16 Jahren in vielen Servern
articles.text:
UEFI-Lücke: Kritischer Bug versteckt sich seit 16 Jahren in vielen Servern
Erst Mitte Oktober 2026 sorgte die Entdeckung schwerwiegender Sicherheitslücken in der weit verbreiteten Programmiersprache PHP für Aufregung. Angreifer:innen sollen die php2shell genannten Schwachstellen schon aktiv ausnutzen und versuchen, ganze Server zu kapern. Allein in Deutschland sollen vier Millionen Dienste betroffen sein.
Schwachstelle in Baustein für UEFI-Firmware
Jetzt ist eine weitere kritische Sicherheitslücke bekannt geworden, von der ein großer Teil der Server weltweit betroffen sein soll. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Schwachstelle in EDK II, dem Open-Source-Code, der vielen UEFI-Firmwares als Basis dient. Diese Firmware ist der moderne Nachfolger von BIOS und startet beim Einschalten eines Computers als erstes, noch vor dem Betriebssystem. Laut Ars Technica setzen die meisten UEFI-Anbieter wie AMI, Insyde und Phoenix auf den Code.
Die Sicherheitslücke in EDK II (CVE-2026-97631), die auf der Schweregradskala CVSS 4.0 9,5 von 10 Punkten erreicht, befindet sich konkret im ICMP-Code des PXE-Netzwerkstarts. PXE sorgt dafür, dass Computer über ein Netzwerk statt von einer eingebauten Festplatte oder SSD starten. In Unternehmen dient diese Funktion dazu, viele Rechner zentral einzurichten oder zu warten.
Nur Geräte mit PXE-Start betroffen
Eine fehlerhafte Speicherbegrenzung bei dieser Art von Start per PXE kann es Angreifer:innen ermöglichen, eigenen Code auszuführen, bevor das Betriebssystem und Schutzmechanismen wie Secure-Boot starten. Dazu benötigen Angreifer:innen Zugang zu dem entsprechenden Netzwerk. Und: Computer, die von Festplatte oder SSD aus starten, sind nicht betroffen.
Bis ein Firmware-Update die Geräte erreicht, sollten Admins prüfen, ob Server und Netzwerkgeräte per PXE starten und ob die Firmware auf EDK II beruht, wie Dr. Web empfiehlt. Sollte PXE nicht benötigt werden, sollte die Funktion bis zu einem Update deaktiviert werden. Andernfalls sollten Admins das Bootnetz abschotten, so dass Arbeitsplatzrechner und Geräte im Gästenetz keine Pakete schicken können.
Verfrühte Korrektur erleichtert Angriffe
Erschwerend für die Bereinigung der schon seit 16 Jahren bestehenden Sicherheitslücke sind die offenbar unzureichend koordinierten Korrekturschritte. So wollten die Entdecker der Lücke, Alex Matrosov von Anthropic und Dan Holmes-Mitra von Google, den Fund eigentlich bis Januar 2027 geheimhalten. Allerdings ist schon Mitte Oktober 2026 eine Korrektur öffentlich einsehbar veröffentlicht worden. Diese zeigt potenziellen Angreifer:innen, wo der Fehler lag.

articles.title: "Es un principio básico de respeto": el veto al burka se cuela en las escuelas españolas por la Comunidad Valenciana
articles.text:
La Comunidad Valenciana ha abierto uno de los melones más espinosos a los que se enfrenta el sistema de educación español: ¿qué hacer con las alumnas (o maestras) que acudan a las aulas con el rostro cubierto por un burka o niqab? Es una cuestión relevante porque, aunque a día de hoy no parece que se den con frecuencia casos así, resulta igualmente innegable que España es cada vez más un país diverso, con una importante población inmigrante y musulmana.
Con ese telón de fondo, en la Comunidad Valenciana lo han tenido claro: los rostros, siempre a la vista.
Rompiendo el melón. Las leyes de acompañamiento de los presupuestos suelen actuar como grandes ‘cajones de sastre’, textos en los que se cuelan medidas que afectan al uso de los recursos públicos y el día a día de las administraciones. La Ley 5/2026 de la Comunidad Valenciana no es una excepción. En su amplio articulado (aprobado el 31 de julio, aunque se publicó hace un mes en el BOE) encontramos medidas relacionadas con tributos, competencias y regulaciones.
Entre esa amalgama hay una medida que, aunque esperada, ha despertado un interés especial: la regulación de ciertas prendas asociadas al mundo islámico en espacios públicos. La ley no habla expresamente de burkas, niqabs o hijabs (de hecho, ni se citan); pero hace algo igual de efectivo: modifica ciertos reglamentos que afectan a los usuarios del transporte público, hospitales y recintos escolares.
“Sustancialmente descubierto”. El cambio que introduce la ley es tan sutil como relevante. El reglamento sobre convivencia en las escuelas e institutos de la Comunidad Valenciana pasa a incluir una nueva exigencia que afecta a los alumnos y alumnas. ¿Cuál? “Mantener el rostro sustancialmente descubierto durante toda la jornada académica, tanto en el interior de las aulas como en el resto de las dependencias e instalaciones del recinto escolar”.
No hacerlo, aclara la ley, se considerará una falta grave.
“Este deber es un principio básico de respeto y convivencia, esencial para garantizar la interacción socioafectiva, la comunicación lingüística, el desarrollo del proceso de enseñanza-aprendizaje y la seguridad organizativa del centro”, insiste. La ley aclara que, tanto los usuarios del transporte público como los de hospitales e instalaciones en las que se ofrecen espectáculos, deben cumplir la misma pauta: “mantener el rostro sustancialmente descubierto”.
¿Por qué es importante? Porque, como recuerda El Mundo, la decisión de la Comunidad Valenciana supone todo un hito. Hasta ahora en España han sido las propias escuelas las que decidían, a través de sus reglamentos de convivencia, si los alumnos podían o no llevar la cabeza cubierta. Ni las leyes estatales ni las regionales se metían en un terreno tan resbaladizo.
Como mucho, en España se aplican normas locales que restringen su presencia en las calles o plazas. Es el caso de Lleida, que hace poco vetó de facto el uso de burkas con multas de entre 400 y 750 euros. O el de Zaragoza, que abrió el mismo melón para regular el acceso a los edificios municipales. En ambos casos, los consistorios se limitan a sus competencias, entre las que no se incluye la educación.
Importa el qué… y el cuándo. Para entender la decisión de la Comunidad Valenciana hay que tener presentes varias claves. Y el contexto. La regulación ha salido adelante gracias al PP y Vox en un ambiente claramente preelectoral, si bien en julio, cuando se aprobó la norma, aún no se habían adelantado las elecciones. Además se da en una de las regiones con las aulas más diversas.
Según un informe reciente presentado por la Fundación Europa Sociedad y Educación y Fundación Ramón Areces, la Comunidad Valenciana fue una de las autonomías con mayor peso del alumnado extranjero durante el curso 2024-2025. Supuso el 18,5%, por encima del promedio nacional, que se situaba en el 12,9%. De hecho, solo la supera Baleares. A modo de referencia, en Extremadura los estudiantes foráneos representan solo el 4,5% y en Galicia el 6,3%.
¿Realmente hace falta regularlo? La pregunta del millón. La Inspección valenciana ha reconocido a El Mundo que, al menos de momento, no le consta ningún caso de alumnas con burka o niqab. Sin embargo, no es descabellado pensar que cada vez será más común encontrarse con aulas diversas formadas por niños y niñas criados en hogares con un acervo islámico. De hecho ya ha habido polémicas puntuales con alumnas que usaban el velo en clase.
Según el Observatorio Demográfico de CEU CEFAS, a comienzos de 2025 residían en España entre 2,4 y 2,5 millones de musulmanes, lo que representa aproximadamente el 5% de la población total. No solo eso. Sus analistas estiman que el 11% de los bebés nacidos en España en 2024 tuvieron al menos un progenitor musulmán. Hay ciertas provincias donde ese porcentaje es superior y roza (incluso supera) el 20%.
“Ni religiosa ni cultural”. Regular el uso de velos no es tarea sencilla. Hacerlo exige abrir un debate espinoso en el que se entrecruzan el derecho a la educación, la libertad religiosa, la igualdad entre hombres y mujeres, la protección del menor, la neutralidad de los espacios públicos o la seguridad ciudadana. De ahí que la norma valenciana no hable directamente de burkas o niqabs y sus pautas dejen fuera los hijabs o shaylas, prendas que no tapan todo el rostro.
“No es una cuestión religiosa ni cultural. Es una cuestión de identificación de la alumna”, aclaran a El Mundo desde la Consejería de Educación valenciana. Otras regiones en las que gobiernan PP y Vox mantienen sin tocar su regulación, lo que deja la pelota en el tejado de cada escuela e instituto.
Por supuesto, hay comunidades autónomas que regulan la indumentaria en las aulas, pero no van tan lejos como la valenciana. El debate no es en cualquier caso exclusivo de la Comunidad Valenciana. Ni de España. En Francia, con una nutrida población musulmana, se abrió hace ya años.

articles.title: Even after PHP2Shell, blast radius matters more than a CVSS score
articles.text:
Here's a prediction: we're about to see a stellar quarter for application security companies. PHP2Shell is about to become the strongest budget argument application security vendors have had in years. AI helped researchers find two remote code execution vulnerabilities in the language behind 69% of the web, attackers targeted it before the patch shipped, and the pitch writes itself: find more bugs and fix them faster.
Enterprises should rethink this idea. Security teams cannot patch at machine speed, but they can reduce what an attacker can reach after exploitation by focusing on identity as the control plane.
Beyond the initial exploitation, the ultimate incident severity depends heavily on which service accounts, API keys, cloud roles, and tokens the compromised workload can use and what they can access.
From vulnerability to exploitation
First, we need to understand just how much faster exploitation is now. The two flaws behind PHP2Shell had been in PHP's code since 2012. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found them in August, with help from OpenAI and Google models, and disclosed them jointly with OpenAI.
Amazon saw an exploitation attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure. PHP shipped the patch on October 21, and watchTowr saw exploitation attempts in the wild the same day. Cloudflare observed attack traffic escalating rapidly after disclosure, and on October 26, CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities.
Exploitation now often starts before disclosure. Unfortunately, things aren't moving as quickly on the remediation side. Verizon's 2026 DBIR states the median time-to-fix of a known exploited vulnerability is 43 days. According to Qualys, the mean remediation time is 21.2 days, and 63% of critical vulnerabilities are still open after a week. All while around 195 new CVEs are published every day.
PHP2Shell will take longer than most to clean up. PHP ships inside appliances and hosting control panels that customers can't patch themselves. Moreover, versions 8.1 and older got no official builds.
As of October 27, Censys counted 32.5 million internet-facing PHP services still running potentially vulnerable versions, and more than 60 million others that don’t report a version at all.
However you look at it, remediation speed will remain slower than the pace of exploitation for the foreseeable future, even when patching itself benefits greatly from AI-driven workflows.
Every Agent Needs an Identity
Agents now act across your systems with access nobody has reviewed.
Token Security’s AI Agent Security finds every agent, links it to an owner, and limits what it can do. Identity-based order to control the chaos of your agentic AI
See Token in Action
Finding isn't fixing
With the exploitation gap widening, it’s tempting to invest everything you can in holding back the tide. But even if an AI-driven scan found 2,000 new zero-day vulnerabilities in your environment tomorrow, that won’t result in a stronger security posture.
It will give you a list. Some items will be easy to patch, while others will need more time than your team has.
For supported PHP branches, the direct fix was simple: install the updated release. Governments and companies still took their sites offline while they waited for it.
Here's another, more optimistic way to look at it. Vulnerabilities lead to exploits, and exploits lead to attacks, but in an enterprise context, the impact of an attack is determined by how far the compromised identities can reach. A shell on a PHP server grants the attacker access to whatever that server can read, from environment variables to cloud keys in config files.
PHP2Shell can also leak worker memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys. An attacker executing code on one host opens a door to a hallway, but the real valuables are usually in locked rooms.
And the controls that limit lateral movement don't depend on winning a race against discovery. Finding vulnerabilities is an open-ended process, and limiting the reach of a service account is a quantifiable task.
Attackers take the easiest path
This approach has limits. If the vulnerability is in the IdP or the secrets manager, lateral movement capabilities come built in. If it's in the database or in the storage provider, the attacker is already where they want to be.
So with limited resources, it's tempting to stay vulnerability-first: catalog what the advisories and scanners found, triage it, work down from the top. But cataloging takes weeks, and fixing the most pressing findings takes even longer. The bet here is that the most exploitable holes in your core systems are the ones you'll close first.
That bet prioritizes the vulnerability’s severity (the CVSS score) over the blast radius. Attackers aren't looking for the most direct path; they're looking for the easiest path. Taking a leaked credential and moving with it is easier than stringing together zero-days to reach a database directly.
October's other headlines show that path. At LiteLLM, attackers used a master key exposed in a public repository to retrieve an unscoped GitHub organization-owner token from an internal agent platform. That identity let them steal two more maintainer tokens, subvert the release workflow, and publish credential-stealing artifacts.
Shrink the blast radius first
You can’t win the race to patch every server before the attackers arrive, but you can determine what a compromised server is worth to them. Discover and inventory every AI agent and non-human identity and start by securing the ones that reach the most.
Assign an owner, scope access to purpose and intent, remove dormant credentials, and continuously govern the identity lifecycle. For AI agents, go further and grant access by intent. That is what it means to treat identity as the control plane.
Patching decides how fast you close a hole. Identity decides how much an attacker gets when you can’t.

articles.title: Colombia tiene ahora un centro de ciberseguridad que detecta ataques en menos de 10 minutos y los resuelve 5 veces más rápido
articles.text:
Indra lanzó en Colombia un Centro de Operaciones de Ciberseguridad (SOC) con inteligencia artificial (IA) para detectar incidentes críticos como ciberataques en menos de 10 minutos y reducir hasta cinco veces los tiempos de investigación y resolución.
El centro incorpora automatización y agentes de IA para clasificar alertas, identificar comportamientos anómalos y priorizar los eventos que requieren intervención, con un alcance que cubre a Colombia y Latinoamérica.
La operación mantiene supervisión humana durante el análisis y la contención de incidentes, según explicó Edwin Balteros, director de ciberseguridad de Indra para Colombia, Ecuador, Centroamérica y el Caribe.
Cómo opera el centro de ciberseguridad
El SOC reúne herramientas de monitoreo que reciben señales desde distintos sistemas de una organización. A partir de esos datos, identifica accesos inusuales, intentos de intrusión, movimientos sospechosos dentro de una red y otros indicios que pueden anticipar un ataque.
La operación busca cubrir el ciclo completo de un incidente: detección, análisis, respuesta, contención y recuperación. El modelo contempla la protección de espacios de tecnologías de la información y de tecnologías operativas, que controlan procesos físicos en sectores como energía, transporte, salud e infraestructura.
Cómo la IA potencia la ciberseguridad
La inteligencia artificial permite filtrar un volumen elevado de alertas y entregar a los analistas una primera evaluación sobre el nivel de riesgo. Los agentes automatizados contrastan eventos, identifican patrones y ayudan a diferenciar una actividad rutinaria de una posible amenaza que requiere una intervención inmediata.
Baltero explicó que los tiempos de revisión se redujeron frente a métodos convencionales. “Generalmente, el tiempo promedio de análisis de una alerta se hacía más o menos entre 25 y 30 minutos. Estamos pasando a hablar de una alerta bien validada entre cuatro y cinco minutos”.
Por qué es clave la rapidez al momento de detectar un incidente de ciberseguridad
La velocidad es uno de los factores que determina la dimensión de un incidente. Un atacante que permanece dentro de una red sin ser detectado puede obtener contraseñas, copiar información, desplazarse entre sistemas, alterar procesos o bloquear archivos y servicios.
“Esta es una competencia de tiempo. Entre más rápido logremos detectar, más rápido garantizamos que no se expanda un ataque dentro de una compañía”, dijo Balteros.
El ejecutivo aclaró que la IA participa en el análisis y la priorización de eventos, aunque los especialistas mantienen la supervisión de las decisiones relacionadas con la respuesta.
Cuáles son los ciberataques más comunes que experimentan usuarios y empresas
El phishing continúa entre las técnicas más utilizadas. “El phishing, que es ese correo malicioso, sigue siendo el top en todos los tipos de ataques”, señaló Balteros. El ataque aprovecha un punto vulnerable que no depende exclusivamente de las defensas tecnológicas: la decisión del usuario que recibe el mensaje.
Según explicó Balteros, los avances en inteligencia artificial mejoraron la redacción, la apariencia y la personalización de mensajes fraudulentos, lo que dificulta reconocerlos a simple vista.
Asimismo, el ransomware mantiene presencia entre las amenazas que enfrentan las organizaciones. En estos casos, los atacantes cifran información o bloquean sistemas y luego exigen un pago.
A ello se suman fraudes que utilizan clonación de voz y videos manipulados para suplantar a directivos, empleados o familiares y obtener transferencias, información reservada o autorizaciones internas.
Qué sectores están más expuestos a ciberataques
El sector financiero continúa entre los objetivos más atractivos por el volumen de recursos e información que administra. A la vez, los ataques contra infraestructuras críticas han ampliado el riesgo a sectores como energía, salud y transporte.
“Hoy en día son todos los sectores”, afirmó Balteros al referirse a los objetivos de los ciberdelincuentes. “Paralizar un hospital es una problemática que pasa más allá del mundo digital. No simplemente la pérdida de una información, sino que puede terminar en afectación de vidas humanas”.

articles.title: Les nouveaux MacBook Pro sont tactiles, voilà la techno qu'Apple a choisi — Frandroid
articles.text:
Apple a officialisé ce mercredi 28 octobre un MacBook Pro qui se pilote au doigt, en 14 et 16 pouces. Avec lui, la marque met fin à vingt ans de refus surtout sous l’ère de Steve Jobs, et rejoint ainsi la myriade de PC portables à écrans tactiles.
En 2010, Steve Jobs jugeait ces écrans « ergonomiquement terribles », parce que le bras fatigue vite à toucher une surface verticale.
L’Apple de 2026 ne semble pas avoir trouvé une parade à ce problème. En revanche, il a renforcé la charnière pour que l’écran ne bascule pas sous le doigt, et ajouté une stabilisation de la webcam pour que l’image ne tremble pas quand on touche l’écran en visio.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Un capteur dans la dalle, comme chez Samsung depuis 2023
Apple insiste sur un détail : le capteur tactile est intégré directement à la dalle, sans couche posée par-dessus, ce qui réduit le délai entre le doigt et l’affichage. Sur un écran tactile classique, on colle entre la dalle et la vitre un film tactile d’environ 40 micromètres, plus sa couche d’adhésif, d’après le schéma publié par Samsung Display.
Le fabricant coréen se passe de ce film depuis 2023 sur les Galaxy Book avec sa technologie OCTA, qui loge les capteurs directement dans l’OLED. Apple applique le même principe, et la finesse de l’OLED lui permet d’affiner le modèle 16 pouces de près d’un millimètre.
macOS 27 traduit tous les appuis
Pour ne pas attendre les développeurs, macOS 27 traduit automatiquement chaque appui en clic, ce qui rend les applications existantes utilisables au doigt dès la sortie des MacBook Pro tactiles. Apple ajoute des gestes propres à son ADN : un double appui sur une fenêtre la passe en plein écran, un mouvement rapide du doigt la range en mosaïque, et le pincement zoome dans une photo.
L’encoche laisse sa place à la Dynamic Island de l’iPhone, qui accueille Spotlight, Siri AI et les activités en direct. On peut également y accepter un AirDrop ou mettre en pause un morceau d’un simple appui. Dans Logic Pro, un clavier polyphonique multipoint s’affiche à l’écran, et Final Cut Pro permet de zoomer sur une coupe en pinçant. Autant d’usages qui seront amenés à se développer.
Les versions tactiles de Word, Excel, Lightroom ou Blender sont promises d’ici la fin de l’année.
Les précommandes sont ouvertes depuis ce mercredi sur l’Apple Store, pour des livraisons à partir du vendredi 6 novembre. Le 14 pouces démarre à 3 299 euros et le 16 pouces à 3 899 euros, donc bien au-delà des 3 000 euros évoqués avant l’annonce. La configuration maximale associe une puce M5 Max, 128 Go de mémoire, 16 To de stockage et un verre nano-texturé, le tout pour plus de 16 000 euros ! Le mini-LED reste au catalogue avec le MacBook Pro 14 pouces M6, vendu à partir de 2 299 euros.
