articles.title: Norton launches new Safe AI tool to stay in control and protect users when using AI - Tech Guide
articles.text:
With the increased use of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude, Norton has released Safe AI to keep an eye on what AI chat apps can do and access on your device.
According to Gen Threat Labs, there has been a 54 per cent increase in malicious content served through AI chatbots in the last 90 days.
Separate research has also found more than two-thirds of people are concerned about privacy, data breaches, or losing control of AI assistants that can act on their behalf.
Safe AI is a new set of protections within Norton 360 and can block actions you did not intend and let you decide which personal files AI tools can access and open.
It can also help you avoid risky links.
AI assistants are making things easier for many people, from finding information to getting things done, but that convenience can bring with it new risks.
Safe AI can address these emerging issues and risks and quell people’s concern while increasing Norton’s protection in AI experiences people are using every day.
“Most of the AI tools people are using today should really come with a warning label that safety isn’t included,” said Dagim Girma, GM for Norton.
“The tools were designed around how to get the job done and not necessarily how to get the job done right, or even safely, despite the best intentions,
“That’s where we come in. People shouldn’t have to become AI security experts to benefit from AI tools.
“With Safe AI, we’re helping people stay in control of their information and embrace the possibilities of AI with greater confidence.”
Safe AI has been with the foundation of Norton 360’s advanced scam protection.
It introduces three capabilities designed to help make using AI tools safer:
– Protects against unwanted AI actions. As AI tools become more capable of performing tasks, malicious instructions and prompt injections can introduce new security risks. Action Shield helps stop unwanted AI actions and potentially harmful prompt injections before they run.
– Gives people more control over AI file access. As people connect AI tools to their personal files and content, understanding what those tools can access becomes increasingly important. Safe Zone lets you choose which connected files and content AI can access, with options for full, read-only or blocked permissions.
– Spots risky links before you click. AI assistants can surface links that appear useful or trustworthy, even when they lead to unsafe destinations. Safe Links helps identify potentially harmful links shared through ChatGPT and Claude before people open them.

articles.title: I tested the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark and that next-gen Nvidia chip gives it superb AI, creative and gaming performance — it’s like a MacBook Pro M5 you can game on
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Not only does the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark have a lightweight form factor and a huge and vibrant OLED screen but that eponymous RTX Spark chip from Nvidia gives it some impressive power. Whether you want to train your own AI agents, edit video or play games on the go, it makes short work of many workloads. The only real stumbling block is that super high price — it costs as much as a top-of-the-range gaming laptop or creative work station, while not besting them for performance, meaning it’s best for those that need power in every area, rather than just one.
Reasons to buy
- + Stunning 3K OLED screen
- + Stylish, lightweight design
- + Strong creative, AI and gaming performance
Reasons to avoid
- - Very expensive
- - Bested by dedicated gaming or creative laptops
- - Some wobble to the screen
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark: two-minute review
The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is one of the new generation of laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. This all-in-one system-on-a-chip is packing 20 ARM CPU cores, 6144 CUDA GPU backed up by 64GB of RAM and promises to offer fantastic AI, creative and gaming performance in a lightweight, portable form factor. So how does this new SoC version of the Asus ProArt P16 laptop fare?
When powering up the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark for the first time, perhaps the first thing I noticed is its huge, vibrant 16-inch OLED screen. With a peak brightness of 1,100 nits and a 100% DCI-P3 color gamut, it looked gorgeous whether I was loading up my digital artworks or watching movies. And its 120Hz VRR makes it perfect for playing games on.
That’s not the only part of the ProArt P16’s design that feels premium. Its overall build quality feels suitably luxe, with the smooth metal of its upper casing feeling wonderfully tactile. Inside, its keyboard is well designed and feels pleasant to type on, while its haptic trackpad is precise and gives snappy feedback, even if I did find it too easy to trigger the right click at first. I will say its lid has a little bit too much wobble for my liking though: if I’m honest, I’d expect a laptop at this price to have a slightly more stable hinge.
But let’s not just focus on the superficial here: the ProArt P16 RTX Spark has a lot going on under the surface. That’s predominantly thanks to that Nvidia SoC, which enables it to tackle a wider range of tasks than even many of the best laptops.
Perhaps the most attention grabbing feature is its AI capabilities. Designed for hybrid workflows, the RTX Spark makes it easy to use a combination of local and cloud models to run your AI agents. Testing it out with the Qwen 3 8B open-source local model, I certainly found it had pretty snappy performance for basic workflows, with a basic data analysis only taking about 12 minutes.
More involved tasks took much more refining and prompting over multiple sessions though — attempting to automate 3DMark benchmarks took many 75 minute runs before the completion time reduced significantly. Still, being able to run these workflows on such a lightweight, portable machine was pretty impressive
Another area the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark delivers potent performance is during creative tasks. Running multiple PugetBench benchmarks for automating Photoshop and Premier Pro workflows, the ProArt P16 was only a little behind Apple’s M5 chip when running image-based tasks and beat it when it came to video tasks. And this was borne out by my own testing: even my largest 4K 300dpi Photoshop file crammed full of clipping masks didn’t make it wince, with filters and generative fills executing smoothly. Even downscaling the whole image to 2K only took around five seconds, which isn’t bad for a nigh-on 2GB file.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Few SoCs to date have been designed with gaming performance in mind. But given Nvidia’s heritage in this space, it’s hardly surprising that the ProArt P16 RTX Spark is capable of some serious gaming power. While it’s not quite able to deliver at the same level as RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs, I enjoyed a very smooth 60fps on Cyberpunk 2077 on Raytracing Medium settings, while Gears of War: E-day ran at more solid than bedrock at over 110fps. So this laptop can achieve some stunning results, even if the performance you’ll get isn’t 100% the top of the range.
Given it can handle all of these tasks on the go, you’d hope it has a pretty capacious battery to back up that powerful chip. And it’s relatively good news on this front. While it only managed 11 hours of continuous video playback during my testing, during productivity based work it lasted well over 14 hours. That’s nowhere near as long-lasting as the Methuselah-like MacBook Pro M5 Pro, which clocked over 21 hours in our testing, but it’s certainly enough to get you through a standard day’s work.
Honestly, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is pretty adept at everything it tries to do: it’s a talented all-rounder. The only caveat really is its price: like many of the RTX Spark laptops, it isn’t cheap. Starting from $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999, it costs just as much as a high-end gaming laptop or a pro-level creative workhorse — so, honestly, if you care more about getting the best performance you can in a specific niche, you may be better off investing in one of those instead.
However, if you need a single bow that can handle every single one of your strings, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is a good shout. It’ll handle running your own AI agents, whipping up creative work and even gaming for your downtime, all in a single, portable package.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: price & availability
Having launched on October 9, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is available now. Unlike its smaller sibling, it ships with the higher-end Nvidia RTX Spark N1X with 6144-core GPU and 20-core CPU.
As a result, it’s a pricey meatball: its list price starts from $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999 for the spec with 64GB RAM, 3K screen and 1TB SSD. That increases to $6,999.99 / £5,999.99 / AU$10,999 if you want the version with 128GB RAM, a 4K screen and a 2TB SSD.
Even with its impressive specs, there’s no getting away from the fact that this is a premium-priced laptop. Both in terms of price and spec, the ProArt P16 RTX Spark is pretty similar to the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra with Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, which will set you back $3,799.99 / £3,649 (around AU$5,410).
Alternatively, this kind of spend could net you the MacBook Pro M5 Pro 16-inch with 64GB for $2,999 / £3,999 / AU$6,299, which should give you a lot of performance and creative power but I wouldn’t expect to get quite as much gaming power for your buck.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: Specs
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark Base Config | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark High end Config | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999 | $6,999.99 / £5,999.99 / AU$10,999 | 
| CPU | NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X 20-core | NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X 20-core CPU | 
| GPU | NVIDIA Blackwell RTX 6144-core | NVIDIA Blackwell RTX 6144-core GPU | 
| RAM | 64GB | 128GB | 
| Storage | 1TB SSD | 2TB SSD | 
| Display | 16.0-inch, 2880 x 1800, 120Hz, 1100 nits OLED | 16.0-inch, 3840 x 2400, 120Hz, 1600 nits OLED | 
| Ports and Connectivity | 3x USB-C, USB, HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack, SD Express 7.0 card reader | 3x USB-C, USB, HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack, SD Express 7.0 card reader | 
| Battery | 99.9Wh | 99.9Wh | 
| Dimensions | 13.94 x 9.57 x 0.63 inches / 354.1 x 243 x 15.9mm | 13.94 x 9.57 x 0.63 inches / 354.1 x 243 x 15.9mm | 
| Weight | 3.9 lbs / 1.77kg | 3.9 lbs / 1.77kg | 
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: design
- Gorgeous 3K OLED display
- Slim, sleek design
- Slightly flimsy hinge
Like all of the initial lineup RTX Spark laptops I’ve seen, the new Asus ProArt P16 is a sleek-looking unit. While its 16-inch span is pretty expansive, it’s still light in terms of weight, clocking in at 1.77 kg compared to my 16-inch MacBook Pro M4’s 2.14kg. It’s also got a pretty sleek silhouette — unlike some of the RTX Spark laptop models I’ve seen, it’s not concealing a much chonkier base with the help of gradually sloping bevels. And its nano black and neo white colorways feel suitably premium, although I marginally prefer the black version I tested here.
It’s not all about style though: the ProArt P16 RTX Spark has plenty of substance too. Manufactured from smooth metal, its external and internal surfaces feel wonderfully tactile, although I’d say the inner ones feel a tiny bit less sturdy than the solid bodywork of the outside. On top of this, there’s a tiny bit of wobble to its screen when you touch it — I’d expect a slightly firmer hinge on a premium laptop like this.
Speaking of that screen, I found Asus’s 3K touchscreen Lumina Pro OLED to be pretty impressive on the whole. Not only can my unit hit a peak brightness of 1,100 nits and a max 120Hz VRR but comparing it to my MacBook Pro M4’s Liquid Retina XDR display while watching Pixar’s Elemental was — sorry for this — pretty illuminating. While the latter can go slightly brighter at 1,600 nits peak, I didn’t find the difference all that pronounced. And the colors of the P16 RTX Spark’s OLED panel were noticeably more vibrant, with the reds, blues and greens of the fire, water and earth elements really popping.
To say laptop keyboards can be hit or miss might be the understatement of the century but, fortunately, the ProArt P16 RTX Spark’s keyboard falls more in the former category than the latter. Although the keys don’t have a huge amount of travel, I still found the typing experience to be pretty fluid. I rarely ever struggled to find my chosen key when touch typing — although I did occasionally knock both parts of the dual enter key, accidentally sticking random #s at the end of sentences. Still, it felt nice to use, whether I was prompting an AI agent or rapidly splatting demons in Doom: The Dark Ages.
For the most part, the P16 RTX Spark’s trackpad is also well designed. It’s very accurate, gives you a huge area for controlling your cursor and the haptic feedback is spot on, feeling exactly like a mechanical click. Really the only issue I found with it is the right click triggers far too far to the left, meaning I’d sometimes accidentally right click on certain elements. Still though, it’s a decent trackpad for the most part.
As you’d expect from a laptop this premium, the P16 RTX Spark comes with access to a wide range of connectivity options as well. On top of offering Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity, it rocks a pretty decent selection of ports for such a slim laptop. These include three USB-C and one standard USB port, an HDMI 2.1 port, a 3.5mm headphone jack and an SD Express card reader. So even for most creative workflows, you should find you’re able to plug in plenty of devices to get things done.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: performance
- Strong all-round performance
- Local AI workflows impressive but require some patience
- Specialist laptops can give better gaming or creative performance
I’ll be honest: by far the most exciting part about getting my hands on the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is that eponymous chip. Similar to Apple’s M-series silicon, Nvidia’s RTX Spark is the company’s first attempt at a full system-on-a-chip architecture. And given Nvidia’s involvement in both the AI and gaming spaces, it’s safe to say I was looking forward to putting the Nvidia Spark RTX through its paces.
Combining CPU, GPU and RAM all in one compact package, the version of the RTX Spark included with the Asus ProArt P16 I tested here rocks 20 ARM CPU cores backed up by 64GB of RAM. Meanwhile, on the graphics side, it wields 6144 CUDA GPU cores with 30GB integrated memory. In terms of raw hardware, it's less cooked and more meaty than steak tartare.
While this is the equivalent of using a steam hammer to obliterate a nut, general productivity tasks ran perfectly smoothly on the ProArt P16 RTX Spark. Whether I was browsing the web, tinkering with spreadsheets or leafing through huge PDFs, I never experienced any awkward hanging or slowdowns. Even on the odd occasion when I had to look something up online while the laptop worked on an AI task, there wasn’t any unpleasant gear-crunching, showing the ProArt P16 is plenty fast enough for general use.
But you’re unlikely to be buying an RTX Spark laptop just for doing a bit of Googling or filing your taxes. Instead, the most obvious use case for the RTX Spark chip in the ProArt P16 is its hybrid agentic AI functionality. Put simply, rather than being forced to choose between using cloud models that potentially jeopardize the security of your data and less powerful local models, this blended approach means you can pick and choose which parts of your workflow you’re going to outsource to the cloud and which you’ll keep under strict local control.
With its integrated fifth-generation Tensor cores, the RTX Spark should be perfectly placed to support this. To see how fast it could run some of these models locally, I used the MLPerf Client benchmarking tool to mimic data analyst and SWE agentic workflows using the Qwen 3 8B local model. And the results felt pretty rapid, with the pipelines completing after an average duration of 63.7 and 50.8 seconds and processing up to 14,005 and 10,238 tokens respectively.
But I wanted to see for myself what it could do. So I fired up Hermes, the open-source AI agent tool, and set it up to run the local open-source model Qwen3.8 27B to see what having my own personal AI version of Alfred could help me achieve.
Some of the basic tasks I threw its way, the RTX Spark practically scoffed at. When I asked Hermes to organize a spreadsheet full of web analytics for me and pull out actionable highlights, it whipped the file up into a pivot table and gave me six bullet points within about 12 minutes. Asking it to convert this info into a presentation with slides and prompts took a little longer at 23 minutes, but it helped highlight the best information to pitch — even if the slides themselves needed a considerable glow up before I’d ever call them up in a Zoom call.
In theory though, these hybrid agentic AI tools can go much further than this. Not only can you convert your prompts into skills or schedule them to run as daily tasks but you can even set them to target your apps and control your screen directly.
Some of my experiments paid off here: after one abortive run, I eventually managed to get Hermes to access my emails and create a daily digest in 70 minutes. But trying to automate some of my 3DMark benchmarking process ended up being a real rabbit hole — even with judicious prompts throughout the process and prompting Hermes to find ways to boost the skill’s efficiency, it took around eight runs to significantly improve its workflow. So it’s important to recognize that while some agentic pipelines may save you time in the long run, without utilizing some cloud models, training them may take a decent investment.
Agentic AI isn’t the only use you can put all of that processing power to though. While I’m not a massive fan of generative AI, I can definitely see how fast the RTX Spark is at whipping up new images and videos. Automating some imagery and video pipelines using ComfyUI, the laptop completed tests of Flux2.Dev - NVFP4 and Flux2.Klein 4B Base - NVFP4 models in just 46.5 and 16.2 seconds, while the LTX 2.5 - Distilled - NVFP4 video model took 88 seconds. Those are pretty swift run times for local generative models.
And if, like me, you prefer creating your own stuff from scratch, my testing showed the ProArt P16 RTX Spark can help here too. Using PugetBench to automate a range of creative workflows, I found Asus’s laptop was capable of some lightning fast processing.
Our standard Photoshop workflow completed in 10.83 minutes and achieved a score of 11,801 — that’s not far short of Apple’s M5 chip at 13,755. And the RTX Spark offered even speedier performance for video work, securing a score in our Premier Pro benchmark of 76,234 in 8.12 minutes, giving the M5 chip a bit of a drubbing at 69,887. Unfortunately, it can’t keep up with the similarly priced Apple MacBook Pro M5 Pro though, which managed to best it for both still imagery and video with scores of 15,204 and 105,580 respectively.
Naturally, I’m not just going to take these numbers on trust though, so I dug out one of my most demanding Photoshop files — a 4K, 300dpi PSD with dozens of clipping masks and adjustment layers — and checked how the ProArt P16 RTX Spark handled it.
Manipulating layers and applying filters caused scarcely any slowdown, in spite of the fact I’d tripled the number of layers in the file. Even downscaling the image to 2K — no small task given the total file size was now in excess of 2GB — only took around five seconds, which is pleasingly swift. And thanks to the optimization work that Adobe has been doing behind the scenes to allow its apps to take advantage of the RTX Spark’s AI capabilities, even generative fills and neural filters didn’t take long to generate.
When it comes to gaming performance, I’d say the ProArt P16 RTX Spark hovers somewhere between mid-range laptops with RTX 5060 and RTX 5070 GPUs. For example, when playing Cyberpunk 2077 on Raytracing Ultra settings at 1080p, I found the Asus hovered around 30.16fps — but, by contrast, the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI with an RTX 5060 only reached a marginally smoother 34.47fps. Other games told a similar story. For example, Doom: The Dark Ages on Ultra settings sat at a pretty decent 48fps on the ProArt P16. In comparison, with its slightly beefier RTX 5070, the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra whipped the game like meringue into a much smoother 63.98fps.
But that’s running things on max settings. In practice, when actually playing games on more moderate settings, they ran plenty smoothly enough, especially those that are already well optimized for the RTX Spark. As I explored Dogtown in Cyberpunk 2077 at Raytracing Medium settings, it chugged along at a perfect stable 60fps. And playing Dogs of War: E-day on Ultra settings, I never saw it drop below 110fps, which shows what wonderfully smooth experiences you should still be able to expect from native gaming on the RTX Spark.
Honestly, I’d say that if you put the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark up against any similarly priced, specialist laptop focused on AI, creative workflows or gaming, you’ll likely find its performance can’t quite keep up. But that’s the point — RTX Spark laptops are a triple threat: they’re designed to be a swiss army knife that can handle every task you might throw at them. So if you want a lightweight laptop that combines the agentic AI hosting of a compact desktop, the creative power of the Apple M5 and the gaming oomph of the Nvidia Geforce RTX 5060, all in one handy package, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark should have your back.
- Performance score: 4.5 / 5
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: battery test
- Battery should last 14 hours of standard use
- Some similar rivals can outlast it
Being able to achieve all of this on the go is impressive. But for that to be sustainable, it needs a battery that can keep up with these kinds of heavy duty tasks. Fortunately, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is capable of decent battery life, even if it’s not quite as exceptional as some of its rivals.
Running it through our standard battery tests, I played a 1080p video at 50% brightness and volume to see how long it took to drain the battery from 100% to 0%. The ProArt P16 RTX Spark ran out of juice after 11h 23m — that’s not at all bad but it’s also not quite at the level I’d expect for a premium laptop like this.
But a video test doesn’t necessarily give you the full picture. One of the big benefits of an SoC is through boosted efficiency during CPU usage, so I wanted to also run some tests that showed how the laptop fared in action. Running PCMark 10’s applications battery test — which runs various Microsoft Office based tasks until the battery is drained — the ProArt P16 lasted 14h 24m.
That’s definitely a better score, even if it falls a little ways short of some of the best laptops for Windows. For example, the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra managed well over 15 hours in our benchmark tests and that wasn’t even the strongest contender. The MacBook Pro M5 Pro 16-inch clocked over 21 hours, which makes the ProArt P16’s look pretty short-lived in comparison.
Fortunately, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark does have one extra trick up its sleeve: its charging rate. Thanks to its 140W fast charging, topping your battery up again should be a relatively speedy affair. Sadly, my US unit didn’t come with a UK plug — slight oversight there — so I wasn’t able to test this as I would have liked. Still, my 65W charger topped it up relatively quickly, so you’ll definitely get pretty speedy charging out that 140W cable.
So I’d say that, all in all, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is capable of competitive battery life. When you’re doing standard office work, it’ll get you through a full day without you having to hunt out a charger. But it’s still not quite able to keep pace with the most enduring batteries on the market and particularly intensive tasks like AI or gaming are going to drain it much faster.
- Battery score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark has a lot of power behind it, an attractive lightweight design and a gorgeous screen. But that price is going to be a stumbling block for many, particularly when specialist gaming or creative laptops achieve better performance for similar cash. | 2.5 / 5 | 
| Design | A stunning 3K OLED screen, lightweight design and premium feeling materials, although it loses a few marks here and there for small details like its wobbly screen and slightly off-balance trackpad. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | While the ProArt P16 RTX Spark doesn’t offer top level performance in creative workflows or gaming, its AI tools and how much power it crams into a small frame are very impressive. Additionally, the fact it performs so well across so many categories makes it a great all rounder. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Battery Life | At roughly 14.5 hours, this laptop’s battery is strong but not exactly exceptional. You’ll comfortably get more than a day’s work out of it but it will definitely tap out sooner than a MacBook Pro during intensive workloads. | 4 / 5 | 
| Total | The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is a good-looking, lightweight laptop that’s perfect for anyone who wants to create, game and use AI agents on a single device. But that high price means that if you care most about performance in a single area, you’ll be better off with a specialist laptop. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if…
You want to game, create and use AI on a single device
Thanks to Nvidia’s RTX Spark SoC, the Asus ProArt P16 puts considerable power behind every task you might throw at it. So if you’re a bit of a polymath, it may well be the only device you need.
You want a seriously portable 16-inch device
Despite that gorgeous and expansive 16-inch display, the laptop’s wonderfully light — at 3.9 lbs / 1.77kg, it’s svelter than other powerful laptops like the MacBook Pro M5 Pro or the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra.
Don’t buy it if…
You want top performance in any one category
If you only really care about gaming or creative work is your sole priority, there are laptops out there that can give you peak performance for a similar spend.
You don’t have loads of money laying around
There’s no getting away from it: this laptop ain’t cheap. Even in its base spec, you’ll be paying $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999, so if you’re not feeling flush, you might want to look elsewhere.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: also consider
Apple MacBook Pro M5 Pro
If you’re wanting a true creative powerhouse, the MacBook Pro M5 Pro will get you there. Despite costing a similar price, this incarnation of Apple’s laptop will absolutely blitz both image and video workflows, while also offering an absurdly long 21-hour battery life. While you’re not going to get top shelf gaming performance out of Apple silicon, this is still a great choice if your main concern is sheer creative thrust. Read our full Apple MacBook Pro M5 Pro review.
Asus Zephyrus G16 2026
With its discrete Nvidia Geforce RTX 5080 GPU, the Asus Zephyrus G16 2026 offers seriously nippy gaming performance, besting the P16 RTX Spark in both benchmarks and in-game frame rates. Okay, it’s not going to unlock the same oomph the P16 can for hybrid AI workflows. But if your main concern is pure gaming punch, the Zephyrus G16 will deliver.
How I tested the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark
- Tested over the course of several weeks
- Ran a huge number of benchmarks for different workflows
- Conducted experiential AI, gaming and creative testing
Testing the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark over the course of several weeks, I ran a wide range of benchmarks. Not only did I run a variety of baseline hardware tests using Geekbench 7.1 and Cinebench R23, but I tested performance across a wide range of tasks as well. I used MLPerf Client to test agentic workflows, ComfyUI to simulate generative workflows, PugetBench to automate creative tasks and 3DMark and gaming benchmarks to test in-game GPU performance.
On top of this, I did a wide range of experiential testing. Not only did I use the laptop for plenty of daily and productivity-based work but I also extensively tested agentic AI workflows using Hermes and the local open-source model Qwen3.8 27B. I also tried carrying out creative work using large, hi-resolution Photoshop files and played a range of games including Cyberpunk 2077, Gears of War: E-day and Planet Zoo 2.
As TechRadar’s reviews editor, I have plenty of experience covering laptops. As well as editing scores of laptop reviews over the last few years, I’ve reviewed multiple gaming handhelds and have used a huge variety of laptops over the years, both Windows and MacOS.
- First reviewed: October 2026
- Read more about how we test
Josh is Reviews Editor at TechRadar. With over ten years of experience covering tech both in print and online, he’s served as editor of T3 and net magazines and written about everything from groundbreaking gadgets to innovative Silicon Valley startups. He’s an expert in a wide range of products from Spatial Audio headphones to gaming handhelds. When he’s not putting trailblazing tech through its paces, he can be found making melodic techno or seeking out the perfect cold brew coffee.

articles.title: AI agents need to be replaceable – without losing your work
articles.text:
AI agents need to be replaceable – without losing your work
An agent receives approval to process a partial refund. It sends the request to a payment API, and the process crashes. Maybe the payment service completed the refund. Maybe the request never went through. A replacement agent spins up and finds an operation record marked dispatched with no outcome written.
This kind of ambiguity isn’t unique to agents. Any distributed worker crashing mid-mutation faces the same problem. But a conventional worker resumes a predetermined workflow from the last checkpoint. An agent does something more dangerous: it reasons on its own. Given the same customer request and no outcome record, it might come up with a different plan, pick different parameters, or decide to issue a new refund instead of continuing the one already approved.
“An agent does something more dangerous: it reasons on its own.”
If the original refund went through, a second attempt refunds the customer twice. The charge still has enough remaining balance to cover another partial refund, so nothing stops it.
The replacement must inherit the original operation, not reinterpret it.
The operation must outlive the agent
An agent’s process, its in-memory variables, its transient reasoning context: all disposable. The business operation is not. The refund, its approval, its parameters, its current status. A long-running agent can preserve useful state for as long as it runs. The requirement: no essential operation should depend on the original execution surviving.
Before dispatching the refund, the application commits a durable operation record to a transactional store. That record includes the approved amount, the applicable authorization, the idempotency key the application sends to the payment provider, the application’s operation identifier in the provider’s metadata, and a status.
“An agent’s process, its in-memory variables, its transient reasoning context: all disposable. The business operation is not.”
The status moves from created to dispatched as the request leaves, and to confirmed or failed only on a provider response. If the agent crashes, the replacement retrieves this record and its correlation identifiers. A record stuck in dispatched indicates a call was attempted, but the outcome was never written.
The replacement inherits the approved operation rather than regenerating it.
When the replacement needs to verify the outcome, it can list refunds against the original charge and match the operation identifier in the returned metadata.
But the durable record isn’t just context for the replacement. The application enforces it at the tool boundary: the dispatch layer validates every outbound request against the committed record. The agent can propose a next step, but only authorized operations with their original parameters and identity reach the provider. The model can’t redefine what was approved.
ClickHouse Managed Postgres holds the business data, including the authoritative operation record that defines what the replacement is allowed to do. Native CDC replicates that data into ClickHouse. Application telemetry ships to ClickStack and agent traces to Langfuse, both configured to use the same ClickHouse service as their backend database.
Because business data, application telemetry, and agent traces land in one database, tying an operation to the agent run that dispatched it and the failed HTTP call is a single-identifier query. Not a reconciliation across three tools.
Two conditions. The application has to propagate that identifier. The operation ID must appear in the Postgres row, in the Langfuse trace attributes, and in the service’s log context, because nothing correlates it for you. And the replacement reads the record from Postgres, not from the replicated copy. CDC runs with seconds of latency. The authoritative row is the one the tool boundary enforces.
Restarting execution isn’t safely resuming work
Durable execution frameworks like LangGraph and Temporal record execution progress and resume after a failure. Both recommend making side effects idempotent, because resuming doesn’t resolve one. If the refund completed while the step was still pending, the framework can restart the agent, but it can’t tell the replacement whether the payment provider committed the original request.
The durable operation record implements that idempotency guidance for an agent whose next step isn’t predetermined.
The idempotency key from the durable record connects the replacement to the original request. If the replacement retries with the same key, the provider can recognize the same operation rather than processing an independent refund. This holds even if the original agent’s in-flight request completed after the crash, or a worker assumed dead has resumed. AWS’s Builders’ Library formalizes this pattern: a caller-provided identifier recorded atomically with the mutation.
But retrying isn’t always safe. The outcome might stay unclear. Stripe documents that a 500 response on a mutation can still produce external effects. When the outcome is unknown, the replacement needs evidence to investigate.
Langfuse can show the previous agent’s tool invocation: a refund request dispatched with the recorded idempotency key. ClickStack can fill in the operational side: an outbound HTTP request to the payment service followed by a connection failure, narrowing the failure window.
Both are available to the replacement directly. The Langfuse MCP server lets it query the previous agent’s trace by operation ID, and the ClickStack MCP server lets it search service events in the same window. Give the replacement the read tools only. It can narrow down what happened, but the tool boundary still controls what the replacement can do.
Neither trace proves the provider committed the refund. And an absent trace doesn’t prove the request was never sent, since Langfuse transmits traces asynchronously and a crash can prevent delivery. The payment provider remains the system of record for the external outcome. Execution telemetry narrows the investigation. It doesn’t replace authoritative confirmation.
Continue the work; don’t start over
The replacement has the durable record and, where the outcome was unclear, the execution evidence. Now it needs to act, but not by re-deciding what to do.
The replacement follows the recovery protocol the application defines, not its own judgment about the customer’s situation.
If the provider confirms the refund is complete, the replacement records the outcome and moves on. If the provider shows the refund is still pending or in progress, the replacement waits. Retrying would risk a duplicate. If the refund definitively failed with no external effect, the replacement revalidates preconditions before a new authorized attempt. If the outcome remains unclear, it escalates rather than guessing. A missing provider record doesn’t prove the refund was never processed. The provider may not have finalized the transaction.
“A stored approval is historical evidence, not current authority to act.”
Even after establishing the external outcome, the replacement has to verify that the world hasn’t changed. The refundable balance may have shifted. A human representative might have processed a separate refund through a different interface. The customer’s account status may have changed. Someone may have revoked the original authorization.
A stored approval is historical evidence, not current authority to act.
The real engineering question is whether a new agent can establish the work’s current objective, outstanding obligations, and uncertain effects, then continue safely without treating the predecessor’s recollections as authority.
The agent is disposable. The work isn’t.

articles.title: Test Samsung Odyssey G8 (G80HF) : 5K, 360 Hz… Samsung veut tout, mais peut-il tout faire ?
articles.text:
Un seul écran pour travailler et jouer, c'est le pari de Samsung avec son Odyssey G8 (G80HF). Ce moniteur de 27 pouces mise sur une dalle Fast IPS capable d'afficher une définition 5K à 180 Hz, tout en proposant un second mode en QHD à 360 Hz. Une polyvalence intéressante pour les créateurs de contenu comme pour les joueurs, même si les performances HDR et quelques concessions matérielles viennent tempérer cette proposition.
Les écrans destinés au gaming et ceux conçus pour la création de contenu ne répondent pas toujours aux mêmes exigences. Les premiers privilégient généralement la fréquence de rafraîchissement et la réactivité, tandis que les seconds mettent davantage l'accent sur la finesse d'affichage et la précision des couleurs. Avec son Odyssey G8 (G80HF), Samsung cherche à réunir ces deux univers au sein d'un même moniteur.
- La finesse d'affichage en 5K sur 27 pouces
- Le Dual Mode QHD à 360 Hz
- Une latence d'affichage bien maîtrisée
- Sa large couverture colorimétrique
- La connectique globalement généreuse
- Absence d'un port USB-C
- Des performances HDR limitées
- Position du joystick de réglages peu ergonomique
- Un contraste et des noirs en retrait de l'OLED
- Des temps de réponse perfectibles à 360 Hz
Pour cela, le constructeur sud-coréen mise sur une dalle Fast IPS de 27 pouces, affichant une définition native de 5 120 × 2 880 pixels, avec une fréquence maximale annoncée de 180 Hz. Sa particularité réside toutefois dans son Dual Mode, qui permet de basculer vers une définition QHD de 2 560 × 1 440 pixels pour atteindre les 360 Hz. De quoi répondre aussi bien aux besoins des créateurs qu'à ceux des amateurs de FPS.
Alors, ce nouvel allié des créateurs comme des gamers est-il convaincant ? Nous l'avons testé pendant deux semaines, voici notre verdict.
Nos mesures sur le Samsung Odyssey G8 (G80HF)
Le Samsung Odyssey G8 (G80HF) étant un écran dual-mode, nous avons testé sa réactivité sur les deux modes disponibles. La latence est globalement bien maîtrisée sur cet écran Samsung, avec des résultats qui évoluent sensiblement selon le mode d’affichage utilisé. En 5K à 180 Hz, nous avons mesuré une latence d’affichage de 4,6 ms, contre seulement 1,7 ms en 1440p à 360 Hz, ce qui est excellent en termes de réactivité.
L’input lag sur le Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HF
| Input lag | Valeur en 5K / 60 Hz | Valeur en 5K / 180 Hz | Valeur en 1440p / 360 Hz | 
| Moyenne* | 13,3 ms | 13,1 ms | 10,6 ms | 
| Minimum | 9,4 ms | 8,2 ms | 9 ms | 
| Maximum | 18,3 ms | 17,5 ms | 12,2 ms | 
| Affichage seul | 4,7 ms | 4,6 ms | 1,7 ms | 
*Moyennes établies sur 200 mesures.
Les mesures click-to-photon confirment cette différence entre les deux configurations. Selon notre protocole habituel, à 60 Hz, l'input-lag moyen atteint 13,3 ms, avec un minimum à 9,4 ms et un maximum à 18,3 ms, avec un écart relativement marqué entre les valeurs minimales et maximales. À 180 Hz, l'input-lag atteint 13,1 ms en moyenne, avec des valeurs comprises entre 8,2 et 17,5 ms. On observe ici encore une certaine dispersion entre les valeurs minimales et maximales relevées. En passant à 360 Hz, la moyenne descend à 10,6 ms, oscillant entre 9 et 12,2 ms.
Outre la diminution de la latence, les mesures sont donc plus resserrées dans cette configuration, signe d'un comportement plus régulier. En pratique, cet avantage est particulièrement intéressant dans des jeux demandant une grande réactivité, comme de nombreux FPS.
| Mesure GtG | Valeur en 5K / 180 Hz | Valeur en 1440p / 360 Hz | 
| Temps de réponse moyen | 3,7 ms | 2,5 ms | 
| Temps de réponse max | 4,8 ms | 4,3 ms | 
| Overshoot moyen | 4,1 % | 1,2 % | 
| Overshoot max | 15,2 % | 16,3 % | 
| Transitions < 1 ms | 0 % | 0 % | 
Concernant le temps de réponse, les mesures LDAT mettent également en évidence une différence entre les deux modes. En 5K à 180 Hz, le temps de réponse GtG moyen s'établit à 3,7 ms, avec un maximum de 4,8 ms. Des valeurs encourageantes, qui permettent à la dalle de suivre la fréquence de rafraîchissement de 180 Hz. En QHD à 360 Hz, la moyenne descend à 2,5 ms, tandis que le maximum atteint 4,3 ms. Si la moyenne reste inférieure aux 2,78 ms séparant deux rafraîchissements à cette fréquence, certaines transitions demandent davantage de temps à la dalle pour s'effectuer.
Le Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HF offre une image en 5K à 180 Hz. Toutefois, pour en profiter, il faut disposer d'une carte graphique récente, comme une GeForce RTX 50 côté NVIDIA, ou bien une Radeon RX 7000 ou RX 9000 côté AMD, équipées d'un DisplayPort 2.1. Les cartes de série RTX 30 et RTX 40 se limitent à une image en 5K à 120 Hz. Nos mesures ici ont été réalisés avec une RTX 5080 prêtée par ASUS, connectée en DisplayPort.
Du côté de l'overshoot, la moyenne diminue sensiblement en passant à 360 Hz, de 4,1 % à 1,2 %. Le maximum grimpe toutefois à 16,3 %, ce qui traduit quelques dépassements plus importants susceptibles de provoquer du reverse ghosting. Ces résultats témoignent d'une réactivité globalement satisfaisante, même si toutes les transitions ne sont pas parfaitement maîtrisées à la fréquence maximale.
Autre élément que nous avons constaté : aucune des transitions mesurées ne passe sous la barre des 1 ms, tant en 180 Hz qu'en 360 Hz. Malgré un temps de réponse moyen de 2,5 ms avec la fréquence la plus élevée, les performances restent assez éloignées de ce que peuvent atteindre les meilleures dalles OLED.
Cliquez ici pour voir nos mesures SDR 
Avec cet Odyssey G8 G80HF, Samsung mise sur une dalle LCD Fast IPS de 27 pouces avec un ratio de 16:9, un format on ne peut plus classique. Cette dalle, capable d'atteindre les 360 Hz, offre une polyvalence certaine sur le papier.
En SDR, les résultats sont contrastés. Nous avons relevé un delta E moyen de 2,77 et un maximum de 4,4. La majorité des écarts reste donc relativement contenue, même si certaines teintes s'éloignent davantage de leur référence. Dans l'ensemble, la restitution des couleurs reste suffisante pour les usages courants. Pour les photographes professionnels ou les monteurs vidéo exigeant une grande fidélité colorimétrique, une calibration de l'écran est vivement recommandée.
L'échelle de gris affiche quant à elle de meilleurs résultats, avec un delta E moyen de seulement 1,7. La température moyenne de couleur, mesurée à 6 329 K, se situe légèrement sous la référence de 6 500 K, ce qui se traduit par une image très légèrement plus chaude que la normale. L'écart reste toutefois très contenu. Enfin, le gamma moyen, relevé à 2,145, se montre quant à lui très proche de la cible à 2,2. L'image est donc assez naturelle, mais les réglages d'usine n'atteignent pas la précision attendue par les plus exigeants.
La suite de nos mesures en HDR 
En HDR, le Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HF affiche certaines limites. La dalle prend en charge les contenus en HDR10 ainsi que la technologie HDR10+ pour le gaming. Cette dernière permet, sur les jeux compatibles, d'adapter le rendu HDR en fonction des caractéristiques de l'écran. Une caractéristique intéressante sur le papier, mais qui ne garantit pas nécessairement une expérience HDR spectaculaire.
Avec un delta E moyen de 2,66 et un maximum de 3,83, la précision se montre globalement convenable, même si certains écarts peuvent rester perceptibles.
Selon le mode sélectionné, nous avons relevé une luminosité maximale d'environ 370 cd/m² en HDR. Cette valeur reste toutefois modeste pour un affichage HDR et limite l'intensité des hautes lumières. Sur une petite surface, la luminosité reste particulièrement faible, avec environ 75 à 85 cd/m² sur des fenêtres de 1 et 2 %, puis près de 200 cd/m² sur une fenêtre de 5 %.
En cause, une gestion particulièrement rudimentaire de la gradation locale du rétroéclairage (local dimming). Le G80HF ne dispose en effet que de quelques grandes zones de gradation verticales, ce qui limite fortement sa capacité à ajuster précisément la luminosité des différentes parties de l'image. Pour éviter des écarts trop visibles entre les zones claires et sombres, le traitement tend notamment à réduire l'intensité des petits éléments lumineux.
La luminosité augmente ensuite sensiblement pour atteindre environ 355 cd/m² sur une fenêtre de 10 %, avant de se stabiliser autour de 350 cd/m² jusqu’à une fenêtre couvrant la totalité de l’écran. La luminosité reste ainsi relativement stable lorsque la surface affichée augmente, sans toutefois atteindre un niveau suffisant pour donner beaucoup d'éclat aux contenus HDR.
La couverture colorimétrique constitue en revanche l'un des atouts majeurs de cet écran. Nous avons mesuré 94,48 % de l'espace DCI-P3 et 69,82 % du BT.2020. Ce Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HF couvre une très large partie de l'espace P3, lui permettant de restituer des couleurs riches et suffisamment variées pour la majorité des jeux et contenus vidéo compatibles. La couverture du BT.2020 reste plus limitée, mais elle reste cohérente avec les capacités colorimétriques de nombreux moniteurs actuels.
Le bilan est donc globalement positif pour ce Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HF. Les performances en SDR sont dans l'ensemble convenables. Les performances en HDR se montrent toutefois plus mitigées. Malgré une couverture DCI-P3 étendue et une luminosité relativement stable sur les grandes surfaces, l'image manque parfois d'éclat face à la concurrence.
Nos impressions sur le rendu à l'image
L'une des particularités du Samsung Odyssey G8 (G80HF) réside dans la finesse qu'offre sa définition native. Sur une dalle de 27 pouces, une définition 5K (5 120 x 2 880 pixels) permet de proposer une image extrêmement détaillée, même à une distance relativement courte.
Dans les jeux comportant de nombreux éléments fins, les textures, petits objets et détails éloignés peuvent apparaître plus nets. Si cette définition se prête aussi bien aux jeux d'aventure qu'aux RPG, c'est surtout pour travailler que la 5K présente un réel intérêt face à la 4K Ultra HD plus conventionnelle.
En retouche photo notamment, cette finesse d'affichage facilite l'identification des petits défauts, comme une poussière ou une imperfection qu'il devient plus simple de repérer et de corriger. La dalle propose par ailleurs une fréquence de rafraîchissement de 180 Hz. À diagonale égale, cet Odyssey G8 atteint une densité de 218 pixels par pouce, contre 163 ppp sur un écran 4K comme le Asus ROG Strix XG27UCS, également équipé d'une dalle Fast IPS.
Côté couleurs, le rendu se montre vif et agréable à l'œil, sans saturation excessive. Les teintes conservent un aspect relativement naturel, même si nos mesures montrent qu'une calibration reste préférable pour les travaux exigeant une colorimétrie particulièrement précise.
Les angles de vision sont également très bons à l'usage. Samsung annonce 178° horizontalement comme verticalement, une valeur classique pour une dalle Fast IPS. Cette valeur ne garantit toutefois pas une restitution identique sous tous les angles, notamment en matière de contraste. Sur ce dernier point, le contraste reste soumis aux limites de la technologie d'affichage. Samsung annonce un rapport de contraste natif de 1 000:1, une valeur classique pour une dalle IPS, qui ne permet pas d'obtenir des noirs aussi profonds que ceux d'une dalle OLED.
Au-delà de la retouche photo ou du montage vidéo en 5K, l'autre particularité de cette dalle Fast IPS réside dans son mode QHD (2 560 × 1 440 pixels) à 360 Hz. De quoi rivaliser avec des moniteurs destinés au jeu compétitif, comme le Acer Predator XB273U F5 récemment testé.
La qualité d'image reste très satisfaisante à cette définition, tandis que la fréquence de 360 Hz apporte un gain de fluidité appréciable dans les FPS comme Counter-Strike 2, à condition de disposer d'une configuration suffisamment performante. Certains tons sombres restent cependant difficiles à discerner, notamment dans Alan Wake 2.
Le HDR constitue toutefois l'une des principales limites de cet Odyssey G8. Malgré une couverture colorimétrique étendue, la luminosité maximale relativement modeste ne permet pas aux hautes lumières de se détacher avec autant d'intensité que sur les meilleurs écrans Mini-LED ou OLED. Le contraste limité de la dalle IPS joue également en sa défaveur, avec des noirs qui manquent de profondeur dans les scènes sombres. Le rendu reste agréable dans l'ensemble, mais le passage du SDR au HDR n'apporte pas le gain de dynamique que l'on pourrait espérer sur un moniteur de cette catégorie.
Expérience au quotidien
Audio
Samsung a fait le choix de ne pas intégrer de haut-parleurs à son Odyssey G8. Une absence qui n'est pas rédhibitoire pour un moniteur gaming, mais un système audio d'appoint aurait été appréciable, notamment pour les usages bureautiques ou multimédias.
Une prise jack 3,5 mm est néanmoins présente à l'arrière du moniteur pour brancher un casque, des écouteurs ou des enceintes.
Interface et fonctionnalités
Le menu OSD du Samsung Odyssey G8 G80HF se montre assez simple d'utilisation. Un premier volet présente les options de jeu, avec notamment la possibilité d'activer l'Adaptive-Sync et le "Mode double". Ce dernier permet de basculer en QHD à 360 Hz, une fréquence qui nécessite d'activer cette option directement dans l'OSD du moniteur.
Un viseur virtuel est également disponible sous l'intitulé "Pt de visée virtuel". L'OSD propose aussi quelques fonctionnalités destinées aux joueurs, notamment un égaliseur des noirs, même si les possibilités de personnalisation restent assez classiques.
Les paramètres d'image donnent accès à plusieurs préréglages (FPS, RPG, Cinéma, etc.), ainsi qu'aux ajustements habituels de luminosité, de contraste, de couleur et de teinte.
Enfin, le volet "Système" regroupe notamment les paramètres d'économie d'énergie et le changement automatique de source, étonnamment désactivé par défaut.
Consommation électrique
Nous avons relevé une consommation électrique à 150 nits assez importante, de l'ordre de 179,2 W/m2. Autant dire que cet écran ne se place certainement pas parmi les plus économes de sa catégorie. Si son impact sur la facture d'électricité devrait rester modéré, il se fera tout de même ressentir.
Design et connectiques
Pour ce qui est de l'esthétique, Samsung fait le choix de la sobriété avec son Odyssey G8. Pas de rétroéclairage RGB particulièrement voyant ni d'éléments décoratifs superflus. Le constructeur privilégie un design relativement discret, qui permet à l'écran de trouver aussi bien sa place sur un bureau professionnel que dans une configuration gaming.
On peut toutefois noter des bordures latérales un peu épaisses, qui ne seront pas du goût de tous les usagers, surtout ceux souhaitant mettre deux moniteurs côte à côte.
Côté réglages, l'écran peut pivoter jusqu'à 92° dans les deux sens pour une utilisation en mode portrait, s'incliner de -2° à +25° et être orienté horizontalement de -30° à +30°. Il est également doté d'un pied permettant de régler sa hauteur, sur une amplitude de 12 centimètres.
Le pied intègre un passe-câbles et repose sur un socle assez large. Ce dernier présente une surface plane, qui permet de poser quelques objets ou d'y ranger un clavier au besoin. L'écran peut être fixé à l'aide d'un support VESA 100 x 100, si le pied ne convient pas à l'utilisateur.
Côté connectique, c'est convenable, mais sans plus, avec deux entrées HDMI 2.1 et un DisplayPort 2.1 côté vidéo.
La connectique se complète avec une sortie audio jack 3,5 mm et un hub USB comprenant un port USB-B pour la liaison avec l'ordinateur, ainsi que deux ports USB-A pour les périphériques. L'absence de port USB-C sur un modèle de 2026 est toutefois regrettable.
Test Samsung Odyssey G8 (G80HF) : l'avis de Clubic
Avec son Odyssey G8 (G80HF), Samsung propose un moniteur qui cherche à concilier les exigences des créateurs de contenu et celles des joueurs. Sa définition 5K sur une diagonale de 27 pouces offre une finesse d'affichage très appréciable au quotidien, notamment pour la retouche photo et les travaux nécessitant une image détaillée. L'intérêt de cet écran réside toutefois dans son Dual Mode, qui permet de basculer en QHD à 360 Hz pour privilégier la fluidité.
Les performances sont dans l'ensemble satisfaisantes, avec une latence d'affichage bien maîtrisée, une colorimétrie convenable et une ergonomie soignée. Le G80HF montre néanmoins certaines limites, particulièrement en HDR, où sa luminosité modeste peine à donner suffisamment d'éclat aux hautes lumières. À cela s'ajoutent des temps de réponse qui restent en retrait des meilleures références gaming et l'absence d'une connectique USB-C pourtant instaurée sur bon nombre de moniteurs en 2026.
Il conviendra particulièrement à ceux qui privilégient la finesse d'affichage sans vouloir renoncer à une fréquence élevée pour jouer occasionnellement ou régulièrement. En revanche, les amateurs de HDR spectaculaire et les joueurs compétitifs les plus exigeants trouveront des alternatives davantage adaptées à leurs attentes.
- La finesse d'affichage en 5K sur 27 pouces
- Le Dual Mode QHD à 360 Hz
- Une latence d'affichage bien maîtrisée
- Sa large couverture colorimétrique
- La connectique globalement généreuse
- Absence d'un port USB-C
- Des performances HDR limitées
- Position du joystick de réglages peu ergonomique
- Un contraste et des noirs en retrait de l'OLED
- Des temps de réponse perfectibles à 360 Hz
Toutes les mesures réalisées dans le cadre de ce test ont été enregistrées avec le logiciel CalMAN Ultimate, une sonde Calibrite Display Plus HL et un boîtier de mesure d'Input Lag NVIDIA LDAT v2.
