articles.title: Le MacBook Pro M6 est lancé, mais le 16" M5 Max est bradé à -22% chez Amazon 🔥
articles.text:
Apple a présenté le 27 octobre ses MacBook Pro à puce M6, de quoi relancer la question pour qui hésitait sur la génération M5 et sa puce Max, taillée pour la vidéo, la 3D et l’IA en local. Amazon affiche le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max (36 Go, 2 To) à 3 999 €, 1 100 € sous le prix de Darty : une machine de création qui reste chère, et livrée sans chargeur.
Lancé au printemps 2026, le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max associe ici une puce à processeur 18 cœurs et GPU 32 cœurs à 36 Go de mémoire unifiée et 2 To de SSD, en coloris Noir sidéral. Amazon le vend à 3 999 €, alors que Darty l’affichait encore à 5 099 € le 27 octobre.
L’offre s’adresse aux monteurs vidéo, aux graphistes 3D et aux développeurs qui font tourner des modèles d’IA en local, pour qui la puissance graphique compte davantage que le prix. Pour la bureautique, cette configuration reste nettement surdimensionnée.
Le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max 36 Go et 2 To est à 3 999 € chez Amazon, contre 5 099 € chez Darty lors de notre dernier relevé.
Pourquoi choisir le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max ?
- Un GPU de 32 cœurs : Chaque cœur graphique intègre un accélérateur neuronal, et la mémoire atteint 460 Go/s de bande passante. Les exports vidéo, le rendu 3D et l’inférence de modèles d’IA en profitent directement.
- Un écran taillé pour l’image : La dalle Mini-LED de 16,2 pouces monte à 1 600 nits en HDR, à 120 Hz. Notre test de la version M5 Pro, qui partage cet écran, y a mesuré des couleurs très fidèles.
- Jusqu’à quatre écrans externes : Trois ports Thunderbolt 5, un HDMI et un lecteur SDXC accompagnent une puce M5 Max qui pilote quatre moniteurs, un de plus que la M5 Pro. Les cartes SD de vos caméras se lisent sans adaptateur.
Montage, 3D, IA locale : là où la puce Max fait la différence
Les 36 Go de mémoire unifiée sont partagés entre le processeur et le GPU, ce qui laisse de la marge aux timelines 4K chargées et aux scènes 3D lourdes. Le SSD de 2 To accueille plusieurs projets vidéo sans disque externe. Apple la présente aussi comme capable de faire tourner et d’entraîner des modèles de langage en local, un argument concret pour les développeurs.
Ce modèle vise d’abord les monteurs, les motion designers et les studios qui facturent leur temps de rendu. Il pèse en revanche plus de 2 kg et ne se recharge qu’avec un adaptateur d’au moins 94 W, absent de la boîte : un nomade s’en lassera vite. Le jeu n’est pas non plus sa vocation, puisque notre test de la version M5 Pro situait ses performances au niveau d’une RTX 4060.
M5 Pro, M5 Max ou M6 : ce que vous payez vraiment
Face au MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Pro, proposé à partir de 2 999 € à sa sortie, la version M5 Max apporte surtout un GPU de 32 cœurs, contre 20 sur le modèle que nous avons testé, et la prise en charge d’un quatrième écran. Le processeur de la M5 Pro testée comptait déjà 18 cœurs, si bien que le gain se concentre sur le rendu graphique et l’IA. Les MacBook Pro M6 présentés le 27 octobre restent à confronter à cette offre, faute de test à ce jour. Face aux alternatives sous Windows, notre comparatif des meilleurs PC portables fait le point.
✅ Les points forts
- GPU de 32 cœurs avec un accélérateur neuronal dans chaque cœur
- 36 Go de mémoire unifiée à 460 Go/s
- Écran Mini-LED de 16,2 pouces à 120 Hz, 1 600 nits en HDR
- Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, lecteur SDXC et jusqu’à quatre écrans externes
- 1 100 € sous le prix affiché par Darty
❌ Les limites
- Adaptateur secteur non fourni, 94 W minimum requis
- Mémoire et stockage impossibles à faire évoluer après l’achat
- Plus de 2 kg, peu adapté aux déplacements quotidiens
- Wi-Fi 7 limité aux canaux de 160 MHz, selon notre test de la version M5 Pro
Amazon n’indiquait plus que deux exemplaires en stock lors de notre relevé de 6 h : vérifiez la disponibilité de cette configuration avant de commander.
À 3 999 €, le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max reste un investissement lourd, mais il coûte 1 100 € de moins que chez Darty pour une configuration de création complète. Son GPU, son écran et sa connectique justifient l’écart avec la version M5 Pro pour qui exporte, rend ou entraîne des modèles au quotidien. Ajoutez au budget un adaptateur d’au moins 94 W.
Si votre activité se mesure en heures de rendu, l’offre mérite un examen sérieux, d’autant que la mémoire et le stockage ne se changent pas après l’achat : 36 Go et 2 To doivent tenir plusieurs années. Pour de la retouche photo ou du montage occasionnel, en revanche, une version M5 Pro ou un MacBook Air répondront au besoin pour bien moins cher. Les premiers tests des MacBook Pro M6 diront ce que la nouvelle génération change.

articles.title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime, a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched.
Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it.
A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image.
This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository, and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough.
What you get without building anything
The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. The tag this sample pulls, public.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/ray:train-ml-cuda-v1.1, replaces a build that would otherwise look like this:
| Layer | What you would otherwise build and keep aligned | In the Ray Train DLC | 
| Distributed runtime | Ray with the dashboard and job server, at a version KubeRay supports | Ray 2.58.0 with Train, Tune and Data | 
| Framework | PyTorch compiled for your CUDA version | PyTorch 2.13.0, torchvision 0.28.0 | 
| GPU runtime | CUDA, cuDNN and NCCL releases that agree with each other | CUDA 13.0.2, cuDNN, NCCL 2.29.7 | 
| Networking | EFA installer, libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl, built against that NCCL | EFA latest, AWS OFI NCCL plugin, GDRCopy | 
| Training libraries | DeepSpeed, flash-attn and Transformer Engine compiled for your CUDA | DeepSpeed, flash-attn, Transformer Engine, PyTorch Lightning, Hugging Face libraries | 
| Diagnostics | NCCL tests built from source | all_reduce_perf already on the path | 
The networking row is the one most teams would least like to own. A mismatch there doesn’t produce an error. NCCL drops to TCP sockets, and the job runs to completion at a fraction of the speed. In the DLC, those libraries are built and tested together, and AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests, which are exactly the paths this sample uses.
A few more properties remove work that you would otherwise do per cluster:
- No registry setup – The image is public, so nodes pull it without credentials and nothing is built or pushed on the way.
- No driver matching – On startup the entrypoint checks the host’s NVIDIA driver and, if it is older than the image’s CUDA, turns on the bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries automatically.
- No head-versus-worker images – The image has no fixed role. Whatever starts the container supplies the ray start command, so one tag serves every pod.
- No separate inference image family – Ray Train shares the ray ECR repository with the Ray Serve DLC and Ray LLM DLCs, under the train-ml tag prefix.
Configure it, don’t rebuild it
Everything that differs between one training job and the next is set around the image. The sample uses each of these mechanisms:
| What you control | How you set it | In this sample | 
| Head or worker role | KubeRay rayStartParams per pod group | Same DLC_IMAGE for both. Head runs with num-gpus: "0" | 
| GPUs and EFA per pod | Kubernetes resource requests | nvidia.com/gpu: 4, vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 1 | 
| Network transport | Environment variables on the pod or the job | FI_PROVIDER, NCCL_NET_PLUGIN, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_DEBUG | 
| Extra Python packages | Ray runtime_env at submit time | Any package a job needs, installed at submit time | 
| Image version | Versioned or digest-pinned tag in DLC_IMAGE | train-ml-cuda-v1.1 | 
| Cluster shape | Variables in scripts/ env.sh | Instance type, node count, GPUs per node, Region, AZ | 
| Training job | Arguments to train.py | Model, steps, sequence length, batch size | 
Packages per job. The image ships the HuggingFace training stack, so this sample’s job needs nothing added. When an experiment does need a library the image does not carry, Ray installs it for that job at submit time through runtime_env and the image is unchanged. No new image, no new tag.
Transport per job. The image defaults to FI_PROVIDER=efa, and its NCCL configuration excludes the loopback and Docker bridge interfaces. On EKS you point NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME at the pod’s eth0. The sample sets all four networking variables in the manifest anyway, so the behavior is visible in one file and doesn’t depend on image defaults. Because these are plain environment variables, a single job can override them through its runtime_env.
Versions you choose. The sample pins train-ml-cuda-v1.1, the current minor release, so a cluster is reproducible from one run to the next. The vX.Y tags move with security rebuilds. The fully qualified vX.Y.Z tags stay frozen at the original release build, so pin a digest when you need a byte-identical run. The same image is also available from private ECR URIs.
How the cluster is laid out
All nodes sit in private subnets of one virtual private cloud (VPC) and reach the internet only through a NAT Gateway, which is how every node pulls the DLC from Amazon ECR Public and how workers download model weights from Hugging Face. One m7i.xlarge forms the system node group, hosting kube-system add-ons, the KubeRay operator and the Ray head. The head runs the job server on port 8265 and Ray’s control store on 6379, and it advertises no GPUs, so no training work lands on it. Jobs are submitted from inside the head pod with kubectl exec, through the EKS API, so port 8265 is never exposed outside the cluster.
Training runs on two g6.12xlarge instances, each with four NVIDIA L4 GPUs, 48 vCPUs, 192 GiB of memory, 40 Gbps of networking and one EFA interface. Each runs one Ray worker pod that claims all four GPUs and the EFA interface, and Ray Train places four workers in each pod: ranks 0–3 on one instance, 4–7 on the other. Because EFA traffic doesn’t cross Availability Zones, the scripts place both instances in a single zone that has been checked to offer g6.12xlarge.
What Ray Train does inside the container
The DLC provides the stack. Ray Train provides the part that would otherwise be launcher code. Multi-node PyTorch normally means starting a process per GPU on every host and giving each one its rank, the world size and a rendezvous address. With Ray Train you write the training loop as a function and pass it to TorchTrainer with a ScalingConfig. Ray starts one worker per GPU wherever the cluster has GPUs, forms the torch.distributed process group, and runs your function on each worker.
This sample asks Ray Train for FSDP, which splits the model’s weights, gradients and optimizer state across all eight GPUs rather than copying them to each one. Qwen2.5-1.5B in bfloat16 needs about 12 GB for those four tensors. Sharded eight ways, each L4 GPU holds roughly 1.5 GB. The price is communication: FSDP gathers each layer’s weights before using it and reduce-scatters gradients afterwards, so the whole model crosses between ranks on every step. Between the two instances, that traffic is what the DLC’s EFA stack carries.
Prerequisites
You must have the following in place before you start:
- Tools: AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 signed in to the target account, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, and envsubst from GNU gettext.
- Quota: 96 vCPUs of G-family On-Demand capacity for the two g6.12xlarge instances, in an AWS Region where at least one zone offers them. If you already hold an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the instances, set CAPACITY_RESERVATION_ID instead. The scripts launch the node group into it and skip the capacity search.
- Budget: about $9.50 an hour while the GPU instances are up, covering both instances, the EKS control plane and the NAT Gateway.
A quick way to confirm that the CLI is pointed at the account that you expect:
The training code: One function and a trainer
code/train.py is the whole job, and it contains nothing specific to the container, the cluster or the network. Ray runs train_func once per GPU. It asks Ray for its rank, loads the model, hands it to prepare_model for FSDP, and runs an ordinary PyTorch loop:
code/train.py — the per-GPU function (abridged)
The driver joins the running cluster, counts its GPUs and starts the trainer. Because the worker count comes from the cluster, the same script runs unchanged on one node or many:
code/train.py — the driver (abridged)
The batches are random token IDs so that the run depends on nothing but the cluster. The sample is judged on whether real FSDP collectives crossed both nodes and the job completed. For a real fine-tune, replace the random tensor with a Ray Data or DataLoader pipeline. Nothing else in the function changes.
The manifest: The only place the DLC is configured
manifest/raycluster.yaml is where the image meets the cluster, and it is short because the image needs so little. The head’s only special setting is NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void, which stops the container runtime’s NVIDIA hook from failing on a node that has no GPU. The worker group holds everything else:
manifest/raycluster.yaml — worker group (abridged)
Read it as three decisions.
Which image: ${DLC_IMAGE}, unmodified, for both head and workers.
Which hardware: four GPUs and the node’s single EFA interface per pod. Requesting vpc.amazonaws.com/efa is what makes the EFA device plugin mount the interface into the container. Without it, NCCL can’t see EFA and falls back to sockets.
Which transport: four environment variables, so nothing is left to auto-detection.
Two smaller details keep a multi-node job stable. First, requests should equal limits, which places the workers in Kubernetes’ Guaranteed Quality of Service (QoS) class. This matters because a single throttled or evicted rank stalls the other seven. Second, num-gpus is derived from the same variable as the GPU request, so Ray’s view of capacity always matches Kubernetes’.
Bringing it up: One command for the infrastructure, then the job
Configuration lives in one place, scripts/env.sh: cluster name, Region, Kubernetes version, node types and counts, the image, pinned versions of KubeRay and both device plugins, and the training parameters. Export any of them to change it for a run. All five scripts are idempotent and safe to re-run. deploy_cluster.sh, deploy_node_group.sh, and deploy_ray_train_job.sh each prompt before creating or touching cluster resources. install_gpu_plugins.sh and install_kuberay.sh are reconcilers and run straight through.
./deploy_all.sh – Finds where the capacity actually is, then builds the infrastructure there.
g6.12xlarge capacity shifts between Regions and Availability Zones day to day, so this is the starting point rather than a Region guessed up front in env.sh. It first runs find_gpu_capacity.sh, which checks, per candidate Region: whether g6.12xlarge is offered in each Availability Zone, whether the account’s On-Demand G/VT-family vCPU quota has room for the requested node count, and the EC2 Spot placement score as a capacity signal. With --probe, which deploy_all.sh passes by default, it gets a definitive answer by creating and immediately canceling a real Capacity Reservation in each candidate zone. It then shows the plan and asks once:
Answering y runs, in order, deploy_cluster.sh, deploy_node_group.sh, install_gpu_plugins.sh, and install_kuberay.sh in the recommended Region, each skipping its own repeat confirmation because this one already asked (-y skips this prompt too, and --plan shows the plan without creating anything). If the GPU node group can’t launch in the best zone, the script removes it and tries the next zone the probe confirmed. GPU_AZ is also cross-checked against the cluster’s actual private subnets, not only where g6.12xlarge happens to be offered, so the GPU node group can’t end up pinned to an Availability Zone the cluster has no subnet in. The chosen Region and zone are saved to scripts/.placement.env, which every other script reads, so later commands target the same place without re-exporting anything. Together the four steps take 20 to 30 minutes on a fresh Region. An existing cluster or node group is detected and reused.
deploy_cluster.sh creates the EKS control plane, VPC, OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, core add-ons, and the m7i.xlarge system node group, choosing subnets in zones that actually offer g6.12xlarge. deploy_node_group.sh adds the two g6.12xlarge instances with EFA turned on, labeled role=gpu-worker and nvidia.com/gpu.present=true. The second label is one that teams often overlook. Without it, the NVIDIA device plugin chart’s DaemonSet runs on zero nodes, with no error pointing at the cause. install_gpu_plugins.sh makes sure both device plugins are present. Recent eksctl bundles them into an EFA-enabled node group, so on a fresh cluster it finds them and skips. Otherwise it installs them at pinned chart versions. Either way it verifies nvidia.com/gpu and vpc.amazonaws.com/efa are allocatable on every GPU node rather than trusting a successful Helm release. install_kuberay.sh installs the KubeRay operator onto the system node, keeping it off the GPU instances.
What deploy_all.sh does not do by default is run the training job. That stays a separate step you can re-run as often as you like, because it is a real job run rather than infrastructure, and a failed job then never sends you back through cluster setup. Pass --train to chain it:
./deploy_ray_train_job.sh — the RayCluster, the job, and the checks.
Renders the manifest with envsubst and applies it. It then re-reads each GPU node’s allocatable resources before waiting on any pod: if a device plugin didn’t come up, you get a clear error here rather than a pod that sits in Pending until a timeout. Once the head is Ready and both workers are Ready, it copies code/ onto the head and, through kubectl exec, submits from inside it:
The submit call streams logs from all eight ranks and returns when the job does. The script then inspects which transport NCCL used and exits with an error if the job failed or EFA wasn’t in the path, which also makes it usable as a continuous integration (CI) gate. ./deploy_ray_train_job.sh status prints the RayCluster state, which instance hosts each pod, and GPU capacity. A correctly provisioned cluster looks like this:
Adapting it to your workload
Because the image is used as published and the job learns its scale from the cluster, most changes touch exactly one file:
| You want to change | Where | No changes needed to | 
| The model | MODEL_ID | Code, manifest, image | 
| Steps, sequence length, batch size | STEPS, SEQ_LEN, BATCH_SIZE | Code, manifest, image | 
| The training loop itself | Body of train_func | Trainer, manifest, image, scripts | 
| An additional Python package | --runtime-env-json pip list | Image | 
| A pinned DLC release | DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag | Everything else | 
| The GPU instance family | GPU_NODE_TYPE, GPUS_PER_NODE | Code, image | 
| How many GPU instances | GPU_NODE_COUNT, plus replicas, minReplicas and maxReplicas in the manifest | Code (it counts the GPUs) | 
| Region or zone | REGION, optionally GPU_AZ | Everything else | 
Variables in the table live in env.sh unless stated otherwise. When switching instance families, GPUS_PER_NODE has to match the hardware, and the family needs EFA support plus a place on the EFA device plugin’s list of allowed instance types. The plugin version pinned here is known to include g6.12xlarge. Moving to p5 or another GPUDirect-capable family needs no change to the image or the training code.
Tearing it down
The GPU instances are the expensive part, at around $9.50 an hour together with the control plane and NAT Gateway. Remove things in the opposite order to how they were created:
Where to go next
Two instances and eight GPUs ran a sharded fine-tune on EKS with a container nobody built. The Ray Train DLC supplied a tested stack from CUDA through EFA. KubeRay started it as head and workers from one tag. Ray Train placed the workers and formed the process group. Everything that varied, from hardware to transport to Python packages, was set from outside the image. The EFA path the image ships engaged with four environment variables and doubled throughput over TCP on unchanged code.
Natural next moves:
- Replace the random batches with a real dataset, and checkpoint to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon FSx for Lustre.
- Pin DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag for reproducible runs.
- Turn on FailureConfig so long runs survive a lost instance.
- Move to a larger model on a GPUDirect RDMA family such as p5. The image and code stay the same.

articles.title: Secrets Management Firm Infisical Valued at $600 Million After $40 Million Raise
articles.text:
Infisical has announced a $40 million Series B round that values the San Francisco company at $600 million.
Elad Gil, a returning investor from the Series A, led the round. Gradient and Y Combinator also back the company. The Series B round brings the total funding to nearly $60 million.
Infisical provides tools for managing secrets, encryption keys, and digital certificates, along with privileged access management, covering cloud, on-premises, and AI infrastructure.
More than 1,300 organizations use its products, among them Airbus, Volkswagen, Hugging Face, and Wise.
With Infisical’s Agent Vault, AI agents can reach sensitive systems without ever being given the underlying credentials. The agent works with placeholders, while the actual secrets are injected at a proxy and never reach it. All agent requests pass through Infisical and are logged.
“Agents need access to company systems to do their jobs, but giving them actual passwords and API keys is a major security risk. We let agents get their job done safely without ever having those credentials in their hands,” said Vlad Matsiiako, Infisical’s co-founder and CEO.
Infisical plans to spend the money on speeding up product development, hiring for its engineering and go-to-market teams, and further developing its AI agent security capabilities.
“AI agents are becoming a new class of users inside every enterprise, and securing their access will be one of the biggest cybersecurity challenges of the next decade,” Gil noted.
Related: Former Unit 8200 Officers Raise $34 Million for Agentic SecOps Startup Mave
Related: Indurex Raises $8 Million to Expand Industrial Cybersecurity Platform
Related: Asymptote Labs Lands $5.5 Million Seed for AI Agent Runtime Security

articles.title: Detienen a una mujer en Cangas por una estafa bancaria de más de 47.000 euros
articles.text:
La Guardia Civil ha detenido a una mujer de 29 años en Cangas do Morrazo (Pontevedra) por su presunta participación en múltiples sucesos de hurto y una estafa continuada, con un perjuicio económico superior a los 47.280 euros, según las investigaciones. La mujer habría sustraído carteras y teléfonos móviles al descuido, utilizando los datos y las tarjetas de las víctimas para acceder a sus aplicaciones de banca electrónica.
La sospechosa habría realizado transferencias y compras, enviado dinero mediante Bizum, retirado efectivo de diferentes cajeros automáticos con HalCash y solicitado préstamos personales no autorizados. Los investigadores no especifican cuánto dinero perdió cada una de las víctimas ni la cantidad que corresponde a cada tipo de operación.
La investigación surgió a raíz de tres denuncias presentadas en enero de 2026. Los hurtos eran similares y se produjeron los martes y viernes, días de mercado en Cangas. Las investigaciones revelaron que la misma persona retiraba efectivo en todos los cajeros automáticos.
La detención y el paso por el juzgado
Fue el 17 de octubre cuando la sospechosa intentó robar un bolso en una cafetería y huyó junto a otros dos hombres en un vehículo, que fue interceptado por una patrulla de la Guardia Civil. Al identificarlos, los agentes se dieron cuenta de que la mujer ya estaba siendo investigada por actividades delictivas similares.
Tras su detención, la mujer fue puesta a disposición del Tribunal de Instancia de Cangas junto con las diligencias, y quedó en libertad mientras continúa investigada por los hechos. No hay información sobre cómo accedió a las contraseñas ni qué comprobaciones de autenticación se saltó.
Las funciones antirrobo de Android y iPhone
Los propietarios de teléfonos Android pueden proteger sus dispositivos frente al robo y al acceso no autorizado a sus datos utilizando funciones de protección antirrobo. Estas opciones se pueden encontrar en Ajustes, Google, Todos los servicios y Protección antirrobo, y constan de varias funciones de seguridad.
El bloqueo por detección de robo utiliza los sensores de movimiento y las conexiones del dispositivo y puede bloquear la pantalla si alguien arrebata el móvil y huye. Sin embargo, la disponibilidad de estas funciones puede variar en función del modelo del teléfono; un ajuste atenuado indica que no es compatible con esa función.
La guía de protección antirrobo de Android describe el funcionamiento de las herramientas. El bloqueo remoto exige, entre otros requisitos, que el número de teléfono esté verificado, la tarjeta SIM esté activa y que la función “Localizador” esté activa en el móvil, tal y como se indica en las instrucciones de Google. Si el dispositivo no tiene conexión a internet cuando se solicita el bloqueo remoto, el teléfono se bloqueará automáticamente una vez que se restablezca dicha conexión.
Los iPhones ofrecen funciones de protección antirrobo similares; sin embargo, algunas acciones exigen Face ID o Touch ID, sin que el código pueda usarse como alternativa. Dichas funciones requieren autenticación biométrica para acceder a contraseñas guardadas cuando se cumplen las condiciones de esta protección. Además, si se intenta cambiar las opciones de seguridad, como la contraseña de la Cuenta de Apple, tendrá que esperar una hora y utilizar Face ID/Touch ID una segunda vez para confirmar su identidad.
La protección antirrobo adicional del iPhone se aplica por defecto fuera de lugares conocidos, como casa o el trabajo. La opción “Siempre” permite exigir estas medidas también en esas ubicaciones. Las funciones de protección antirrobo deben activarse antes de que se produzca un robo.
Si ya se han realizado pagos fraudulentos, el Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) aconseja contactar con el banco para intentar anularlos y, en su caso, bloquear la tarjeta y denunciar el problema. El bloqueo del teléfono y la reclamación de las operaciones son actuaciones distintas.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: Radeon 9070 XT vs. Radeon 7900 XTX: 50+ Game Benchmark
articles.text:
In today's market, the Radeon RX 9070 XT is the best-value high-end GPU you can buy, which is brutal considering that pricing starts at around $900 (against a $600 MSRP). Still, that's about how much you'll pay for an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB in some markets, and the Radeon GPU is on average 70% faster at 4K gaming.
With that kind of performance gap, it's hard to make a case for GeForce right now, at least if you're shopping for something with more than 8GB of VRAM.
So, is it an open-and-shut case for the 9070 XT? Well, not so fast. Many readers have been asking us to revisit the Radeon RX 7900 XTX. Some have cited it as a potentially viable purchase in their region, while others simply want to see how AMD's RDNA 3 flagship has aged, and not just across 10 games, but more like 50+ titles. And that's exactly what we're going to do.
There's a lot of data to go over, after all we did test 51 games in total. However, much of it tells a similar story because the 9070 XT and 7900 XTX often deliver very similar gaming performance. So we'll focus on the games where we found notable results before diving into the overall performance summaries.
Test System
As usual, we're using our Ryzen 7 9800X3D GPU test system, equipped with 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory. The latest available display drivers at the time of testing were also used.
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D | 
| Motherboard | MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi [BIOS 7E49v1AA7] | 
| Memory | G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB DDR5-6000 32GB CL30 [CL30-38-38-96] | 
| Graphics Card | Radeon RX 9070 XT, Radeon RX 7900 XTX | 
| ATX Case | MSI Prospect 700R | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 26H2 | 
| Display Driver | AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.9.2 (9070 XT) AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.10.1 (7900 XTX) | 
Gaming Benchmarks
Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced
Believe it or not, the margins we're seeing here in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced are on the larger side of what we observed across the 51 games. In this example, the older 7900 XTX was 6-7% faster using the Very High quality preset, but when we enabled Extended Ray Tracing, that margin dropped to just 3-5%, depending on the resolution.
Black Myth: Wukong
Performance in Black Myth: Wukong is also much the same, though we are seeing up to a 6% performance advantage for the 7900 XTX using the High preset at 4K. That margin is reduced to just 3% when using the Cinematic preset.
Arc Raiders
Arc Raiders is more representative of the typical performance margins we saw. Here, the 9070 XT was 2-3% faster at 1440p, while the 7900 XTX nudged ahead at 4K by just 1%.
Borderlands 4
Borderlands 4 is a mixed bag. For example, the 7900 XTX was up to 7% faster at 1440p using the High preset, and 5% faster at 4K. However, switching over to the Badass preset allowed the 9070 XT to pull out a 4% win at 1440p, though the results were tied at 4K.
Crimson Desert
The older 7900 XTX enjoyed Crimson Desert, delivering 11% greater performance at 1440p when using Medium settings. Beyond that, though, we're looking at margins of around 6% or less.
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
The Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 results are very typical. For the most part, we're seeing nearly identical performance between these two GPUs. The only exception was at 1440p using Medium settings, where the 7900 XTX pulled out a 5% win. That's close enough to call a tie, but in this data set, it stands out as a relatively large margin.
Doom: The Dark Ages
The 9070 XT does quite well in Doom: The Dark Ages. At 1440p, we see no real difference between these two GPUs, but at 4K using the Ultra Nightmare settings, the newer Radeon GPU was 10% faster. However, despite the RDNA 4 architecture offering better ray tracing support, that advantage doesn't matter much with path tracing enabled, as both GPUs get smashed.
F1 25
F1 25 saw the 7900 XTX delivering up to 5% greater performance when using the High preset, as seen at 4K. However, enabling ray tracing favors the 9070 XT, though only slightly, with the newer Radeon GPU pulling ahead by 4-6%.
Hell is Us
Performance in Hell is Us is pretty typical of what we saw across most of the 51 games tested, with just a few frames separating these GPUs. In this example, the 9070 XT was generally ahead, but again, we're talking about low single-digit margins here.
Indiana Jones and the Great Circle
Indiana Jones and the Great Circle is another example where performance was largely the same. The 7900 XTX was up to 5% faster at 1440p using the Supreme preset, but that margin quickly shrank to just 2% at 4K. Then, when enabling full ray tracing, the 9070 XT takes the lead, though only just, offering around 5% better performance.
Lego Batman
Lego Batman provided us with more of the same. For the most part, there's little to nothing separating these two GPUs. At most, we saw a 4% margin at 4K using Medium settings, which favored the 9070 XT.
Monster Hunter Wilds
The same is true of Monster Hunter Wilds. Here, we're looking at identical or near-identical performance for the most part. The only somewhat noteworthy results can be seen at 4K using the High ray tracing settings, where the 7900 XTX was actually faster. So the 9070 XT isn't always superior when using RT effects.
Pragmata
Another typical example can be seen in Pragmata. Here, the 7900 XTX and 9070 XT deliver virtually identical performance, with or without ray tracing enabled.
Marvel Rivals
The same is also true of Marvel Rivals. The two GPUs trade blows using Medium settings, with performance swings no larger than 4%. But once we max out the quality settings, performance is virtually identical.
007 First Light
007 First Light gives us a mixed bag of results. Using Medium settings at 1440p, the 7900 XTX was 4% faster, not a big margin, but at 4K the results are flipped, and now it's the 9070 XT that's faster, leading by a slim 6% margin. Back at 1440p, but this time with Ultra settings, the 7900 XTX gets out to a 9% lead, only for that margin to shrink to 2% at 4K.
Cities: Skylines
Cities: Skylines provides us with some unusual results. In this example, the older 7900 XTX is quite a bit faster, delivering 12-13% greater performance using the Medium preset and then 12% at 1440p using High settings, though just 6% at 4K. Still, overall, the 7900 XTX was the faster GPU in this title.
Counter-Strike 2
The 7900 XTX was also dominant in Counter-Strike 2, delivering 18% greater performance at 1440p with Medium settings and 25% at 4K. These gains were maintained using Very High settings, with the older Radeon delivering 22% greater performance at 1440p and then a massive 32% increase at 4K.
Delta Force
In this example, we see that Delta Force favors the newer 9070 XT. Here, the RDNA 4 GPU delivered 14% more performance at 1440p using Ultra settings, though just 5% more at 4K. We also saw similar scaling using the Ultimate preset.
Forza Horizon 6
Forza Horizon 6 provided the kind of data I expected to see more of, that is, competitive rasterized performance with the newer 9070 XT taking the cake once ray tracing is enabled. Using the Extreme preset, the 9070 XT was 3% faster, but when we switched over to ray tracing, that margin grew substantially to 23%.
Fortnite
Testing with Fortnite, we find the limits of our Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor at 1440p using Performance mode, reaching just over 700 fps, which seems like enough to me, for now. Anyway, at 4K, the 7900 XTX delivered 18% stronger performance, and even with ray tracing enabled, the older RDNA 3 GPU still came out on top, offering 14% better performance.
Grand Theft Auto V
Testing with Grand Theft Auto V shows very similar rasterized performance between these two GPUs, but once we enabled ray tracing using the Maximum RT preset, the 9070 XT takes over, crushing the 7900 XTX by 35% at 1440p and 33% at 4K.
Spider-Man 2
The 9070 XT also dominated our Spider-Man 2 testing, well, at least at 1440p, where it was 9% faster using the Very High preset and then 22% faster with the maximum ray tracing settings enabled. At 4K, the margins were much smaller, in the 5-6% range.
Performance Summary
Across the 51 games tested, how do the 9070 XT and 7900 XTX compare?
Well, they're nearly identical in terms of performance. This data doesn't tell us too much, other than the fact that overall, these GPUs deliver very similar performance. So let's take a closer look at the per-game results.
Average Performance by Game
Please note that this data is based on average frame rates, calculated using the geo mean, and combines the two quality configurations tested, as well as both resolutions.
As you can see, the vast majority of games saw less than a 10% difference in performance between these two GPUs. In fact, just five games exceeded 10%. The worst examples for the 9070 XT were Counter-Strike 2 and Red Dead Redemption 2, while its best results came in GTA V, Forza Horizon 6, and Naraka: Bladepoint.
What We Learned
The Radeon RX 9070 XT has continued to age well, and we've seen plenty of evidence of this recently. We've seen it matching and even beating the RTX 5070 Ti in newer titles such as Gears of War: E-Day, The Witcher 3 Remastered, and Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, to name a few, though that will depend on the settings used.
Not only did most early reviews of the 9070 XT find it trailing the 5070 Ti by a reasonable margin, but also the 7900 XTX. Now the 9070 XT and 7900 XTX appear to be pretty much neck and neck.
Looking across all 51 games tested, the performance margins generally fall into three categories: 1) near-parity in standard rasterization, 2) ray tracing and path tracing gives the advantage to the newer RDNA 4 architecture, and 3) specific titles where the older 7900 XTX flagship flexes its memory bandwidth and compute muscle.
Where the GPUs Differ
At native 4K, the Radeon 7900 XTX's additional bandwidth can help, particularly in memory-intensive games. However, that doesn't translate into a 50% increase in FPS simply because it has 50% more memory bandwidth.
The 7900 XTX also has 50% more VRAM: 24GB versus 16GB for the 9070 XT. But right now that only matters when playing heavily modded games with UHD texture packs, running games at extreme settings, working with large 3D scenes, or using local AI models that exceed 16GB.
With ray tracing enabled, particularly in newer games, the 9070 XT generally comes out on top, sometimes by a substantial margin. Both GPUs now support FSR 4.1 upscaling, as AMD extended support to the RX 7000 series back in June. This means the 7900 XTX is no longer restricted to the lower-quality FSR 3.1 upscaler.
The key difference to note here is that the 9070 XT uses FP8 acceleration to run FSR 4.1 more efficiently. It also supports the newer ML frame generation and ray regeneration features in FSR Redstone. The 7900 XTX, on the other hand, runs FSR 4.1 through INT8 processing, which comes with higher overhead. It still supports older FSR frame generation, but not all the RDNA 4-exclusive Redstone features.
As an example, AMD reports roughly 1.3 ms of FSR 4.1 upscaling processing time at 4K on the 9070 XT, compared with 3.1 ms on the 7900 XTX. In short, this means the 9070 XT can deliver better performance when both GPUs use the same upscaling settings, even in games where the 7900 XTX is faster natively.
Both GPUs support AV1 encoding for streaming, though the 9070 XT also gets PCIe 5.0 support, which can be viewed as a modest future-facing benefit. That said, the 7900 XTX's PCIe 4.0 x16 interface really isn't a limitation, especially given that you're far less likely to exceed its VRAM capacity.
Pricing can vary from month to month, sometimes substantially, but as of writing the 9070 XT costs $900 in the US, or $1,250 in Australia, while secondhand 7900 XTX models are selling on eBay for between $800 and $1,100, or around $1,500 in Australia. At those prices, the 9070 XT makes far more sense for most buyers. Obviously, if you already own the 7900 XTX, upgrading to the 9070 XT would be a sidegrade at best, so don't do that.
Bottom line, the 7900 XTX has continued to age well and remains highly competitive with current generation high-end GPUs. Like the 9070 XT, it has only gotten better since release through updated features such as FSR 4.1, even if AMD did take its sweet time rolling out support.

articles.title: Danish BioTech Samplix secures €25 million in first close of financing round to scale antibody discovery | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Samplix, a Danish BioTech company developing droplet microfluidics technology for functional single-cell analysis, has announced a €25 million first closing of a financing round.
The financing comprises €3 million in new capital and €22 million in shareholder convertible bonds. It was led by WLanholding GmbH, a privately owned European investment firm with participation from all major shareholders. The round remains open to additional investors with a total target of €30 million.
“We are excited to partner with Samplix at this pivotal stage of its growth. The team has built a differentiated single-cell technology platform that solves real, persistent challenges in drug discovery. We believe Samplix is well positioned to become a category leader, and we look forward to supporting the team as they scale their impact across the industry,” said Dr. Werner Lanthaler, founder and Managing Director of WLan.
As part of this new financing round, Dr Lanthaler, former CEO of Evotec, will join Samplix’s Board of Directors within the next year. He will work closely with the management team to guide the company’s next phase of growth.
Headquartered in Birkerød, Samplix was founded in 2013 with the vision of making high-throughput cellular screening accessible without specialised instrumentation. It develops microfluidics technologies for high-throughput, function-first single-cell analysis and provides droplet microfluidics technology for functional single-cell analysis in the biopharmaceutical sector.
Its core offering is the Xdrop platform, which encloses individual living cells and assay reagents in millions of tiny double-emulsion droplets. Each droplet acts as a miniature, self-contained reaction vessel, allowing researchers to observe cell behaviour. The company says its droplets are compatible with standard flow cytometry and cell-sorting equipment, enabling high-throughput analysis and sorting of functional droplets.
The platform is used across antibody discovery, immunotherapy, cell line development, genomic editing, and other functional single-cell research by both biopharmaceutical companies and academic research institutions worldwide.
According to Samplix, its platform is designed to address persistent pain points in early-stage drug development, chief among them being the difficulty of screening cells against hard-to-target proteins such as those embedded in cell membranes.
“This investment is a further validation of the value our Xdrop platform brings to the antibody discovery community. We are now in a strong position to further scale our platform, deepen our partnerships with biopharma and academia, and continue pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in single-cell workflows. This is an important milestone in our mission to make drug-discovery faster, simpler, and more reliable,” said Dr. Henrik Pfundheller, CEO of Samplix.
Samplix intends to use the new capital to strengthen its balance sheet and broaden commercial adoption of the Xdrop platform, particularly in the antibody discovery space. The company also sees a growing opportunity for its platform in AI-driven drug discovery, where large volumes of functional, cell-level data are needed to train predictive models.

articles.title: South Korea's financial industry hit by fresh wave of cyberattacks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
South Korea’s financial institutions have been hit by another wave of cyberattacks, highlighting the growing risk of AI-driven hacking in Asia. The latest incidents affect brokerages Daishin Securities and Mirae Asset Global Investments, as well as the crypto exchange Bithumb.
The incident comes roughly a month after a series of cyberattacks targeting South Korean financial institutions, raising concerns about vulnerabilities beyond just the country’s banking systems. Security researchers linked the September wave of attacks on South Korea to a suspected China-based hacker who relied on an AI penetration testing tool called Artex, though officials are still investigating the root cause of the latest breaches.
According to local news, Daishin reported a cyberattack that exposed the personal information of 38,490 customers, including names, email addresses, and mobile phone numbers. The company has notified affected customers, is cooperating with authorities in the investigation, and will compensate for any losses as required by law.
Meanwhile, Mirae and Bithumb reported separate cybersecurity incidents on Wednesday, per local media, though neither has confirmed that customer data was taken.
South Korea’s financial regulator has called for stronger cybersecurity measures following a string of attacks on financial firms and government agencies, per officials in Seoul on Wednesday. The country also plans to conduct security checks on dozens of IT systems in the private sector.
Yesterday, Japan reported a cybersecurity incident involving GMO Internet, following a series of attacks on its financial institutions. The wave of cyberattacks across Asia underscore growing cybersecurity challenges in the region, often as a result of years of weak cybersecurity; though, investigators have not established a connection between the incidents.
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC), Daishin Securities, Bithumb, and Mirae Asset Global Investments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Three trends to watch from the 2026 Québec FinTech Report | BetaKit
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence is moving deeper into the systems that power financial services, putting pressure on the industry to confront questions about standards, interoperability, and capital.
“The real breakthrough in agentic commerce is not that AI can make decisions, but that ecosystems are being built to let those decisions translate into trusted transactions.”
Surinderjit Kaur Bhatti,
Fathom4sight
Those findings come from a new report released by innovation hub Station FinTech Montréal and Toronto-based Fathom4sight at the 2026 Canada FinTech Forum this week. Now in its fourth year, the report tracks the evolution of Québec’s financial technology ecosystem, including investment activity, sector employment, and vertical trends.
This year’s report zeroed in on one of the sector’s fastest-moving fronts, agentic commerce, which is drawing global firms into a race to write the rules of a new market. It also looked closer to home at the financing and commercialization challenges that could determine how much of Québec’s AI strength can translate into successful products and companies.
Here are three trends from the 2026 Québec FinTech Report that are worth watching.
Agentic commerce creates a new rules race
One of the clearest trends highlighted in this year’s Québec FinTech Report is the emergence of payments infrastructure and protocols designed specifically for AI agents. The report pointed to a new payments stack that is being assembled at several layers simultaneously, without a settled architecture for merchants to plug into.
Agentic commerce refers to transactions in which an AI system can carry out purchases on behalf of a consumer, all the way from product discovery to payment. Making this vision of commerce a functioning market requires a new rulebook for how agents connect to merchants, prove who they are, and move money securely.
Some of the world’s largest payments infrastructure companies have already started building those layers. In April of 2025, Mastercard launched Agent Pay, its own framework for agentic commerce that uses network tokens and biometric authentication. One day later, Visa unveiled its Intelligent Commerce initiative, which also includes tokenization and personalization features.
Agent Pay and Intelligent Commerce primarily address the payment and trust infrastructure needed to authorize agent-led transactions. A separate wave of initiatives is trying to standardize different parts of how agents interact, establish authority, and transact across the commerce ecosystem.
In September of 2025, Google published its Agent Payments Protocol; one month later, Visa launched a Trusted Agent Protocol with Montréal-founded Nuvei among the organizations supporting it. The report also highlighted the Agentic Commerce Protocol launched by OpenAI and Stripe, Google and Shopify’s Universal Commerce Protocol, and x402, a cryptocurrency-based payments protocol built around instant on-chain transactions.
These new protocols span several distinct functions, including checkout orchestration, which coordinates the purchase; delegated payment authority, which allows an agent to transact; agent identity, which verifies what is initiating the transaction; and finally, settlement, which refers to the transfer of funds. With different protocols addressing different and sometimes overlapping parts of the stack, merchants are left deciding which standards they should support, according to the report.
“The sequence shows a market that standardized before it settled,” the report said.
The growing protocol landscape is now pushing the industry toward making all of these standards work together across the commerce ecosystem.
The next hurdle for merchants is interoperability
How do merchants and financial institutions support different approaches to agentic commerce without needing to build separate infrastructure for each one? The 2026 Québec FinTech Report suggests the shift toward standards coordination is already underway.
In April of 2026, Google donated its Agent Payments Protocol to the FIDO Alliance, a neutral standards body, to ensure its protocol remained platform-agnostic. Visa’s Intelligent Commerce Connect was also launched as a single-merchant integration designed to help businesses accept agentic payments across multiple card networks.
“The real breakthrough in agentic commerce is not that AI can make decisions, but that ecosystems are being built to let those decisions translate into trusted transactions,” said Surinderjit Kaur Bhatti, CEO and Founder of Fathom4sight. “The organizations that embrace interoperability today will be best positioned for tomorrow’s autonomous economy.”
The technical pieces may be falling into place, but the business case for agentic commerce is still being tested. In March, OpenAI shut down Instant Checkout, a feature that allowed ChatGPT users to purchase products directly inside the chat interface. The firm cited inaccurate pricing and inventory data, and repositioned ChatGPT around product discovery. The report suggests this is evidence that the commercial model for agentic commerce remains largely unproven.
Interoperability may help solve some of the technical friction around agentic commerce, but adoption will still depend on whether companies have the resources to build and deploy these capabilities. In ecosystems like Québec, that brings the conversation back to dollars and cents.
Capital is the dividing line for Québec
Québec’s FinTech ecosystem has continued to expand over the past five years. According to the report, the province is now home to 296 FinTech companies, up from 294 last year. Thirty of those companies are categorized in the AI and data sector, while the report found that AI is being used in the operations or offerings of a majority of Québec FinTech companies across sectors.
FinTech companies in the province also sit alongside major financial institutions and a globally renowned AI research ecosystem. According to the 2026 Québec FinTech Report, however, Québec’s ability to participate in the next phase of AI-enabled financial services depends partly on who can afford it.
Financing for Québec FinTech companies rebounded in 2026, with companies collectively raising $615 million in 2026, up significantly from $161 million in 2025 and on par with investment in 2022. However, the report identified a gap between organizations that are experimenting with AI and those investing enough capital to build mature capabilities.
Among organizations spending more than $100,000 USD ($138,000 CAD) annually on AI, 62 percent had reached an advanced stage of AI maturity. The same share reported higher profitability from AI, compared to 39 percent of organizations spending below that threshold. Those findings do not establish causation, but suggest organizations making larger AI investments are also more likely to report advanced capabilities and stronger business outcomes.
The report noted that many smaller businesses understand the potential business case for AI, but lack the capital needed to accelerate their plans. In response, development banks are now pairing financing with advisory support, while established institutions are taking a larger role as capital providers.
“AI investment is entering a new phase,” said Samy Bjaiji, Director of Technological Innovation at Finance Montréal. “What was once driven primarily by venture capital is increasingly being shaped by financial institutions, development banks, and corporate balance sheets. This shift signals that AI is no longer an emerging technology trend. It is becoming a strategic economic priority.”
The AI commercialization gap also remains significant, and commercialization is, in part, a capital problem. Data from Mila and Inovia Capital estimate that Canada produces roughly 10 percent of the world’s top AI research talent, while attracting less than two percent of global AI venture capital. Turning research strength into lasting companies requires sustained investment well beyond the early stages.
The 2026 Québec FinTech Report suggests that established financial institutions, development banks, and holding companies may play a larger role in that next phase. Their involvement could determine how much of the province’s strength stays concentrated in research, and how much makes its way into the market.
PRESENTED BY
Want the full picture? Download the 2026 Québec FinTech Report to explore the latest data on AI adoption, investment activity, talent, and emerging opportunities across Québec’s FinTech ecosystem.
Featured image courtesy Station FinTech Montréal.

articles.title: Apple charges $14,549 for a fully specced touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.text:
With an OLED display and touchscreen capabilities, it’s no surprise that the new MacBook Pro Apple announced today is more expensive than the MBP announced earlier this year. But upgrading the base models that start at $2,899 for the 14-inch, and $3,399 for the 16-inch, with every premium hardware option that Apple offers pushes those prices to an eye-watering $14,249 and $14,549, respectively.
Apple charges $14,549 for a fully specced touchscreen MacBook Pro
The maximum configuration is $4,400 more expensive than a fully specced version of the last MacBook Pro.
Both of those premium configurations include the M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, $150 worth of nano-texture glass, 128GB of memory that adds an extra $2,000, and 16TB of storage which is the real budget breaker here thanks to the ongoing memory shortage.
Maximizing the configuration of the previous 16-inch version of the MacBook Pro topped out at $10,149, according to MacRumors, but today’s $14,549 price is a result of the 16TB storage option that Apple now offers which adds an extra $7,000 to the new MacBook Pro’s price. If you only upgrade the new 16-inch model to 8TB of storage, a $3,000 option, the fully specced price is $10,549, or $400 more expensive than its predecessor.

articles.title: Reicht schon ein Macbook mit M1? Diese Hardware brauchst du für lokale KI
articles.text:
Reicht schon ein Macbook mit M1? Diese Hardware brauchst du für lokale KI
Es gibt viele gute Gründe, KI-Modelle herunterzuladen und lokal auf dem eigenen Computer zu betreiben. Ihr behaltet die Hoheit über eure Daten. Nichts wandert in die Cloud eines US‑Anbieters. Weil die Künstliche Intelligenz direkt auf dem Gerät arbeitet, braucht sie schließlich keinen Zugang zum Internet, um zu funktionieren. Und für den vollumfänglichen Zugriff müsst ihr auch kein Abo abschließen.
Je nach Modell kann euch die KI direkt auf dem Speicher wie gewohnt beim Formulieren von Texten, beim Coden oder bei der Bilderstellung zur Seite stehen. Verknüpft man das Modell mit agentenbasierter Software wie Hermes, kann es auch Aufgaben auf dem Computer erledigen, etwa den Download-Ordner aufräumen.
All das klingt gut, ist aber nicht immer ganz trivial. Denn wie gut so ein lokales Modell läuft, hängt entscheidend von der Hardware ab, die euch zur Verfügung steht – oder vom Budget, falls ihr einen Neukauf plant.
