articles.title: Antivirus : le prix de la première année cache parfois une forte hausse au renouvellement
articles.text:
Prix antivirus 2026 : tarifs, renouvellements et appareils couverts
Combien coûte un antivirus en 2026 ? Ce guide compare les prix de première année, les renouvellements, le nombre d’appareils couverts et les fonctions réellement incluses pour mesurer le coût réel de chaque abonnement.
Avis : le prix affiché la première année ne suffit pas pour comparer deux antivirus. Le renouvellement, la durée de l’engagement, le nombre d’appareils couverts et les services inclus peuvent faire varier fortement le coût réel sur deux ou trois ans.
Points forts
• Plusieurs offres sous les 80 € la première année
• Comparaison des prix de lancement et des renouvellements
• VPN et couverture multi-appareils pris en compte
Points faibles
• Les promotions peuvent changer rapidement
• Les fonctions varient selon le système d’exploitation
• Certaines suites deviennent nettement plus chères au renouvellement
Prix des antivirus en 2026 : les abonnements à comparer
Cinq abonnements antivirus passés au crible côté prix
Comparer le prix d’un antivirus ne consiste pas seulement à regarder la remise de départ. Il faut aussi vérifier le tarif de renouvellement, le nombre d’appareils couverts et les fonctions réellement incluses. Un VPN, un gestionnaire de mots de passe ou une protection contre les arnaques peuvent justifier un abonnement plus cher, à condition d’en avoir l’usage.
Norton 360 (Standard / Deluxe)
Norton 360 se décline en plusieurs formules qui couvrent de 1 à 10 appareils. Standard vise un seul appareil, Deluxe en couvre 5 et Advanced monte à 10. Les trois incluent un VPN, tandis que Deluxe et Advanced ajoutent des services plus adaptés aux foyers.
L’intérêt des formules Deluxe et Advanced tient surtout à la gestion multi-appareils. Deluxe couvre 5 appareils avec 50 Go de sauvegarde cloud, le contrôle parental et le Dark Web Monitoring. Advanced passe à 10 appareils et 200 Go de sauvegarde cloud, avec des services supplémentaires liés à l’identité.
Avast (Premium Security / Ultimate)
Avast vise clairement le grand public avec une installation simple et une protection qui travaille surtout en arrière-plan. Premium Security ajoute notamment des protections contre les arnaques, les sites frauduleux, les ransomwares et certaines menaces liées au réseau.
Les formules payantes sont surtout intéressantes lorsqu’il faut couvrir plusieurs appareils. Premium Security protège jusqu’à 10 appareils et Ultimate ajoute SecureLine VPN, AntiTrack et Cleanup Premium. La différence tient donc moins au moteur antivirus qu’aux services supplémentaires intégrés au pack.
Bitdefender (Antivirus Plus / Total / Premium Security)
Bitdefender reste une référence pour ceux qui recherchent une protection complète sans multiplier les réglages. La gamme va d’Antivirus Plus à Total Security et Premium Security, avec des différences importantes sur les plateformes couvertes et le VPN.
Antivirus Plus reste surtout orienté Windows. Total Security Individual couvre jusqu’à 5 appareils sous Windows, macOS, Android et iOS avec un VPN standard limité à 200 Mo par jour et par appareil. Premium Security ajoute notamment un VPN illimité et des protections anti-arnaques plus avancées.
Surfshark One (Antivirus)
Surfshark One part d’un VPN et y ajoute un antivirus, Alert, Alternative ID et des fonctions de protection contre les arnaques. Cette logique le distingue des suites antivirus plus classiques : le VPN reste utilisable sur un nombre illimité d’appareils, alors que l’antivirus est limité à 5 appareils.
Le pack peut convenir à ceux qui utilisent régulièrement un VPN et veulent éviter de multiplier les abonnements. L’antivirus surveille les fichiers et les menaces en temps réel sur les plateformes compatibles, tandis que le VPN chiffre la connexion sur les réseaux publics ou domestiques.
ESET HOME (Essential / Premium / Ultimate)
ESET mise davantage sur une protection sobre que sur l’accumulation de modules. Les offres HOME Security Essential, Premium et Ultimate couvrent Windows, macOS, Android et iOS, avec des fonctions qui varient selon le niveau choisi.
ESET HOME Security Premium ajoute notamment Password Manager et le VPN, tandis qu’Ultimate ajoute Identity Protection. Le nombre d’appareils et le nombre d’activations VPN dépendent de l’abonnement choisi.
Deux remarques rapides avant de choisir
• Un antivirus ne remplace pas les bons réflexes : prudence face aux pièces jointes, téléchargements douteux, faux sites et messages qui cherchent à créer un sentiment d’urgence.
• McAfee reste une autre option à considérer, mais son intérêt dépend fortement de la formule choisie, du prix promotionnel et du tarif de renouvellement.
Comment comparer le prix d’un antivirus sans se tromper ?
Commencez par vos usages, pas par la promesse “total”
À un moment, la question n’est plus “quel est le meilleur antivirus”, mais “lequel colle à votre vie”. Parce qu’entre un ordinateur fixe sous Windows, un mac de boulot, un smartphone android et une tablette ios, vos appareils n’ont pas les mêmes faiblesses, ni les mêmes habitudes. Et c’est souvent là que les ennuis arrivent : vous ouvrez une pièce jointe “facture.pdf”, vous cliquez sur un lien reçu par SMS, vous lancez un telechargement un peu trop rapide… Les menaces modernes passent rarement par un gros virus spectaculaire. C’est plus discret : du phishing, un faux site, un formulaire qui pompe vos données, un fichier piégé. Du coup, premier tri : cherchez un logiciel qui protège vraiment la navigation web, qui sait gérer les sites risqués, et qui ne se contente pas de scanner vos fichiers une fois de temps en temps. Les listes de fonctionnalités font joli, mais dans la vraie vie, ce qui compte c’est ce qui tourne, là, en arrière-plan, quand vous êtes pressé.
L’interface, c’est la moitié de la sécurité
On n’y pense pas, mais l’interface fait souvent la différence. Si votre antivirus vous harcèle de pop-ups, vous finirez par le couper. S’il cache les réglages derrière trois menus, vous ne saurez même plus si la protection est active. Et puis il y a le piège des versions : sur ios, l’appli sera forcément plus limitée (Apple verrouille), alors que sur android ou sur Windows certains outils sont plus complets. C’est là qu’il faut lire entre les lignes : “security premium” sur la boîte ne veut pas dire la même chose sur tous les systèmes. Vérifiez aussi ce qui est réellement inclus : un vpn peut être utile si vous bossez souvent en ligne sur des Wi-Fi publics, mais si vous êtes surtout chez vous, ce n’est pas forcément le critère numéro un. Et si le VPN est là, mieux vaut qu’il soit intégré proprement, pas planqué dans un onglet que vous n’ouvrirez jamais.
Licence, appareils, renouvellement : les points à vérifier avant de payer
Cette partie mérite autant d’attention que le prix d’appel. Vérifiez combien d’appareils sont couverts et sur quelles plateformes. Une licence pour un seul poste peut sembler économique, mais devenir moins intéressante dès qu’il faut aussi protéger plusieurs smartphones ou tablettes. Regardez également le prix de renouvellement, souvent bien supérieur au tarif de la première année, ainsi que les limites éventuelles du contrôle parental ou du VPN.
Et les marques dans tout ça ? Prenez-les pour ce qu’elles sont
Vous verrez revenir les mêmes grands noms : Avast (et son cousin AVG), Bitdefender, ESET, Norton, parfois McAfee, et chacun a sa manière de faire. Certains éditeurs misent sur la simplicité, d’autres sur des suites très complètes, d’autres encore sur un bon équilibre performance/outil. Ne vous fiez pas uniquement à une “note” vue au détour d’un comparatif sur internet : un bon score ne garantit pas que vous supporterez le logiciel au quotidien. L’objectif est simple : un produit que vous gardez activé, qui protège vos usages réels (liens, sites, fichiers, téléchargements), et qui ne vous donne pas envie de le désinstaller au bout d’une semaine. Ça paraît évident, pourtant c’est souvent là que se joue la vraie protection.
Antivirus gratuit ou payant : quel impact sur le coût réel ?
On le sait, les antivirus gratuits rendent service. Ils assurent une couche de protection de base contre les logiciels malveillants, bloquent certaines menaces web, parfois même détectent du phishing. Mais leurs limites apparaissent vite : pas de pare-feu solide, pas d’outils de contrôle parental, une interface qui pousse sans cesse vers l’offre premium, et surtout une couverture minimale dès qu’on multiplie les appareils.
Avira ou AVG gratuits font le job pour un ordinateur Windows. Les gratuits peuvent aussi exister sur Mac et mobile, mais la couverture et les options varient davantage selon la plateforme (iOS étant souvent plus limité), et certaines fonctions restent bridées hors premium. Et là, on comprend que la gratuité a un prix caché.
En gratuit, l’interface pousse régulièrement vers l’offre premium et plusieurs fonctionnalités restent limitées (confidentialité, anti-tracking, options avancées, support).
Les versions payantes ajoutent surtout des services et une couverture plus large.
Bitdefender inclut parfois un VPN, mais l’usage peut être limité selon la formule ; l’illimité est réservé à certaines offres premium.
Norton ajoute notamment le VPN, le stockage cloud et, selon la formule, des outils de contrôle parental ou de protection de l’identité. Bitdefender et Avast proposent eux aussi des packs plus complets avec VPN et outils de confidentialité. Ces fonctions répondent à des usages concrets, mais elles n’ont d’intérêt que si elles sont réellement utilisées.
Mais la vraie question reste celle du rapport qualité-prix.
Les promotions de première année peuvent descendre sous les 30 € sur certaines formules, mais elles ne sont ni permanentes ni représentatives du prix de renouvellement. L’écart peut être important : le coût réel doit donc être évalué sur plusieurs années et en fonction du nombre d’appareils couverts.
Pourtant, il ne s’agit pas de dire que gratuit rime avec inutile. Pour un utilisateur qui ne consulte que ses mails, qui ne stocke rien de sensible et qui navigue prudemment, un antivirus gratuit reste une solution viable. Mais pour la plupart, l’enjeu est ailleurs : trouver l’équilibre entre budget et sécurité, entre un outil basique qui alerte quand il est déjà trop tard et une suite complète qui anticipe les menaces. Et là, l’offre payante, surtout quand elle est abordable, finit par s’imposer comme un choix pragmatique.
Avantages et inconvénients des antivirus populaires
Quatre suites connues, quatre manières de vous suivre au quotidien
Vous le voyez vite : sur le web, on n’attrape plus seulement des virus “à l’ancienne”.
Le vrai risque, c’est le phishing, le faux site de livraison, le telechargement d’un fichier piégé, ou un lien qui traîne sur internet.
Donc oui, tous ces antivirus promettent la sécurité… mais ce qui compte, c’est la manière dont la protection se comporte sur vos appareils.
Un PC windows à la maison, un mac au bureau, un mobile android, un iPad sous ios : la même version ne se vit pas pareil.
Et puis il y a la partie “réalité” : le prix, l’abonnement, la licence multi-appareil, et ce qui est vraiment inclus.
Avast Premium Security / Ultimate : simple, large, parfois un peu trop insistant
Avast, c’est l’éditeur qui vise les utilisateurs pressés.
Vous installez le logiciel, l’interface est lisible, et ça se met à travailler tout de suite sur les sites risqués.
Premium Security regroupe l’essentiel : antivirus, protection contre les ransomwares, détection des arnaques et protections web.
Ultimate ajoute une logique “boîte à outils” : VPN SecureLine, Cleanup, AntiTrack… pratique si vous aimez les packs.
Mais on ne va pas se mentir : Avast sait vous rappeler, ligne après ligne, qu’il existe une formule premium.
• Avantages : protection web complète, couverture jusqu’à 10 appareils avec Premium Security ou Ultimate, et plusieurs outils additionnels dans Ultimate
•	Inconvénients : upsell régulier, beaucoup de modules, et la sensation que tout n’est pas indispensable selon votre usage home.
Et si vous venez d’AVG ou d’Avira, vous ne serez pas dépaysé : même famille, même logique “grand public”.
Norton 360 : rassurant, familial, mais il faut choisir la bonne formule
Norton 360 adopte une approche de suite de sécurité complète.
La gamme comprend Standard pour 1 appareil, Deluxe pour 5 appareils et Advanced pour 10 appareils.
Dans la pratique, ça parle aux foyers : un seul tableau de bord, moins de bricolage, et une protection web solide quand vous naviguez en ligne.
Le VPN est inclus dans les formules Norton 360. Deluxe ajoute notamment Dark Web Monitoring, contrôle parental et 50 Go de sauvegarde cloud, tandis qu’Advanced monte à 200 Go et ajoute plusieurs services liés à l’identité.
Le revers, c’est que vous payez un pack : si vous n’utilisez pas certaines fonctionnalités, vous les financez quand même.
Et il faut garder un œil sur le renouvellement : ce n’est pas toujours le même prix que l’offre de départ.
•	Avantages : gestion multi-appareils, protection web/anti-phishing, suite assez complète, efficace quand un clic part trop vite sur un site douteux.
•	Inconvénients : bundle parfois “total” alors que vous vouliez juste un antivirus simple, et écarts de contenu entre versions à comparer avant achat.
À titre de repère, on retrouve un esprit voisin chez McAfee Total : suite large, utile, mais pas toujours minimale.
Surfshark Antivirus : parfait si le VPN fait partie de votre routine
Surfshark repose d’abord sur son VPN, auquel l’antivirus vient s’ajouter dans la formule One.
Si vous bossez souvent en mobilité, en Wi-Fi public, ou si vous aimez cloisonner vos données, la proposition est cohérente.
L’app surveille les fichiers pendant que vous les téléchargez, et la partie VPN suit pour la connexion.
Le pack comprend aussi Alert, Alternative ID, Search et des outils de blocage des contenus malveillants, des publicités et des traqueurs.
En revanche, si vous cherchez une suite antivirus ultra traditionnelle avec une tonne de réglages, Surfshark peut sembler moins “outil de sécurité historique”.
Tout dépend de votre profil : vous voulez un pack simple qui couvre la confidentialité, ou une boîte à outils purement antivirus ?
•	Avantages : approche “one” (VPN + antivirus), utile sur plusieurs appareils, pratique pour sécuriser vos usages internet sans multiplier les applis.
•	Inconvénients : intérêt réel lié à votre besoin de VPN, et un positionnement moins classique que Bitdefender ou Norton sur certaines attentes “pro”.
Bitdefender : efficace, discret, mais l’offre peut demander deux minutes de lecture
Bitdefender garde cette réputation d’antivirus solide qui ne transforme pas votre ordinateur en moulin à vent.
Sur Windows, c’est souvent apprécié : ça protège sans vous couper le rythme.
Sur macOS aussi, l’idée est la même : une protection efficace contre malwares et ransomwares, avec une couche web anti-arnaques.
La gamme actuelle s’articule notamment autour d’Antivirus Plus, Total Security Individual et Premium Security Individual.
Le VPN peut être présent, mais parfois avec un quota dans certaines formules, et illimité dans d’autres : il faut lire l’astérisque.
Et c’est là le petit défaut : l’offre est riche, donc le bon choix dépend de votre usage réel, pas d’une “note” trouvée en vitesse.
•	Avantages : protection robuste, impact souvent limité sur les performances, bon équilibre sur fichiers, sites et menaces courantes.
•	Inconvénients : segmentation des offres, différences de fonctionnalités selon la version, et un choix moins évident si vous voulez “juste installer”.
Pour les amateurs de solutions plus sobres, ESET reste souvent une alternative intéressante, plus “outil” que “super pack”.
Au final, vous n’achetez pas un logo : vous choisissez un logiciel que vous garderez actif.
Et ça, ça vaut plus qu’une promesse premium sur une page marketing.
Prix des antivirus en 2026 : première année, renouvellement et durée d’engagement
Ce que changent réellement les prix actuels
En 2026, les éditeurs ne vendent plus un simple antivirus, ils vendent un petit écosystème. La base, c’est toujours la protection contre les virus et les menaces qui traînent sur le web. Mais l’argument qui fait mouche, c’est tout ce qui vient autour : VPN, anti-phishing, outils anti-arnaques, alertes, parfois même de l’optimisation.
Et là, les promos servent d’accroche : “1ère année” très agressive, puis renouvellement plus salé. Ce n’est pas forcément un piège, mais il faut le savoir avant de sortir la carte.
Norton 360 Deluxe est actuellement affiché à 39,99 € la première année pour 5 appareils, avec un renouvellement à 109,99 €/an. Norton 360 Advanced coûte 44,99 € la première année pour 10 appareils, puis 139,99 €/an.
Dans l’idée, vous payez une suite familiale : plusieurs appareils, un VPN intégré, du contrôle parental selon la formule. C’est pratique si vous voulez couvrir un PC Windows, un Mac et deux mobiles sans vous disperser.
En revanche, c’est typiquement le genre d’abonnement où il faut regarder le tarif de renouvellement, sinon la surprise arrive l’année suivante.
Avast Premium Security est actuellement affiché à 54,04 € la première année pour 10 appareils, puis 99,99 €/an. L’offre Ultimate passe à 79,04 € la première année pour 10 appareils, avec un renouvellement à 139,99 €/an.
Ultimate ajoute une couche “boîte à outils” (VPN SecureLine, nettoyage, anti-tracking), utile… si vous vous en servez vraiment. Le point faible, c’est que l’expérience peut devenir très “suite” : modules partout, et beaucoup d’invitations à explorer les options.
Surfshark One suit une logique différente : le VPN reste au centre du pack, avec l’antivirus et les outils de confidentialité autour. L’offre 24 mois est actuellement affichée à 2,79 €/mois avec 3 mois supplémentaires, soit 75,33 € pour les 27 premiers mois, avec une garantie de remboursement de 30 jours.
Cela parle surtout aux gens souvent en déplacement, souvent connectés, qui veulent une solution simple à activer partout.
Si vous cherchez juste un antivirus “minimal”, l’approche pack peut sembler surdimensionnée.
Chez Bitdefender, Antivirus Plus est affiché à 24,98 € la première année pour 3 appareils. Total Security Individual coûte 49,99 € la première année pour 5 appareils, tandis que Premium Security Individual monte à 69,98 € pour 5 appareils.
Le VPN peut être inclus, mais parfois avec un quota (et l’illimité dépend de la formule).
Bref : bonne promo, oui, mais choisissez la bonne version.

FAQ - Prix des antivirus en 2026
1) Un antivirus va-t-il ralentir mon ordinateur Windows ou mon Mac ?
Pas forcément. Sur une machine récente, vous ne verrez souvent rien au quotidien. Là où ça se ressent, c’est surtout pendant un scan complet, ou sur un vieux PC déjà chargé. Et puis il y a un paradoxe : un bon antivirus peut parfois rendre l’ordinateur plus fluide… simplement parce qu’il empêche un logiciel indésirable de tourner en douce et de manger les ressources.
2) J’ai déjà “l’antivirus de base” : est-ce suffisant pour être en sécurité ?
Pour un usage très calme, oui, ça peut tenir. Mais dès que vous vivez un peu en ligne — achats, banque, mails, réseaux sociaux — la différence se fait sur la protection web : anti-phishing, blocage de sites piégés, alertes quand un téléchargement sent l’embrouille. C’est souvent là que les suites comme Norton, Avast ou Bitdefender marquent des points.
3) Est-ce que les antivirus protègent vraiment Android et iOS comme sur Windows ?
Sur Android, vous avez souvent une vraie marge : analyse d’applis, surveillance, protections web. Sur iOS, c’est plus limité, parce qu’Apple verrouille beaucoup. Du coup, la “version iOS” d’un produit peut ressembler à un pack sécurité autour (VPN, navigation, anti-phishing) plus qu’à un antivirus classique. C’est normal, mais il vaut mieux le savoir avant de payer une licence “multi-appareils”.
4) Le VPN inclus, c’est un gadget ou un vrai plus ?
Ça dépend de votre vie. Si vous bossez en déplacement, Wi-Fi d’hôtel, café, train… le VPN devient une protection simple et utile, parce qu’il chiffre la connexion. En revanche, si vous êtes surtout à la maison sur un réseau stable, ce n’est pas forcément le critère numéro un. Et attention au détail : “VPN inclus” ne veut pas toujours dire “illimité”, selon les offres.
5) Comment éviter le piège du prix promo la première année ?
Regardez toujours deux lignes : “prix la 1ère année” et “prix au renouvellement”. C’est là que tout se joue. Les éditeurs cassent souvent les tarifs pour vous faire entrer, puis l’abonnement remonte. Donc si vous comparez, comparez à horizon 2 ans, pas juste sur l’étiquette qui brille.
6) Qu’est-ce qui change vraiment entre Avast Premium Security et Avast Ultimate ?
Premium Security se concentre sur l’antivirus et les protections web, tandis qu’Ultimate ajoute SecureLine VPN, Cleanup Premium et AntiTrack. L’écart de prix n’a de sens que si ces outils supplémentaires correspondent réellement à vos usages.
7) Comment choisir une licence pour plusieurs appareils ?
Commencez par compter les appareils à protéger et vérifiez leur système. Norton 360 Deluxe couvre 5 appareils, Advanced 10, Avast Premium Security et Ultimate jusqu’à 10, Bitdefender Total Security et Premium Security 5, tandis que Surfshark autorise un nombre illimité d’appareils pour le VPN mais limite son antivirus à 5 appareils.

articles.title: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3
As quality assurance (QA) automation adoption grows inside an organization, a new problem appears that has nothing to do with writing tests. A platform team stands up test automation, then a second team wants to join, then a dozen more. Soon hundreds of test cases belong to different products and squads, and everyone can see everyone else’s tests. No one can answer a basic question at a glance: is this application’s test coverage healthy right now? Test authoring stops being the bottleneck. Organizing tests and controlling who can touch them becomes the work.
A second, related question follows close behind: who owns this application and its tests, and who is accountable when coverage slips? Without a clear owner, health problems have no one to land on.
In the first post, we introduced QA Studio, a reference solution built with Amazon Nova Act. Teams use it to define tests in natural language and run them through AI-powered visual navigation. In the second post, we added test suites and a CLI for batch regression testing in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. In this post, we cover two capabilities that help QA Studio scale across an organization. The first, applications, organizes tests and reports health metrics. The second, team-based user management, controls who can see and change what.
Organizing tests with applications
An application in QA Studio represents the system under test: a website, a web app, a service front end. It’s the container that gives a collection of tests, a home, and an owner. Use cases (the individual tests from Part 1) and test suites (the regression collections from Part 2) belong to an application, and they inherit its ownership. Instead of one flat list of every test in the deployment, each team works inside the applications they own.
Creating an application takes a name, a base URL, and an optional set of environments such as development, staging, and production. From the application page, teams create new use cases directly in context, add existing ones, and group them into test suites. This is also where QA Studio reports on the health of the tests it runs.
Understanding application health with metrics
Tests produce results. Understanding those results over time is what tells a team whether the development lifecycle for an application is healthy, not only whether a single build is ready for release. QA Studio records the outcome of every execution as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by application and by environment. It turns these metrics into a health view on the application page.
The top of the page answers the immediate question with three figures: the pass rate over the selected window, the total number of executions, and the current failure count. Alongside them, QA Studio computes a health score of 0–100. The score starts from the pass rate and subtracts a penalty for flaky tests. That way, an application whose tests pass but flip between pass and fail doesn’t present a falsely perfect picture. A team scanning a portfolio of applications can tell the stable ones from the ones that need attention without opening each result.
The metrics tab moves from the current snapshot to trends. Teams choose a 7-day window with hourly granularity or a 30-day window with daily granularity, and QA Studio charts executions, successes, failures, and average duration across that period. Because the underlying metrics carry an environment dimension, teams filter the view to a single environment. For example, they can compare how staging behaves against production for the same set of tests.
Two views target the tests that cost teams the most time. The flaky tests view ranks use cases by how often they flipped between passing and failing over the last seven days. This surfaces the intermittent failures that erode trust in a suite before they turn into a production miss. The recent failures view lists the latest failed executions for quick triage. Each one links back to the Amazon Nova Act trajectory logs and session recordings described in Part 1. That way, moving from “this test is failing” to “here is exactly what the agent saw” takes one click.
Controlling access with teams and roles
Metrics tell a team how their applications are doing. Team-based user management decides which applications are theirs in the first place. QA Studio organizes access around teams, and an application belongs to exactly one team. Members of that team work with its applications. Everyone else doesn’t see them.
Every team member holds one of five roles, and each role includes the permissions of the ones below it:
- Admin: Studio-wide access to every team, application, and user, including creating teams and assigning applications. Admin is a studio-wide role rather than a per-team assignment.
- Team Lead: Manages their own team members and creates applications for the team.
- Editor: Creates and edits use cases and test suites within the team’s applications.
- Executor: Runs use cases and suites but doesn’t modify them.
- Viewer: Read-only access to the team’s applications and results.
Because roles are cumulative, a Team Lead has everything an Editor has, and so on down to Viewer. Access to a use case or a test suite follows the application that contains it. If a member can work with the application, they can work with its tests, bounded by their role. This keeps permission management at the application level instead of on thousands of individual tests.
An administrator sees the whole studio. The Users page lists every account with its team and role in one place. An admin can tell who holds Team Lead on which team and who carries Studio-wide Administrator rights. In the reference deployment shown here, four users span two teams: two Team Leads, one Viewer, and one Studio-wide Administrator. The Teams page rolls the same data up by team, showing each team’s member count and application count side by side. An admin can see which teams are expanding before opening any one of them.
The same membership data, rolled up by team, appears on the Teams page.
Switching from teams to applications, the studio-wide Applications list shows every application across all teams.
Sharing applications between teams
Teams rarely work in complete isolation. A platform team might own an application that a feature team needs to run against, without handing over the ability to change it. QA Studio supports this with shared access: the owning team grants another team access to an application at a view, execute, or full level.
Shared access follows a ceiling rule. A user’s effective permission on a shared application is the lower of their own role and the level of the grant. A Viewer who is given full access to a shared application remains view-only, because their role is the ceiling. This way, an owning team can share widely without granting more than a recipient’s role allows.
What a team lead sees
A team lead works inside a single team rather than the whole studio. Opening My Team presents four tabs that cover everything the lead controls: Members, Applications, Use Cases, and Shared Access. The Members tab lists the people on the team. The lead can change any member’s role inline or add a new one, so day-to-day access management stays with the person closest to the work. In the AWS Team shown here, the lead manages two members, one Team Lead and one Viewer.
The Applications tab shows only the applications the team owns, each with its test-case count and last-run time. This keeps the lead focused on their own surface rather than the full studio inventory. The Shared Access tab is where cross-team sharing becomes concrete. Here the AWS Team has granted the AMZN Team view access to an application, and the lead can grant, revoke, or change the level of that access. Because the grant was view level, an AMZN Team Editor still sees the shared application read-only: the ceiling rule from the previous section, applied in practice.
The same Team Lead’s Shared Access tab records which other teams can reach the team’s applications, and at what level.
How it works
QA Studio builds team-based access control and metrics on the same serverless foundation described in the earlier posts, adding a few AWS services to the mix:
- Amazon Cognito: Each team maps to a set of Cognito groups, one per role. An AWS Lambda authorizer resolves a caller’s groups into API scopes and team context on every request.
- Amazon DynamoDB: Teams, memberships, application ownership, and cross-team share grants are stored in the existing single-table design.
- Amazon CloudWatch: Every execution emits custom metrics in the QAStudio/Executions namespace, dimensioned by application and environment. The metrics API reads them back to build the health view and trend charts.
- AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway: The backend enforces access at two layers: the scope a caller’s role grants, and a resource check that confirms the caller’s team owns or has been shared with the application.
Because access is derived from Cognito group membership, the OAuth client credentials flow from Part 2 fits the same model. A CI pipeline authenticates as a machine identity with the scopes it needs and no more.
Getting started
Applications, metrics, and team-based access control are part of the QA Studio reference solution, which you deploy in your own AWS account with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). All test data, results, and metrics stay within your account boundaries. After deploying, an administrator creates teams, assigns members and roles, and assigns applications to teams. Each team’s health metrics begin populating as their tests run.
For deployment instructions and configuration details, see the QA Studio GitHub repository and its documentation.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how QA Studio scales agentic QA automation from individual tests to an organization. Applications give every team a home for their use cases and test suites. They report health through pass rate, trend charts, a flaky-adjusted health score, and failure triage built on Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Team-based user management, backed by Amazon Cognito, keeps each team working within the applications they own, with cross-team sharing bounded by a clear ceiling rule.
These capabilities build on the natural language test authoring from Part 1 and the suites and CI/CD integration from Part 2. Together, they help QA automation grow across many teams without losing visibility or control. To try it in your own environment, deploy the reference solution from the QA Studio GitHub repository, create your first team and application, and run a few use cases to watch the metrics take shape. To learn more about the agent behind it, see the Amazon Nova Act product page.

articles.title: UK considering forcing data centers to invest in local communities as part of AI “covenant” — and it shows getting angry at developers can massively benefit working people
articles.text:
UK considering forcing data centers to invest in local communities as part of AI “covenant” — and it shows getting angry at developers can massively benefit working people
The UK government wants to make data centers more appealing
- Data center developers could be required to invest in local communities as part of new UK government plans for an AI "covenant"
- This could come in the form of payments to residents or investment plans for local infrastructure
- Multiple sites in AI Growth Zones have seen widespread opposition over fears that the data centers don't offer enough benefit for local residents
The UK is attempting to position itself as a world-leader in AI technology, but a data center buildout is a necessary step in realizing that ambition and those living in the immediate vicinity of planned sites aren’t too happy.
In an effort to reduce the dissatisfaction of local communities, the UK government is considering setting a list of criteria a developer must meet to have a data center approved for construction.
The current list of criteria include investments in local communities, as well as meeting sustainability requirements and set agreements on energy use as part of an AI “covenant” with the British public.
British AI to be “distinctly Labour”
The current buildout of AI data centers in the UK has been fraught with delays in planning processes, a significant backlog of grid connections, and bottlenecks in hardware and cabling.
Microsoft recently pulled out of residency plans at the UK’s largest planned data center after learning the facility would not be connected to the grid until the early 2030s.
UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan has said developers should be “able to build British infrastructure, especially in areas like AI that are driving growth and creating revenue for public services.”
Data center developers who meet the “covenant” could be given priority access to power grids and fast-tracked planning approval, helping to secure funding for local areas while also helping to meet the UK’s AI goals. While no solid plans exist for how this investment could look, it could involve contributions to local infrastructure or payments to residents.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Speaking to the Financial Times, Narayan said that the government would not let the AI buildout purely serve “foreign firms and foreign billionaires,” adding that the government would seek a “distinctly Labour approach to British AI” that would help better serve the British public.
Several areas of the UK have been designated as AI Growth Zones by the UK government, providing developers with preferential energy rates in regions with excess - such as areas with strong renewable energy generation - while also allowing local authorities to keep 100% of the additional business rates generated by new developments.
AI buildout isn’t all sunshine and roses
The proposed AI “covenant” isn’t purely out of the goodwill of the British government. There has been significant opposition to data centers across the UK.
One data center planned to be built in Auchertool in Fife, Scotland, has attracted over 1,600 objections. The site - with a 600MW capacity - would be the second largest in the world once operational. The Scottish Parliament also backed a de facto moratorium on hyperscale data centers in September.
Similar plans for a 450MW data center on a former factory site in North Wales are being opposed by local residents and an online petition that has exceeded 26,000 signatures. The campus would occupy a brownfield site that has been derelict since 2008, but locals say the plans for the data center do not include clear and sustainable benefit for residents.

Benedict provides detailed analysis on state-sponsored threat actors, APT groups, and the protection of critical national infrastructure, with his reporting bridging the gap between technical threat intelligence and B2B security strategy.
Benedict holds an MA (Distinction) in Security, Intelligence, and Diplomacy from the University of Buckingham Centre for Security and Intelligence Studies (BUCSIS), with his specialization providing him with a robust academic framework for deconstructing complex international conflicts and intelligence operations, and the ability to translate intricate security data into actionable insights.

articles.title: Hackers Start Probing Fresh Oracle EBS Vulnerability
articles.text:
Threat actors have started probing for a newly patched critical vulnerability in Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS), threat intelligence firm Defused reports.
The exploited flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS score of 9.8), was patched last week in Oracle’s October CPU.
It is described as an SQL injection issue in the Application Object Library product of EBS that could be exploited by remote, unauthenticated attackers over HTTP.
Successful exploitation of the bug could allow attackers to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and completely take over the Application Object Library.
According to Defused, the first exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-101767 were observed on October 27.
“Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767 this morning, Oct 27,” the company warned on X.
The security defect was discovered and reported by Horizon3.ai and there have been no other reports regarding its in-the-wild exploitation.
Oracle EBS vulnerabilities are often targeted by threat actors. In June, Defused warned of attacks exploiting CVE-2026-46817, a critical issue in the File Transmissions component of E-Business Suite’s Payments product.
Last year, the Cl0p ransomware and extortion group exploited zero-day bugs in Oracle’s enterprise management software to access stored data.
The large-scale EBS hacking campaign potentially impacted over 100 organizations across consumer goods, energy, engineering, entertainment, finance, heavy industry, manufacturing, media, software, technology, telecommunications, and other industries.

articles.title: Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI
articles.text:
Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.
AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.
The problem, not the title
Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.
Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.
That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.
The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.
Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.
The importance of systems thinking
Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.
AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.
An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.
This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.
Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.
New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.
In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.
Human judgment is important
AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.
Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.
An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.
The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.
An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.
IEEE’s vital role
The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.
IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.
IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.
Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.
A larger definition of the engineer
AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.
An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.
That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.
The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

articles.title: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech
articles.text:
What do drones, routers, and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones from entering the country. They’re the first consumer gadgets that are facing de facto import bans because of the US government’s xenophobic stance — and they might not be the last.
Originally, the US government was just worried about US networks. It’s been distrustful of Chinese telecom equipment providers Huawei and ZTE for well over a decade, eventually requiring telecom providers to “rip and replace” their gear. (Many telecoms have still failed to do so.) It established an “Entity List” for companies whose gear should be banned from import, marketing, and sale.
But under the second Trump administration, that list has been weaponized against entire home consumer gadget categories too — starting in December 2025 when Trump and Brendan Carr’s FCC banned all future foreign drones unless their companies obtained a waiver.
Next was a ban on all future foreign routers, all future foreign robots and power inverters, and within the robot ban, all future foreign robovacs. In each case, the government claims it’s because those gadgets fundamentally pose an unacceptable threat to US national security. But in each case, the US has provided zero public evidence of a threat, has done nothing about existing drones and routers and robots that might pose such a threat, and hasn’t given us any reason to trust that its waivers have anything to do with security.
Besides, there are rarely any US companies to fill the gaps left by foreign ones. Consumer gadgets are largely made overseas, including practically all routers and practically all drones — just like how your Apple, Dell, and HP laptops are not made in the US.
In this StoryStream, we’re following the latest on the foreign gadget bans.
- MSI just got a router ban waiver — but not a blanket one. As PCMag notes, Taiwan’s MSI has gotten conditional approval to bring two specific routers into the United States, pending certification: the Radix GRBE94 and GRBE34, which’ll likely have friendlier names when they go on sale. Netgear and Asus inexplicably got blanket approvals for all new routers earlier this year, while TP-Link is fighting for its Wi-Fi 8 ones.
- Will TP-Link really make routers in the US? Here’s what it told us TP-Link, one of the world’s leading manufacturers of consumer Wi-Fi routers, is in a precarious position in the US. The company just launched its first Wi-Fi 8 routers, but can’t bring them here because of President Donald Trump’s foreign router ban. Even though competitors Netgear and Asus make their routers in Asia, they’ve mysteriously obtained blanket waivers for all their new gear; perhaps because of alleged ties to China, TP-Link hasn’t managed to get such a waiver yet. But TP-Link is willing to do something those companies weren’t — to invest nearly $1 billion to make routers in the United States, creating “hundreds of high-paying research and development, manufacturing, and construction jobs for American workers over the next four years,” according to a letter TP-Link sent to the FCC. Read Article >
- Another ‘DJI front company’ bites the dust. In July, we told you how the FCC — and its subcontractor TÜV Rheinland — didn’t bother to do basic Google searches before legally approving banned DJI technology for import and sale. But a new game of whack-a-drone was more successful. Public records show TÜV Rheinland asked the FCC to block applications from another “DJI front company,” Jovistar. The FCC agreed, and Jovistar is now on notice.
- It sure would be nice if these congresspeople would say why DJI is a threat. The FCC would like you to know that its DJI ban is justified — because of the contents of sealed letters from the Pentagon that it has now forwarded to 16 congresspeople. Do they know something they’re not saying out loud? So far, the government hasn’t revealed a single shred of public evidence about a national security threat.
- Unlike Netgear and Asus, TP-Link says it’s prepared to spend $1 billion to make Wi-Fi routers in the US. “TP-Link would begin assembling these Wi-Fi 8 devices in the United States by next year,” it claims in a letter to the FCC — if the FCC will exempt its routers from the foreign router ban. Notably, both Netgear and Asus got exemptions without promising to make routers in the US, even though the FCC’s paperwork requires companies to commit to US manufacturing to get that exemption.
- The FCC plans to ban all Chinese labs from testing US gadgets by 2029. The FCC has been cracking down on some Chinese test labs that improperly helped authorize gadgets for import into the US — now, it wants to get rid of Chinese labs altogether starting December 2028, only authorizing labs if they have a reciprocal economic relationship with the US. It’ll vote on October 29th; you can read the whole argument here.
- The FCC has decertified two more Chinese test labs. The US has been finding ways to stem the tide of imported Chinese gadgets, including decertifying “bad labs” that are “apparently controlled by China.” It’s now pulled credentials from two more: SLG-CPC Test Laboratory, and Shenzhen STS Test Services, “for willfully providing incorrect or false equipment test results in connection with applications for equipment authorization.” It’s also planning to do the same to Shenzhen CTB Testing.
- The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it’s also now the first to escape the FCC’s Roomba ban. Well, sort of — because the Matic wasn’t banned to begin with. Read Article >
- Asus won’t say how it escaped the US router ban This spring, the United States banned all future foreign-made consumer routers — effectively all future routers — unless their makers could 1) convince the US government that they weren’t a national security threat, and 2) submit “a detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.” As of September 9th, Asus now has an exemption from the ban, just in time to bring its first early Wi-Fi 8 routers here. But Asus has not publicly announced any plan to bring manufacturing to the US. It would not even confirm to The Verge whether it had submitted a US manufacturing plan. Read Article >
- Etsy is worried it’ll get caught up in the FCC’s gadget bans. Remember when it was cheap and easy for me to buy DJI’s banned camera? The FCC is currently taking comments on a plan to ban online marketplaces from listing gadgets like that. Platforms would need to validate each device’s FCC status before they list it for sale. Etsy wants its “micro-entrepreneurs” to be exempt.
- We flew the banned drone with snap-on propeller wings. Dom says it’s quick and easy to snap a propeller backback onto the HoverAir Versa, and then… it can fly! Shame that HoverAir isn’t transparently telling backers that this camera has been banned in the US, and shame on the Trump administration for creating the dumb drone ban to begin with.
- HoverAir’s transforming modular drone has already been halted in the US I am so sorry, fellow US gadget fans: the FCC’s drone ban appears to have struck again. The HoverAir Versa — a baby steadycam with snap-on propeller wings that transform it into a drone — has already stopped taking US orders just three days after its Indiegogo debut, and may be forced to abandon shipping plans in the US. HoverAir is now telling backers it’s only shipping its camera to the US, not the piece that turns it into a drone, “due to a few remaining logistics updates with the Flight Kit.” But those “logistics” may actually be a euphemism for “we’ve been banned by the federal government.” The FCC’s database no longer has an entry for the HoverAir Versa at all, suggesting that its authorization grant has been pulled. Read Article >
- I bought DJI’s banned camera — it was cheap and easy As a kid, I always imagined the “black market” would be like the movies: Shady vendors hawking illicit goods along dusty streets. But if you want a banned DJI Osmo Pocket 4 or Pocket 4 Pro camera in the US, you can just reach for your phone. They’re on Temu, AliExpress, eBay, Mercari — even Amazon and Newegg — with fast, free shipping and no risk of tariffs or seizures. That’s because these cameras are already inside the United States, despite rules that ban them from entering the country. Read Article >
- Does giving a camera wings dodge the FCC’s drone ban? HoverAir drones always have intriguing gimmicks. This one folds flat to fit in your pocket. This one can land on water. Another can charge inside its carrying case. But the brand’s latest trick might be its riskiest: it’s attempting to sneak a drone past the FCC. In December 2025, the US government banned future foreign drones from reaching our shores, and HoverAir’s floating Aqua drone was one of the first casualties. But this time, brand owner Zero Zero Robotics might have found a loophole: its latest $750 Versa drone isn’t a drone, it claims, but rather a DJI Pocket-style mini steadycam with optional snap-on propellers that let it fly. Read Article >
- That lying drone company we caught? The FCC has now banned Odyssey Robot. Empty offices. Bald-faced lies. No real consequences. Our investigation suggests it’s cheap and easy to dodge the US drone ban — but at least the FCC is revoking Odyssey Robot’s authorizations after we made the agency aware. The FCC’s order doesn’t begin to explore whether Odyssey might be DJI in disguise.
- The ban on robot vacuums won’t make them safer, only worse No other gadget knows as much about your home as a robot vacuum. They map your space, learn your routines, and many now carry a camera and microphone into every room in your house. As AI gives them a better understanding of what they see, the privacy and security risks these autonomous robots pose are only growing. That’s why greater scrutiny makes sense, but the ban on foreign-made mobile robots issued by the Federal Communications Commission earlier this week — implemented to address “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” — doesn’t actually judge products by how secure they are, just where they’re built. It effectively means no new robot vacuums from major companies can enter the US market unless they are built here. And spoiler alert: none are. Read Article >
- The US government just banned Roombas When the Trump administration announced yesterday that it was banning “advanced robotic devices” from entering the United States, the headlines were all about humanoids. But spying doesn’t require legs — and neither does the FCC’s robot ban. The robot ban will sweep up robot vacuum cleaners too, FCC media relations director Katie Gorscak confirms to The Verge. Read Article >
- DJI camera clone company Xtra claims it’s ‘in close communication’ with the FCC. If so, that would be new — the FCC proposed a $25,000 fine against Xtra for failing to respond to its letters, and has since revealed plans to ban Xtra from importing and selling more of its existing cameras in the US. Xtra might be canceling its new DJI Osmo Pocket 4 Pro variant, too.
- DJI camera clone company Xtra is halting and refunding all preorders After selling a barely disguised version of the hit DJI Osmo Pocket 3 in the United States last year, Xtra Technology seemed ready to sneak in its version of the new dual-lens Osmo Pocket 4 Pro, too. But today, Xtra has abruptly removed the new Xtra Muse 2 Pro from its website landing page, is pausing preorders indefinitely, and says it’ll refund all the $20 deposits that it’s already collected. Just days after showing off the camera at a Los Angeles launch event, the company is no longer necessarily committing to launch at all: “XTRA has not made a final announcement regarding future product availability. We have not announced a new product launch timeline at this time. Further information will be shared separately once the relevant plans are confirmed,” it writes. Read Article >
- The US government can’t enforce its own drone ban In Pasadena, California, there’s a cute red brick courtyard where one storefront isn’t like the rest. The glass doors open onto a sparse industrial hallway, which leads to a sunlit foyer with a large spiral staircase. Go up, and you’ll see a typical coworking space: open tables, healthy snacks, a collection of meeting rooms with glass walls. Follow one hallway most of the way back, and you’ll find Office 18. There are no signs of life in this tiny private office that’s supposed to be the headquarters of Odyssey Robot, an upstart US drone company. We saw three small desks and chairs, but no power strips, no monitors, no keyboards or chargers or decorations. Two of the desks were covered with sealed cardboard packages. Read Article >
- The FCC is planning to retroactively ban disguised DJI gadgets Last October, we told you how the FCC had given itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets that have already received its approval to be imported and sold in the United States. Now, the FCC’s getting ready to wield that power for the first time, by cracking down on the “DJI front companies” suspected of sneaking the Chinese company’s tech past its foreign drone ban. Two Fridays ago, the FCC had already proposed a $25,000 fine on eight of those “front companies,” including the ones behind the Skyrover drones and Xtra cameras. But now, the FCC is proposing a lot more than a slap on the wrist — it’s planning to ban those same companies from continuing to import, distribute, market, and sell their existing drones and cameras. Read Article >
- The FCC is cracking down on DJI tech that dodged the foreign drone ban Last year, we told you about Xtra, the company that lets DJI sneak its popular cameras into the US, and Skyrover, a brand seemingly selling DJI drones in disguise. They’re just two of the many firms DJI is suspected of starting to skirt the United States’ foreign drone ban. But it appears the FCC is finally doing something about “DJI front companies,” as watcher Konrad Iturbe dubbed them last year. Today, the FCC is fining eight of them $25,000 each — and giving them until Monday, July 20th, just 10 calendar days, to answer the FCC’s questions before the agency takes further action. Read Article >
- The FCC is saving Amazon’s Eero and Leo routers from its ban, too. The FCC is giving Amazon conditional approval to import future routers into the US, following its decision to grant Netgear conditional approval earlier this month. ”We remain committed to delivering innovative, reliable products our customers can depend on,” Eero says.
- Netgear and the FCC have not responded to our emails. It’s been 24 hours. I tried them again five hours ago too. Note that we did not ask if Netgear “bribed the government” to escape the router ban as readers keep suggesting, or anything like that. We simply asked if Netgear followed the FCC’s own rules by submitting a detailed plan for US manufacturing.
- The FCC just saved Netgear from its router ban for no obvious reason The United States’ foreign router ban didn’t make a whole lot of sense, and today may not change that. The FCC has just granted Netgear a conditional approval to import its future consumer routers, cable modems, and cable gateways into the US through October 1st, 2027 — even though the company builds those devices in Asia and has not announced any plan to bring manufacturing to the United States. Neither the FCC’s announcement nor Netgear’s announcement explain why Netgear was granted the temporary exemption. The FCC only states that the Pentagon has now made “a specific determination” that “such devices do not pose risks to U.S. national security.” Read Article >
More Stories

articles.title: Android 18: Neue Funktion soll deine Kontakte besser schützen
articles.text:
Android 18: Neue Funktion soll deine Kontakte besser schützen
In Android 18 schließt Google nach Jahren ein Einfallstor für Manipulationen im Adressbuch. Im kommenden Betriebssystem sollen Apps nicht mehr ohne die aktive Zustimmung der Nutzer:innen auf die Kontakte in deinem Smartphone zugreifen.
Dies erklärte Mishaal Rahman, der bei Google als Community-Manager für Android zuständig ist, in einem ausführlichen Thread bei X. Google hatte bereits am 21. Oktober 2026 Änderungen beim Zugriff auf das Adressbuch angekündigt. Für Rahman ging dieses wichtige Update dabei jedoch unter.
Android: App-Berechtigung als Freifahrtsschein
Bisher galt ein im Rückblick verblüffend sorgloses Prinzip. Hattest du einer App über die entsprechende Berechtigung einmal gestattet, auf dein Adressbuch zuzugreifen, konnte sie dort tun und lassen, was sie wollte. Ohne dass du davon etwas mitbekommen hast. Selbst Apps, die nur einen einzigen Kontakt hinzufügen wollten, hatten vollen Zugriff.
Dies bedeutete, dass böswillige Anwendungen oder manipulierte Apps etwa die Handynummern deiner Kontakte ändern konnten. Wenn dann deine Bank anrief, konnte es sein, dass du mit Betrügerinnen sprichst.
Android 18: Bei Kontaktaufnahme öffnet sich Interface
Wenn Apps künftig unter Android 18 auf dein Adressbuch zugreifen wollen, soll sich eine Benutzerfläche öffnen. Darin siehst du genau, welchen Kontakt die Anwendung wie verändern will.
Bei neuen Einträgen im Adressbuch öffnet sich künftig der Kontakt-Editor in Halbbildansicht. Du siehst darin genau, wer sich in deine Kontakte eintragen will. Du kannst darüber auch bestehende Kontakte durchsuchen.
Neue Berechtigung für Spamfilter und Co.
Für Anwendungen wie Wählhilfen oder Spamfilter, die zwingend Zugriff auf mehrere Kontakte benötigen, wird es eine andere Lösung geben. Für sie führt Google eine neue Berechtigungsform ein. Sie soll bereits ab dem Update Android 17 QPR2 verfügbar sein.
Mit dem Start von Android 18 im Jahr 2027 müssen Apps, die im großen Stil Zugriff auf die Adressbücher von Nutzer:innen wünschen, eine Erklärung in der Google Play Console einreichen. Darin müssen sie nachweisen, warum sie massenhaft auf Kontakte zugreifen wollen.
