articles.title: Amazon debuts the Alexa Photo Frame and Echo Time smart clock, plus other upgraded devices | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon unveiled five new Alexa devices today, including two new kinds of hardware: the Alexa Photo Frame, a smart picture frame, and the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock.
The Alexa Photo Frame is Amazon’s foray into the world of digital photo displays, a product category that has transcended from a clunky, last-minute holiday gift to a sleek, attractive way to look through your camera roll.
Aura is responsible for much of the growth in this category, so it’s no coincidence that the Alexa Photo Frame has a similar aesthetic feel: The screen is much easier on the eyes than the old, bright photo frames from years past. The device is said to be specifically calibrated for sharing photos, featuring a semi-matte, anti-glare display that makes it look more like a Samsung Frame TV than a laptop screen.
Also like Aura, the Photo Frame’s 10-inch screen looks like a matte photograph, helping it blend in with other artwork on your wall.
Amazon’s new device, though, adds the value of integration with users’ existing Amazon accounts. Prime members get unlimited storage on Amazon Photos, and Alexa+ is supposed to intelligently choose how and when to display photos.
“It knows to choose photos where you’re smiling and the lighting is right, and it matches the season you’re in, so you see last year’s family Halloween costumes in October instead of the middle of spring. It also knows what to skip, like screenshots and receipts,” Amazon said in a press release. You can also add voice notes to photos, and images sync automatically as you take them.
The Alexa Photo Frame is on sale now, and starts at $199.99 in Black, and $229 in Birch or Walnut wood.
Meanwhile, the Echo Time clock seems to be a response to the growing sentiment that people don’t want to rely on their phones for alarms, setting morning reminders, or checking the weather.
“Millions of customers start and end their days with Alexa — checking the weather and turning on the lights from bed in the morning or winding down with white noise at night,” Amazon wrote. “But the bedroom asks for something different from a device than the kitchen or living room does — so we designed an Echo specifically for it.”
Amazon says that the Echo Time, which costs $199.99, or $209.99 for a Kids version, has opt-in sleep sensing tools. You can choose to set a smart alarm feature that wakes you up within a 10 to 60 minute window of your alarm time, and can wake you when it detects you’re in a lighter phase of sleep, so that it’s less jarring to begin your day.
Like the popular Hatch alarm clocks, the clock can also mimic sunrise features to ease you awake.
Amazon also showed off updates to its existing lines of devices. We now get the Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and Echo Studio with Home Camera.
The biggest upgrade to the Echo Dot is that it now includes a built-in smart home hub, which also includes an eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage, helping it connect to lights, locks, and thermostats around your home. The new Echo Dot is also powered by Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon chip, which is said to make it better at on-device processing to speed up conversations with its AI, Alexa+.
Amazon says its most advanced speaker, however, is the Echo Studio with Home Camera. This speaker doubles as a camera so you can check on your home while you’re out, and also has visual intelligence features.
“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time,” Amazon explained. “Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.”
The Echo Dot is available at $99.99, and the Echo Studio with Home Camera costs $249.99.
Finally, Amazon unveiled the new Echo Show 16, which includes a 16-inch display. Amazon says the device has a 10% larger viewing area than its predecessor, but with a 40% smaller frame. It has Fire TV built in, plus Smart Home tools like Family Organizer. It can also function like a digital photo frame.
The Echo Show 16 is available for preorder for $499.99.

articles.title: Q&A: Koho’s Daniel Eberhard on unicorns, leadership, and striving to stay humble | BetaKit
articles.text:
Daniel Eberhard has hit some milestones not many founders have. Last summer, the CEO and founder of Toronto FinTech company Koho saw the company’s valuation reach unicorn status following a $130-million Series E round, joining an increasingly exclusive club of non-AI startups to do so in the post-2023 era.
En route to securing a banking license that, if obtained, will vault Koho into the Canadian challenger bank category, Eberhard sat down with BetaKit Editor-in-Chief Douglas Soltys for a conversation about what he’s learned about leadership on the road from startup to billion-dollar valuation, why he’s not game for prediction markets, and the very peculiar list he keeps in his office. An excerpt from that conversation is below.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
You raised a Series E round earlier this year that got Koho over a $1-billion valuation. What does that mean for the company after a decade?
Internally, I still don’t really think of Koho as a unicorn, even though we are. The cool part is it’s a validation of the team, the work that we’ve done to get here, and the capital in itself is very useful.
There are on the order of 150 unicorns minted each year in the world. Roughly 70 percent of those are AI companies right now. So it’s 40 companies each year that do what we’ve done.
The other part is that only eight percent of companies that make billion-dollar valuations go on to build $10-billion businesses. Fifty percent of them never raise another round, never get acquired. So, 50 percent of them are zombie unicorns. If you just do that math, you’re like: OK, we have a one-in-10 shot.
On the other side, what keeps you humble is that we didn’t do this to be a unicorn. In that respect—who cares? It’s incidental to what we’re trying to do as a business.
Has the perspective around valuation changed in the post-2023 AI era? Do you see Koho and FinTech in a different space relative to what’s going on in AI?
I don’t really care. We are not out to chase valuations; we’re here to build a wonderful business. There’s a nature of cyclicality to what we do, and I don’t spend a lot of time losing sleep over it.
It’s been a 10-year journey for Koho, and you’re coming up to this major milestone of obtaining a banking license. I’m wondering what’s still driving you to get to the end of the beginning?
The team is really good, and I’m having a lot of fun. If the job today was like it was during the first five to eight years, I don’t think I’d have the gas in the tank. I’m at a different phase in life now. I have two young kids, and I’m trying to figure out how I can do this job for the next 25 to 30 years. At the same time, even if I did stop, what would I do? I like this business. I think we’re positioned better than anyone in the country to go solve our version of the problem. We’ve worked our butts off for a decade plus to position ourselves this way, and I do think it takes 25 to 30 years to build a truly generational company.
RELATED: Koho secures $190 million CAD in equity and debt to bolster banking licence efforts
What changed from those first seven or eight years to the point where you’re now having fun?
It’s a confluence of factors. Certainly part of it is existential risk that is not present in Koho the way it used to be. Before, if we ran out of money, we died. We’re in a better position now, and it makes it much easier. The distribution of outcomes is very different.
The other thing is that the team is really good. As you get to this stage, the folks you have around the table are very competent and much better than me in many ways.
There was a Maclean’s interview you did recently; it was revealed that on the wall of your office, you have several motivating, inspirational things. But there’s also a list of names of people that have burned you, or didn’t believe in you. What’s going on there?
I’m happy to talk about it. There are two things on my wall. One of them is a poem called If by Rudyard Kipling and another called Defeat by Kahlil Gibran. But yes, I have a list of people. I used to lean on it a lot more. I kind of consider it dirty fuel and I think there’s a certain utility to that which is like anger or spite. There’s a part of you that’s like “Fuck you, I’m going to prove you wrong.” I think that’s important and useful. There’s obviously much healthier ways to get your energy, though, and building from a place of wholeness and completeness, and that’s what I’m trying to do now.
In the Maclean’s article, there was a reference to what happened in 2021, kind of at the very end of the zero interest rate period (ZIRP) and the end of Tiger Global coming in and throwing checks at a bunch of Canadian companies. What happened at that moment?
In 2021 it was really interesting because it was ZIRP and I was listening to certain members of my board a lot, and I kind of thought of them as the adults in the room; these folks were telling me to grow, grow, grow, double headcount every year, that kind of stuff. Then ZIRP went away, and I was way too deferential to these folks, and they were like, “Why is your burn so high?” It was a total 180-degree flip, and it got really contentious, and I just remember thinking I could follow these people’s advice perfectly, and even then, if it doesn’t work, the bag’s with me. So, I may as well fail or succeed on my terms. That was a really clarifying moment for me as a CEO. It almost killed the company.
So, there is this kind of thing of people that I do want to prove wrong. I don’t look at it that much anymore.
Are you still in contact with those people?
Yeah. We have a great relationship. They’re still on my board. We still have to have productive working relationships. We have a really good board with a lot of healthy conversation and mutual respect.
RELATED: Koho wants to be the new bank on Bay Street
At NACO Summit this year, you talked about the idea of launching a telco. Talk to me about the strategy there.
We don’t have anything to announce right now, but the question we always ask ourselves is: can we give people more agency in their life if we give them better financial tools? If part of that better financial tool is a telco, or access to phone plans at $20 a month, then we’re fairly agnostic about what types of things we’re delivering, assuming it’s useful for the user and we can deliver it in a cohesive way.
There’s been some new competition in Canada, and it mostly seems to be coming from international FinTechs. We’re starting to see some US-Canadian partnerships. Is the real competition going to be international incumbents or disruptors?
I welcome competition, one, for the reason that it makes us better as a company, and two, that it makes the products and services better in Canada. I don’t want Koho to win because we’ve had an insulated market where we didn’t go up against the best companies in the world. That’s not interesting to me. And we like our position because it’s taken us five years to get a banking license, and we may bank some of these entities as they come into Canada. We have a lot of call options in terms of how we think about it.
We’ve seen that the 2015 cohort of young, shiny FinTechs has grown up to capture a meaningful share of the market, yet I haven’t seen too much change from the larger financial institutions. How do you see the market changing?
I think the banks have proven they largely, with few exceptions, have a very, very hard time changing. That said, we are all still incredibly small relative to the banks. So when we talk about this at Koho, with 2.5 million accounts, we think, cool, let’s go directly impact two-and-a-half million people. The way you indirectly impact the entire landscape of the country is when you start showing up on a bank’s earnings reports. That’s how they go: oh yeah, maybe we should stop paying savings rates of 0.01 percent.
Watch and listen to the full conversaion on The BetaKit Podcast:
Feature image courtsy The BetaKit Podcast.

articles.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
articles.text:
Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters.
Today at GitHub Universe, we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it.
Our vision: From idea to completed software
The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better.
This agentic software delivery system solves for three things:
Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible
Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it
Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship
GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost.
New features and products that move the work forward
Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app.
GitHub Copilot app: From issue to merge, in one app
The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface.
Copilot Fusion: Multi-model orchestration at its finest
Different tasks need different models. Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task.
Copilot projects: Give Copilot a goal
Available natively in the GitHub Copilot app starting today, Copilot projects let you run agent work across multiple repos in fully managed, parallel sessions. You have one place to track progress, make decisions, and direct what happens next. That means you can spend less time managing execution and more time deciding what’s worth building.
Session continuity: Keep working across surfaces
Your work shouldn’t restart when you switch devices or tools. Session continuity lets you start and follow the same cloud agent session across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. Start from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check in on it from github.com at lunch. The agent keeps working in the cloud. Our multi-model harness that enables it is powerful, fast, and cost-efficient.
Copilot automations: Learning from the results
Copilot automations let you create AI-powered workflows within your repo. They run in the cloud, and you can kick them off manually or set them up to respond to an event or run on a schedule. That lets you coordinate agents to handle tasks such as issue triage and code review. And now, automations can learn from their outcomes and propose improvements for you to review and approve. That’s the learning engine in practice. Use the results of the completed work to make the next run better.
Copilot code review Max: A deeper look at what ships
More code means more pull requests and more demand for review. Moving faster only helps if we can maintain the quality of what ships. Copilot code review surfaces meaningful, actionable bugs that developers need to catch. Today, we introduced Copilot code review Max, which posted the highest F1 score on ReviewBench for high-severity issues. Lite and Balanced keep everyday reviews fast; the new Max provides a deeper look when a change needs it.
Copilot features without a separate enterprise subscription
Starting today, GitHub Enterprise customers can use all Copilot features without buying a separate subscription. That includes GitHub Copilot app, code review, automations, and more. You pay for the AI credits you use.
This is available through GitHub Sales today, with self-serve coming soon. Existing Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise customers can keep their current plans or move over when they’re ready. GitHub also remains open and extensible. Keep using the tools your team depends on, including Cloudflare, Datadog, Figma, and more.
Our continued infrastructure investments
All of this depends on a foundation that’s fast, reliable, and built to scale. Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture.
So far this year, we’ve added:
4 million CPU cores
160 PB of high-speed storage
50 Tb/s network capacity
We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure, while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world. We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work.
We’ve scaled Git for years as activity on GitHub has grown. The agentic era calls for a different ceiling on throughput and reliability. Three principles guide our new Git architecture: simplify the primitives, decouple storage from compute, and minimize coordination.
Git’s just one example of the work we’re doing to scale the platform. We’ve done a lot of work across GitHub’s AI gateway, the harness, and much more.
Beyond the first 1%
Our jobs are changing, but developers are more important than ever. I think all the software we’ve written to date will amount to less than 1% of the software we’ll write in the next five years. The opportunity isn’t just to produce more code. It’s to solve problems we couldn’t solve before.
That’s why we’re connecting the full software delivery system, giving developers better ways to work with agents, and evolving the infrastructure for what comes next. And we’re doing it on GitHub, where we can build together.
Jay Parikh is a seasoned executive, board member, and advisor to some of the world’s fastest growing and most successful consumer, developer, and enterprise technology companies. As Executive Vice President of CoreAI at Microsoft, Parikh leads the organization building the end-to-end agentic system required to build, ship, and run AI agents in the Enterprise. His teams, including GitHub, also build the tools and platforms developers need to create the next generation of software.
Previously, Parikh was CEO of a cloud security startup and, before that, was Facebook’s global head of engineering and infrastructure. For more than a decade, he led the teams that built and operated the physical infrastructure and software that supported the company’s growth from 300 million people to more than 3 billion. His teams worked across the stack, from data centers, servers, and subsea cables to software, data, AI, and security systems. Through leadership roles in the Open Compute Project and Telecom Infra Project, he helped extend infrastructure innovation beyond a single company to benefit entire industries.
Earlier in his career, Parikh held leadership roles at Akamai and Ning. He brings a systems thinker’s perspective to a deeply human challenge: how to build teams that keep learning, moving, and delivering as the world changes around them.
AI, agents, voice, and physical controls are shifting software development from operating tools to expressing intent—and helping developers stay focused on building.

articles.title: The impossible equation of being a researcher mother, striving to make ends meet
articles.text:
How can we encourage women to pursue scientific careers? In recent years, a number of mentoring or awareness campaigns have been put in place to encourage French high school students to study maths, physics or engineering sciences, while they remain underrepresented in these fields. One of the last large-scale initiatives is the Filles et Maths program, launched in 2025, including work on gender bias, the implementation of “role models” or timetables featuring flexible hours.
The program was nonetheless met with criticism: while women remain under-represented in some disciplines, they also remain a minority in the highest positions across the board in the academic world, from mathematics to social sciences.
In France, gender inequalities are therefore not limited to access to scientific studies: they cut across all university careers and make many women leave French Higher Education and Research before securing tenure. This “drain” is explained by several factors among which motherhood holds an important place. A survey in Denmark illustrates that unlike men, one in three women abandon their scientific career after the birth of their first child.
The survey I have been conducting among doctoral students and social scientists highlights the difficulties faced by women who became mothers before becoming permanent employees. Since the 1980s, recruitment requirements have become tougher with candidates needing to have written a good PhD paper, regularly have their work published, participate in scientific events and get involved in the life of research labs. Much of this work falls under hope labour, that is, unpaid work done in the hope of future employment.
In this context, what could be called the myth of the “total researcher” takes shape. This is based on the double penalty of being a productive scientist (without necessarily receiving any financial reward) and embodying the ideal of a career woman, devoted companion, and dedicated mother all rolled into one.
However, this ideal of the “total researcher” clashes with the actual conditions of scientific work and motherhood.
Paying the motherhood penalty in academia
Becoming a full-time researcher requires mothers who aren’t tenured researchers to reorganise their lives. Some cram several days’ work into one by doing casual work, part-time teaching, unpaid scientific projects, and parental responsibilities. The pace often makes women work under pressure, sometimes at the expense of the quantity and quality of their scientific work.
Other women choose to remain unemployed or take parental leave and thus link their career to that of their spouse if they earn enough. If this strategy of linked career is favourable for scientific production when you have a child, it also creates material dependence that could lead to sexist and sexual violence within the family unit, which this testimony from Jeanne, a doctor and mother of a little girl, illustrates:
“I sometimes feel like I have to [‘have sex’], telling myself that ‘I owe him’ and ‘He lets me know it’.”
In a professional context, where every moment must count, maternity, parental or sick leave become scientific working hours in themselves.
Rebecca, for example, shared that she continued writing her final thesis when her son was sent to hospital in an emergency. This situation feeds a feeling of double guilt: the respondents believe they are never up to par, neither as mothers nor as researchers. Joana explains:
“I took parental leave from work, but I feel bad about working when I see my son next to me.”
Some non-tenured researcher dads, on the other hand, benefit from an academic paternity bonus. The gendered division of domestic and parental tasks, as well as taking paternity leave, sometimes allows them to devote more time to their research. To quote Marion’s doctor of History husband’s words: “I have completed nearly two articles in one month of paternity leave!”
The ‘initiatory rite of passage’ rhetoric
Even when they reorganise their lives to ensure their scientific activity, non-tenured researcher mothers face disqualification mechanisms from their peers.
Some remarks that seem kind on the surface often come back to motherhood: “You should spend more time with your children,” “they must miss you”, or “where is your child?”
Other colleagues, often women incumbents, the difficulties that non-incumbents face in reconciling motherhood and scientific work seem perfectly normal, presenting them as inevitable trials. Louise reports how one female colleague explained to her:
“What you’re going through is normal; it’s an uphill battle. We’ve all been there.”
While such pep talks are meant to be comforting, the constraints related to motherhood appear as an obligatory rite of passage to becoming a ‘total’ researcher.
Motherhood-related constraints that become faults
Due to increasing competition in the French Higher Education & Research system, motherhood can be used against some women as a means of sidelining them. Some respondents said they were excluded from scientific events on the basis that they now had “better things to do” with their children.
When precarious researchers voice their concerns at meetings, their difficulties in reconciling scientific work and motherhood are disqualified on the grounds that they “knew” what having a child meant before becoming a tenured researcher.
The constraints related to motherhood end up remaining invisible behind criticism about a supposed lack of scientific productivity, which tends to arise from pregnancy onwards, through comments on untenured researcher mothers-to-be’s physical appearance and how they supposedly mismanage stress with regards to important deadlines in their careers.
Anouk recounts that, after auditioning for a position as a lecturer when she was pregnant, a member of the jury who said she wanted to help her “reminded him” that committees were looking for “nice people to chat to at the coffee machine”, before offering her the following advice:
“Are you pregnant? You looked pale. Next time, apply some blush on your cheeks so you don’t make a bad impression.”
The complaints also concern the routes travelled to academia: not attending certain events organised during the school holidays, taking on casual work or failing to develop other research subjects that are unrelated to their PhD; are frequently associated with a lack of scientific commitment, thus obscuring the financial and family-related constraints these women face.
A case of the fate of Sisyphus?
Faced with the impossibility of achieving the tenured researcher ideal, many respondents end up internalising their challenges as individual failures and gradually abandon academia.
This distance from academia is actually the result of structural constraints that make it difficult to reconcile motherhood and careers in research. Élodie expresses a sense of exhaustion with the predicament:
“I am like Sisyphus! My fate is to do work that will never be recognised, that will never lead to anything because I had a child at the end of my PhD studies.”
In this context, in Higher Education and Research, schemes like France’s Filles et Maths Maths program are not going to be enough to reduce inequalities. More broadly, rethinking the criteria around tenure is what needs to happen.
The current requirements favour women with sufficient material resources and time, to the detriment of people experiencing family, social or financial constraints. This marginalisation is not only unequal: it is harmful to research. By depriving people of certain talents, it also deprives them of certain knowledge.
A weekly e-mail in English featuring expertise from scholars and researchers. It provides an introduction to the diversity of research coming out of the continent and considers some of the key issues facing European countries. Get the newsletter!

articles.title: Ifo-Beschäftigungsbarometer: Unternehmen werden beim Stellenabbau vorsichtiger – aber nicht in allen Branchen
articles.text:
Stellenabbau: Wo Unternehmen jetzt noch kürzen und wo wieder gesucht wird
Die Unternehmen in Deutschland planen nach Einschätzung des Ifo-Instituts, insgesamt etwas weniger Stellen abzubauen. Das Ifo-Beschäftigungsbarometer stieg im Oktober leicht auf 95,5 Punkte, nach 95,1 Punkten im September. „Die Unternehmen werden beim Stellenabbau etwas vorsichtiger. Für einen breiten Beschäftigungsaufbau fehlt dem Aufschwung aber noch die Stärke“, sagte Klaus Wohlrabe, Leiter der Ifo-Umfragen.
In der Industrie habe sich die Situation gegenüber September leicht verschlechtert. Die Unternehmen planten weiter mit weniger Personal. Vor allem in der Autoindustrie sollen weitere Stellen abgebaut werden. Bei den Herstellern von Datenverarbeitungsgeräten sowie elektronischen und optischen Erzeugnissen seien dagegen mehr Neueinstellungen vorgesehen. Zuletzt plante die Industrie Anfang 2023 einen Personalaufbau.
Die Dienstleister wollen dem Ifo zufolge eher Stellen aufbauen. Auch bei Leiharbeitsfirmen wachse angesichts der verbesserten Konjunkturaussichten die Zuversicht. Im Handel planten die Unternehmen dagegen unverändert mit weniger Personal. Auch im Baugewerbe zeichne sich ein leichter Stellenabbau ab.
Ökonomen erwarten mehr Wachstum
Die Stimmung in den Chefetagen der deutschen Wirtschaft hatte sich zuletzt erneut verbessert – laut Ifo-Institut den sechsten Monat in Folge. Für die Konjunktur wächst die Zuversicht: Die Bundesregierung rechnet mit 1,3 Prozent Wachstum der deutschen Wirtschaft im laufenden Jahr. Das Ifo erwartet ein Plus von 1,4 Prozent. Damit würde die jahrelange Flaute enden: 2025 hatte das Bruttoinlandsprodukt nur um 0,2 Prozent zugelegt, in den beiden Jahren davor war die Wirtschaft geschrumpft.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6

articles.title: CISA Warns of Node2Shell Exploitation as Honeypots Log Attack Attempts
articles.text:
The US cybersecurity agency CISA has added the Brotli vulnerability known as Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Separately, two security firms say they have recorded exploitation attempts against their honeypots.
Tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and also known as HTTP2Shell and Broccoli2Shell, the flaw is an out-of-bounds write in the decoder of Brotli, the data compression library developed by Google.
It impacts Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0. With specially crafted compressed data, an attacker could crash the application, expose the contents of its memory, and potentially execute arbitrary code.
The bug was reported by researchers at OpenAI, and Node.js and Google released fixes on October 21. Microsoft, the maintainers of two Python packages, Bun, Envoy and Istio have also released fixes, and Palo Alto Networks is rolling out hotfixes for PAN-OS.
Imperva has demonstrated that the vulnerability can be exploited for code execution on an official Node.js image.
CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to the KEV catalog on October 27, but provided no information on the attacks. Federal civilian agencies have been instructed to address the flaw by November 10.
Previdian, which monitors exploitation activity through its own network of sensors, says it recorded one exploitation attempt targeting CVE-2026-111497 on October 27, coming from a US-based IP address. The company rates its confidence in the exploitation as ‘confirmed’.
“Confidence is how strongly the evidence supports treating this as exploitation of this vulnerability. It does not mean the attempt succeeded,” Previdian explains.
ELLIO, a cybersecurity lab that monitors reconnaissance and mass exploitation activity, says its sensors caught a malicious request targeting Node.js 24.22.0 running on x86-64 systems on October 26. The previous day, a publicly available tool had sent Brotli-compressed data to its sensors to determine which hosts process such data.
The exploitation attempt came from an IP address that ELLIO previously saw targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and probing Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet VPN devices. “This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation,” ELLIO said.
According to ELLIO’s analysis, however, the exploit used in the attack was broken. Its delivery components matched public proof-of-concept code, but the final stage, which the attacker wrote themselves, did not result in a shell in any of the 50 tests ELLIO ran against a vulnerable Node.js instance.
“This was likely a first-generation attempt fired in the wild before the operator fully tested the final stage against a live target – a working framework with a defective last 12 instructions,” ELLIO noted.
The company has itself achieved code execution against four different setups running an official Node.js build on x86-64. It also warns that failed exploitation attempts can crash the targeted process, which means they can be used in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.
VMware patches pending
Broadcom warned on October 27 that SDDC Manager in VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation is affected by CVE-2026-111497 because it uses Node.js.
The company rates the issue critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, for SDDC Manager 9.1.1. For versions 9.0.x, 9.1.0 and 5.2.x, it rates the bug important, with a CVSS score of 7.5.
“A malicious actor with network access to SDDC Manager may exploit this issue to execute arbitrary code,” Broadcom said.
Patches are pending for all affected versions, and Broadcom has published workarounds in two knowledge base articles. Its advisory does not mention exploitation in the wild.

articles.title: Can This Vermont Company Remake the Electric Aviation Industry?
articles.text:
How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight
It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network
In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.
At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.
Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.
Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.
What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”
At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies
This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.
Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.
To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta says its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.
RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO
“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.
Reducing the Risk of FAA Certification
Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.
| 3 Competing Paths to Electric Aviation The top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful. | 
| aspect_ratio | 
| Joby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas. | 
| Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights. | 
| Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later. | 
Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.
The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.
The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.
On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.
The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”
“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”
How Redundancy Enhances Safety
A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.
But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.
The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.
Beta Technologies
Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.
To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.
“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.
The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.
Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.
Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.
For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.
Innovation in eVTOLs
Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.
“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.
Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.
There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.
Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont
Beta Technologies
According to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.
As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.
Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.
That helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.
Beta’s Approach to Batteries
In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.
Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies
By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.
While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.
“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”
In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.
Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.
The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.
On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.
The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.
Beta Technologies’ Electric Ecosystem
What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.
For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.
Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies
Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.
The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.
For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.
Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.
Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.
